items.t: 0 · What the name means: Subsidiary, or Subordinate, Alliance
items.x: Story so far: the whole chapter is about one unequal treaty. Keep the picture: Amritsar is a level line, Hyderabad is a slope. Ask: who is on top? Three things are added to the title by hand. (1) "Richard" above the surname: the Governor General is Richard Wellesley 98-05.(2) "Subordinate [SA]" under the word Subsidiary: read Subsidiary Alliance as Subordinate Alliance.(3) "[BRO: ARTHUR (Br Royal Military), HENRY (eic)]": his two brothers, Arthur in the British Royal Military and Henry with the EIC. The whole chapter turns on these two ideas: an unequal alliance, and three brothers working together. Teacher's board: the meaning of Subordinate Alliance 1. Alliance Between equals, that is, equal rights of both parties A level line between two dots Treaty of Amritsar 1809: Sikh and EIC on the same level 2. Subordinate One party's rights are less respected A line sloping down from the EIC to the Indian State 1798: EIC above, Hyderabad (HYD) below Read the two words in the teacher's order: first "Alliance", then "Subordinate". An alliance by itself is a treaty between equals. The word "Subordinate" then cancels that equality: one party's rights are less respected. So a Subordinate (Subsidiary) Alliance looks like an alliance on paper, but the two dots are not on the same level: the EIC is on top. The teacher draws the same sloping line again on slide 43 under the word "Imbalance."

Because the chapter is a family story, meet the three brothers first. Ask: which one fought, which one governed, which one handled diplomacy, and who was NOT an EIC officer? Richard Wellesley 98-05 Governor General of Bengal from 1798 to 1805. He was joined in India by both his brothers, Arthur and Henry Wellesley. An empire builder Henry Wellesley Handled the administration and diplomacy of the EIC Arthur Wellesley A military commander, but NOT an EIC officer: a commissioned officer in the British Royal Army Wellesley 98-05 was an empire builder. He understood that expanding the empire raised his profile among a nationalistic British public, which was useful for his political ambitions back home. He established Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800 to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs before posting them to the districts. The yellow underlines on this slide are "empire builder", "Fort William College, Calcutta 1800", "train British civil servants" and "Indian languages, laws". These are exactly the words UPSC has used: the founder pair and the purpose. Fort William College has been tested in UPSC Prelims three times.Prelims 2018: the institution and founder pair (alongside Sanskrit College Banaras and Calcutta Madarsa). Prelims 2020 and Prelims 2021: the purpose of establishment. Learn: Wellesley 98-05, Calcutta, 1800, to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs. 1.1 Arthur Wellesley: a Royal Army officer, not an EIC officer Arthur Wellesley was a military commander, but he was NOT an EIC officer. He was a commissioned officer in the British Royal Army, commanding the 33rd Regiment of Foot (that is, infantry). He led his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99), including the Siege of Seringapatam (1799), and in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05), including the Battle of Assaye (1803). He also fought Napoleon's army between 1808 and 1815. Written beside the Arthur row: "Br State helped EIC in India, e.g. 3rd CW 1756-63; therefore the EIC GOT HELP of the Br State in Empire BUILDING in India." The reasoning: Arthur is proof that the British State's own army fought the EIC's wars. This was not new in 1798: Royal help goes back to the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63). So the empire was built by the Company and the British State together, not by a private company alone. 1.2 Two European armies in India (3rd Carnatic War 1756–63 till 1858) From the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63) till 1858, two separate European military forces operated in India side by side: Company's Army The EIC's own private military.Majorly Indian sepoys, but it also had European sepoys.Senior officers were always European, that is, British Paid for by the EIC King's Army (Royal Military) The official British State's regiments sent to India to support the EIC The EIC had to reimburse the British State for the cost of Royal troops deployed in India Both forces fought together, but they were legally and institutionally distinct. The handout's note: the Company State in India received direct military support from the British Crown. Hence the British State cannot escape responsibility for empire building in India. (The teacher underlined "EIC had to reimburse the British State" in yellow: the Crown lent its regiments, and the Company paid the bill.) 1.3 Arthur's own verdict on the Marathas Arthur Wellesley on record stated that the Marathas were the most formidable enemy he ever faced, and that the Battle of Assaye (1803) against them was the toughest fight of his entire military career. The Marathas were harder to defeat militarily. The handout's conclusion: had India not been a fragmented polity, that is, had there been one State ruling the whole of India, India would not have been colonised. This is a ready Mains line on why the EIC won.

items.t: 2 · Pitt's India Act 1784 banned conquest: how Wellesley 98-05 re-initiated it
items.x: Because conquest cost money, Parliament banned it in 1784. Ask: how does Wellesley 98-05 still go to war? Answer: an overhyped threat and a middle path. 2.1 Context of Pitt's India Act 1784 (the teacher's board) Teacher's board: "Context of PIA 1784 [passed by Br (P), William PITT = PM]" Why Pitt's India Act 1784 was passed (teacher's board) GBF 1770 (as written on the board) By 1772 the EIC is bankrupt; it seeks the help of the British State The British State gives money (a loan) to the EIC, BUT brings the EIC under its supervision via the Regulating Act 1773 Core goal of 1773: the EIC shall not waste British taxpayers' money on wars and go bankrupt again 1st Anglo-Maratha War plus 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84): high war expenditure; the British State is anxious Pitt's India Act 1784 bans conquest: the EIC can defend but cannot start wars on its own The heading reads "Context of PIA 1784 [passed by Br (P), William PITT = PM]": the Act was passed by the British Parliament (the circled P) when William Pitt was Prime Minister. The logic of the chain is money: the British State had already rescued a bankrupt Company once (the loan, with supervision through the Regulating Act 1773). Its core goal was that the EIC should not waste British taxpayers' money on wars and go bankrupt again. When two more wars again produced high war expenditure, the State grew anxious and wrote the ban into law. The teacher underlined in yellow: "Cannot START WARS." 2.2 The ban and the reason for it The ban Pitt's India Act of 1784 had banned conquest. The Governor-General (GG) could not start an offensive war without the express command and authority of either the Court of Directors of the EIC or the Board of Control of the British State (discussed in a later chapter) The exception The GG had the right to enter war on grounds of defence The reason High war expenditure The wars that drained Company finances The Three Carnatic Wars (1746–63), the Battle of Buxar (1764),two Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–69 and 1780–84) and the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) What Parliament mandated instead Diplomacy rather than war, in the form of the Policy of Indirect Rule (PoIR) and maintaining a balance of power among Indian States, instead of pursuing direct conquest The handout's recall: the pacifist policy of the Mughals after 1707 was also for the same reason (the cost of war). And the handout's note: Wellesley 98-05 could not legally start an offensive war without prior authorisation. 2.3 The Napoleon threat: there, but not real Teacher's board headed "WORLD HISTORY" (underlined in yellow) The Napoleon-threat diagram (teacher's World History board) 1798: France (Napoleon) attacks Egypt; the dotted line on the board runs France to Egypt, marked 1798 Aim: the Middle East; to hurt the British trade of the Arabian Sea (three arrows on the board) Diplomatic contact with Tipu 82-99 of Mysore Threat: a Napoleon and Mysore alliance, or Napoleon attacking British India But the threat was "there, not real"; the British Navy was superior, so the French would not have been able to reach India This is the board marked PRELIMS. The teacher splits the word "threat" into two kinds: Real = high chance; Unreal = less chance. His verdict: "THREAT was THERE BUT not Real", that is, a threat existed, but with a low chance. The reason he writes beside it: "because Br NAVY = SUPERIOR [would not have been able to reach India]." So in an exam statement, "Napoleonic danger" is a correct feature of the Subsidiary Alliance (the danger was there), even though the danger was not a real, high-chance one. Wellesley 98-05 re-initiated conquest by overhyping the threat of a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance. Napoleon had attacked Egypt in 1798 with the goal of controlling the Middle East and hurting British trade, and he was in communication with Tipu 82-99 of Mysore. A threat existed, but not a real one.Britain's navy was superior to France's, and a French fleet heading for India through the Arabian Sea would have been destroyed before arriving. The handout's note: the British had already burnt French ships in the Mediterranean once Napoleon landed in Egypt, leaving his army stranded with no way home. But the British State agreed anyway, because protecting India from European rivals was the primary goal of British foreign policy and it did not want to take any risks. Wellesley 98-05 also offered a middle path: the Subsidiary Alliance. It gave political domination without the cost, the administrative burden and the symbolism of full annexation. Beside "Middle path" the teacher wrote "= SA = CONTROL w/o annexation." He also added a handwritten "w/o" before "symbolism", so the phrase reads: without the cost, without the administrative burden and without the symbolism of full annexation. This is the one-line definition to carry: the Subsidiary Alliance is control without annexation. It suited a State that had banned conquest because conquest was costly: the SA promised the gains of conquest without its bill. How Wellesley 98-05 got round the ban Pitt's India Act 1784: no offensive war without the Court of Directors or the Board of Control; war only in defence 1798: Napoleon attacks Egypt and is in communication with Tipu 82-99 Wellesley 98-05 overhypes the threat of a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance The British State agrees anyway: protecting India from European rivals is its primary foreign-policy goal; it will not take risks Middle path: the Subsidiary Alliance; control without annexation Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021: option (b) was a TRUE statement: "Napoleonic danger was a feature of the SA."The danger was not real (less chance of a Napoleonic attack on India), but the danger was there (a chance existed). Do not mark it false. Prelims 1999: "At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors General kept the British flag flying high in India?" Options: (a) Warren Hastings 73-85, (b) Lord Cornwallis 86-93, (c) Lord Wellesley 98-05 (correct), (d) Lord Hastings. The trap: two different Governors General share the surname Hastings.Warren Hastings 73-85 is the pre-Napoleon era: wrong.Francis Hastings 13-23 (also called Lord Hastings) is the post-Napoleon era: wrong.Why (c): the tenure of Wellesley 98-05 (1798–1805) overlaps with Napoleon's offensive phase (1796–1812). Students sometimes pick (d) Lord Hastings because the name sounds Napoleon-era. It is NOT.

items.t: 3 · Two roots of the SA: Dupleix 42-54 and ToA 1765
items.x: Because the Subsidiary Alliance was not invented in 1798, ask who used the template first. Ask: French or British, 1751 or 1765, and what did Wellesley 98-05 add? The Policy of Subsidiary Alliance did not appear from nowhere. It has two roots: one French and one British. Who Dupleix 42-54, as Governor General of French Establishments in India (GG of the French EIC) Robert Clive 57-67 What he set up The first mini or proto-form of the Subsidiary Alliance, at Hyderabad in 1751 The mini Subsidiary Alliance planted at Awadh via the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) The occasion Salabat Jung 51-62 became Nizam of Hyderabad with French backing The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) with Awadh The army A French force under Bussy was permanently stationed An EIC army in Awadh Who paid Paid out in the form of Northern Sarkars revenues (and control) Paid by subsidy from Awadh The ruler's own army Not stated in the handout Size of the Nawab's controlled army reduced (not disbanded) The man at court A foreign adviser at court who would not just advise but establish indirect rule A British Resident stationed Dupleix 42-54 had discovered the template: an external army at the Indian State's cost, with a foreign adviser at court who would not just advise but establish indirect rule. Clive 57-67's mini SA at Awadh was the British version, very close to the French template that Dupleix 42-54 had pioneered. 3.1 Wellesley 98-05's step: from a device to a policy Wellesley 98-05 took the next step. He formalised the relationship in a written treaty,took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy explicitly, and disbanded its army. The Subsidiary Alliance was NOT a Wellesley 98-05 invention. BUT the Policy of Subsidiary Alliance was initiated by him. Why "policy": a policy means a pre-meditated, formalised plan of action with a pre-decided intent, which is reflected in a series of events executed in line with that policy. Wellesley 98-05 formalised the SA into a policy,added the takeover of Foreign Policy and the disbanding of the Indian State's army, and implemented this policy State by State across India. Invention versus policy. The idea is older: Dupleix 42-54 (Hyderabad, 1751) and Clive 57-67 (Awadh, ToA 1765). The policy is Wellesley 98-05's: a written treaty, Foreign Policy taken over, the army disbanded, applied State by State. If a statement says "Wellesley 98-05 invented the Subsidiary Alliance", it is wrong; if it says he "initiated the Policy of Subsidiary Alliance", it is right. From proto-SA to the full Policy of Subsidiary Alliance 1751, Hyderabad (Dupleix 42-54): French force under Bussy stationed, paid from the Northern Sarkars; a foreign adviser at court 1765, Awadh (Clive 57-67, ToA 1765); EIC army paid by Awadh's subsidy, Nawab's army reduced, British Resident stationed Wellesley 98-05: written treaty, Foreign Policy taken over explicitly, the State's army disbanded A policy, not a one-off: implemented State by State across India

items.t: 4 · The model treaty of the Subsidiary Alliance and its legal logic
items.x: Because the idea became a policy, the treaty was written down. Ask: what did the EIC get (five), what did the ruler get (two), and why did Foreign Policy matter? The standard terms of any Subsidiary Alliance fell into two groups, though the actual terms varied a little from State to State, depending on context. 4.0 The teacher's board: how the SA splits sovereignty Teacher's board headed "SA" (circled, underlined in yellow) Symbolic Sovereignty The throne and the title The Indian king External Sovereign Functions: D, C, FA Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs Taken by the EIC Domestic Sovereign Functions Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc. The Indian king The teacher starts from the word Sovereignty and separates Symbolic Sovereignty (who is called king) from the "power to do" (the three circled letters L, E, J; the board does not expand them here). The power to do is then cut in two. External Sovereign Functions (D, C, FA: Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs) are "[Taken by EIC]".Domestic Sovereign Functions (Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc.) stay with the "[Indian king]". Under Def he writes the heart of the SA: "EIC will maintain the Army BUT TAKES money = SUBSIDY: Def BD [Decided by EIC]." That is: the subsidy is simply the Indian State's defence budget (Def BD), but the size of that budget is decided by the EIC, not by the ruler who pays it. Teacher's board: "Symbolic Sovereignty" with a line splitting into two branches The same split, now in the Mughal vocabulary of Nizamat and Diwani.Diwani = civil administration plus Finance.Nizamat (minus Military) = Criminal Jurisdiction. The teacher's own summary line: "Simple: MILITARY and Foreign Policy with the EIC; the rest of Nizamat, and Diwani, and Symbolic Sovereignty with the Indian King." This is why the handout writes the ruler's promise as non-interference in "succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military)". 4.0b The same board, redrawn at the start of Lecture 15 (Treaty of SA) Lecture 15 opens with the teacher's board "Treaty of SA" Symbolic Sovereignty The Indian king The title and throne External Sovereign Functions The EIC D (Defence), C (Communications), FA (Foreign Affairs) Domestic Sovereign Functions The Indian king Fin (Finance), Home, Admin, Health etc, infra Lecture 15 begins by redrawing the Lecture 14 board (slide 40) so that the model treaty can be revised in one picture. The two terms he writes at the left are the first two of the five EIC terms: "Br Resident" (underlined) and "Military alliance between the EIC and the Indian State". The "Def BD" (defence budget) box carries the third and fourth: the Indian king pays an annual subsidy, and it "has to be used for military", so it is not income for the Company. That is exactly why option (c) "secure a fixed income for the Company" is false in the Prelims 2018 and 2021 question (Section 8). Two small differences from the Lecture 14 board.(1) The domestic list is written Fin, Home, Admin, Health etc, infra here, against Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc on slide 40. Same idea (domestic functions stay with the king); learn the idea, not the exact list. (2) The circled L, E, J after "Power to" are not expanded on the slide (the same as on slide 40). Reading them as Legislature, Executive, Judiciary is a natural guess but is not written:. The symbol before "income" in the bottom note is also slightly unclear; the sense is "used for military, so not income". 4.1 What the EIC got (5 terms) Model Treaty: What the EIC Got (5 terms) 1 A British Resident stationed permanently in the Indian ruler's court, with the ruler as a puppet Elements 1 and 2 of PoIR, but not yet element 3: the British promised non-interference in internal affairs by the British Resident. This promise was seldom kept, and the British breached the treaty in many cases 2 A formal military alliance between the EIC and the Indian State  3 The Indian State's own army was disbanded and replaced by an EIC-maintained army permanently stationed in the State  4 The Indian State paid an annual subsidy to fund this EIC army So technically this army is owned by the Indian State; the EIC only maintains it. But because of the 5th point, this ownership of the Indian State was lost 5 The EIC took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy Decisions on war and peace, diplomacy, the defence budget and foreign trade. The GG's consent was needed before any European could be stationed at the court. The ruler had to consult the GG before negotiating with any other Indian State or foreign power. The subsidy, that is, the defence budget of the Indian State, was decided by the EIC Ink on the five terms (slide 42), with the reasoning.Term 1: the teacher writes "(1) Puppet Nawab (2) Br Resident" and draws both into a circled "(3) CONTROL", which he crosses with dotted lines and labels "= promise in SA TREATY". Meaning: the three elements of indirect rule are a puppet ruler, a Resident, and control through the Resident. The SA treaty openly had the first two; the third (control) was promised away on paper by the non-interference clause. Term 2:"So the MILITARY maintained for the Indian State can be used FOR Br India as well." An alliance cuts both ways: the army paid for by the ruler is now also the EIC's army for British India's needs. Term 4:"= Def BD". The annual subsidy is nothing but the State's defence budget.Term 5:"The money will GO TO the Indian State BUT the Decisions are the EIC's." The State keeps earning and paying; the EIC decides. The handout's note: the annual subsidy money was NOT surplus income that the EIC could use for anything. The subsidy was to be spent only for maintaining the army. The slide adds: the subsidy was earmarked for that army, but the EIC commanded it, so operational control was fully with the EIC. 4.2 What the Indian ruler got (2 terms) Model Treaty: What the Indian Ruler Got (2 terms) 1 EIC protection against neighbours and domestic threats 2 A formal promise of non-interference in internal affairs:succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military) The imbalance. The slide's own line: the ruler gets 2 promises; the EIC takes 5 operational levers. The non-interference promise was routinely broken via the Resident: "creeping PoIR through the back door". Under the word Imbalance the teacher redraws the sloping line: EIC on top, Indian State below (the same picture as on slide 29). His comparison:"[Compare with DUAL GOVT (1765-72) in Bengal]". Then: "From 1772 everything in Bengal with the EIC [symbolically the Nawabs continued into the 19th century]." The point of the comparison: in both cases an Indian ruler keeps the name and the responsibility while the Company holds real power. In Bengal the split ended in 1772 with everything going to the EIC; the SA sets up a similar split in State after State. 4.3 Why the EIC took Foreign Policy: the legal logic The legal logic of Term 5 The EIC maintains the army using the Indian State's own subsidy money Loophole: one could argue that legal ownership, and the right to deploy that army, still belong to the Indian ruler The EIC takes Foreign Policy: the decision of war and peace Loophole closed: the right to deploy the army now legally rests with the EIC There is a legal logic to why the EIC specifically demanded Foreign Policy. The EIC maintained the army using the Indian State's own subsidy money. One could therefore argue that legal ownership, and the right to deploy that army, still belonged to the Indian ruler. The EIC closed this loophole by taking Foreign Policy. The decision of war and peace, and therefore the right to deploy the army, now legally rested with the EIC. Why ToA 1765 was only a "mini" Subsidiary Alliance: an EIC army was stationed there at Awadh's expense, BUT Awadh's own army was not disbanded and Foreign Policy was not taken over.The proper SA (the full package) came only in 1801. The formula: PoSA = PoIR (informally) + PoRF + EIC Military replacing the Indian State's Military + annual subsidy + loss of Foreign Policy. (PoSA = Policy of Subsidiary Alliance; PoIR = Policy of Indirect Rule; PoRF = Policy of Ring Fence, from Chapter 10. "Informally" because the treaty itself promised non-interference.) 4.4 The PYQ on SA features (Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021) UPSC asked the same question in both Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021: "Which statement does NOT apply to the Subsidiary Alliance?" The four options tested the features of the SA. The false option was (c) "Secure a fixed income for the Company." The SA's annual subsidy was earmarked for maintaining the EIC army stationed in the host State. It was NOT surplus income for the EIC.The other three options were true: to maintain a large standing army, to defend against Napoleonic danger, and to establish British paramountcy.

items.t: 5 · The vicious chain: consequences of the Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States
items.x: Because the EIC held the army and Foreign Policy, the chain of harm followed. Ask: at which link did the ruler lose his State? Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance 1 Disbanded armies, so mass unemployment Disbanding Indian State armies caused mass unemployment for military men:Mansabdars lost their positions (the teacher corrects this to "military role"), sepoys lost their livelihoods 2 The EIC's compounded military power at the host State's expense The EIC maintained and commanded the army in the Indian State, so operational control was entirely with the EIC. Having taken over Foreign Policy, it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere. The EIC could now maintain a large army at the expense of Indian States 3 High and rising subsidy, so Drain of Wealth Subsidy payments were high to begin with and the EIC gradually increased its demands. The same money could have been used by the ruler for his own State's development. Instead there was Drain of Wealth 4 Tax hikes, so unrest To pay the ever-rising subsidy, rulers had to raise taxes. High taxes made rulers unpopular, fuelled peasant resentment and created conditions for unrest 5 Maladministration accusations, so grounds for annexation The EIC then accused Indian rulers of maladministration. In reality the ruler had no real power left 6 Territory in lieu of cash When the subsidy could not be paid in cash, the EIC simply took territory as payment 7 Permanent loss of alliance-forming capacity By losing Foreign Policy and military control, Indian States permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the EIC 5.1 Links 1 and 2: unemployment and the EIC's free army Link 1. Disbanding Indian State armies caused mass unemployment for military men.Mansabdars lost their positions; sepoys lost their livelihoods. The handout's note: the EIC also recruited sepoys from outside the host State, to reduce any chance of loyalty to the Nawab in case he revolted: a classic Divide and Rule strategy. Link 2. Since the EIC maintained and commanded the army in the Indian State, operational control was entirely with the EIC. Since it had also taken over Foreign Policy, it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere. Hence the EIC could now maintain a large army at the expense of Indian States. The handout's note: EIC Armies = the army of the Indian State maintained by the EIC using the Indian State's subsidy + the EIC's own army maintained from its own money. Both were available to the EIC for its own wars. Teacher's correction on slide 45. In the line "Mansabdars lost their positions", the teacher struck out "positions" and wrote "MILITARY ROLE" above it. The handout prints "positions". Use the teacher's wording: Mansabdars lost their military role. Divide and Rule (the circled "DnR"). Beside the note on recruiting outsiders the teacher wrote: "DnR: the EIC will NOT keep sepoys from Bengal in the Bengal Army", with "(Less)" written above "NOT". So read it as: the EIC would keep few or no local men in the army of their own region. The reasoning is in the handout's note: a sepoy from outside has no loyalty to the local Nawab if he revolts. Who pays? The teacher asks: "WHO PAYS for the EIC army in an Indian State (SA)?" Answer: "the Indian State / King", therefore a "FREE army" for the Company (his written phrase is "Free of ARMY"). The boxed conclusion: "[Every SA leads to a free-of-cost increase in the EIC army]". Each new treaty adds a paid-for army to the Company's strength without adding a rupee to its costs. Teacher's board, the analogy: "SA Concept LIKE BALI of Ramayana" (the word LIKE underlined, BALI inside a large circle, "Concept" written small under SA) The Bali analogy. The board reads: "SA concept LIKE BALI of Ramayana" (BALI in a big circle), and under it "SA LED TO MILITARY POWER SHIFT." Read it together with the previous board: under every SA the Indian State's military strength moves across to the EIC. The State pays, its own army is disbanded, and the army it pays for fights for the Company. So with each alliance the ally grows weaker and the EIC grows stronger: a shift of military power. The board gives only the name of the analogy ("like Bali of Ramayana") and its conclusion ("military power shift"). The story behind the analogy was explained orally and is not written on the slide. Check your class notebook for the spoken explanation before using it in an answer. 5.2 Links 3 and 4: Drain of Wealth and tax hikes Link 3.Subsidy payments were high to begin with, and the EIC gradually increased its demands. The same money could have been used by the Indian ruler for his own State's development.Instead there was Drain of Wealth. Link 4.To pay the ever-rising subsidy, Indian rulers had to raise taxes. High taxes made rulers unpopular,fuelled peasant resentment and created conditions for unrest. After the words "for unrest" the teacher wrote "Peasant Revolts". That is where this link ends: rising subsidy, then higher taxes, then peasant resentment, then peasant revolts. His underlines pick out the cause ("rulers had to raise taxes") and the cost (the "same money could have funded" the "State development"). 5.3 Links 5 and 6: maladministration and territory in lieu of cash Link 5. The EIC then accused Indian rulers of maladministration. In reality the ruler had no real power left. The British Resident had in many cases established Indirect Rule illegally, in direct breach of the treaty's own promise of non-interference. The ruler had no power, but all the responsibility. The most stark example was Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh: accused of maladministration, his State annexed in 1856. Link 6. When the subsidy could not be paid in cash, the EIC simply took territory as payment. In 1801, half of Awadh was annexed as permanent subsidy payment. In 1853, Hyderabad was made to give Berar. The handout's aside: the EIC can say "Thanks, Dupleix 42-54". He gave this idea when he took the Northern Sarkars from Hyderabad in 1751. Under "Territory in lieu of cash" the teacher wrote: "Subsidy = TOOL of empire building." The subsidy was not only a payment. It was set high, it kept rising, and when the ruler defaulted the EIC took land. So the subsidy itself was the instrument that turned an "alliance" into annexation. He underlined the two examples to memorise: 1801, half of Awadh; 1853, Berar from Hyderabad. 5.4 Link 7 and the takeaway Link 7. By losing Foreign Policy and military control, Indian States permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the EIC. Hence the Subsidiary Alliance was, in effect, a sophisticated Divide and Rule instrument at the level of an entire subcontinent. Takeaway: the EIC via the SA got all military and diplomatic powers, with no responsibility of ruling and no burden of finances. The seven vicious-chain links explain why every single SA signatory ended up either annexed or permanently dependent. The vicious chain in one line The State's army is disbanded: Mansabdars lose their military role, sepoys their livelihood The EIC's army grows free of cost and can be used for the EIC's own wars Subsidy high and rising: Drain of Wealth Taxes raised: rulers unpopular, peasant resentment, peasant revolts "Maladministration": the ruler has no power but all the responsibility (Awadh annexed 1856) Territory in lieu of cash: half of Awadh 1801, Berar 1853 No alliances possible against the EIC: annexed or permanently dependent

items.t: 6 · Which States signed, and under what circumstances
items.x: Because the harm was slow, many rulers signed willingly or after a war. Ask: factionalism or war, and under which Governor General? Sections 6 and 7 combine the handout with the teacher's ink from Lecture 15 (slides 2 to 10). The Lecture 14 slides stop at the vicious chain (slide 49); Lecture 15 picks the chapter up with the five arguments, the signatories (his corrected count is ten), the annexations and the recall, and then ends the chapter with the PYQ slides (11 to 23), which are in Section 8. Where the slide's typed text disagrees with the teacher's pen or with the handout, an alert says which to use. 6.1 Why some rulers walked in willingly The SA was not forced on every signatory at sword-point. In several cases the Indian ruler walked in willingly, persuaded by five arguments: 1 Protection against internal revolts A guaranteed EIC army inside the palace walls was attractive insurance against rival claimants or mutinous nobles 2 Protection against external threats Small States feared Maratha Chauth raids, Mysorean expansion or Rohilla incursions far more than the distant British 3 Better than annexation The subsidy was, on paper, cheaper than annexation or a losing war against the EIC 4 Preservation of royal dignity The ruler's title, court and ceremonial status were formally preserved.The flag of sovereignty flew, even after its substance had been handed over 5 For winning succession disputes and for protection from neighbours In many cases rulers sought EIC help in succession disputes and for protection from other Indian States. The EIC used this as an opportunity by making military help conditional upon the Indian ruler signing the SA Under the fifth argument, "Winning succession disputes", the teacher writes one word: "FACTIONALISM". That is the label for argument 5: the rulers did not sign only out of fear of outsiders; they signed because groups inside the ruling family or court fought over the throne or the regency, and the side that wanted the EIC's help had to sign the SA to get it. He returns to the word on slide 7 (Nagpur regency) and draws a five-way tag for the Marathas (see 6.2). The first four arguments (slide 2) carry no ink. 6.2 The ten signatories (1798–1818) 1 1798 Hyderabad The Nizam signed first, to get EIC protection against the Marathas and Mysore Wellesley 98-05 2 1799 Mysore (Wodeyar dynasty) Forced to sign after defeat in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99).Tipu 82-99 was killed at the Battle of Seringapatam (1799); the Wodeyars were restored as a subsidiary throne Wellesley 98-05 3 1801 Awadh Sadat Ali Khan II defaulted on the subsidy; Henry Wellesley imposed a full Subsidiary Alliance;half of Awadh annexed (details below) Wellesley 98-05 4 June 1802 Gaikwad of Baroda (Treaty of Cambay) Signed in exchange for EIC help in a Gaikwad succession dispute Wellesley 98-05 5 December 1802 Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 (Treaty of Bassein / Vasai) Defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar, he fled and signed to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support Wellesley 98-05 6 1803 Scindia of Gwalior Forced to sign during the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) Wellesley 98-05 7 1803-05 Jats, Rajputs, Bundelas (a group entry) During the war the EIC forced them to sign Subsidiary Alliances. They had earlier paid Chauth and Sardeshmukhi to the Marathas; now they paid subsidy to the new regional power, the EIC Wellesley 98-05 8 1805 Travancore Signed in exchange for EIC help in crushing a mutiny by Nair troops, who had revolted over non-payment of salary.The last SA signed under Wellesley 98-05 before his recall Wellesley 98-05 9 1816 Bhonsle of Nagpur (Treaty of Nagpur) Appa Sahib finally signed, using EIC backing to win the faction fight over who would be regent Francis Hastings 13-23 10 1818 Holkar of Indore (Treaty of Mandsaur) Forced to sign after decisive defeat in the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817–19) Francis Hastings 13-23 Signatories (1798-1818): Hyderabad and Mysore The title is corrected from "Nine" to "10". The same strike-through and "10" appear on every signatory slide (slides 4 to 8). Counting rule for this notebook: TEN entries, with Jats-Rajputs-Bundelas as no. 7 (a group entry); see the alert below. Count conflict: typed slides and handout say "Nine"; the teacher says TEN. The handout heading reads "The Nine Signatories" and its takeaway says "9 SAs in 20 years; the first seven under Wellesley 98-05". On slides 4 to 8 the teacher struck "Nine" and wrote 10, struck "9" and wrote 10, and struck "seven" and wrote 8 (slide 8). The list itself has ten bullets, so 10 and 8 are right.Use: ten SAs; the first eight (Hyderabad to Travancore, counting Jats-Rajputs-Bundelas as no. 7) under Wellesley 98-05; the last two (Bhonsle, Holkar) under Francis Hastings 13-23. Only if a question counts just the named States is the number nine. A line written under the Hyderabad and Mysore rows, with a dotted line from the 1798 and 1799 entries: "Had India had one common centre, i.e. one State ruling all (T) of Indian, then this would not have happened." The circled T is not expanded on the slide (the sense is a single State over all the territory). It is the same lesson as the handout's conclusion in 1.3: a fragmented polity is why India was colonised. The bracket beside it, tagged (IR) (a tag he uses for an international-relations lesson), adds: "enemy/rival should not be ONE". The slide does not spell out the logic; my reading is that the lesson is about facing a united rival: the Indian States were many, the EIC was one. [Reading, not written: check your notebook.] Against the Mysore row, a dotted line leads to a second (IR) bracket: "Don't lose WARS." Mysore is the clearest case on the list: the 4th Anglo-Mysore War was lost, Tipu 82-99 was killed at Seringapatam (1799), and the State was forced into an SA with the Wodeyars restored on a subsidiary throne. A war lost is an SA signed. Takeaway: 10 SAs in 20 years, 1798 to 1818.The first eight (Hyderabad to Travancore) were signed under Wellesley 98-05; the last two under Francis Hastings 13-23.First: Hyderabad (1798). Last under Wellesley 98-05: Travancore (1805). Last of all: Holkar (1818). Signatories (contd.): the takeaway row Two corrections in the takeaway: "9" becomes "10" and "seven" becomes "8". Then he adds a list of "empire builders", four names in time order:Clive 57-67, Wellesley 98-05, F. Hastings 13-23, Dalhousie 48-56. He groups them by century: Clive 57-67 and Wellesley 98-05 in the "18th c" bracket; F. Hastings 13-23 and Dalhousie 48-56 in the "19th c" bracket (Wellesley 98-05 starts in 1798, which is why he sits with the 18th century even though his term runs to 1805). The circle on the "#" before Wellesley 98-05 and F. Hastings 13-23 is not explained on the slide. One likely reason: these two are exactly the Governors General under whom the ten SAs were signed (8 and 2).[Reading, not written: check your notebook.] Dalhousie 48-56 is the subject of Chapter 14. On the count. The handout's list has ten bullets, and this table numbers all ten. The Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas (1803-05) are one group entry (several rulers under one bullet); if a question counts only the named States, the number is nine. Read the question for which count it wants. Signatories (contd.): Awadh and the Gaikwad of Baroda The oval is Awadh cut in two. The left half "1801" is the half annexed in 1801 (the Doab, Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand): an arrow takes it to "NWP 1836", the full province status given to the Ceded Districts. The right half "1856" is the rest of Awadh, annexed in 1856 (Wajid Ali Shah, maladministration; see 5.3). Under it he writes "1877: Both merged" (1877 underlined): the two halves, the NWP territories annexed in 1801 and Awadh annexed in 1856, were merged in 1877. Dashed underlines mark what to remember in the handout text: "Shore 93-98 obliged" (the favour that started the story), "permanent subsidy" and "Ceded Districts". The Nawab list in the margin gives the dynasty in order, which makes the 1797-98 episode easy to follow: Sadat 22-39, Safdar Jung 39-53, Shuja 54-75, Asaf-ud-Dowla 75-97, Wazir Ali [1797-98], and then, with an arrow from Wazir Ali, "uncle Sadat II Ali Khan [1798+]". So the man the SA was bought for was the uncle who replaced his nephew Wazir Ali, and the same uncle defaulted by 1801. "Whole" Awadh and "half" Awadh are the same story, not a conflict. The memory line "Awadh: 01 half, 56 whole" in Section 5.3 means: the first half went in 1801 and the rest in 1856, which the teacher's oval shows as two halves. Do not write "Awadh annexed in 1801" for the whole State; 1801 = half (Ceded Districts), 1856 = the remainder. Awadh, 1798 to 1801, step by step: How Awadh came under the full Subsidiary Alliance 1798: Sadat Ali Khan II offers the EIC Rs 76 lakh as annual subsidy; in exchange John Shore 93-98 is to remove his nephew Wazir Ali (1797-98) from the Nawabship Shore 93-98 obliges By 1801 Sadat Ali Khan II defaults Wellesley 98-05 sends his brother Henry Wellesley to impose a full Subsidiary Alliance Half of Awadh annexed as permanent subsidy payment: the Doab, Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand 1801, Awadh. In 1798, Sadat Ali Khan II had offered the EIC Rs 76 lakh as annual subsidy in exchange for John Shore 93-98 removing his nephew Wazir Ali (1797-98) from the Nawabship.Shore 93-98 obliged.By 1801, Sadat Ali Khan II defaulted.Wellesley 98-05 sent his brother Henry Wellesley to impose a full Subsidiary Alliance.Half of Awadh (the Doab, Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand) was annexed as permanent subsidy payment. The handout's note: this was unfair. The revenue from this territory was twice the Rs 76 lakh annual subsidy it was meant to cover. These territories became the Ceded Districts, and in 1836 were given full province status as the North-West Provinces (NWP 1836) of British India. Recall on Rohilkhand:most of Rohilkhand was annexed by Awadh with EIC help in 1774. The EIC had helped because of the ToA 1765 military alliance. The remaining small part of Rohilkhand became the autonomous State of Rampur, but under Awadh legally, and from 1801 under the EIC legally. Three small inks on this slide.(1) "Treaty of Bassein/Vasai" is underlined: know both names, Bassein and Vasai. (2) Under Scindia: "or 1804". The slide and handout print 1803; the teacher adds that the date may also be given as 1804.(3) "2nd A-Ma" over "the war" in the Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas row: the war in which they were forced to sign is the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Scindia's date: 1803 (handout and slide) or 1804 (teacher's ink). Both are inside the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Learn 1803 as the base date and know that 1804 is also acceptable. If an exam option shows only one of them, check the other options before deciding; the safe anchor is "during the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War". The Peshwa and the Treaty of Bassein, 1802: From Bassein to the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War Yashwantrao Holkar defeats Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18; he was avenging his brother's death Bajirao II 96-18 flees December 1802, Treaty of Bassein (Vasai): he signs the SA to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support Scindia and Bhonsle read this as a Peshwa selling the Confederacy to the British The 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) follows December 1802, Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18. He had been defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar (avenging his brother's death). He fled, and signed the Treaty of Bassein (1802) to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support. The handout's note:Scindia and Bhonsle read this as a Peshwa selling the Confederacy to the British, and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) followed. The full treatment of Bassein 1802 and the war is in the Anglo-Maratha Wars chapter (Chapter 13). Recall: the Marathas captured Bassein from the Portuguese via the Treaty of Bassein (1739), and brought it under Peshwa control along with Salsette. So there are two Treaties of Bassein: 1739 (Marathas and the Portuguese) and 1802 (Peshwa and the EIC). 1816, Bhonsle of Nagpur. After defeat in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the Bhonsles had resisted signing a full Subsidiary Alliance for over a decade. In 1816 Appa Sahib finally signed, using EIC backing to win the faction fight over who would be regent of the Bhonsle of Nagpur. (The story belongs to the Anglo-Maratha Wars chapter, Chapter 13.) Signatories (contd.): Travancore 1805, Bhonsle of Nagpur 1816, Holkar of Indore 1818 The Nagpur row defines the word. So factionalism means rival groups fighting over who rules, here over the regency of Nagpur. The five-way tree: what happened to each Maratha power after 1761. items.t: 7 · Direct annexations and the recall of Wellesley 98-05
items.x: Because alliances were not enough, land was also taken, and wars again cost money. Ask: what did he annex, and why was he recalled? What territory did Wellesley 98-05 directly annex, and why was he eventually recalled? Beyond Subsidiary Alliances, Wellesley 98-05 also directly annexed territory: 1799 Mysore territory Significant territory taken from Mysore after the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799 Early 1801 Half of Awadh (the Ceded Districts) Annexed as permanent subsidy payment (the NWP 1836 territories, covered in section 6) 1801 Carnatic Annexed on grounds of maladministration, six years after the death of Md Ali 52-95 (1752–1795), who had been the EIC's loyal ally since the 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54 1803–05 2nd Anglo-Maratha War: Bhonsle Bhonsle of Nagpur lost significant territory, including Orissa (which Bhonsle had himself taken from Bengal in 1751) 1803–05 2nd Anglo-Maratha War: Scindia Scindia lost territory in Gujarat and all territory north of the River Yamuna, including Delhi Direct Annexations + Wellesley 98-05's Recall Ink beside each annexation, row by row (slide 9).Mysore 1799: "To MADRAS PRESIDENCY". The territory taken from Mysore after the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799 went to the EIC's Madras Presidency.Half of Awadh, early 1801: "SUBSIDY as TOOL or empire BUILDING". The same sentence as on slide 48 of Lecture 14 ("Subsidy = TOOL of empire building"): the subsidy was the tool through which an alliance became territory.Carnatic 1801: "(not on RECORD REASON)" ... "BUT an imp context". The reason on record is maladministration (the handout's wording). The teacher says the important context behind it is that "the Nawab HAD taken MANY loans from the EIC and its officers", which he labels "Financial maladmin". So "maladministration" here means financial mismanagement and debt to the Company and its officers.2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05: he underlines the five things to remember: Bhonsle, Orissa, Scindia, Gujarat, and "all territory north of the River Yamuna, including Delhi". Beside the Delhi line: "[Now PoIR in Delhi]" and, below it, a bracketed "[1771 - 1803]". The slide does not explain either note, and the letters "PoIR" are themselves hard to read.  for his spoken reason. All that is certain from the text is that Scindia lost Delhi and everything north of the Yamuna in 1803-05. Mysore territory 1799 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799 Went to the Madras Presidency Half of Awadh 1801 Permanent subsidy payment (default) Subsidy as tool of empire building Carnatic 1801 Maladministration, six years after Md Ali 52-95 died Not the real record reason: the Nawab's many loans from the EIC and its officers (financial maladministration) Orissa, Gujarat, Delhi side 1803-05 2nd Anglo-Maratha War "Now PoIR in Delhi"; "[1771 - 1803]" (unclear) Carnatic: use "maladministration" as the recorded ground, and add the teacher's context. The handout gives only "annexed on grounds of maladministration". The teacher's two additions ("not on record reason", "Nawab had taken many loans from the EIC and its officers") do not contradict it; they explain what the word covered. In a Mains answer write: annexed on the ground of maladministration, in the background of the Nawab's heavy debts to the Company and its officers. Wellesley 98-05 was eventually recalled to London due to high war expenditure. Empire building was profitable only if wars were short and cheap. His were neither. Direct Annexations + Wellesley 98-05's Recall (contd.): why recalled The teacher's board: why even a winning war got Wellesley 98-05 recalled GBF 1770; 1772 bankruptcy of the EIC Loan from the British State, with supervision through the Regulating Act 1773 BUT STILL wars (sad face): the EIC keeps fighting Pitt's India Act 1784 bans offensive war BUT STILL wars (circled): under Wellesley 98-05 the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799 and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 Wars are expensive for both, winner and loser: high war expenditure, so he is recalled The board repeats the money chain of slide 34 (GBF 1770, bankruptcy 1772, loan from the British State, Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784) and adds the punch line: "BUT STILL wars", twice. Two laws, one rescue loan, and the wars did not stop. Under Wellesley 98-05 (underlined) he lists the two wars that cost him his post: 4th A-My 1799 and 2nd A-Ma 1803-05. In the box: "Wars are expensive for both," with the branches Winner and Loser. The point: even the winner pays, so a Governor General who wins two big wars can still be recalled for the bill. The (IR) note at the top says the same: "Wars HURT the economy of both sides." The chapter comes full circle on money.High war expenditure produced the ban on conquest in Pitt's India Act 1784. Wellesley 98-05 got round the ban with the Napoleon threat and the Subsidiary Alliance. And high war expenditure is what finally got Wellesley 98-05 recalled. The handout page for this chapter ends with an index of the next chapter (Mysore's four wars, Dhondia Wagh, Tipu 82-99's religious policy, the Carnatic annexed in 1801, Travancore and Velu Thampi Dalawa). That material belongs to Chapter 12, not here.

Two ink differences from the handout; the handout and slide answer still win.(1) Napoleon's dates: the teacher writes 1799-1815; the handout alert says Wellesley 98-05's tenure overlaps Napoleon's offensive phase (1796-1812). The two ranges frame the same era and give the same answer, (c). Learn 1796-1812 (handout) if a question gives dates, and treat 1799-1815 as the teacher's quick bracket for the same era. (2) The code beside (d): the ink reads "13-93", which looks like a slip; Francis Hastings 13-23 is the right code (handout, slide 14 and Section 2.3). Use 13-23. Answer: (c) Lord Wellesley 98-05 (slide 13). Slide 14's explanation: (a) wrong, Warren Hastings 73-85 was Governor General 1773-85, well before the Napoleonic era;(b) wrong, Cornwallis 86-93 was "a quiet phase, not a Napoleonic-era expansionist";(d) wrong, Francis Hastings 13-23 fought after Napoleon's defeat in 1815.Bank check: the bank's answer key reads (a), which is a key error (its own explanation says (c)); use (c). 8.2 PYQ 2 and PYQ 3: "Which does NOT apply to the Subsidiary Alliance" (Prelims 2018, Prelims 2021; slides 15 to 18) PYQ 1, Prelims 1999: "At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors General kept the British flag fly PYQ 2, Prelims 2018, answer slide with the teacher's marks (a) Maintain standing army T "BALI", "FREE of ARMY" Bali analogy and the free army at the State's cost (5.1) (b) Keep India safe from Napoleon T "THREAT", split REAL or UNREAL The threat was there but not real (2.3) (c) Secure fixed income for Company F none Subsidy is the Def BD, earmarked for the army, not income (4.0b, 4.4) (d) Establish British paramountcy T "LOSS of D, C, FA"; on slide 15 "[SUPREMACY]" Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs lost to the EIC (4.0): paramountcy = supremacy The T-T-F-T drill. Three brothers, one mission. Richard Wellesley 98-05 becomes Governor General of Bengal in 1798, an empire builder who knows expansion raises his profile with a nationalistic British public. His brothers join him: Arthur, a Royal Army officer commanding the 33rd Regiment of Foot (not an EIC officer), and Henry, who handles the administration and diplomacy of the EIC. In 1800 Richard founds Fort William College, Calcutta, to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs. The money rule. GBF 1770 leads to the EIC's bankruptcy by 1772; the British State lends money but brings the EIC under supervision through the Regulating Act 1773, so it will not waste taxpayers' money on wars. Then the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84) mean high war expenditure, and Pitt's India Act 1784 bans conquest: the Governor General may fight only in defence, otherwise he needs the Court of Directors or the Board of Control. Napoleon knocks at Egypt. In 1798 Napoleon attacks Egypt to control the Middle East and hurt British trade, and he is in contact with Tipu 82-99 of Mysore. Wellesley 98-05 overhypes a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance. The threat was there but not real: Britain's navy was superior, and the British had already burnt French ships in the Mediterranean. The middle path. Protecting India from European rivals is the primary goal of British foreign policy, so the State does not take risks. Wellesley 98-05 offers the Subsidiary Alliance: political domination without the cost, administrative burden and symbolism of full annexation. The teacher's line: SA = control without annexation. The idea is older: Dupleix 42-54 at Hyderabad in 1751 and Clive 57-67 at Awadh in 1765 (a mini SA). The model treaty. Wellesley 98-05 formalises the relationship in a written treaty, takes over Foreign Policy and disbands the State's army, State by State. The EIC gets five things: a Resident, a military alliance, the State's army disbanded and replaced, an annual subsidy and Foreign Policy. The ruler gets two promises: protection, and non-interference in succession, Diwani and Nizamat (minus military). Taking Foreign Policy closes a loophole: the army was paid by the State's subsidy, so only war and peace in EIC hands gave the EIC the right to deploy it. Why rulers walked in. Five arguments: protection against internal revolts, protection against external threats (Chauth raids, Mysore, Rohillas), a subsidy cheaper than annexation, royal dignity preserved, and help in succession disputes and against neighbours. The EIC made military help conditional on signing. The teacher tags the fifth argument FACTIONALISM. The vicious chain. The State's army is disbanded and Mansabdars lose their military role; the EIC army grows free of cost; the subsidy is high and rising (Drain of Wealth); taxes rise and peasants revolt; the EIC charges maladministration though the ruler has no power; territory is taken in lieu of cash (half of Awadh 1801, Berar 1853); and no alliances against the EIC remain possible. The teacher compares it to Bali of Ramayana: a military power shift. The signing spree, 1798-1805. Hyderabad signs first in 1798, for protection against the Marathas and Mysore. Mysore signs in 1799 after Tipu 82-99 is killed at Seringapatam. Awadh in 1801: Sadat Ali Khan II had offered Rs 76 lakh in 1798 for John Shore 93-98 removing his nephew Wazir Ali (1797-98); he defaulted and Henry Wellesley imposed a full SA. The Gaikwad signs at Cambay in June 1802, the Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 at Bassein in December 1802 after Yashwantrao Holkar defeats him, Scindia in 1803, the Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas in 1803-05, and Travancore in 1805 after a Nair mutiny. Land taken outright. Wellesley 98-05 also annexes directly: Mysore territory in 1799 (to the Madras Presidency), half of Awadh in 1801 (the Doab, Gorakhpur, Rohilkhand: revenue twice the Rs 76 lakh subsidy, later the Ceded Districts, NWP 1836), and the Carnatic in 1801 (maladministration on record, the Nawab's many loans as context). In the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) Bhonsle loses Orissa and Scindia loses Gujarat and everything north of the Yamuna, including Delhi. The bill, and the recall. Wars are expensive for both winner and loser. The board repeats: loan and Regulating Act 1773, but still wars; Pitt's India Act 1784, but still wars. Under Wellesley 98-05 the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799 and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 again mean high war expenditure, and he is recalled to London. Travancore in 1805 is the last SA of his term. The last two of ten. Under Francis Hastings 13-23, the Bhonsle of Nagpur signs in 1816 (Appa Sahib wins the Nagpur regency fight with EIC backing) and Holkar of Indore signs at Mandsaur in 1818 after defeat in the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War. The teacher's count: ten SAs in 20 years, eight under Wellesley 98-05 and two under Francis Hastings 13-23. Factionalism brought the Peshwa, Bhonsle and Gaikwad; war brought Scindia and Holkar.
