Ask: what was the teacher's one-line summary of each? Chapter 15 title slide: British Imperial Ideology The master board, a 4-column table: "1765 ORIENTALISM" | "1813" | "1858" under the heading "White Man's Burden" The whole chapter in one board. Four columns on a time line: 1765 Orientalism, 1786-93 Cornwallis 86-93's Authoritarianism, from 1813 Liberalism + Utilitarianism + Evangelicalism, from 1858 Racism + Authoritarianism, all under the roof "White Man's Burden". His one-line summaries are the exam answers: Orientalism = "Rule India the India Way" (Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian languages, Indian syllabus). Authoritarianism = "My way or highway" (Indians removed from all senior positions). Liberalism = "give the best ideas of our time to India, but best = west." Utilitarianism = "civil servant mind" (effectiveness, maximum results, implementable, practical): good laws and a strong State. Evangelicalism = "Christianize India to modernize India." After the Revolt: "Indians are beyond reform... Dogs and Indians not allowed... more Authoritarianism plus more Racism." Slide 66 versus the handout on dates. The teacher's board dates Authoritarianism 1786-93 (the Cornwallis 86-93 years). The handout's summary table (Section 13) gives it 1786-1805 (Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05) and Conservatism 1801-27, which the board does not show as a separate column. Both are consistent: use the board for the sequence, the handout table for the champions. The board also puts the boundaries at 1813 and 1858 (a vertical line at 1858, the year of Queen Victoria's Proclamation in Section 7.1).

Because every ideology was both belief and cover story, policy followed ideas. Ask: what are the two layers, and why show both in Mains? British Imperial Ideologies are the ideas that shaped colonial policy. They were not one fixed set. They changed over time and sometimes competed. They shared one function: they gave the British a way to tell themselves and the world that what they were doing in India was not just profitable but morally right. Every ideology was both a genuine belief held by some Englishmen and a convenient narrative to make imperialism look ethical. Both layers operate at once. For Mains: always show both layers. Sincere belief and convenient cover story together. Many Englishmen were sincere (Section 5.5), and the ideas still served British power.

Because the British were sure of themselves, they felt a duty to civilise. Ask: which five roots of confidence, and which four counter-currents did WMB create? No class notes beyond the board. The typed slides 69-71 repeat the handout; the board on slide 65 is the only ink (below). Teacher's board: WMB (circled) All other ideologies rested on one belief:Western European civilisation was superior, so the British had a responsibility to civilise the rest of the world. This is the White Man's Burden (WMB). WMB = "Civilize the rest of the world" and "We are superior". His bracket gives the reasons for the confidence: the Industrial Revolution 1750-1850: first (Britain was first); the Seven Years' Global War 1756-63: won; the earliest of democracies; and empire. (After "1st" the line trails off, and slide 70 of the handout carries the rest.) 2.1 The roots of British civilisational confidence The British had genuine reasons to believe in their superiority: 1. World's first modern democracy: the English Civil War + Glorious Revolution (17th century). 2. Birthplace of the Industrial Revolution (c. 1750-1850). 3. Won the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63): the top global power. 4. Financially backed the coalition that defeated Napoleon at Leipzig (1813); led the allied armies to final victory with Prussia at Waterloo (1815). 5. Capitalism and science transforming British society at an unprecedented pace. A nation that achieves all this within 150 years can convince itself that it is destined to lead the world.Every major imperial power had its own version of WMB. 2.2 WMB as roof, and the counter-ideologies as reaction WMB was the roof over everything else. The specific ideologies below were different answers to the same question: how exactly should we civilise India? WMB also generated its opposite: powerful anti-colonial counter-ideologies worldwide: 1. American Revolution: a political movement from 1765, War of Independence 1776-83. 2. French Revolution (1789): liberty, equality, fraternity. 3. European revolutions of 1830 and 1848. 4. Irish Home Rule movement (1870-1914) and the Irish armed struggle for independence (1916-21). These challenged imperial-superiority assumptions and inspired colonised peoples, including Indian nationalists. (Section 12 develops this: Mains 2014.) Slide 71 shows only two of the four counter-ideologies (the American Revolution and the Irish struggle). The handout lists all four; Section 12 repeats the four. Use the handout's four.

items.t: 3 · Orientalism (1765-1813): Rule India, the India Way
items.x: Because the EIC was scared and some wanted to spare India, it chose to rule the India way. Ask: which four things, which four institutions, and which one is the Prelims 2020 answer? 3.1 Orientalism defined In the 18th century the British used language and literature as the measure of civilisation. Scholars like William Jones studied Sanskrit and found it older and grammatically more sophisticated than ancient Greek and Latin. The conclusion: India had been a great ancient civilisation, and European and Indian languages belonged to the same family (today's Indo-European family: genuine scholarship, not propaganda). So Orientalism said: India's ancient past was glorious even if its present was degenerate, so the British should study Indian tradition and rule India by its own customs and laws. In short: Rule India, the India Way. A date slip on slide 72. The typed slide writes William Jones as "(late 19th c)"; the handout places this scholarship in the 18th century, and the Asiatic Society that Jones founded is dated 1784. Use the handout: 18th century. On his board the teacher glosses "Oriental" as "related to east" and writes "Rule India the INDIA WAY" with four bullets: Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian languages, Indian syllabus in schools and colleges. These four bullets are the practical content of Orientalism. 3.2 Why the EIC adopted Orientalism Two practical reasons: 1. The EIC was militarily not yet confident before 1813. Victory in the Carnatic, Mysore and Maratha Wars was never guaranteed, and one badly handled cultural insult could trigger mass resistance. Ruling through Indian customs reduced that risk. 2. Some Englishmen believed India was not ready for British modernity. Imposing alien systems would do more damage than good. Warren Hastings 73-85 was Orientalism's most prominent champion. He argued that the more the British understood Indian traditions, the lighter the chains of colonialism would feel. 3.2.1 The four Orientalist institutions 1 1781 Calcutta Madrasa Warren Hastings 73-85, as Governor-General of Bengal; mainly for the study of Islamic law and customs 2 1784 Asiatic Society of Bengal Sir William Jones, as Puisne Judge of the Supreme Court at Calcutta; to study Asian history, antiquities and culture 3 1791 Sanskrit College, Banaras Jonathan Duncan, as British Resident at Benares; for the study of Hindu law and philosophy 4 1800 Fort William College, Calcutta Wellesley 98-05, as Governor-General of Bengal; to train newly recruited EIC civil servants in Indian languages and administration The figure holds names the handout text does not:Colebrooke, Wilson and Prinsep (Brahmi decipherment) and the ASI founded 1861 by Alexander Cunningham. The handout's summary table (Section 13) also lists Colebrooke and Wilson as Orientalism's champions. They are figure-only items; learn them lightly. Wellesley 98-05's second motive for Fort William College: to keep French republican ideas away from his officers. The French Revolution 1789 had overthrown the monarchy by 1792, and Wellesley 98-05 did not want anti-monarchy ideas infecting his men. 3.3 Orientalism's political angle The British supported the Aryan Invasion Theory: ancient India's cultural greatness was actually brought by Europeans who migrated to India in ancient times. Even while praising India, the British claimed credit. The argument of kinship: Europeans and Indians were separated kin connected through language. It was used to reduce Indian opposition: "we are not foreigners, we are cousins who have come home." This was a rhetoric of love to disguise the reality of exploitation. Prelims 2020 trap: answer (d) train British civilians. The three wrong options each sound plausible. (a) the Board of Directors asked: wrong, it was Wellesley 98-05's own initiative. (b) revive oriental learning: wrong, that was the Asiatic Society 1784 and Sanskrit College 1791.(c) employment for William Carey: wrong, Carey was an employee, not the founding purpose. The slide and the handout agree.

Because critics said the past was dead, Cornwallis 86-93 imposed the English way. Ask: which four steps, and what did Munro's formula add? 4.1 The Cornwallis 86-93 shift Orientalism had critics from the beginning. The study of ancient India had only confirmed that India's past was glorious and its present degenerate. That made restoring the past pointless and called for imposing the British system instead. Cornwallis 86-93 was the first Governor-General to implement this vision systematically. He ruled India, the English Way. Four specific measures: 1. All-British senior administration. He replaced all Indians in senior administrative positions with British officials. His argument: Indian administrators were corrupt and incompetent; only British authority could deliver rule of law. (Deeper argument: only by removing Indians from power can the British civilise India. This "corrupt-native-needs-the-honest-foreigner" story was used through 1947 to justify exclusion.) 2. Rule of Law through codification. The Charter Act 1793, influenced by Cornwallis 86-93, established civil law and protection of individual rights and private property. It reintroduced separation of powers at the district level: the District Collector would no longer also be the District Judge. 3. Permanent Settlement (1793) in Bengal, converting zamindars into large landlords on the English model. (Full treatment in the Land Revenue Systems chapter, Chapter 16.) 4. Aloof Elite. EIC officials were discouraged from mixing with Indians.Indian wives were discouraged.Eurasians were barred from EIC service. Officials having Indian wives were barred from purchasing land in India. Authoritarianism = "MY WAY OR HIGHWAY" and "Removed Indians from all senior positions." About the Permanent Settlement he wrote: "PS 1793 based on English way of agriculture = OUTLIER to Orientalism." That is the reasoning: Orientalism meant ruling the Indian way, but the Permanent Settlement copied the English landlord model, so it breaks the Orientalist pattern and belongs with Authoritarianism. 4.2 The Aloof-Elite doctrine Cornwallis 86-93 had personally commanded the British army's defeat in the American War of Independence (1776-83). He had watched British settlers in the 13 American colonies develop deep roots (family, property, identity) and then fight for independence as their homeland. He was determined not to let the same happen in India. The rule: keep the rulers separate from the ruled. Never let India become home. Wellesley 98-05 shared this authoritarian instinct. Both administrations were control-oriented, centralised and mistrustful of Indian agency. 4.3 Conservatism: Munro, Malcolm, Elphinstone, Metcalfe Thomas Munro (Governor of Madras 1820-27) was a hybrid of Orientalism and Authoritarianism. India should be governed through its own traditions, but the British would govern, with no leadership role for Indians.Total power centralised in EIC hands, but exercised through Indian forms (Indian laws and customs). His Ryotwari Settlement (1801-07, 1820+) in the Madras Presidency was inspired by the ancient Indian model of the State collecting revenue directly from the peasant, without intermediaries. But all collection was done by EIC officials, with no Indians in senior roles. The formula: Orientalist in form, Authoritarian in substance. Mountstuart Elphinstone, John Malcolm and Charles Metcalfe followed the same school. Elphinstone, a disciple of Munro, later implemented the Ryotwari Settlement in Bombay. No class notes beyond the typed slide for Conservatism. The master board (slide 66) has no column for it.

items.t: 5 · Three new ideologies (post 1813): Liberalism, Utilitarianism, Evangelicalism
items.x: Because the EIC was confident by 1813, three reform ideas took over. Ask: what did each want, and who was the champion of each? 5.1 The post-1813 sharp turn By 1813 the landscape had changed dramatically: 1. The EIC had defeated all major Indian powers; only Holkar, Bhonsle and the Sikh State remained as potential rivals. 2. The Company's army had grown huge. 3. Britain had defeated Napoleon. 4. The Industrial Revolution was in full swing. The EIC was now confident enough to rule India the British way: openly, aggressively, without apology. There was also a new economic motive: an India with western tastes and western education would become a market for British manufactured goods.Three ideologies filled the space Orientalism had occupied: Liberalism, Utilitarianism, Evangelicalism. 5.2 Liberalism Liberals argued that the EIC had governed India badly under Orientalism. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (one crore Indians perished while the EIC doubled land revenue) was cited as proof. India needed to be modernised through the best ideas of the age (best meaning western). Goal: liberate India from feudalism:feudal polity (no democracy), feudal economy (agrarian, closed, unequal), feudal society (birth-based discrimination, no women's rights), and replace it with modern British institutions. Thomas Macaulay, legal member of the GG's council under the Charter Act 1833, was the most prominent Liberal. His three signature interventions: 1. Law Commission (1834): codified western-style laws for British India by 1837. 2. Minute on Indian Education (1835): proposed western education in English to create Brown Sahibs (brown on the outside, British on the inside): a class of Indians as cultural intermediaries between British rulers and the Indian masses. 3. Charter Act 1813 (a Liberal-influenced reform): ended the EIC's monopoly over Indian trade and let non-EIC British businesses enter India freely. This was economic liberalism for British businesses, not for Indian ones. Social reform followed too: Bentinck 28-35 brought the Sati Abolition Act 1829 under Liberal influence (full treatment in Chapter 19). A date wrinkle. The slide and the handout list the Charter Act 1813 among Macaulay's "interventions", yet his seat on the GG's council came under the Charter Act 1833. The handout itself calls the 1813 Act a "Liberal-influenced reform", so read it as a Liberal-era measure that opened trade, not as Macaulay's own act. Learn the pair: Law Commission 1834, Minute 1835 are his. 5.3 Utilitarianism Associated with Jeremy Bentham and James Mill. India needed not culture change but good policy and a strong rule of law. The State's job: design laws that maximise benefit for the largest number of people. James Mill's History of British India (1818) declared India's great past a myth and argued India needed an effective schoolmaster: someone to impose good governance from above. Mill joined the Court of Directors of the EIC in London and pushed for the Law Commission in 1834 under Macaulay. Utilitarianism contains an inherent authoritarian streak. Utilitarianism = "civil servant mind" with four words: effectiveness, max results, implementable, practical. Then: "Bring good laws and a strong State for rule of law." The reasoning: a utilitarian cares about what works, not what is traditional or Christian, so the answer is laws and a strong State. 5.4 Evangelicalism Evangelists argued India's fundamental problem was its religion, which promoted superstition, ignorance, idolatry and tyranny of priests and blocked scientific thinking.Religion shapes values; values shape society. Change the religion, change everything. Their model was Protestant Christianity in western Europe, where Protestant ethics supported the rise of capitalism and modernity. Charles Grant, a member of the Court of Directors and later an MP, influenced the Charter Act 1813 to legalise the entry of Christian missionaries into India. The Lex Loci Act / Removal of Religious-Caste Disabilities Act (1850) allowed a convert to retain inheritance rights in family property, removing one practical obstacle to conversion (full treatment in Chapter 19). "Evangelicalism: CHRISTIANIZE India to MODERNIZE India." Charter Act 1813 appears under two ideologies. Liberal side: ended the EIC's trade monopoly (section 5.2). Evangelical side: allowed missionaries (this section). Both are in the handout. Keep the two effects apart. 5.5 Common ground across the three All three pushed for reform of the colonial State and together built the narrative of Benevolent Colonialism: "we are here to help you." Many Englishmen who believed in these ideologies were sincere. And yet all three together contributed to the conditions that produced the Revolt of 1857:cultural, economic and political resistance to a colonial project that had touched almost every aspect of Indian life.

Because Liberal confidence peaked in 1828-35, four interventions followed. Ask: which four, and what is the Charter Act 1833 trap? The short window from Bentinck 28-35 through the Charter Act 1833 to Macaulay's 1835 Minute is the high-water mark of Liberal confidence in India. Four headline interventions: 1. Sati Abolition Act 1829: criminalised widow-burning (full treatment in Chapter 19). 2. Thuggee Suppression (1830s-40s): under Captain William Sleeman; restored police order on the Grand Trunk roads (Section 8; Prelims 1997). 3. Macaulay's Education Minute 1835: made English the medium of higher instruction, displacing Persian. 4. Cornwallis 86-93 Code progressively revised into a uniform criminal procedure: the foundation Macaulay's 1834 Law Commission would build on. Charter Act 1833: the trap (slide 104). The slide warns: the Charter Act 1833 did NOT make the provision that an Indian be appointed as a law member in the GG's council (Prelims 2003, answer (d) in the bank). Macaulay, the law member, was a Briton.

Because 1857 shocked the British, reform retreated and race hardened. Ask: which six fronts, and which two architects? The Revolt of 1857 shook the British not just militarily but psychologically. The scale of Indian violence against British rule (soldiers, civilians, women, children) broke the paternalistic narrative. The British had told themselves they were trustees and reformers. 1857 told them that a very large number of Indians did not see it that way. Column 4 of the board: "1857 Revolt = SHOCK for British.""Indians are beyond Reform.""Ideology = DOGS & Indians not allowed.""Up-up Authoritarianism (+) up-up RACISM." (The teacher underlined "Dogs", "Indians" and "not allowed" in green.) 7.1 The six-front sharp shift after 1857 1. Reformist impulse retreated sharply. Liberalism, Utilitarianism and Evangelicalism (Section 5) collapsed. Many concluded that Indians were beyond redemption through reform. 2. Racial sciences shift. European racial classification in the second half of the 19th century shifted from language (the Orientalist criterion) to physical features. Indians were now classed as an inferior and fundamentally different race: not separated kin (Section 3) but a lower order of humanity. 3. Aryan Invasion Theory kept but twisted. Europeans had founded the Vedic civilisation, but by intermarrying with indigenous Indians over millennia they lost their racial superiority and degraded. Even India's ancient greatness was now used as evidence of Indian inferiority. 4. "Dogs and Indians not allowed": seen on signs at clubs and parks in colonial India; it captures the spirit of post-1857 attitudes. 5. Authoritarianism increased. The British became distrustful of sharing power with Indians in any meaningful way. 6. Social reforms slowed sharply.Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 explicitly promised religious tolerance and non-interference in Indian customs: a direct acknowledgement that missionary and reformer interference had been a major grievance of 1857. From here, social and political reforms came mainly in response to pressure from Indian leaders, not British initiative. The table below contrasts the two uses of the Aryan idea and of race. Criterion of race Language Physical features Indians seen as Separated kin, cousins Inferior, different race, a lower order Aryan Invasion Theory Europeans brought India's greatness: "cousins come home" Europeans founded Vedic civilisation but intermarried and degraded Policy mood Rule India the India Way Reform retreated; more Authoritarianism 7.2 Post-1857 architects: Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05 The architects of this harder imperialism were Lytton 76-80 and Curzon 99-05: men for whom empire was a project of prestige, paramountcy and racial hierarchy. 1. Lytton 76-80: the Vernacular Press Act 1878 and Arms Act 1878 reinstated racial privilege (VPA in Chapter 19). 2. Curzon 99-05: the Partition of Bengal (1905) was the same mindset applied administratively (in Chapter 29).

items.t: 8 · Law and order paternalism: Sleeman and the Thugs
items.x: Because the roads were unsafe, a parallel track of law-and-order paternalism ran. Ask: whose department, which three tools, and which distractors in Prelims 1997? Between Orientalism and Liberalism the EIC also ran a parallel track of law-and-order paternalism:reclaiming the roads, the courts and rural policing in the name of the peasant's physical safety. The flagship was the Thuggee and Dacoity Suppression campaign of the 1830s-40s, built around Captain (later Major-General Sir) William Sleeman, under Bentinck 28-35. His Thuggee and Dacoity Department (set up 1835) used three tools: 1. Informant networks infiltrating Thug bands. 2. Approver testimony: captured Thugs gave evidence against their associates in exchange for lighter sentences. 3. Swift judicial commissions: dedicated tribunals delivering rapid trials. Together these dismantled organised highway murder cults that had made long-distance trade on the Grand Trunk Road a life-and-death gamble. Over 3,000 Thugs were convicted between 1831 and 1841. Prelims 1997 trap: answer (b) Captain Sleeman.Prendergast = Upper Burma 1885-86 (Section 10). Burnes = Afghan frontier, killed in the 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1841 (Section 9). Pemberton = Assam/Burma frontier officer. The slide and the handout agree.

items.t: 9 · The Forward Policy in Afghanistan: from Auckland 36-42 to Lytton 76-80
items.x: Because Russia was feared, the frontier was pushed into Afghanistan. Ask: which four Governors-General, and what did Gandamak 1879 give? The Forward Policy was the militarised face of post-1840s British imperialism on the north-west frontier: Britain should actively push its effective frontier into Afghanistan to pre-empt Tsarist Russian influence, rather than defend a fixed line at the Indus. Its arc ran through multiple Governors-General and is a classic PYQ trap: 1. Auckland 36-42 launched the disastrous 1st Anglo-Afghan War (1839-42) to reinstall Shah Shuja against Dost Mohammad. The retreat from Kabul (January 1842) wiped out almost an entire British-Indian army. 2. Ellenborough 42-44 initiated what later came to be called the Forward Policy: a punitive return to Kabul in 1842 to restore British prestige, followed by a doctrine of pushing the frontier outward. 3. Lytton 76-80 carried forward the Forward Policy and launched the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War (1878-80), forcing the Treaty of Gandamak 1879. The war continued into its 2nd phase after the massacre of British Resident Louis Cavagnari at Kabul. 4. Ripon 80-84reversed the Forward Policy and withdrew British forces from Afghanistan: the pendulum swing that Liberal governments in London demanded. Slide versus handout on Ellenborough 42-44. The handout says he initiated the Forward Policy (a punitive return to Kabul 1842 to restore prestige; the handout's flow chart says the same). Slide 91 says he "Ended Forward Policy (*Correct this in notes)", and the slide itself carries the typed reminder to correct it, so the slide is flagged by its own author as unsettled. This notebook follows the handout: Ellenborough 42-44 = punitive return to Kabul 1842, then the frontier-outward doctrine. For the exam the safe core is the same either way: Auckland 36-42 = 1st war 1839-42; Lytton 76-80 = carried forward the Forward Policy (2nd war 1878-80); Ripon 80-84 = reversed it. The slide also spells the name "Aukland"; the handout spells "Auckland 36-42". 9.1 The Treaty of Gandamak 1879 The handout calls Gandamak 1879 a mini subsidiary alliance, with five terms: British Resident stationed At the Amir's court Army stationed British forces Foreign policy taken By the British Territory Khyber Pass and some other lands to the British In return The British pay 6 lakh annually to the Amir Prelims 1999 trap: answer (d) Lytton 76-80. (a) Minto (Minto II 1905-10) belongs to a different era, after Curzon 99-05. (b) Dufferin 84-88 is famous for Upper Burma 1886, not Afghanistan. (c) Elgin (I 1862-63 or II 1894-99) is a different era. This slide's answer text says Lytton 76-80 carried forward the policy "initiated by Ellenborough 42-44", which supports the handout over slide 91. 9.2 Revision: Russophobia and the Great Game Russophobia: the British fear that Czarist Russia, expanding through Central Asia, would one day reach the north-west land approach to India. The Great Game: this Anglo-Russian rivalry over Central Asia. It shaped British frontier and foreign policy far more than trade. Offensive answer: the Forward Policy, pushing the effective frontier outward through the two Anglo-Afghan Wars (1839-42 and 1878-80). Defensive twin: the Policy of Ring Fence: keeping strong, friendly border States as a buffer around British India, with Afghanistan and Punjab as the buffer in the north-west. The 1838 Tripartite Treaty (Sikh State, EIC and Shah Shuja) was built on this buffer logic (see Chapter 6, Chapter 14). The Persian flank: the same logic produced the Anglo-Persian War 1856-57 and finally the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907, which split Iran into three: a Russian sphere in the north, a neutral buffer in the middle and a British sphere in the south (see Chapter 14). This is a "Revision" box with no ink. It belongs with the policies chapter: the Ring Fence idea began with Clive 57-67 in 1765 (Chapter 10) and the Five-Policy Arc is in Chapter 14.

Because the land-grab ended in Burma, one year matters. Ask: which Viceroy, which year, and what is the slide's nuance? The last major territorial extension of British India was Upper Burma, annexed in January 1886 after the 3rd Anglo-Burmese War 1885-86. The Viceroy was Dufferin 84-88.King Thibaw was deposed and exiled to Ratnagiri. The field commander was General Henry Prendergast, the same man who appeared as a distractor in the Prelims 1997 Thuggee question. Upper Burma was merged with Lower Burma (British from 1852) and governed as a province of British India until the 1937 separation. "Lower Burma, British from 1852" is the 2nd Anglo-Burmese War (1852-53) of Dalhousie 48-56 (Chapter 14). The handout's Ch 14 section on it is the home for that war. Prelims 2000: Dufferin 84-88 (a), with a slide nuance.Handout: Dufferin 84-88 added Upper Burma in January 1886: (a). Traps: Dalhousie 48-56 (Punjab 1849, Awadh 1856, Doctrine of Lapse) was the big annexation GG, but his last major extension was Awadh 1856;Lytton 76-80 made no territorial extension (he tightened Paramountcy-era instruments, such as the Treaty of Jacobabad 1876, without annexing); Curzon 99-05's Partition of Bengal 1905 was administrative, not territorial. Slide 108 adds a real-exam wrinkle: because Burma was not traditionally part of India, the "famous" answer is Dalhousie 48-56 and the official key might say that, but the question says "British Indian territory", so (a) Dufferin 84-88 is the legally correct answer. Use (a), as the handout and bank do, and keep the Dalhousie 48-56 possibility in mind as the slide's warning.

Because trade was bent to the empire, tariffs favoured Britain. Ask: what is the key word, and where was it formalised? "Imperial Preference" was a commercial tariff arrangement: the constituent units of the British Empire (Britain, the Dominions and India) granted one another preferential (lower) tariff rates denied to non-Empire competitors. Formalised at the Ottawa Conference of 1932, locking India's trade into an Empire-first structure that subordinated Indian industrial interests to British manufacturing needs. (Full treatment in the Drain Theory chapter, Chapter 27.) Effect on India:British goods entered Indian ports at a lower tariff than German, Japanese or American competitors. India's tariff regime systematically advantaged the very British manufacturing economy that Indian industries were trying to compete with. Prelims 1999 trap: answer (a) special privileges on British imports in India. (b) racial discrimination is a different phenomenon (Section 7). (c) subordination of Indian interest is too vague, a general description of colonialism and not the specific definition. (d) preference to British political agents over Princes is Political Department protocol.The key word is tariff. 11.1 The stray table of five antiquarians (Prelims 2023) 1 Alexander Rea Excavated at Amaravati and Bhattiprolu 2 A.H. Longhurst Excavated at Nagarjunakonda and Hampi 3 Robert Sewell Wrote "A Forgotten Empire" (Vijayanagara) 4 James Burgess First Director of the Archaeological Survey of Western and Southern India 5 Walter Elliot Of the Madras Civil Service; catalogued Andhra Buddhist sites and coins This table is out of place in the handout and slide. It sits between Imperial Preference (Section 11) and the foreign ideologies (Section 12) with no heading or link to the ideology story; it answers Prelims 2023: all five were associated with archaeological excavations (a). The handout's flow chart ties it to Orientalist scholarship through the ASI (founded 1861, Alexander Cunningham) (see section 3.2.1). The rest of the 2023 bank item mentions the ASI reorganisation in its explanation; the full story is not in this chapter. Names only in the figure:Wilkins (Orientalism) and Trevelyan (Liberal-era) are not in the handout text. Use the figure as a picture of the sequence, and the text for facts.

items.t: 12 · Foreign ideologies motivating India's anti-colonial struggle
items.x: Because the burden produced its opposite, world events fed Indian nationalism. Ask: which three buckets and which two carriers answer Mains 2014? Handout numbering glitch. Section 12's sub-points are numbered 13.1 to 13.3 in the handout (and the heading before the summary is "Sec. 13"). Here they are called 12.1 to 12.3. WMB (Section 2) produced its opposite: powerful anti-colonial counter-ideologies across the globe that travelled back into India through newspapers, returning students and political exiles. 12.1 Pre-1900 political and ideological currents 1. American Revolution (1765-83): political movement from 1765, War of Independence 1776-83. 2. French Revolution of 1789: liberty, equality, fraternity. 3. European revolutions of 1830 and 1848: democratic uprisings across the continent. 4. Irish Home Rule (1870-1914) and Irish armed struggle (1916-21) against Britain: direct anti-British inspiration. All challenged imperial superiority and inspired colonised peoples worldwide. 12.2 Three 20th-century shocks that radicalised Indian nationalism 1. Industrial Revolution's destructive impact on Indian handloom:deindustrialisation fed the Drain Theory of Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt. 2. Russian Revolution of 1917: gave the Indian left a peasant-worker mobilisation model and an anti-imperial vocabulary. 3. Post-WWI principle of self-determination (Wilson's Fourteen Points, 1918) and rising anti-racism: made continued British rule increasingly indefensible in international forums. 12.3 Returning Indian leaders brought these currents home The world-developments travelled through people, not ideas alone: 1. Gandhi from South Africa: anti-colonial training from Indian-diaspora struggles in South Africa (1893-1915). 2. Nehru from Cambridge:Western liberal-democratic political theory absorbed during his Cambridge studies, applied in Indian Congress politics. Mains 2014 (10M, 150 words): "What were the major political, economic and social developments in the world which motivated the anti-colonial struggle in India?" The handout's three-bucket answer:Enlightenment + American + French + Irish revolutions (political and ideological) then Industrial Revolution deindustrialisation (economic) then Russian Revolution 1917 + Wilson's self-determination + anti-racism (social and ideological) then returning leaders (Gandhi from South Africa, Nehru from Cambridge). The handout points to a companion Appendix FYQ_Mains with the full five-part treatment; that appendix is not in this notebook. The skeleton is in the Exam lens.

Last scene: the eight ideologies with champions and measures. Ask: which champion goes with which ideology, and which three share 1813? A nation sure of itself. Britain had reasons for pride: the first modern democracy, the Industrial Revolution (c. 1750-1850), victory in the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63), Napoleon beaten (Leipzig 1813, Waterloo 1815) and the rise of capitalism and science. Within 150 years it could convince itself it was destined to lead, and that it owed the world its civilisation. This is the White Man's Burden. Scared, so Orientalist. Before 1813 the EIC was not militarily confident, and one badly handled insult could trigger mass resistance. Scholars like William Jones found Sanskrit older and more sophisticated than Greek and Latin. So Orientalism said: rule India the India way, with Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian languages and an Indian syllabus. Warren Hastings 73-85 was its champion. Four Orientalist institutions. The Calcutta Madrasa came in 1781 (Warren Hastings 73-85), the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784 (Sir William Jones), the Sanskrit College at Banaras in 1791 (Jonathan Duncan) and Fort William College in 1800 (Wellesley 98-05) to train British civilians. The Aryan Invasion Theory and kinship through language added a rhetoric of love: we are cousins who have come home. My way or highway. The critics said the study of India showed a glorious past and a degenerate present, so restoring the past was pointless. Cornwallis 86-93 ruled India the English way: all-British senior posts, rule of law with the Collector no longer also Judge (Charter Act 1793), the Permanent Settlement 1793 and an Aloof Elite. He had lost America and did not want settlers putting down roots. Indian coat, British hand. Thomas Munro, Governor of Madras 1820-27, governed through Indian forms but kept all power with the EIC: Orientalist in form, Authoritarian in substance. His Ryotwari Settlement copied the ancient State-peasant model but all collection was by EIC officials. Elphinstone, Malcolm and Metcalfe followed him. 1813: confidence, then three ideas. Indian powers had been beaten except Holkar, Bhonsle and the Sikh State, the army was huge, Napoleon was beaten and the Industrial Revolution was in full swing, with a market for British goods to win. Liberalism (Macaulay: Law Commission 1834, Minute on Education 1835, Brown Sahibs), Utilitarianism (Bentham and James Mill: good laws, a strong State, the schoolmaster) and Evangelicalism (Charles Grant, Charter Act 1813, Lex Loci Act 1850) filled the space. The Liberal window, 1828-35. From Bentinck 28-35 through the Charter Act 1833 to Macaulay's Minute 1835, Liberal confidence peaked: the Sati Abolition Act 1829, Thuggee suppression under Captain Sleeman (three tools: informants, approvers, swift commissions; over 3,000 Thugs convicted 1831-41), English replacing Persian in higher instruction, and Cornwallis 86-93's Code revised into uniform criminal procedure. The shock of 1857. The Revolt shook the British psychologically and broke the paternalistic narrative. Six fronts shifted: reform retreated, race was read by physical features, the Aryan theory was twisted, Dogs and Indians not allowed, Authoritarianism rose and social reforms slowed after Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858. Lytton 76-80 (Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act 1878) and Curzon 99-05 (Partition of Bengal 1905) were its architects. The Forward Policy and the Great Game. Fearing Tsarist Russia, the British pushed the frontier into Afghanistan: Auckland 36-42's 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1839-42, Ellenborough 42-44's punitive return to Kabul, Lytton 76-80's 2nd war 1878-80 and the Treaty of Gandamak 1879, then Ripon 80-84's reversal. The defensive twin was the Ring Fence, and the Persian flank ended with the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907. Upper Burma and Imperial Preference. Dufferin 84-88 annexed Upper Burma in January 1886, the last major extension, deposing King Thibaw. Trade was also bent to the empire: Imperial Preference, formalised at Ottawa in 1932, let British goods enter Indian ports at lower tariffs than German, Japanese or American goods. The ideas come home. The White Man's Burden produced its opposite: the American Revolution, the French Revolution 1789, the European revolutions of 1830 and 1848 and the Irish struggle. Later shocks added deindustrialisation and the Drain Theory, the Russian Revolution 1917, Wilson's self-determination and anti-racism. They travelled through people: Gandhi from South Africa (1893-1915) and Nehru from Cambridge.

Because the State's duty to its people is economic security in an agrarian economy, every land system is judged on five questions. Ask: who owns, how is it assessed, who settles, who collects, and what do tenants get? Chapter 16 title slide Why this chapter matters for UPSC: the State's duty to its people is economic security, and in a pre-industrial country that means the agrarian economy: agriculture is the big share of GDP, and ryots are the big share of the work profile. Then he gives the five-question frame he repeats for the Mughal system, Ijaradari, PS 1793, Ryotwari and Mahalwari: who is the landowner, how is the revenue assessed, with whom is the settlement made, who collects, and what rights do tenants have. Learn every system as a row of those five answers.

items.t: 1 · The Mughal blueprint for land revenue
items.x: Because the British inherited the Mughal chain, you must know it first: it is the yardstick the later systems fall short of. Ask: where did the Khudkasht's protection come from, and who really owned the land? Teacher's board: State, intermediaries and ryots The Khudkasht was the actual cultivator. He held customary occupancy rights over his land (he could not simply be thrown off). He paid land revenue by the Patta system: a document (patta) recorded the amount he owed, a legal safeguard against arbitrary over-extraction. He also paid abwabs (informal tributes) to his Primary Zamindar. The Mughal revenue chain: who collected, who paid up Khudkasht (cultivator): customary occupancy rights; pays LR per his patta; pays abwabs to the Primary Zamindar Primary Zamindar: keeps his commission, passes the rest up Intermediary Zamindar: collects, keeps his cut, passes the rest up Jagirdar if the land was a jagir; the State if it was khalisa land The figure's bottom box says "Amlas" (state-appointed, audit chain). The handout's text names the supervising State officers as Amils and Amalguzars. The teacher and the Mahalwari section stress that Amlas are different: private employees of Zamindars, not State officers (Section 4.1). Treat "Amlas" in the figure as a label slip and use Amils and Amalguzars for the State's supervisors. Amils and Amalguzars (government officers) supervised the chain so that Zamindars did not under-report collections. Critical point: the Zamindar was not the owner of land. He was a revenue collector on commission (the teacher's board: Vatan right to collect LR and keep a 10% commission). He also had police duties alongside revenue work. Legal private ownership of property was not a Mughal idea; it was British, imported from English law. Ijaradari: when the State needed money in a hurry it auctioned the right to collect land revenue to the highest bidder. The British would replicate this (Section 2.2). Teacher's board, pre-British era Legal against customary. In the Mughal era only the King was the legal owner and no individual legal property rights existed. The Khudkasht's right was customary (from custom, not from a law made by the State), recorded in his patta. Land was not a commodity: it changed hands only by conquest or gift, so there was no land market. The market in land develops with the British, from 1793. (The ink "Ded" beside "This" reads like "dev(elops)"; check your notebook.) Mughal LR system on the five-question frame Landowner Khudkasht (practically his milkiyat; legally only the King owned) Ryot or Khudkasht (practical) Assessment Detailed survey; % of gross produce (e.g. one-third); revisable Summary, by auction; an amount Settlement with The ryot (he gives a Qubuliyat to the State; the State gives him a patta) The Ijaradar, via auction Collection by A non-State actor: the Zamindar The Ijaradar Tenants Rightless, landless Pahikashts (not written)

Because the EIC held the Diwani from 1765, it had to collect land revenue, and Bengal became the laboratory. Ask: what did each of the three experiments do to the ryot, and why did the next one follow? 2.1 Experiment 1: Dual Government (1765-72) In 1765 the EIC received the Diwani (right to collect land revenue) of Bengal, Orissa and Bihar through the Treaty of Allahabad (ToA 1765) (the treaty itself is in Chapter 10). It did not administer directly. It appointed Deputy Subadar Muhammad Reza Khan as its Diwan. The Mughal collection system continued: the EIC followed Orientalism (Indian traditions are best administered on their own terms). Ideology did not stop greed. In five years: frantic experiments to squeeze more revenue; the Patta system was ignored; rents were extracted far beyond what pattas recorded. Then back-to-back droughts. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed between 50 lakh and 1 crore. The EIC doubled the revenue demand in 1770 and used brutality to collect. For the first time some British men acted as whistleblowers, writing to London newspapers. Reza Khan was made a scapegoat: imprisoned without trial on corruption charges, 1772-74. In the Pre-British era the words "rent" and "revenue" were used interchangeably (his note beside the slide). Underlines: Deputy Subadar, Orientalism, Patta ignored, back-to-back droughts, doubled in 1770, brutality, imprisoned without trial, 1772-74. The famine fits his nature factor and human factor idea from Chapter 10: droughts were nature; the doubled demand, ignored pattas and brutality were human. The handout here gives the famine toll as 50 lakh to 1 crore. Chapter 10's handout says about 1 crore, one-third of Bengal. Quote the range in this chapter's answers; "about one crore" is the upper end. Since 1757 the EIC had bought Indian goods with India's own land revenue rather than gold from England, so a famine hit its income directly (the Drain logic of Chapter 10). Famine destroyed the agrarian economy and land revenue collapsed. By 1772 the EIC was on the verge of bankruptcy: rampant corruption by its officials (the "Nabobs"), the 1770 famine, and heavy expenses of the army and the Dual System. The EIC asked the British Government for an emergency bailout. Parliament granted 1.4 million pounds at 4% interest, on the strict condition of parliamentary oversight, which led directly to the Regulating Act of 1773 (Chapter 17). 2.2 Experiment 2: the Farming System of Warren Hastings 73-85 (1772) Farming System = the English name for Ijaradari; Revenue Farmer = Ijaradar. Warren Hastings 73-85 was Governor of the Bengal Presidency. The ryot's sad face carries three blows in a row: 1757+ high LR, 1770 Great Bengal Famine, 1772 Ijaradari. On the right he lists events of Hastings's years (as written: "To Purandhar 1776 @ Ma", "To Salbai 1782", "HA 61-82: military alliance 1769", "2nd A-My 1780-84"); "To" reads as his shorthand for Treaty, "Ma" for Marathas, "HA" for Haidar Ali 61-82 (). They belong to Chapter 12 and Chapter 13. Till 1813 the ideology was Orientalism: "Rule India the India way." That is why the EIC kept Mughal collection after 1765 and revived Ijaradari in 1772 (and why Hastings 73-85 is called an Orientalist). The turn away from it follows the Charter Act of 1813 (Chapter 17). Warren Hastings 73-85, himself an Orientalist, revived the Mughal Ijaradari system. The right to collect LR in each district was auctioned to the highest bidder: the Revenue Farmer (so named because, like a farmer, he aimed to extract profit through a contract; not a farmer who tills soil). Bengal Experiment 2: Hastings's Farming System (1772) The Revenue Farmer worked under a European District Collector (DC) (European = English, Scottish or Irish, not English alone). Outcome: farmers squeezed the maximum from ryots to recover their bids and make profit. The demand was often so high that peasants paid nothing: self-defeating. Revenue did not improve; the rural population was ruined. 2.3 Primer: tax, property, settlement (taught first in the lecture) The lecture teaches these concepts before the Mughal system (Lecture 17, slides 5 to 12, 21, 22); the handout puts them here as Section 2.3. Read them before the pillars of PS 1793. Teacher's board: rights Rights in land have five layers: a) The ryot's right to cultivate and occupy his plot b) The right to fair rents (tenant ryot) or fair land revenue (owner) c) The landowner's right to sell, lease, rent and mortgage land and receive those proceeds d) The right to collect taxes (State, or Vatan right holders such as Zamindars) e) The right to receive tax proceeds and revise tax rates (State; Jagirdars receive but by the State's grant) Two kinds of rights on his board (Lecture 17, slide 3): rights given by law (made by the State, an organisation, through rules) and customary or traditional rights (from the conventions of a society), e.g. the Vatan rights of Zamindars. (The star note "MIH" and the small "7 ... PPT" beside the law branch are.) Teacher's board: taxes and rents Teacher's board: the word "Zamindar" changes meaning Meaning of words changes, the word stays the same. Zamindar before 1793 = collector of LR, not owner; after 1793 = legal landowner (he stars "conditional ownership": the Sunset Clause can take the land); after 1947 "Zamindari abolition" meant abolishing big landownership. Assessment = deciding how much tax is owed, by detailed field survey (soil quality, irrigation, crop type, plot size, rainfall; the board adds frequency of drought or flood and past LR trends) or summarily (a rough estimate). The demand is a fixed absolute amount or a percentage of produce; it is permanent or revisable. Settlement = with whom the State negotiates the tax demand, and who is responsible for depositing it. Teacher's board: settlement with Mr XYZ Settlement = agreement on LR plus the duty to deposit it. His analogy: in GST the shopkeeper deposits a tax that the buyer bears, so the depositor need not be the one who bears the tax. In the land systems the owner always bears the tax, but the settlement may or may not be with the owner:PS 1793: with the landowner (Zamindar); Ryotwari: with the landowner (ryot); Mahalwari 1822: not the landowner (the Mahal, via its Lambardar). Rent is always paid by a tenant to a property owner. Taxes are always borne by the property owner. The State is always the ultimate recipient but may collect through its own officers or non-State intermediaries. In the Farming System of 1772, assessment was by auction and settlement was with the Revenue Farmer. 2.4 Experiment 3: the Permanent Settlement Act, 1793 Applied in:Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras, Benaras. Cornwallis 86-93 (GG of Bengal 1786-93) was sent with one primary assignment: fix the land revenue problem. After several experiments he passed the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793 through the GG(Bengal)'s Council and extended it to Madras on his instructions. By 1801 Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in London to replace it with Ryotwari in Madras, though it survived in North Madras. Permanent Settlement Act, 1793 AUTHORITARIANISM under Cornwallis 86-93: "my way or highway." He came from a landlord family and was inspired by how agriculture was done in England (agrarian capitalism); his own words: CW 86-93 = Believer (a believer in English landlordism). The belief explains the model: see Pillar 1 below. Teacher's board: PS 1793 on the five questions Landowner The Zamindar Assessment No field survey; summary; an absolute amount (not %); not revisable Settlement with The Zamindar Collection by The District Collector (DC) Tenants No rights: the Zamindar can charge whatever rent and remove them from the plot Pillar 1: landownership went to the Zamindar. Zamindars got full proprietary rights for the first time, making them legal owners. Land became a commodity: sold, purchased, leased, rented, mortgaged. Hereditary, transferable within the family. Why? (a) Ideology: belief in English-style landlordism; convert Zamindars into agrarian capitalists like England's landed gentry; security of property would induce investment. (b) Agrarian capitalism would improve food security, boost agricultural trade and grow the EIC's LR income. (c) Loyalty of Zamindars, the traditional leaders of rural society, would buy political stability. Revenue Farmers, though wealthy, were not made landowners: they were not part of the traditional agrarian economy and lacked agricultural expertise. Teacher's board: landowner criteria = a big landowner Teacher's board: why Zamindar chosen Why a big landowner? A rich man invests (irrigation, better equipment and machines as in England's Industrial Revolution of 1750-1850, hired labour), produces for profit, so production rises: food security and government LR income rise. Whom to make big landowner? An already rich person: the Zamindar (ticked; by 1727, 15 Intermediary Zamindars collected 50% of Bengal Suba's LR, the group Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) had built), a moneylender, or a merchant of urban areas. Why the Zamindar over the rest? He is part of the rural economy and the traditional leader of rural society, and thinks about agriculture 24x7 because his commission depends on production; merchants and moneylenders (Ijaradars) think about margin and interest and are outsiders to the rural economy. "PS 1793 = DnR" (Divide and Rule). His general picture: in any setting (company, country, society, politics, family, geopolitics) there are leaders and followers; DnR can pit leader against leader, follower against follower, or favour one tier over the other (L happy, F sad or L sad, F happy, the last with "Bangladesh, Nepal" as examples). The slide does not write which pattern PS 1793 is. Read from Section 2.5, it is leaders (Zamindars) rewarded, masses (ryots) stripped of rights; that is a reading, not his ink. Pillar 2: settlement with the Zamindar.Fewer, bigger counterparties (the teacher writes "LR payers" above "counterparties") made collection simpler. The State negotiated with Zamindars; the Zamindar was responsible for depositing LR. Pillar 3: assessment was permanent. LR was fixed at 10/11 of the Zamindar's pre-existing revenue (what he had collected from ryots before deducting his commission), with 1789-90 as the base year.Fixed forever, as an absolute annual amount, not a percentage. The arithmetic (Lecture 17, slide 30). Before 1793: ryot's produce Rs 100; LR = two-thirds = 66% = Rs 66, which the Zamindar collects (Z's revenue); ryot keeps Rs 34; Zamindar keeps 10% of 66 = Rs 6.6; the State gets Rs 59.4. After 1793: 10/11 x 66 = Rs 60, and Rs 60 is fixed forever (boxed FOREVER = Permanent-ly, "FIG not %"). Anything above Rs 60 the Zamindar can keep: in his example the Zamindar takes Rs 13 and the ryot keeps 40 - 13 = Rs 27 (the ink does not explain where the 40 comes from;). Teacher's board: why LR fixed so high Teacher's worked example Why so high and why in rupees:inflation shrinks what the State receives each year (practically nothing in 100 years), so the initial demand was fixed very high to compensate the State for the long-term loss. And because it is a fixed amount, not a percentage: if the ryots produce Rs 120 in 1794 the State still gets Rs 60, so the Zamindar keeps the gain and is incentivised to invest; if they produce Rs 0 in 1795 the State still gets Rs 60 (the Zamindar carries the risk). Why permanent and absolute? (a) To incentivise the Zamindar: revenue would not rise however profits grew, so he had every reason to invest and produce more. (b) Certainty for the State: even in a drought year the State knew what it would receive. (c) Less administration: no repeat assessment surveys (the teacher adds: corruption would fall, since no officer could reduce the demand). (d) Trade-off: since the State gave up future increases, it set the initial demand very high. Estimates vary: some historians say double the 1765 level; others, 20% above 1757 levels. Pillar 4: the Sunset Clause. If a Zamindar did not pay LR by the evening of a pre-set deadline, his land was auctioned to anyone who agreed to pay the required land revenue. The buyer only had to agree to pay (not pay in full at once), given the large amounts. Collection was by State officers: the District Collector. The buyer bids for the LR, not the land's value. In his example the buyer agrees to pay Rs 60 a year; the board asks "who can pay the value of the land of 300 villages?" and answers "No one." That is why the Sunset Clause is workable. Prelims 2024: answer (b) 2 only.Statement 1 (F): Ryotwari is not Cornwallis 86-93's, and a bad harvest earned remission (a reduction of LR), not exemption (zero LR): the teacher ticks "Remit" and crosses "Exempt = zero LR." Statement 2 (T): a Zamindar who failed to pay lost his land at auction: the Sunset Clause. 2.5 Impact of PS 1793 The results diverged sharply from Cornwallis 86-93's intentions. 1. Short term:frequent land auctions; the demand was so high that many Zamindars defaulted. Buyers: Jotedars (rich farmers, less wealthy than Zamindars) and the Zamindar's own family members, who bid to keep land in the family. Over time it stabilised and Zamindars became loyal (in 1857 Bengal's Zamindars largely stayed on the British side). 2. Long term: the British got certainty and regularity of LR income. That objective was achieved. 3. But the core economic vision failed: Zamindars did not invest. The demand left little surplus, and they would not risk old family wealth in an uncertain colonial environment (the teacher writes "therefore LR" above "the demand"). 4. Absentee landlordism: Zamindars leased lands to intermediaries for a lease amount and moved to cities. The hands-on agrarian-capitalist vision was abandoned. 5. The ryot's situation became catastrophic. PS gave legal rights to Zamindars but did not recognise the ryot's customary rights. The ryot became a "tenant at will," evicted without legal protection; Patta ignored; high rents; abwabs, now illegal for lack of legal basis, still collected. Underlines: Auctions, frequent, Buyers, Jotedars, the Zamindar's own family, later stabilised, Zamindars became loyal; certainty and regularity; Zamindars did not invest; absentee landlordism, moved to cities, the agrarian-capitalist vision was abandoned; "tenant at will," Patta ignored, high rents, abwabs still collected. The loyalty is exactly the "Sustained" half of his DnR Mains question (Section 0). 6. Zamindars regained coercive powers in 1799. Cornwallis 86-93 had removed their police powers (a Zamindar is a businessman, not law enforcement). Wellesley 98-05 reversed this through Regulation VII of 1799. The Zamindar could now: (a) seize a tenant's property (crops, cattle) without a court order on rent default; (b) imprison tenants; (c) increase rents at will. (Class slide: the result was a wave of peasant revolts after 1793.) 7. Increased litigation after 1793 came from the Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (judicial changes that made the system inefficient in practice): (a) the District Collector was stripped of all judicial and magisterial powers, so revenue disputes once settled swiftly and informally on the spot had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats; (b) court fees were abolished to make justice "accessible," which flooded the courts with genuine and frivolous suits (fees reimposed in 1795); (c) formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) with a rigid hierarchy of appeals let cases be deliberately prolonged. "Not of this chapter, but here so the student knows" (his words on slide 36). The judicial reforms themselves belong to Chapter 18; here you only need the three points because of Prelims 2011. Prelims 2011: answer (d). The three options on offer are not the cause; the cause is the Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (point 7). (a) strong Zamindars did not mean more suits: ryots had no means to sue. (b) the EIC was already the overlord of the Zamindars' region since 1765 (the Diwani).(c) the courts became less efficient. Prelims 2001: answer (b) "no official check upon the Zamindar." The slide adds: Bengal Regulation VIII of 1793 required Zamindars to issue pattas (specifying rent and tenancy terms, so a patta is a rent agreement); the ryot could demand a patta. The gap was enforcement: the government cared about punctual payment of its fixed revenue. (a) trust does not explain it; (c) issuing pattas was the Zamindar's duty; (d) pattas protected cultivators. Mains FYQ on the board: "British empire in India was BUILT (1) and SUSTAINED (2) by policies and tactics of DnR FYQ-M: built and sustained by DnR.Built = created division (the Triple Alliance and the Treaty of Amritsar 1809; the Subsidiary Alliance, which takes over external affairs) and used division (factionalism as opportunity, e.g. the Treaty of Bassein 1802, an SA with Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18). Sustained = PS 1793 (his arrow). Treaties belong to Chapter 11, Chapter 13 and Chapter 6; here you only need to hang PS 1793 on the "Sustained" hook. 2.6 The Rent Act of 1859 and the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 After decades of peasant revolts the British were compelled to act. The Rent Act of 1859 (Bengal Presidency): a) A tenant who cultivated the same plot continuously for more than 12 years gained occupancy rights: no eviction without a court order; rent not raised without the Zamindar showing just cause b) With fewer than 12 years on a plot, rents could not be increased frequently c) The Patta system was revived: Zamindars had to collect rents at recorded rates d) Zamindars lost the power to imprison tenants "No more tenant at will of the Zamindar" (top right of slide 38). In practice it was poorly implemented: the loophole was to evict the tenant just before he completed 12 years, permanently denying him occupancy rights; Zamindars kept private armed men ("Z contd to keep LATHIYALS," the Zamindar's club-men, paid through bribery) and officials turned a blind eye. The failure drove the Indigo Revolt (1859-63) and the Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), where ryots fought specifically for occupancy rights (the revolts themselves: Chapter 20, Chapter 22). The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 (Act III of 1885) The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 (Act III of 1885) followed Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission of 1880 (passed under Dufferin 84-88's tenure, enacted by the Bengal Legislative Council): Rights of all stakeholders, Zamindars and ryots, clearly defined in law. Powers of Zamindars significantly reduced. Occupancy rights strengthened: even tenants who cultivated different plots in the same village for a total of more than 12 years now got occupancy rights over the last plot cultivated, closing the loophole. The government implemented it sincerely this time. He boxes "Tenancy" and ticks both "Tenancy" and "Act" with a note "only for ..." and sketches three circles joined by arrows (State, Zamindar and a third, unclear) (). Underlines: Rent Commission in 1880, dufferin's tenure, Bengal Legislative Council, "even tenants who cultivated different plots ... more than 12 years", "got occupancy rights", "sincerely".

Because the Permanent Settlement could not be copied where Madras lacked big Zamindars, Munro built another model around the ryot. Ask: what made the field survey the crux, and why did assessment drift from gross to net? Ryotwari: where applied Applied in: Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras and Bombay. Ryotwari followed annexations. Sind 1843 (Charles Napier), Coorg 1834 (famous for coffee plantations), Assam 1824-26 (First Anglo-Burmese War; Yandabo 1826, written "Toyandobo 1826"), Bombay 1817-19 (Third Anglo-Maratha War). Madras came in pieces: 1766 Northern Sarkars; the Third and Fourth Anglo-Mysore Wars (Malabar and Baramahal from the 3rd, Kanara from the 4th, Dindigul too, as drawn); 1801 the Carnatic (see Chapter 12). Circled 1 and 2 above the table:. The class map (Lecture 18, slide 24) lists Berar under Ryotwari as well; the handout's list does not. Both agree on the five places above. 3.1 Ryotwari in Madras (1801 onward, firmly from 1820) The first attempt in Madras was the same as Bengal: extend PS.Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 tried to create big Zamindars by recognising the Poligars as landowners. The experiment failed.Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in London in 1801 to replace it with Ryotwari in Madras. He had first experimented in parts of Madras in 1792 under Alexander Read (the slide: in Baramahal, annexed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War 1790-92). 1801-07 Ryotwari applied in Madras. It was diluted after he left for Britain in 1807; he re-established it firmly as Governor of Madras (1820-27). He died in India. Ryotwari in Madras: from the PS 1793 attempt to Munro Prelims 2017: answer (c) 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is wrong: Lord Cornwallis 86-93 was the PS 1793 architect and even tried PS in Madras through the Poligars. Read (1792) and Munro (1801-07, and 1820) are the Ryotwari pair. The teacher's years on the slide are the answer key. Handout hook: Read and Munro = Ryotwari (Scottish, yeoman); Cornwallis 86-93 = Permanent (English landlordism). Why Munro pushed Ryotwari over PS: five reasons. a) Scottish ideology Munro was from Scotland, where the hero of agrarian society was the Yeoman farmer (a landowner who also cultivates his own land, a more prosperous Khudkasht). As an Orientalist he argued ancient India had no intermediaries between the State and the cultivator b) No big Zamindars In Bengal, Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) created super-rich Intermediary Zamindars: by 1727, 15 of them collected 50% of Bengal's LR, which made PS viable. Madras had no such class c) State finances Madras was under stress from low productivity and past wars: three Carnatic Wars (1746-63) and four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767-99). PS fixes LR forever in amount, not %, so there is no room to grow State income d) Eliminate intermediaries Poligars' profits came at the State's expense (the slide adds Deshmukhs). Remove them: the share can go partly to the State, partly to lighter burden on ryots e) Political stability Removing Poligars as a class of powerful non-State actors reduces resistance; loyalty of the masses comes from giving them land (the teacher: "To bar political authority") He ticks (a) Scottish ideology and writes beside (e)"To bar POLITICAL AUTHORITY" (the Poligars' private armies and autonomy are what he means). On slide 2 he restates the logic of PS: big landlords must be very rich, so they can pay the LR (10/11) and invest huge sums in land; Bengal had them (15 Zs, 50%), Madras did not. 3.2 Under Ryotwari Under Ryotwari Landowner The ryot, who held legal title Settlement Directly with the ryot: the State dealt with each cultivator individually Assessment Detailed field surveys (soil productivity, irrigation, acreage, crops, past trends), in %, revisable, with revision and remission in bad harvests Collection By State officers: the DC and his juniors (Indians) Tenants (not stated on the slides) Teacher's board: the field survey is the most crucial thing in Ryotwari, and very tough The field survey is the crux of Ryotwari (very tough). Improper survey → unjust LR demand → landlessness. Three roads to loss of land from high LR: people abandon the land;default on LR → government auction;higher interest on a moneylender's loan → default → loss of the mortgaged land. And: "name of officers who designed and implemented the survey = imp" (underlined imp), with "Bombay: Wingate Settlement = Ryotwari." Learn the surveyors' names. Assessment evolved in two phases. Where and when Madras, by Alexander Read and Thomas Munro (1792-1820) Bombay (Pringle 1830, Wingate 1835) and Madras (1855, 1864) Demand 33% to 50% of estimated gross produce Based on net produce (gross crop value minus cost of cultivation: seeds, manure, bullocks, labour, implements): the Ricardian theory of Economic Rent Flaw or fix Surveys often improper; method arbitrary and ignored the cost of cultivation Reformed after the ruin of the agrarian economy Result Severe over-assessment: poverty, land abandonment ("Kheti hi chhod diye"); crop failure → borrow from moneylenders at high interest → default → lose mortgaged land or lose it in government auctions Bombay: Wingate fixes it; Madras: capped at 50% Phase 2 in Bombay. Elphinstone brought Ryotwari to Bombay (the slide dates it 1819 and says he did no fresh survey and used existing Maratha revenue records and assessments). R.K. Pringle (1830) first applied the Economic Rent theory but faulty calculations gave an excessive 55% demand. The Wingate Settlement of 1835 (Bombay Survey System, by Wingate and Goldsmid, implemented across the Bombay Deccan by 1847) fixed the flaw: it assessed LR fairly and fixed a reasonable annual amount for 30 years. Beside "reasonable annual amount for 30 years" he writes "Check it was %" (is the Wingate demand a percentage?; the handout says annual amount). His sketch splits the Deccan into the Bombay Deccan and the Hyderabad Deccan: Wingate applied to the Bombay part. Ryotwari assessment phase 2 reforms: Bombay Pringle's date. The handout says R.K. Pringle (1830); the teacher's ink on the comparison slide (Lecture 18, slide 23) reads "PRINGLE 1830" (next to a partly unclear "Bomb 44",); the milestone slide (slide 22) places "Pringle's revenue survey" at 1824-1828. Use 1830 for the Economic Rent application, and treat 1824-28 as the survey years on that card. Phase 2 in Madras. Madras Torture Commission Report (1855) exposed severe oppression in revenue collection. The Madras Rules (1855/1864) capped LR at 50% of net produce or rental value for 30 years (the slide: the Court of Directors ordered 30-year settlements with lower LR in 1855; in 1864 SoS Charles Wood directed the half-of-net-produce cap). The handout adds that addressing these grievances kept Madras relatively quiet during the 1857 revolt. Corruption: the lower bureaucracy relied on Mirasidars (rich landowner-cultivators acting as village-level revenue officers). Ryotwari assessment phase 2 reforms: Madras Because the DC and his officers held concentrated judicial, police and revenue powers, Mirasidars oppressed ryots, forced defaults and bought the best lands in auctions. The goal of removing big intermediaries failed: Mirasidars became big landowners themselves. "Over concentration of powers": the DC and his juniors (the Mirasidars) held admin (LR collection), judicial and police powers together, so a village official could squeeze the ryot, force default and then buy the land. Prelims 2012 (handout and class agree): answer (c) 1, 2 and 3. (1) Rent paid directly by peasants to the government: settlement is with the ryot. (2) Pattas given to ryots: the patta system was preserved. (3) Surveyed and assessed before taxed: detailed field surveys. 3.3 Impact in Bombay Collection: after annexing the Maratha Svarajya (3rd Anglo-Maratha War 1817-19) the EIC first used Patils (village headmen) and Deshmukhs to collect revenue, a nod to Orientalism; later it used officers. a) Patils lost their historic status. Earlier a Patil held executive, judicial, revenue and police powers and earned a commission (the teacher: "earlier commission"); now he was an ordinary salaried officer. b) Massive indebtedness to Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders swept the central Deccan in the 1850s. c) Not solely Ryotwari:crop failures and the collapse of cotton prices after the US Civil War (1861-65). Collection at Ryotwari (Bombay) Indian cotton boomed in 1861-65 because the Union naval blockade cut off Confederate cotton; when the war ended, US cotton flooded markets again and the premium vanished. Combined result: the Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875. Underlines: Patils demoted, executive, judicial, revenue and police powers and a commission, indebtedness, Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders, "crop failures played a role", "collapse of cotton prices after the US Civil War (1861-65)", Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875.

Because neither clean model fitted Awadh and the north-west, a compromise grew from the Taluqdars' fall. Ask: who is the owner, who settles, and why did it feed 1857? Mahalwari: where applied Applied in: Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab. UP = Awadh, undivided, taken in two parts: 1801 and 1856. The 1801 ceded districts were the first part; they got Mahalwari in 1822 and were organised as the North-Western Provinces (NWP) in 1836; Awadh was annexed in 1856;Punjab was annexed in 1849.The name changed in four steps: 1877 "NWP and Oudh;" 1902 "UP of Agra and Oudh;" 1937 "UP;" 1950 "Uttar Pradesh." (The handout's note says the "UP of 1937 = United Provinces of Agra and Oudh created in 1902": the board untangles it: 1902 is when it was named so; 1937 the short form UP; 1950 the modern name.) 4.1 Origin in Awadh Before the British, Taluqdars (Intermediary Zamindars) and Primary Zamindars dominated Awadh's agrarian economy. Half of Awadh came under British administration in 1801 (the nucleus of the North-Western Provinces). 1801-22: severe over-extraction.Taluqdars who resisted lost their milkiyats (landed estates): an entire class of landed magnates was crushed. In Mahalwari areas the Mughal-era revenue officers (Amils and Amalguzars at the district level, Tehsildars at the sub-district level) grew powerful and bought the best lands in auctions (note: Amlas are different, private employees of Zamindars, not State officers). Moneylenders, bankers and merchants also acquired milkiyat lands. Holt Mackenzie's recommendations were implemented through Regulation VII of 1822, creating the Mahalwari Settlement.Mahal = a community of people at the village, estate or district level. Taluqdar = a traditional leader of rural society;milkiyat = personal lands (so milkiyat holders = big landowners). He writes "7th Law of 1822" against Regulation VII of 1822 (as he did "7th Law of 1799" in Section 2.5): two Regulation VIIs, 1799 for Zamindar powers, 1822 for Mahalwari. Teacher's board: Mahal = community of people at village level, or district level, or estate level [some other size] 4.2 The hybrid structure Teacher's board: a circle split in two Mahalwari: the final hybrid structure Landowner Most areas: the ryot.Some areas: the Taluqdar Settlement Most areas: with the Mahal, through the Lambardar (its representative; he is the interface between State and community, preserving village autonomy; the Mahal decides internally how to spread the total demand). Some areas: with the Taluqdar Assessment Mahal-level after 1833 (before: per field or ryot); 66% of rental value for 30 years, revisable Collection State officers (the teacher: DC) Tenants Where the Taluqdar was owner, the law recognised ryots' occupancy rights and required recording of rents: the Patta had legal backing Mahalwari = a HYBRID of Ryotwari and Zamindari (on landownership). The slide's rule of thumb: type A = Ryotwari minus settlement with the ryot (it is with the Mahal); type B = PS 1793 minus permanent assessment. 4.3 The Revised Mahalwari System (R.M. Bird, 1833) Initially LR was assessed at the individual field or ryot level, but improper surveys led to excessive demands. In 1833, R.M. Bird introduced the Revised Mahalwari System in the NWP: (a) assessment at the Mahal level, not plot level, respecting the community's collective character; (b) individual contributions decided by the community; (c) if the Mahal's collective LR fell short, the State could auction individual ryots' lands; (d) LR fixed at 66% of the Rental Value (Net Assets, the teacher: net produce) for 30 years, subject to State revision. Dalhousie 48-56 extended Mahalwari to Punjab and Central India. 4.4 Why Mahalwari failed Improper field surveys → unjust land revenue → ryots lose land in State auctions or fall into debt and lose mortgaged land. When Awadh was finally annexed in 1856 a summary settlement was made (revenue without field surveys, because surveys take time): unjust demands and landlessness. Crushing of Taluqdars (1801-22), unjust demands, the summary settlement of 1856 and landlessness of ryots fed directly into the 1857 revolt in the NWP and Awadh (see Chapter 21). Two sad groups, both heading to 1857.Taluqdars (the leaders) were crushed; the ryot may have gained in the short term (smiley) but suffered in the long term (sad: landlessness in the long term). Both arrows end at the boxed "1857 REVOLT." Why Mahalwari failed

Because all three systems demanded cash, the ryot turned to cash crops and the moneylender. Ask: how does the chain run from cash demand to famine? Teacher's board Commercialisation of agriculture: the cash-revenue chain Handout figure of the same chain: British land revenue demanded in cash (not kind); ryots pressured to generate cash and shift from food to cash crops; moneylenders and t Under the Mughals much of the demand could be met in kind (grain for grain). The British demanded revenue in cash. To get cash, ryots were compelled, or induced by moneylenders and traders, to shift from food crops (feed the family, low market price) to cash crops: indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane. The higher the demand, the greater the pressure to grow cash crops: a structural transformation. Land that grew rice, wheat and millets now served British factories or global commodity markets. Food security declined: less food grain in reserve when drought or flood struck. This is one of the most important long-term legacies of British land policy and fed directly into the famines of the late 19th century. Two Indias.Before the Industrial Revolution (1750-1850) India was a source of finished goods (e.g. finished cotton); after it, India became an export market for British machine-made goods and a source of raw materials (raw cotton to British factories). Britain wanted Indians to grow more cash crops (B) and fewer food crops (A) = commercialisation of agriculture, so a higher chance of famine. His starred Mains prompt: "Why so many famines in British India?" And on slide 20 he adds that the moneylender's role rises along with cash demand ("More role of Rs Lenders", and a circled AND joining cash demand and the shift). The handout figure also names tea and coffee (plantation crops), oilseeds and a debt trap, and ends with peasant revolts (1857, Pabna, Deccan 1875). The handout's text lists indigo, cotton, opium, jute and sugarcane; use the text's list for Prelims, and the figure's extras only as colour in a Mains answer. Prelims 2021: answer (c) commercialisation of Indian agriculture. Teacher: (a) F (before the IR India exported finished goods; in the 19th century, the mature IR stage, India became a source of raw materials and an export market, so handicraft exports fell: deindustrialisation); (b) F (no conclusive evidence of growing Indian-owned factories); (c) T ("RM": raw materials need cash crops); (d) F (no conclusive evidence of rapid urbanisation).

Because the three systems answered the same five questions differently, line them up side by side. Ask: what did Cornwallis 86-93, Munro and Mackenzie with Bird each believe, and what did the ryot suffer in all three? Why three systems?Ideology, geography and fiscal pressure pulled in different directions. Cornwallis 86-93, an Englishman who believed in landlordism, made the Permanent Settlement.Munro, a Scotsman who believed in the yeoman farmer, made Ryotwari.Mahalwari was a practical compromise where neither clean model fit. 6.1 Permanent Settlement against Ryotwari against Mahalwari Comparison: Permanent Settlement (1793) / Ryotwari (1801, 1820+) / Mahalwari (1822, rev Landowner Zamindar Ryot Mostly ryot; sometimes Taluqdar (hybrid) Settlement with Zamindar Ryot directly Mahal (via the Lambardar) or Taluqdar Assessment Permanent: fixed forever (10/11 of pre-existing revenue) Detailed field surveys;50% of net rental value (Madras Rules 1855/1864) for 30 years Mahal-level;66% of Rental Value (Net Assets) for 30 years Collection by District Collector State officers (teacher: / DC) State officers (teacher: / DC) Where applied Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, Benaras, North Madras (BOB + Benaras + N. Madras) Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras, Bombay (SCAM-B) Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab (CUP) Architect or driver Cornwallis 86-93 (English landlordism) Alexander Read + Thomas Munro (Scottish yeoman); slide adds Elphinstone (Bombay) Holt Mackenzie + R.M. Bird (hybrid, practical) Key failure Absentee landlordism; ryot a "tenant at will"; Patta collapses Over-assessment;Mirasidar abuse;Bombay Deccan Riots 1875 Improper surveys;summary settlement 1856; 1857 NWP and Awadh epicentre Class map: Land Revenue Systems under the British (1793-1858) Reading the map. It shades by today's state and shows the dominant system only. Princely states (grey) had their own revenue arrangements and are not among the three. The north coastal Andhra and Benaras pockets belong to PS (the handout's "North Madras" and "Benaras"). Berar appears under Ryotwari on the map but not in the handout's list. 6.2 Common causes of ryot suffering What united all three was a common outcome: ryots suffered. Whoever the landowner was (Zamindar, ryot, Taluqdar), the mix of high land revenue demands, faulty surveys, legal vulnerability and predatory moneylending left the cultivating class worse off than under the imperfect but customary protections of the Mughal system. Prelims 2000, the handout and the class slide disagree on the first two rows (see the alert in the Exam lens). Handout: A = Zamindari, B = Jagirdari, code A-4 B-1 C-2 D-3 = (b); class slide and teacher's circles: A = Jagirdari, B = Zamindari, code A-1 B-4 C-2 D-3 = (b). The letter (b) is common. C = Ryotwari and D = Mahalwari are common. If you remember only one rule: peasant with the right to sell = Ryotwari; village level = Mahalwari.
