The Mughal patta. The Khudkasht (cultivator) holds customary occupancy rights and pays by a patta, a written record of what he owes, plus abwabs to his Primary Zamindar. The chain runs Khudkasht, Primary Zamindar, Intermediary Zamindar, then the Jagirdar or State, with Amils and Amalguzars checking. The Zamindar is a commission collector (Vatan right, 10%) and not the owner: only the King is legal owner. When the State needs money in a hurry it auctions the collection (Ijaradari). Diwani, but the old chain (1765-70). The Treaty of Allahabad gives the EIC the Diwani of Bengal, Orissa and Bihar. It keeps the Mughal collection (Orientalism) under Deputy Subadar Muhammad Reza Khan as Diwan. But the patta is ignored and rents run far beyond the record, then back-to-back droughts strike: the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 kills 50 lakh to 1 crore, the demand is doubled and brutality is used. Reza Khan is jailed without trial 1772-74 as scapegoat. Bankrupt (1772). Since 1757 the EIC bought Indian goods with India's own land revenue, so the famine hit its income directly. Nabobs' corruption, the famine and the army and Dual System expenses bring it to the verge of bankruptcy. Parliament lends 1.4 million pounds at 4% on condition of parliamentary oversight, which leads to the Regulating Act 1773. The auction year (1772). Warren Hastings 73-85, an Orientalist, revives Ijaradari as the Farming System: each district's collection is auctioned to the Revenue Farmer, who works under a European District Collector. The farmers squeeze the ryots to recover their bids, the demand is so high that peasants pay nothing, and revenue does not improve. Cornwallis 86-93, the Believer (1793). Cornwallis 86-93 comes from a landlord family and believes in English landlordism ('my way or highway'). His Permanent Settlement Act 1793 covers Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras and Benaras. Four pillars: the Zamindar becomes legal owner; settlement is with him; LR is fixed at 10/11 of the 1789-90 revenue forever (Rs 66 becomes Rs 60); and the Sunset Clause auctions his land if he misses the evening deadline. What the Permanent Settlement did. Frequent auctions at first (Jotedars and the Zamindar's family buy), later loyal Zamindars (largely on the British side in 1857) and certain revenue. But Zamindars do not invest, become absentee, and the ryot is a tenant at will with the patta ignored. Wellesley 98-05 gives back seizure, imprisonment and rent rises (Regulation VII of 1799), and the Cornwallis 86-93 Code clogs the courts. Patching the ryot's rights (1859 and 1885). The Rent Act 1859 gives occupancy rights after 12 years on the same plot, revives the patta and bans imprisonment, but Zamindars evict at year 11 and keep lathiyals; the Indigo Revolt 1859-63 and the Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873 follow. After Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission of 1880, the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 under Dufferin 84-88 counts 12 years across plots in a village and is implemented sincerely. Munro's Ryotwari (1792-1820). Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 tried to create big Zamindars in Madras through the Poligars; it failed. Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in 1801: Read had begun in Baramahal in 1792, Munro applied it 1801-07, and as Governor of Madras 1820-27 re-established it. His reasons: Scottish yeoman ideology, no big Zamindars, stressed finances, eliminating Poligars, political stability. The ryot owns, is settled with directly, after a field survey (SCAM-B). Over-assessment and the Deccan riots. Phase 1 took 33% to 50% of gross produce and ignored costs: ruin, abandoned land, moneylender debt. Phase 2 used net produce (Ricardian Economic Rent): Pringle 1830 reached 55%, the Wingate Settlement 1835 fixed it for 30 years; in Madras the Torture Commission 1855 led to a 50% cap. Mirasidars wore three hats, Patils were demoted, and when the cotton boom of the US Civil War years (1861-65) collapsed, debts to Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders plus crop failures led to the Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875. Mahalwari (1822-1856). In Awadh half came under British rule in 1801 and the Taluqdars were crushed 1801-22. Holt Mackenzie's recommendations became Regulation VII of 1822: settlement with the Mahal through its Lambardar, a hybrid where the Taluqdar owns in some areas. R.M. Bird's Revised Mahalwari of 1833 assesses at Mahal level, 66% of rental value for 30 years; Dalhousie 48-56 carries it to Punjab and Central India (CUP). Improper surveys and the summary settlement of Awadh in 1856 feed the 1857 revolt. Cash instead of grain. The Mughals took much in kind; the British demanded cash. Ryots, compelled or induced by moneylenders and traders, shifted from food crops to indigo, cotton, opium, jute and sugarcane. Land that grew rice, wheat and millets served British factories (after the Industrial Revolution India became an export market and a source of raw materials). Less grain in reserve fed the famines of the late 19th century. Why three systems, and why the ryot lost. Cornwallis 86-93 the landlordist made PS, Munro the yeoman man made Ryotwari, and Mahalwari was a practical compromise: ideology, geography and fiscal pressure. In all three, high demand, faulty surveys, legal vulnerability and predatory moneylending left the cultivating class worse off than under the Mughal patta.

Because the Br State held that only a State may hold power over territory, it faced a Company State it could neither ignore nor end. Ask: why regulate only CMR and not trade, and what are the two lenses? Chapter 17 title slide Br State versus EIC versus Company State. The Br State has no problem with the EIC as a trader. It has "problem and anxiety" with the Company State (1765-1858), because only a State may hold power over territory:"Br State wants monopoly in State matters." The slide also repeats his definition of a State: an organisation with a territory motive (see Chapter 10 for Company, State and Company State). Board only Why the State did not end the Company State. The positives: (1) more income by the EIC, from two incomes,trade (to the EIC) and land revenue (LR) (to the Company State), so Britain gets rich and the government's tax collection goes up; (2) the burden of ruling a far-away India is borne by the EIC, not by the State; (3) Company State of EIC of Britain, so the British empire goes up (indirectly) and so does geopolitical power.Therefore, instead of ending the Company State, the Br State regulated it, that is the EIC's political matters, from 1773. Board only The two affairs of the EIC.Commercial (business, private trade) since 31 December 1600.Political or public since 1765 (the Treaty of Allahabad, Chapter 10), that is Civil, Military, Revenue (CMR) = State matters.In capitalism in Britain the State does not interfere in business, therefore the focus of regulation = CMR matters. He also glosses "affairs" = function = work. Study Method for this Chapter The two lenses fixed on one board.@GG = the Company State and its Governors, the GG of the EIC = India (British India).@Br State = the Court of Directors (CoD) of the EIC and the Br State = Britain. Every provision below is placed in one of these two boxes, which is the frame the teacher uses for the act-by-act tables later in the chapter. @GG Provisions that shaped the structure and functions of the Company State in India: the GG, the Governors, the councils, law-making India [Br India] @Br State Provisions that shaped the relationship between the EIC and the Br State or Crown: how much control London had over the Company Britain (CoD of the EIC and the Br State) [Britain]

items.t: 1 · Why the Br State wanted to regulate the EIC
items.x: Because the EIC grew rich and powerful after 1765, London grew anxious. Ask: which of the five drivers were about money, which about fear, which about conscience? The 1857 revolt is often seen as the reason EIC rule ended. But if one reads the laws Parliament passed from 1773 onwards, the story is clear: the decline of the EIC's autonomy began nearly a century before 1857. Each Charter Act and Regulating Act slowly stripped the EIC of powers and transferred them to the British State. 1857 was the final nail, not the first wound. 1.1 The five drivers Why the Br State Wanted to Regulate EIC 1. Money After Plassey (1757) and the ToA 1765, the EIC got both plunder and Bengal's land revenue. In 1767 the Br State demanded 400,000 pounds a year from the EIC, arguing the State had helped the EIC in conquest. The State wanted its share 2. Fear of another America The American Revolution began in 1765 (the Stamp Act crisis marks the start of the political revolution) and by 1783 the USA was created. The armed War of Independence began in 1775. What if EIC officials, growing rich and powerful in India, did the same? 3. Protecting the taxpayer In 1772 the EIC went bankrupt and was bailed out with a 1.4 million pound loan from the State ("too big to fail"). The State wanted oversight to prevent reckless war expenditure 4. White Man's Burden betrayed The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 and the "Nabobs" (corrupt EIC officers who returned to Britain filthy rich) embarrassed the State and went against the civilising mission narrative 5. Career ambitions of EIC men Senior officials such as Robert Clive 57-67 and Warren Hastings 73-85 also wanted a formal relationship with the State: the Crown gave legitimacy and career advancement "EIC shall never do AR65-83 in India" (the American Revolution, 1765-83). The sketch shows 13 colonies on one side with Br (Britain) tied by a line, and the cone with an upward arrow marked ToA 1765: the Company's Bengal income rising just as the colonies were slipping away. The 400,000 pounds a year (1767) is underlined. 1.2 Select Committee of Parliament (1772) Parliament set up a Select Committee to study the EIC's affairs in India and to advise on the relationship between the British State and the EIC with regard to the EIC's territorial possessions. Only political functions were examined (in capitalism the State does not interfere in a company's business). Result: the EIC kept its monopoly over trade with India. But the Court of Directors (CoD) in London was now made accountable for the EIC's political functions in India. This led directly to the Regulating Act of 1773. Why regulation, and why in 1773 1765 ToA: the EIC becomes a Company State, with two incomes, trade and land revenue 1767: the State demands 400,000 pounds a year; 1765-83: the American Revolution; 1770: famine and Nabobs 1772: the EIC goes bankrupt; the State lends 1.4 million pounds; Select Committee of Parliament Result: trade monopoly kept; the CoD made accountable for political functions Regulating Act 1773: the State regulates the EIC's CMR matters, not its trade

Because the five worries peaked in 1772, Parliament regulated in 1773. Ask: what did the Act do in India (@GG) and in London (@Br State), and where did it leak? 2.1 @GG: provisions shaping the Company State in India 1. The Governor of the Bengal Presidency was elevated to Governor-General of the Bengal Presidency (GG/Bengal). He stayed Governor of Bengal but was now a General over the Governors of Bombay and Madras in specific matters. 2. The Governors of Bombay and Madras were subordinated to GG(Bengal) in matters of war and peace, except in emergency circumstances. They could be suspended if they disobeyed. Board only, "RA 1773" The logic: high war expenditure caused the 1772 bankruptcy, so the GG was made accountable; and accountability without power is meaningless. 3. Commercial affairs were untouched. In commerce the Governors stayed independent regional managers. 4. A Supreme Council of Bengal was created with four councillors (GG + 4). All decisions were by majority vote of the four councillors. The GG had only a casting vote, a tiebreaker. This was a check on any empire-building ambitions of the GG. 5. Legislative function was given to the GG's Council: it could make laws governing Bengal and on matters of war and peace. "GG is not boss in commerce matters" (row 3): in commerce the Governors stayed independent. "[Treaty = Law]" (row 5): in the teacher's reading, a treaty on war and peace is made by law of the GG's Council. The Governor in "Governor-General" = ruler of the Bengal Presidency, in charge of making laws and implementing them; the General = he is senior to G(Bo) and G(Ma) (Lecture 19, slide 27, below). Board only, "Decision making" with "[* Check vs Empire BUILDER GG]" Decision making in the Supreme Council.The council is a check against the empire-builder GG.(1) The GG proposes. (2) Only the four councillors C1 to C4 vote. (3) If it is a tie, the tie-breaker (casting) vote is the GG's. So the GG needs the support of at least 2 councillors to get his decision passed (2 for and 2 against is a tie, which he then breaks). 2.2 @Br State: provisions shaping the EIC-State relationship Handout flow chart: GG (Bengal), Supreme Council of 4 Councillors, majority vote decides, GG = casting vote (only on tie). 1. For the first time Parliament's right to regulate the EIC's political affairs was legally recognised. Commercial affairs stayed outside supervision. (Since 1600 the EIC had commercial functions; since 1765 also political functions, civil, military and revenue.) 2. The GG collects information on commercial and political matters and sends it to the Court of Directors (CoD) in London. The CoD submits information on political matters to the British State. 3. A Supreme Court in Calcutta:one Chief Justice and three puisne judges ("puny", junior judges), all chosen by the Crown. The first Chief Justice was Sir Elijah Impey (1774). It heard cases involving British-born subjects and their Indian servants in the Bengal Presidency, under British law. Similar courts followed at Madras in 1800 and Bombay in 1823 (earlier cases involving British subjects went to Mayor's Courts): thus 3 Supreme Courts. 4. To curb corruption, EIC officials were barred from accepting gifts from Indians. 5. Tenures:Directors of the EIC 4 years, not immediately re-eligible; GG(Bengal) 5 years, re-appointable;Councillors 4 years;all first appointees were named in the Act itself, future ones by the CoD. "[not today's SC]": this Supreme Court is not today's Supreme Court of India; it is a British-law court at Calcutta."(not BY EIC)": the judges were chosen by the Crown, not by the EIC, so the court was the State's own instrument. "Hastings 73-85 [GG's terms]": the first GG's 5 years is the tenure on the slide. Slide typeset detail: "Sir" is struck through before Elijah Impey on slide 52 (the first Chief Justice is simply Elijah Impey, 1774). The handout writes "Sir Elijah Impey". Either is fine for the exam. Source note on the code: slide 53 types "Warren Hastings 73-85" and the teacher's ink on slide 52 is also 73-85 (the last digit is hard to read, it could look like 86). Use 73-85, as the handout, the typed slide and the PYQ ink (Lecture 19, slide 52) all write. Directors of the EIC 4 years Not immediately re-eligible GG(Bengal) 5 years Re-appointable (Warren Hastings 73-85 the first) Councillors 4 years First ones named in the Act; later ones by the CoD 2.3 Impact of the 1773 Act 1. The Supreme Court was set up at Calcutta in 1774. (The Act was passed in 1773; Warren Hastings 73-85 assumed office as the first GG of Bengal in 1774.) Conflict arose between the Supreme Court and the GG's Council over cases arising from acts done by EIC officials in their official capacity. 2. Poor supervision: the huge distance between India and London and no modern communication. 3. Centralisation of power in the GG began: the journey of India's central executive and central legislature starts here. (The teacher's sketch: three equal G's become one GG with two G's below.) 4. Bombay and Madras still acted independently because of the vague phrase "emergency circumstances." Example: the Treaty of Surat (1775) was signed by the Governor of Bombay without the GG's approval, leading directly to the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82). 5. The GG had no veto over his council. With factional politics this led to paralysis, the indecision problem.Philip Francis, a councillor who wanted to replace Hastings 73-85, kept opposing the GG and wrote complaint letters to London. This contributed to Edmund Burke leading an impeachment trial against Hastings 73-85 in Parliament on corruption charges; he spent his life savings and was acquitted. (Robert Clive 57-67 was likewise tried in Parliament in 1773 and acquitted.) 2.4 Amending Act of 1781 (Bengal Judicature Act) The Amending Act of 1781 (also called the Bengal Judicature Act or Declaratory Act) resolved the jurisdiction conflict. The Supreme Court's jurisdiction was now: All cases within Calcutta's territory. All cases of British subjects in the Bengal Presidency (excluding cases arising from official acts of EIC officials, which went to the GG's Council). All cases related to EIC property in Fort William. Prelims 2005 trap (full question in the Exam lens). (1) Warren Hastings 73-85 and the regular police force on the British pattern: WRONG, it is Cornwallis 86-93's reform under the Cornwallis 86-93 Code 1793 (Chapter 18). (2) Supreme Court at Calcutta by the Regulating Act 1773: CORRECT. (3) IPC in 1860: CORRECT (Macaulay's draft from the 1834 Law Commission). Answer (b) 2 and 3. The teacher also inked, beside statement 1, "Till 1813 orientalism. Rule India, the India way": until 1813 the policy was to rule India by its own ways (orientalism), which is why a British-pattern police is out of place under Hastings 73-85. No class notes on Pitt's India Act 1784 sections appear in Lecture 18 after slide 62; the same Pitt's Act slides are repeated and extended with board work in Lecture 19 (slides 1 to 15). The section below uses both.

items.t: 3 · Pitt's India Act, also the East India Company Act (1784)
items.x: Because the Regulating Act leaked and America was lost, London moved from supervision to control. Ask: who is the top authority for commerce, for CMR, and who bosses the GG? Named after the British PM William Pitt.Context: Britain lost its 13 North American colonies in 1783 (American War of Independence 1776-83, USA created). The Br State became anxious about India, so it shifted from supervision to direct control of the EIC. Board: context of Pitt's India Act Two roads lead to the 1784 shift to control.Road 1 (top): the American Revolution 1765-83 produced the USA in 1783, so anxiety in the Br State that the EIC in India might declare independence (circled). Road 2 (bottom):GBF 1770, then the 1772 bankruptcy and the 1.4 million pound loan, then the Regulating Act 1773, then the Wars: the 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82 (he writes "Ma" with a smiley beside it) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War 1780-84 (he writes "Tie"). Both roads end at "shift to control of PIA 1784." The smiley and the "Tie" are the teacher's own result notes on the two wars (the 1st Anglo-Maratha War marked "Ma" with a smile, the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War marked "Tie"). The handout does not give these outcomes; they are covered in Chapter 13 and Chapter 12. Starred question: who chose the Directors in the CoD? Answer, boxed: the SHAREHOLDERS of the EIC. (The CoD is the EIC's own body; the BoC is the State's body.) 3.1 The concept of Double Government (1784-1833) The whole 1784 structure on one board. The CoD of the EIC sits with the English EIC and private people; the BoC sits in the Br State box. The BoC = "ministry for Indian Affairs."From the CoD, all incoming and outgoing letters go to the BoC.BoC to CoD = binding orders; BoC to GG(Be) = binding orders, bypassing the CoD. Bottom: the council shrinks from C1 to C4 (RA 1773) to C1 to C3 (PIA 1784). The summary: "Shift from regulation / supervision to CONTROL: PIA 1784." Board: "Concept: DOUBLE GOVT of EIC AFFAIRS", 1784-1833 above it, and a bracket "not the same as Dual Govt in Bengal Suba, not the same as SA" Board diagram Board: "DUAL GOVT: Bengal 1765-72: Diwani → EIC, Nizamat → Nawab" Double Government of EIC affairs (1784-1833) is not the same as the Dual Government in Bengal (1765-72), and is not the same as the Subsidiary Alliance (SA). The EIC's work is split into two parts and put under two top bosses.Top authority (final) = the one with no one above:commerce: the CoD of the EIC; CMR (political): the BoC of the Br State.1833: the commercial function of the EIC ended, so only one work, so only one top authority, the BoC. To keep them apart he lists three look-alike splits: Dual Government Bengal 1765-72 (Diwani with the EIC, Nizamat with the Nawab); SA (external affairs with the EIC, domestic with the Indian king); the UT with Legislature split (public order, police, land with the Union Government through the LG; the rest with the CM and State Legislative Assembly), and a family joke, "Mera Ghar": ABC = Papa, PQR = Mumma. Double Government of EIC affairs Commerce: CoD of the EIC. CMR (political): BoC of the Br State 1784-1833 Dual Government in Bengal Diwani: the EIC. Nizamat: the Nawab 1765-72 ([[10 Chapter 10]]) Subsidiary Alliance External affairs: the EIC. Domestic affairs: the Indian king From 1798 ([[11 Chapter 11]]) 3.2 @Br State: provisions shaping the EIC-State relationship Handout diagram: PRE-1784 Parliament supervises EIC (informal) versus POST-1784 Double Government (1784-1833): Board of Control (British State) and Court of Directors (EI 1. The Act used the phrase "British territorial possessions in India" (for the first time) but left it ambiguous whether British India belonged to the EIC or the British State. 2. Double Government of EIC affairs (1784-1833): political affairs went under the supreme control of the Br State through a new Board of Control (BoC) in London, effectively a ministry for Indian affairs. On commercial affairs the top authority remained the CoD of the EIC; on political affairs it was now the BoC. 3. The BoC had six members:one Secretary of State (a Cabinet minister) as President of the BoC, the Chancellor of the Exchequer (the Finance Minister) and four members of the Privy Council. (The Privy Council is the Crown's advisory body; earlier it worked like the Mughal Darbar or the Chhatrapati's Ashtapradhan.) Its role: to superintend, direct and control all acts relating to Civil, Military and Revenue government of the British territorial possessions in the East Indies."East Indies" was deliberate: territories annexed outside India (for example Burma later) also came under the BoC. 4. A Secret Committee of three directors within the CoD, through which the BoC could send confidential orders directly to India, bypassing the full CoD, for sensitive military and diplomatic matters. 5. The CoD now had to send all incoming and outgoing letters on India to the BoC. (In 1773 it was information; now original letters: the State's anxiety had grown after 1776-83.) 6. The EIC retained commerce and patronage in 1784: the right to independently appoint EIC officials, including the Principal Servants (GG, Governors, C-in-C, Councillors). The CoD kept the exclusive power to nominate them; the Crown's prior approval was not required (a doubt on this was settled by the Amending Act of 1786). The Crown's control ran through the BoC (policy) and the Crown's power to recall or remove officers. 7. Dual Control over GG (1784-1858): the BoC could pass binding orders both to the CoD and directly to the GG, bypassing the CoD. So the GG had two bosses in political, civil, military and revenue matters, the CoD and the BoC. In commerce only one boss, the CoD. "Power to give job" = patronage."= imp = GG, Governors, Councillors, C-in-C of EIC army" = the Principal Servants, marked imp."= Br STATE" is the teacher's bracket for Crown (the one who got the power to recall or remove). Source conflict inside the handout on the Principal Servants. Section 3.1 #6 says the CoD appointed them without Crown approval in 1784; Section 3.3 #6 and the slide "System that lasted to 1858" say they were appointed only after Crown approval. The teacher resolves it by inking "Done in [1793]" (Lecture 19, slide 15): Crown approval comes with the Charter Act 1793 (see Section 4). In 1784 the Crown only gets the power to recall or remove. Board: "next concept" "1 DUAL CONTROL, 2 OVER GG in C,M,R matters", with "1784-1858" above and "= Two Bosses of GG in C,M,R [Political matters / Company State]", a note " Dual Control over the GG (1784-1858) = two bosses of the GG in C, M, R matters (political matters, the Company State). A boss = a person who can give a direct order. In single control the chain would be BoC → CoD → GG → Governors. In dual control the BoC also orders the GG directly (arrow 2), so there is a breach of the chain of command: "everyone has only one boss" is the rule it breaks. Years 1784-1833 1784-1858 What is split The EIC's work: commerce (CoD) and CMR (BoC) The GG's bosses: CoD and BoC in CMR matters Who is the top authority Commerce: CoD; CMR: BoC In CMR: both, each can give direct orders When it ended 1833, when the commercial function ended (one work, one top authority = BoC) 1858, when the India Council and the SoS replaced the BoC and CoD (the GG reports only to the SoS) 3.3 @GG: provisions shaping the Company State in India Pitt's India Act 1784 @GG (India structure) Aim: resolve the indecision problem of 1773. 1. GG(Bengal)'s council cut from 4 councillors to 3. One seat was mandated for the Commander-in-Chief (CIC) of the EIC army as an ex-officio ordinary member. (Ordinary = mandated in the Act; ex-officio = member because he is the CIC; extra-ordinary = the CoD chooses whether to appoint him.) Council of 1784 = GG + 2 councillors + CIC. 2. The GG was given both a regular vote and a casting vote. With just one councillor's support the GG could create a tie and break it in his favour. (Earlier he needed at least two. In effect one councillor was removed and his vote was given to the GG.) 3. Bombay and Madras Governors were now subordinated to GG(Bengal) in war, peace and revenue (earlier only war and peace). This is how the Permanent Settlement of 1793 could extend to parts of Madras (the Northern Sarkars; see Chapter 16). 4. Responsibilities of the GG and the Governors were more clearly defined, removing the vagueness of "except in emergency circumstances" (RA 1773). 5. A Council of 3 was created under each of the Governors of Bombay and Madras (the beginning of today's State assemblies and Council of Ministers, without separation of powers). 6. "Conquest in India is repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of this nation." The Act thus banned imperial expansion, a response to the heavy war expenditure of the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). (The handout's aside: in reality only fiscal decline was repugnant, not empire-building.) Board: casting vote with 4 councillors (before) versus 3 councillors + GG vote (after 1784) Why the 1784 council helps the GG.Before (1773): the GG proposes and the votes are 2 for, 2 against, a tie, he uses the casting vote: 3 against 2.After (1784): the council is C1, C2, C3, and the GG now also votes: with only C3 for him and C1, C2 against, the votes are 2-2 (C3 + GG against C1 + C2), a tie, he casts: 3 against 2. So C4's normal vote is given to the GG. The aim, as he writes: to end factionalism and indecision and make the GG more powerful. Board: "Concept" (circled) Ordinary versus extra-ordinary member.Ordinary: the law itself says that a person will be a member of the council.Extra-ordinary: the law does not say so, but gives someone, for example the CoD, the power to appoint that person.1784 (PIA): the C-in-C was made an ordinary member of the GG's council; 1793: the C-in-C can be an extra-ordinary member if the CoD wants. Board: the GG's council compared, 1773, 1784, 1793 3.4 Impact of the 1784 Act and the Amending Act of 1786 1. Dual control in practice meant no effective control: the GG could play his two masters (CoD and BoC) against each other, given the distance and no modern communication. 2. The GG still had no veto over his council: if all three councillors opposed him, the indecision problem continued. (The teacher's note: "indecision continued, BUT" the position improved because he needed only one councillor.) 3. Conflict between the GG and the C-in-C: the decision of war and peace rested with the GG, but the right to use the army rested with the C-in-C. 4. The Amending Act of 1786 amended Pitt's Act by: (i) giving the GG a veto over his council in extraordinary circumstances; (ii) letting the EIC appoint the same person to both posts, GG and C-in-C, to avoid the rift (the posts were not merged, and it was not compulsory, just permitted). This was done on the insistence of Cornwallis 86-93 (GG 1786-93), who became the first person to hold both posts. 1st GG (Bengal) Warren Hastings 73-85 1773 (RA 1773; he took office 1774) 1st GG (India) William Bentinck 28-35 1833 (Charter Act 1833) 1st "Viceroy and GG" Charles Canning 56-62 1858 (GOI Act 1858) 1st GG of partitioned India Louis Mountbatten From 15 Aug 1947 (a now symbolic head) 1st Indian GG C. Rajagopalachari June 1948 to 26 Jan 1950 1st President of the Republic Rajendra Prasad After 26 Jan 1950 "To understand: GG = PM of Br India" (starred): before 1858 the GG ran British India as a Prime Minister would. "(Powerless) GG = President of India": after 1947 the GG is only a symbolic head, like the President. The same line appears on the 1853 slide: since 1833 the GG was effectively the PM of Br India and the CM of Bengal. The system of controlling the EIC's political affairs built in 1773-1786 continued till 1858 with very little structural change: binding orders by the BoC to the CoD and to the GG; Principal Servants appointed only after Crown approval (done in 1793); original letters to the BoC; the GG as the main authority in India. Prelims 2002 and 2004 trap cluster.Prelims 2002 (match):A-2 Charter Act 1813 (trade monopoly ended), B-4 Regulating Act 1773 (Directors report to the State), C-3 Act of 1858 (power to the Crown), D-1 Pitt's India Act 1784 (BoC). Correct option (a). The teacher wrote "BoC 1784", "1813", "1858".Prelims 2004 (pair NOT matched): (a) Pitt's India Act : Warren Hastings 73-85 is loose (Hastings 73-85 was GG of Bengal under the Regulating Act 1773); (c) Vernacular Press Act : Curzon 99-05 is the flagrant error (1878, Lytton 76-80). UPSC's key: (c). The teacher marked F on (c) and T under (d) (Ilbert Bill : Ripon 80-84).

Because Pitt's Act left the Company choosing its own top men, the Crown claimed the head. Ask: what does 'sovereignty only on behalf of the Crown' change for the EIC? 4.1 @Br State 1. "Subjects of the Crown cannot acquire sovereign powers over territory on their own but only on behalf of the Crown." So the EIC was now only a manager or agent of the British State.Sovereignty over British India was with the British State, not the EIC. (However, Mughal sovereignty over the whole of India was accepted until 1858.) 2. The size of the BoC was decreased: the President was retained with only two junior members under him, who need not be Privy Councillors. This concentrated real authority in the President and reduced factionalism. Charter Act 1793 @Br State (EIC-State): 1 3. The salary of BoC members was now paid by the EIC. (This later connects to the Home Charges under the Drain of Wealth theory of the Moderates, Chapter 27.) 4. The EIC's charter was renewed for 20 years, and for the first time by Parliament, not the Monarch. 5. Principal Servants (GG, Governors, C-in-C, Councillors) were appointed by the EIC but only after the approval of the Crown. The State took hold of the head of the Company State in India while its body stayed under the EIC, making a declaration of independence impossible. 6. The EIC retained commerce and patronage: it independently appointed officials other than the Principal Servants. The diagram on the right shows who owned what.India = Mughal + Sikh (and, the teacher adds, names such as Tipu 82-99 and the Nizam) on one side, Indian States, and British India [of the EIC → of the Br Crown] on the other: after 1793 British India belongs to the Br Crown, not the EIC, while the Mughal claim over the whole of India is still allowed to stand until 1858. The right-hand margin of the 1813 slide gives the three-step chain: 1784 "Br (T) possessions" (circled T, territorial), 1793 "sovereign powers only on behalf of Crown", 1813 (blank, then "undoubted sovereignty of Crown"). Board: boxed "PRINCIPAL SERVANTS", "now = more LOYAL to Br STATE than EIC" Principal Servants: now more loyal to the Br State than the EIC, because they are appointed by the EIC (the appointment letter and the salary are the EIC's) but only after Crown approval. That is the head taken by the State while the body stays with the EIC. 4.2 @GG 1. GG(Bengal)'s power over his council and over the Governors of Bombay and Madras increased further. When present in Madras or Bombay, the GG could supersede their Governors; even when absent from Bengal he could issue directives to the presidencies without consulting his own council. (Teacher: "Not imp.") 2. The CIC's seat was given to a civilian. The CIC could be appointed an extraordinary member by the CoD (and was). GG's council 1793 = GG + CIC (extraordinary) + 3 ordinary councillors. 3. Hallmark: Civil Law. A code of all regulations governing Bengal was to be framed, dealing with rights of persons and property;courts were bound to follow them; all laws were printed in the vernacular so people knew their rights. (This is Cornwallis 86-93's belief in the rule of law and anti-corruption; the laws included Hindu and Islamic laws and the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793 for land revenue and property.) "Written law, written judgement": the hallmark of 1793 is that law becomes written, and so do court judgements. He underlines "Hindu and Islamic laws + Permanent Settlement Act 1793" (the Cornwallis 86-93 Code, Chapter 18). Board: Law [Code = WRITTEN law] is on Civil matters or Criminal matters What "code" means.A code = written law. Law is on civil matters or criminal matters.Civil, personal (inheritance, marriage and divorce, parent-child relations) is handled by the customs of that community, i.e. the personal law of that religion; the State can make law for social reforms (his list: Sati Abolition Act 1829, Removal of Religious Disabilities Act 1850, Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856, Hindu Succession Act, Triple Talaq, UCC, abolition of untouchability by the COI 1950). Civil, non-personal (secular) (property, contracts) is handled by civil law made by the State.Criminal is always non-personal: State versus the accused, not accused versus victim, therefore law and order is the State's responsibility. 1773 Regulating Act GG + 4 councillors (all civilians) None 1784 Pitt's India Act GG + 2 councillors + CIC (GG's regular and casting vote) Ordinary, ex-officio (mandated by the Act) 1793 Charter Act GG + CIC + 3 councillors (3 civilians) Extra-ordinary (CoD may appoint; he was)

Because Britain's interest shifted with the Industrial Revolution, the trade monopoly became a burden. Ask: what stayed with the EIC, and what arrived with the missionaries? 5.1 Context 1. The narrative for ending the monopoly.Adam Smith's "Wealth of Nations" (1776) argued for a free market (laissez faire), so the monopoly was under intellectual attack since 1776.Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists argued that British manufacturers would industrialise India through technology transfer and FDI, fulfilling the White Man's Burden (WMB). There was also heavy lobbying by manufacturers and non-EIC traders. (Teacher: "[Recall: interlopers]", the non-EIC British traders of Chapter 10.) 2. British national interest. The Industrial Revolution (1750-1850) was progressing; British manufacturers wanted India as a source of raw materials and an export market. It was no longer in the British national interest for a trading company to hold the monopoly over British business with India. 3. The push to westernisation. Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists argued that the idea of a Great Ancient India was a myth and that westernising India fulfilled the White Man's Burden. Board: "Br National interest 1813" Br national interest in 1813: before and after the Industrial Revolution matured.Till the IR (1750-1850) matured: Britain wanted finished goods (FGs) from India to sell at a profit to the rest of the world, so it wanted a big MNC, the EIC, to buy Indian FG in bulk, therefore monopoly to the trader EIC.Once the IR matured: Britain wanted raw material (RM) from India, not FGs, and India as an export market to sell British machine-made FG, therefore the monopoly of a trader is not in the British national interest. Board: "WESTERNIZATION" in three branches Westernisation has three arms:polity and administration (west like), economy (west like: machines, factories of manufacturers, machine-based industry) and society (education, and customs and religion, which leads to social reforms). Board: "Economic Nationalism" Slide 24 is a teaching aside on economic nationalism (weak economy turns protectionist, strong economy turns globalist). It explains why Britain, now strong, wanted free trade in 1813. Nothing in the handout text matches it. 5.2 @Br State 1. "Undoubted sovereignty of the Crown over Indian territorial possessions." Sovereignty was of the British State, not the EIC. (At this stage the Crown was not challenging Mughal sovereignty over India as a whole.) 2. The EIC's monopoly over (British) trade with India was ended, but the EIC retained the monopoly over Tea, Opium and trade with China. (The teacher inserted "Br": the monopoly was over British trade with India.) 3. Cultural Colonialism began.Christian missionaries could enter India for conversions with a licence from the CoD or the BoC. A push to education and social reforms was mandated: the EIC was to spend Rs 1 lakh a year on education. The debate on western versus Indian education and medium continued till 1835, when it was settled in favour of western education in English. 4. The 1813 Act contributed to the 1857 revolt by enabling cultural colonialism and undermining Indian institutions and social structures. 5. The Charter was renewed for 20 years. Prelims 2019 trap (full question in the Exam lens). (1) Ended the trade monopoly except tea and China: CORRECT. (2) Asserted the sovereignty of the Crown over Indian territories: CORRECT. (3) Revenues of India controlled by Parliament: WRONG for 1813 (see the source-conflict alert in the Exam lens: BoC revenue supervision 1784; Budget under Parliament 1853; the teacher inked 1858). Answer (a) 1 and 2.

items.t: 6 · Charter Act of 1833, also the St. Helena Act
items.x: Because the trade monopoly was gone, the Company was left a political agent. Ask: how did one GG, one law and one legislature emerge, and what did the Governors lose? 6.1 @Br State 1. The EIC lost its monopoly over Tea, Opium and China trade. Its commercial function was fully ended: the EIC would no longer conduct business and had only a political function, and that only as an agent of the British State. (The Double Government of EIC affairs (1784-1833) thus ended: no more dual identity of trader and ruler. The slide adds that books still use the phrase till 1858.) 2. The BoC's supervisory power was extended to all administrative affairs in India: not just policy and laws, but supervision over implementation, officers, their transfers and postings. (The handout links this to the 2023 Supreme Court case on administrative control between the Centre and Delhi's elected executive.) 3. The President of the BoC was renamed Minister for Indian Affairs in 1833. The "8 ✓" in the right margin of slide 26 cannot be read with confidence (it could be the teacher marking the 8 numbered points of the Act or a shorthand).  6.2 @GG GG(Bengal) versus GG(India) in one word-play.1773: "Governor" = ruler of the Bengal Presidency, in charge of making laws and implementing them; "General" = senior to the Governors of Bombay and Madras.1833: "General" is the same as before; "Governor" is now the ruler of all British India (Bengal, Bombay, Madras), therefore he is now a true PM of British India, and the law-making powers of the Governors of Bombay and Madras are taken away. 1. A landmark: GG(Bengal)-in-Council was elevated to GG(India)-in-Council. As the EIC's territory expanded and Britishers entered India in larger numbers after 1813, uniform laws and administration across British India became necessary: one country, one law, one executive (like GST today or the Napoleonic Code of 1804). (Teacher: "implementation of law.") 2. The GG(India) was made Executive and Legislative head of British India: empowered to make and administer laws for the whole of British India, equally applicable to Indians and Britishers. Board: "GG(Be) vs GG(I)" 3. The legislative powers of the Governors of Bombay and Madras were taken away (restored by the Indian Councils Act 1861, Chapter 25). 4. Centralisation in the GG peaked in 1833; decentralisation to the provinces began in 1861 and peaked in 1935 (the journey of federalism and Centre-State relations). Charter Act 1833 @GG (contd.): 5 5. One Law Member (Thomas Macaulay) was added to the GG(India)'s council to draft uniform laws. This introduced the grain of separation of the executive and legislative functions at the council level (not at the GG's level, he still headed both). The journey of a separate legislature begins here. 6. In 1834 a Law Commission was set up under Macaulay for codification of laws. Work was completed by 1837, but deliberation went on. Full implementation post-1857:Civil Procedure Code (1859), Indian Penal Code (1860), Criminal Procedure Code (1861). (In 2024 India replaced these with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam.) The teacher adds the Indian Evidence Act to the list. 7. Racial equality promised:"No person to be deprived of chance to enter EIC service on grounds of religion, race, birth or colour." The Uncovenanted Civil Services (UCS, roughly today's Group B) and subordinate judicial positions below the district judge (e.g. Munsifs) were opened to Indians to reduce the cost of administration. (Teacher: "not imp.") 8. The Charter was renewed for 20 years. A triangle for the services:Br at the top, Indians at the base: UCS opened to Indians in 1833; the CCS (Group A) opened to Indians in 1853. GG's title GG(India)-in-Council Same Law-making Only the GG's council for all British India; Governors of Bombay and Madras lose it Same, but 4 provincial members can draft province laws Added to council 1 Law Member (Macaulay), for legislative sittings only The Law Member is promoted to the 4th ordinary member;6 Legal Members added Executive meetings GG + CIC + 3 ordinary GG + CIC + 4 ordinary Legislative meetings Executive + Law Member [GG + CIC + 4] + 6 = 12 persons The handout figure above calls the 1793 CIC "ex-officio." The text and the teacher say extra-ordinary (see the source-conflict alert in the Exam lens). Use the text and the teacher. Prelims 2003, 2007 and 2023 trap cluster.Prelims 2003 (NOT in 1833): (a) trading abolished: in 1833; (b) GG of India in Council: in 1833; (c) all law-making to the GG in Council: in 1833;(d) an Indian as law member: NOT in 1833 (Macaulay was an Englishman; an Indian Law Member came much later). Answer (d).Prelims 2007: (1) Clive 57-67 first GG of Bengal: WRONG (Hastings 73-85, under RA 1773; the teacher: "RA 1773: G → GG"); (2) Bentinck 28-35 first GG of India: CORRECT (Charter 1833). Answer (b).Prelims 2023: the Act that redesignated GG of Bengal as GG of India: Charter Act 1833 (d). RA 1773 only created GG/Bengal; PIA 1784 created the BoC and Double Government; Charter 1793 raised the GG's power but did not rename him.

Because the Company was now only an agent, its last powers were removed. Ask: what did it lose (term, jobs, Budget) and how did the council grow? 7.1 @Br State 1. The Charter was valid only "till Parliament specifies otherwise":no fixed renewal period. (A sword permanently hanging over the EIC's neck, since the Charter was its founding document.) 2. The EIC lost patronage (the power to independently appoint its officials) because a Civil Services Examination was introduced. The first exam was held in 1855 in London. From this point the EIC hardly controlled policies in India. (Teacher: "[* UPSC exam]".) 3. The Covenanted Civil Services (CCS) were opened to Indians (the UCS had been opened in 1833). 4. The revenues of British India (the Budget) were placed under the control of the British Parliament. 7.2 @GG 1. Deeper separation of the executive and legislative functions within the GG(India)'s council by adding 6 more Legal Members. 2. Provincial law-making. Since 1833 only the GG's council could make laws for all British India, but every country has issues that need province-specific laws. The four provincial representatives in the council would draft such laws (for example the Rent Act of 1859 for Bengal by the Bengal member). 3. A Lieutenant-Governor (LG) for Bengal. The GG was empowered to appoint an LG to reduce his workload (since 1833 the GG was effectively PM of British India and CM of Bengal, an impossible dual burden). Board: "2 KIND of LAWS": all country level, and at province level "because of unique problems, context of each province", "e.g.: PS 1793 → Bengal; Ryotwari 1801-07, 1820  In 1854 Dalhousie 48-56 appointed Frederick James Halliday as the first LG of Bengal. Two kinds of laws:all-country-level and province-level (because of the unique problems and context of each province). Examples of province-level subjects: the Permanent Settlement 1793 for Bengal; the Ryotwari system 1801-07 and 1820 (the slide reads "SCAM-B" beside it).Solution: since 1833 only the GG(I)'s council can make law, so 1853 adds 6 more legal members: Bengal, Bombay, Madras and NWP (the North-Western Provinces, "NWP 1836") = the 4 provincial representatives. Provincial representatives (Bengal, Bombay, Madras, North-Western Provinces) 4 Drafted province-specific laws (e.g. Rent Act 1859 by the Bengal member) Chief Justice of the Calcutta Supreme Court 1 Legal weight in the legislature A regular judge of the Calcutta Supreme Court 1 Legal weight in the legislature Total added 6 Legislative meetings: [GG + CIC + 4] + 6 = 12 persons 7.3 Governor versus Lieutenant-Governor (post 1858) "Curiosity but not imp" and "post 1858": this comparison is about the post-1858 Governors and LGs and is not a priority for the exam. Jurisdiction Presidencies (Bengal, Bombay, Madras): the oldest, most prestigious centres of power Provinces (e.g. Punjab, UP, Bihar): newer or subdivided territories Appointed by The British Crown directly The Governor-General of India (with Crown approval) Background Usually British aristocrats, peers or high-profile politicians imported from London Usually veteran ICS officers, career bureaucrats Autonomy and reporting High: could correspond directly with the Secretary of State in London Low: strictly subordinate, all communication through the GG Executive council Yes: ruled collectively as the "Governor-in-Council" No: ruled as a sole executive for most of the colonial period 7.4 Evolution of the council (1833 to 1853) "One council, two avatars." The same council meets as the Executive (he writes "[Cabinet meeting]") for day-to-day administration, taxes and war, and as the Legislative with extra members to draft laws. In 1833: executive = GG + CIC + 3 ordinary (since 1793); legislative = the same + 1 Law Member (Macaulay).In 1853: executive = GG + CIC + 4 ordinary (the Law Member of 1833 is promoted to the 4th ordinary member); legislative = [GG + CIC + 4] + 6 = 12. For Prelims, "members" means councillors only, unless the question explicitly says "total strength of the council." Do not count the GG. Regulating Act 1773 Parliament's right to regulate political affairs recognised; CoD reports to the State; Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) chosen by the Crown; no gifts GG(Bengal) over Bombay and Madras in war and peace (except emergency); law-making for Bengal and war and peace GG + 4 (majority vote; casting vote only) Kept trade and patronage; political affairs now accountable Pitt's India Act 1784 BoC (6 members, minister-level) and Double Government 1784-1833; Secret Committee; Dual Control 1784-1858; original letters; ban on conquest Governors under the GG in war, peace and revenue; Councils of 3 under the Governors GG + 2 + CIC (ordinary); GG: regular + casting vote; Amending Act 1786 gives a veto Kept commerce and patronage; Crown may recall or remove Principal Servants Charter Act 1793 Crown sovereignty; EIC = agent; BoC cut to a President + 2; BoC salary paid by EIC; first Parliament renewal (20 years);Principal Servants after Crown approval GG can supersede Governors; directives without council; Cornwallis 86-93 Code (written law) GG + CIC (extra-ordinary) + 3 Kept commerce and lesser patronage; lost the head of the Company State Charter Act 1813 Undoubted sovereignty of the Crown;India trade monopoly ended (Tea, Opium, China kept); missionaries; Rs 1 lakh; 20 years (Westernisation of polity, economy and society begins) No change Lost the India trade monopoly; kept Tea, Opium, China Charter Act 1833 Commercial function fully ended; BoC supervises all administration;President of BoC = Minister for Indian Affairs; St Helena taken over; 20 years GG(India)-in-Council; one executive and legislative head; Bombay and Madras lose legislative power; UCS and judicial posts opened Executive GG + CIC + 3; legislative + 1 Law Member (Macaulay) Lost all trade;only a political agent of the State Charter Act 1853 No fixed term ("till Parliament specifies otherwise"); Civil Services exam (1855, London);Budget to Parliament; CCS opened to Indians 6 Legal Members;LG of Bengal (Halliday, 1854) Executive GG + CIC + 4; legislative [GG + CIC + 4] + 6 = 12 Lost patronage and control of policy GOI Act 1858 EIC rule replaced by the Crown;Secretary of State and the 15-member India Council;Dual Control ended; Paramountcy; Mughal sovereignty ended Viceroy and GG (Canning 56-62); powers unchanged (GG's council continues) EIC abolished (formally dissolved 1874) Evolution of GG's Council (1773 to 1853)

items.t: 8 · Government of India Act 1858, also the Act for Better Government of India
items.x: Because the revolt gave the occasion and the Acts had done the work, the Crown took over. Ask: what replaced the BoC and the CoD, and what do the princes keep under Paramountcy? 8.1 Background 1. EIC blamed for 1857 The EIC was blamed for mismanagement of Indian affairs and for the 1857 revolt, in which many British were killed and the EIC's monopoly on violence was broken 2. Public demand The British public demanded an end to EIC rule, replacing Absentee Sovereignty with direct rule of the British State (since Charter 1793 sovereignty was with the State, but it was absent and ruled through its agent, the EIC) 3. Free traders Non-EIC merchants wanted direct British rule, claiming the EIC ignored their business interests 4. WEMC The Indian Western-Educated Middle Class wanted direct British rule for accountability and modernisation (the Industrial Revolution and democracy came under State rule in Britain, not under a company) 5. Stronger control Britain wanted stronger control over India after 1857 8.2 @Br State 1. EIC rule was replaced by the direct rule of the British State in British India. (Irony: in 1856 the EIC annexed Awadh on grounds of maladministration; now the EIC was removed on the same grounds. The EIC was formally dissolved in 1874.) 2. Policy of Subordinate Union towards Indian rulers.Mughal sovereignty over Indian territory was legally ended (Mughal State 1526-40 and 1556-1858). GOI Act 1858 @Br State (EIC-State): 1 Note: Mughal sovereignty was not over the whole of India (Travancore was never part of the Mughal State and the Sikh State was legally independent). The British Crown was now sovereign over the whole of India: (i) British India (about 63% of the territory and 78% of the population) was ruled directly by the GG; (ii) Princely States were ruled by Indian princes under Paramountcy, a legal relationship in which Sovereignty, Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs (Sov, D, C, FA) rested with the Crown and domestic affairs with the Prince (the handout's analogy: "Article 370 without democracy"). 3. Zafar 37-57 (Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, the last Mughal Emperor) was pensioned off to Rangoon in Burma. 4. The Secretary of State for India (SoS) replaced the President of the BoC / Minister for Indian Affairs as the main authority and director of policy in India. The board for Paramountcy.India = [symbolic sovereign: the Br Monarch], split into British India (external and domestic both with the British) and the 565 Princely States (external with the British, domestic with the Prince). The bracket "Paramountcy" sits under the 565 PS side. Beside the Proclamation (slide 39) he writes "Rule of Indian Princes in 565 PS" and "Rule of Br State in Br India" (Section 8.3). GOI Act 1858 @Br State (contd.): 5 5. The Council of India (India Council) replaced the Board of Control (BoC 1784) in London, headed by the SoS with 15 members. (Seven members of the EIC's CoD were absorbed into the India Council for continuity and experience.) 6. Dual Control over the GG (1784-1858) ended: as "Viceroy and GG" he now reported only to the SoS. (As GG he is the ruler of British India; as Viceroy he is the representative of the Crown in India, like a Vice-Captain representing the Captain when the Captain is not on the field.) 7. No change in the actual powers of the GG(India) as "Viceroy and GG." 8. In 1858 Charles Canning 56-62 became the first Viceroy. 9. The same Civil Services examination continued and was still held only in London. "[*vice captain]": Viceroy = the Crown's vice-captain. The diagram: before (left) the BoC orders the GG and the CoD orders the GG (the CoD is crossed out "xx/" with the BoC): dual control.After (right): the SoS for India orders the GG, one boss. Body in London BoC (1784) and CoD (EIC) Council of India (15 members) headed by the Secretary of State (SoS) Policy head President of the BoC / Minister for Indian Affairs (1833) Secretary of State for India Bosses of the GG Two: CoD and BoC (Dual Control 1784-1858) One: the SoS GG's title GG(India) Viceroy and GG (Canning 56-62 first) Civil Services exam Held in London Still only in London 8.3 Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) The Proclamation announced the transfer of governance from the East India Company to the British Crown. It specifically: (a) Disclaimed any intention to annex Indian States (a walk-back from Dalhousie 48-56's Doctrine of Lapse and the Awadh annexation 1856). Teacher: "Rule of Indian Princes in 565 PS." (b) Placed the Indian administration (British India) under the British Crown. Teacher: "Rule of Br State in Br India." (c) Promised religious non-interference, fair treatment of all subjects and opportunity in public service without discrimination of race or creed (re-affirming the Charter Act 1833 racial-equality clause). Religious non-interference is underlined. (d) Granted amnesty to those who took part in the 1857 revolt, with limited exceptions. The word "Queen" is struck through in the slide title (the teacher's ink). The handout uses "Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858)" throughout and the Prelims 2014 question says "Queen Victoria's Proclamation". No fact changes. Prelims 2014 and 2006 trap cluster.Prelims 2014: objects of the Proclamation: (1) disclaim annexation: CORRECT; (2) administration under the Crown: CORRECT; (3) regulate the EIC's trade with India: WRONG (the teacher: "ended 1813"; the EIC's commercial function was over by 1833 and the Company was being dissolved). Answer (a) 1 and 2.Prelims 2006: (1) Charter 1833 abolished the EIC's monopoly of Indian trade: WRONG (1813 did that; 1833 ended Tea, Opium, China); (2) under GOI 1858 Parliament abolished the EIC altogether and took over direct rule: CORRECT.Answer (b). 8.4 Royal Titles Act (1876) 1. The Royal Titles Act (1876) by the British Parliament empowered Queen Victoria to take the title of Kaesar-i-Hind (Empress of India). 2. In 1877 Lytton 76-80 organised the Imperial (Delhi) Darbar where Victoria was coronated as Kaesar-i-Hind. (She had been unofficially using the title since 1858.) He completes the slide's word "corona" + "TED" with underlines under Imperial / Delhi Darbar and Victoria got: the point is the ceremony (coronation) at the 1877 Delhi Darbar under Lytton 76-80.

items.t: 9 · Conquest in India: policy versus drift
items.x: Because the 1784 Act banned conquest yet the empire grew, the State's role needs explaining. Ask: was conquest policy or drift, and where was the State involved? No class slides on this section until Lecture 19, slides 41 to 43 (typed "MMP" slides without ink); the handout gives the same points. It is the "Br State responsibility for conquest" Mains angle. 9.1 No official policy of conquest On the surface, Britain had no official policy of conquest. Imperial expansion was largely driven by Sub-Imperialism: the policies, actions and personal ambitions of senior EIC officials in India, many of whom built political careers back home after their India tenures. Pitt's India Act (1784) explicitly banned conquest in India, a response to the heavy expenditure of the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). 9.2 British State responsibility However, the British State was responsible for conquest, for these reasons: a) Tools of conquest given by the State: the EIC's Charter gave it the right to wage war, acquire and administer territory; the Charter was issued first by the Crown and later by Parliament. b) Military aid at critical junctures:Plassey (1757) was won with the help of the Royal British Military (Chapter 10); when the 1857 revolt nearly overthrew Company rule, the arrival of the Royal Military in October 1857 turned the tide. The State helped both the initiation and the survival of conquest. c) The State financed the Company:trade monopoly over Britain's East Indies trade (1600-1813).King Charles II 60-85 rented Bombay (received as a dowry from the Portuguese in 1661) to the EIC for just 10 pounds a year in 1668.Thomas Roe was sent as a State representative to Jahangir 05-27's court to lobby. The State bailed out the EIC with a 1.4 million pound loan in 1772. d) Follow the money trail: over 1,50,000 pounds to the Monarch in the 17th century for Charter renewals; in 1698 Parliament gave the monopoly to a "New Company" because it offered a 2 million pound loan against the EIC's 7,00,000; in 1767 the EIC had to pay 4,00,000 pounds a year; many Parliamentarians and even Queen Elizabeth I 58-03 were shareholders receiving dividends. e) The State controlled the empire-builders: after 1784 Principal Servants (the sub-imperialists themselves) could be appointed only after Crown approval, and binding orders could go directly to the GG (empire-builders were, in effect, favourites of the State). f) The EIC as a foreign-policy tool: Britain dominated world trade through the EIC, as large MNCs today serve a State's foreign policy (the handout's examples: Google or private banks for sanctions on Russia, Airtel in Africa). The 1st Afghan War (1838-42) fought by the EIC was part of the Great Game between Britain and Russia.

items.t: 10 · The Governor General across the Acts (Prelims 1996) and the Sepoy Mutiny question
items.x: Because the GG's title changed with each Act, the teacher drills it by matches. Ask: which famous holder goes with each Act, and where does 1857 fall? A. A trader turned ruler (1765). The EIC has done business since 31 December 1600; since the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765 it also runs Civil, Military and Revenue (CMR) affairs, a Company State. The Br State has no problem with a trader but 'problem and anxiety' with a Company State, since only a State holds power over territory. Yet it does not end it: the EIC brings two incomes (trade and land revenue), bears the burden of ruling far-away India, and raises Britain's empire and geopolitical power indirectly. So from 1773 the State regulates the EIC's political matters. Five worries. Money: in 1767 the State demanded 400,000 pounds a year. America: the revolution of 1765-83 ended with the USA in 1783, so what if EIC men did the same? The taxpayer: the EIC went bankrupt in 1772 and was lent 1.4 million pounds. Conscience: the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 and the Nabobs. Careers: Clive 57-67 and Hastings 73-85 wanted a Crown link. The Select Committee of 1772 kept the EIC's trade monopoly but made the Court of Directors accountable for its political functions. The Regulating Act 1773 in India. The Governor of Bengal becomes GG(Bengal) and is made senior to Bombay and Madras in war and peace, except in emergency; commerce is untouched. A Supreme Council of GG + 4 decides by majority and the GG has only a casting vote, so he needs at least two councillors: a check on an empire-builder. Law-making for Bengal and on war and peace goes to the council. The Regulating Act 1773 in London. For the first time Parliament's right to regulate the EIC's political affairs is recognised. The GG sends information to the Court of Directors and the Directors send political matters to the State. A Supreme Court at Calcutta (a Chief Justice and three puisne judges, all chosen by the Crown, Elijah Impey first in 1774) is created, officials may not take gifts, and the tenures are 4, 5 and 4 years. The leaks of 1773. The Supreme Court clashes with the GG's council over officials' official acts; distance blunts supervision; Bombay signs the Treaty of Surat in 1775 without the GG, starting the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82). With no veto, the GG is blocked by factions: Philip Francis opposes Hastings 73-85 and Edmund Burke leads an impeachment, which ends in acquittal. The Amending Act of 1781 fixes the Supreme Court's jurisdiction. Pitt's India Act 1784. Britain lost 13 colonies in 1783, so the State fears an Indian declaration of independence. A Board of Control (six members, a ministry for Indian affairs) takes political affairs while the Court of Directors keeps commerce: Double Government 1784-1833. The BoC can also order the GG directly: Dual Control 1784-1858. The council shrinks to GG + 2 + CIC and the GG gets a regular and a casting vote. Conquest is declared 'repugnant'. The Amending Act of 1786 gives a veto and lets Cornwallis 86-93 hold both GG and C-in-C. 1793: the Crown takes the head. Subjects of the Crown cannot acquire sovereign power except on behalf of the Crown, so the EIC is an agent. Principal Servants (GG, Governors, C-in-C, Councillors) are appointed by the EIC but only after Crown approval, and Parliament renews the Charter for the first time. The head of the Company State belongs to the State while the body stays with the EIC. In India the GG can supersede Governors, the CIC becomes an extra-ordinary member, and Cornwallis 86-93's Code makes law written. 1813: the monopoly breaks. Adam Smith (1776), Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists, and lobbying manufacturers attack the monopoly; the Industrial Revolution makes Britain want India's raw material and an export market. The India trade monopoly ends (Tea, Opium and China stay), Crown sovereignty is stated as undoubted, missionaries enter with a licence and Rs 1 lakh a year goes to education. The Act contributes to 1857. 1833: one India, one law. The St Helena Act ends the EIC's commercial function: no more business, only a political agent. The BoC supervises all administration and its President is renamed Minister for Indian Affairs. The GG(Bengal)-in-Council becomes GG(India)-in-Council (Bentinck 28-35 first), the Governors of Bombay and Madras lose law-making, Macaulay joins as Law Member, the Law Commission of 1834 begins codification and the UCS opens to Indians. Centralisation peaks. 1853: no term, no jobs, no Budget. The Charter lasts only 'till Parliament specifies otherwise'; a Civil Services exam (first held in London in 1855) ends the EIC's patronage and opens the CCS to Indians; the Budget goes to Parliament. Six Legal Members (four provincial, a Chief Justice and a judge) make a legislative council of twelve, and in 1854 Dalhousie 48-56 appoints Halliday as first LG of Bengal. 1858: the Crown takes the body. The EIC is blamed for 1857; the public, free traders and the western-educated middle class want direct rule. The GOI Act 1858 ends Company rule: a Secretary of State with a 15-member India Council replaces the BoC, Dual Control ends, and Canning 56-62 is first Viceroy. Mughal sovereignty is ended (Zafar 37-57 goes to Rangoon) and the princes of the 565 PS live under Paramountcy. The Proclamation promises no annexation, Crown administration, religious non-interference and amnesty; the Royal Titles Act 1876 makes Victoria Kaesar-i-Hind. Whose conquest? Britain claimed no official policy of conquest; Sub-Imperialism by EIC officials drove it, and Pitt's India Act 1784 banned it. Yet the State gave the Charter (the tools), sent the Royal Military at Plassey and in October 1857, financed the EIC, followed the money, controlled the empire-builders and used the EIC as a foreign-policy tool (the 1st Afghan War, the Great Game).
