Story so far: the EIC holds the territory; now it must run it. The teacher's four verdicts set the weight of this chapter. Ask: why does he call the whole thing PubAd in British India? Chapter 18 title slide: EIC Administration: Judiciary, Civil Services, Police Four verdicts on this chapter:no questions in Mains, few and rare questions in Prelims, it still troubles aspirants in every book, and this handout is the best version. He calls the whole subject the history of Public Administration (PubAd) in British India. That is how to read it: not as a list of Acts but as how a Company State built its working machinery. Administration: Machinery of the State

items.t: 1 · Administration as the machinery of the State
items.x: Because the State needs machinery to work, the EIC had to build or borrow it. Ask: which three pillars carry the chapter, and what are 'T' and 'Ppl'? Administration is the machinery of the State: how the State implements its policies, laws and schemes on the ground. When the EIC changed from a trading company into a Company State (the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function; the slide dates the Company State 1765-1858), it had to build this machinery from scratch. More accurately, it had to decide how much of the existing Indian machinery to keep and how much to replace. The chapter covers three pillars: Judiciary, Civil Services and Police. ORG with three arrows up: the organisation (the State) is made of its three machines. "WORK = RULE", and rule splits into T (territory) and Ppl (people). The State's work is to rule a territory and its people, and administration is how it does that work every day. This links to his L, E, J shorthand (legislative, executive, judicial power) from Chapter 8 and Chapter 10: the Company State had taken the territory; this chapter is about how it handled the people. Note for Mains (the handout's own warning). UPSC Mains PYQs mapped to administration overwhelmingly ask about the economic impact of British rule: Drain of Wealth, de-industrialisation and the Sepoy Army as an imperial tool. They cannot be answered from this chapter alone: Drain of Wealth and the economic critique are in the Moderates / Drain Theory chapter; de-industrialisation and the destruction of handicrafts are in the British Imperial Ideology and Land Revenue Systems chapters; Sepoy Army composition and grievances are in the 1857 Revolt chapter. This chapter provides the administrative skeleton; those chapters supply the economic and military flesh.

Because law was sensitive, the EIC began with Mughal courts and changed them only step by step. Ask: which six questions did every reform have to answer? 2.1 Why judicial reform was so complicated The EIC was not walking into a blank slate. It entered a society with established legal traditions, different religious communities and a functioning (though imperfect) court system. It had to answer six questions: 1 Which law should apply: Hindu, Islamic or British? Personal laws kept; Anglo-Muhammadan law; Supreme Court on British law 2 Should laws be written down or left to the judges' discretion? Codification: Gentoo Code, Hedaya, Code of 1781, Cornwallis 86-93 Code 3 What hierarchy of courts? 1772, 1773, 1793, Bentinck 28-35 4 Should lawyers be allowed to represent parties? Yes, from 1793 5 Should judges be Indians or British? All senior posts European under Cornwallis 86-93; lower posts opened from 1833 6 In which language should courts function? Persian replaced in 1835 Each question carried political, social and financial implications, and the answers changed as British confidence, ambition and administrative needs evolved. 2.2 The Mughal judicial system in Bengal (before 1772) The Mughal system in Bengal had two separate hierarchies, one for civil and one for criminal matters. Civil matters (Diwani = finance, land revenue and civil justice): Courts ran from the local level up to the Sadar Diwani Adalat (SDA) at the suba (provincial) level. In inter-personal matters (marriage, inheritance) the personal laws of Hindus and Muslims applied. Teacher's board: Traditional Mughal (J) system in Provinces Pandits judged Hindu cases and Maulvis judged Muslim cases. At the top the Diwan served as Chief Justice of the SDA. For land revenue and non-personal civil disputes, the original jurisdiction lay with the Zamindar at the local level, in his revenue court, the Kachari. Appeals went up: Zamindar, then Amil (the provincial revenue officer at district level), then the SDA at the provincial capital (Murshidabad), presided over by the Diwan or Naib Diwan. Around this time Muhammad Reza Khan, the Naib Nazim, held the posts of Chief Justice of both the SDA and the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. "Amil" versus "Amalguzar." The handout uses Amil only because it is a snapshot of the corrupted, mutated system of 18th-century Bengal; the canonical Mughal-administrative term is Amalguzar. The teacher's general board (slide 5) writes Amalguzar = revenue officer at district level; his Bengal board (slide 6) writes Amil (Rev officer). Same post. Criminal matters: Nizamat Adalats (commonly called Faujdari Adalats) sat at the district level, with the Sadar Nizamat Adalat (SNA) at the top. The Mughal State was an Islamic state, so Islamic law governed criminal proceedings, applied uniformly regardless of religion. At the village level the Zamindar held petty criminal jurisdiction alongside his police duties. Major crimes bypassed the Zamindar and went straight to the district Faujdari Adalat. Strict division of labour: the Kazis were the actual judges who pronounced verdicts (the board calls it a "2 People Bench," Kazi with Mufti), the Muftis gave expert interpretation of Islamic law, and the district Faujdar (executive police chief) secured the accused and physically executed the sentence. The Naib Nazim headed the SNA. Civil courts were religion-specific (your judge depended on your faith); criminal courts were State-uniform (the law of the ruling State applied to everyone). On the board: civil has two tracks under the SDA: the personal-law track (Diwani Adalat, Pandits and Maulvis) and the LR / non-personal track (Amalguzar, then the Zamindar's Kachari). Criminal has one track, with "Law = Islamic Law." Teacher's board: 18th c BENGAL at the SUBA level Who is Chief Justice of the SNA? Two boards, two answers, one reason. The teacher's general Mughal board (slide 5) writes SNA [CJ = Nazim / Subadar]; his 18th-century Bengal boards (slides 6, 7, 12) and the handout write CJ = Naib Nazim. The difference is the date: by the 18th century the real Subadar had become a distant authority and the Naib Nazim (Muhammad Reza Khan) ran the courts. For Bengal before 1772, use Naib Nazim for the SNA, and for the SDA the handout says Diwan (the board adds that Reza Khan, the Naib Nazim, held both chief justiceships, having been made the EIC's Diwan in 1765). Teacher's board: "Standard Books focus = Personal matters in Civil AND Criminal matters", with a circled "Remember" Most standard books stop at "personal law in civil matters AND criminal law in criminal matters," and the teacher tells you to remember exactly that pair. Civil = Hindu law for Hindus, Muslim law for Muslims. Criminal = Islamic law for everyone. Teacher's board: "FAUJDAR = Like SP at DISTRICT", with a brace giving two functions: "LEO" and "execute Judgement of NA/FA". The Faujdar is like today's SP (Superintendent of Police) at the district, and he did two jobs, which the board lists as LEO (as written on the board; the handout describes the Faujdar as the executive police chief who secured the accused) and executing the judgement of the Nizamat or Faujdari Adalat. He does not judge; the Kazi judges. Teacher's board: PRE 1772 Suba (province) Sadar Diwani Adalat (SDA), CJ the Diwan (Reza Khan held both chief justiceships) Sadar Nizamat Adalat (SNA), headed by the Naib Nazim District Diwani Adalat: Pandits (Hindu cases) and Maulvis (Muslim cases); revenue side: Amil (Amalguzar) Nizamat or Faujdari Adalat: Kazi judges, Mufti interprets, Faujdar executes Local Zamindar's Kachari: land revenue and non-personal disputes Zamindar: petty crimes only; major crimes go straight to the district court Law applied Personal law (Hindu law, Muslim law) Islamic law for all 2.3 The Dual Government period (1765-1772) After the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 the EIC gained the Diwani rights over Bengal:revenue administration, Treasury and control of property / civil courts. (Modern welfare duties such as health and education were not included: they were traditionally handled by private or religious patronage, not by the Mughal government.) The Nawab retained the Nizamat (law and order). This created the Dual Government. Guided by Orientalism ("rule India the Indian way"), the EIC did not rush to impose its own system.Muhammad Reza Khan continued to head both the Diwani (on the EIC's behalf) and the Nizamat (on the Nawab's behalf).Indian officials remained the effective decision-makers on the ground. The EIC was mainly concerned with collecting land revenue. Outcome: revenue collection was poor; law and order deteriorated, made catastrophic by the Great Bengal Famine of 1770, which killed roughly one-third of Bengal's population. There is no ink on slide 11, but its typed outcome row carries a starred note: "Poverty leads to Crimes". Hunger pushed people into crime, so law and order failed because of the famine, and the famine was worsened by a hands-off administration. (For the Dual Government itself, Diwani versus Nizamat and Reza Khan as the EIC's Diwan, see Chapter 10.) 2.4 Direct Government (1772) and the judicial plan of Hastings 73-85 In 1772Hastings 73-85 (Governor from 1772, GG of Bengal 1773-1785) ended the Dual Government and took direct administration of both the Diwani and the Nizamat. Rationale: EIC administration, based on rule of law and equality before law, would be fairer and more efficient and would firmly establish British authority. (The ideology shifts slightly from pure Orientalism to a hybrid: rule more directly, but still use Indian legal frameworks.) Diwani (civil) courts at the district The British DC is the judge, assisted by Pandits and Maulvis Personal laws continued in marriage and inheritance Nizamat (criminal) courts at the district Kazis and Muftis continue as judges, now supervised by the European DC The British thought law and order too sensitive to replace fully Sadar Diwani Adalat and Sadar Nizamat Adalat Headed by the Governor (from 1773, the GG of Bengal) and his Council members The top of both ladders passes to the Company Teacher's board: 1772 CHANGES Muhammad Reza Khan (Naib Nazim) was imprisoned without trial from 1772 to 1774, accused of corruption and poor law-and-order maintenance. Conditions did not improve, so he was released in 1774 and reinstated as head of the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Why Kazis and Muftis stayed in the criminal courts: "Law and order (L and O) = sensitive, therefore the British continue with K and M as J." Taking over civil justice was safe; taking over criminal justice from the Muslim judges was too risky, so the DC only supervises there. Civil: the DC sits as judge. Criminal: the DC watches. 2.4.1 The changes of 1773 Two further adjustments: 1. A proper attempt at separation of revenue and judicial powers: an officer serving as DC was not to serve as judge too. In practice the overlap remained, but the principle was established. 2. To bring justice physically closer to the people, the district-level Diwani Adalats were replaced by 18 Mofussil courts, each headed by a European judge. Teacher's board: 1773 Act (Mofussil = rural areas and countryside districts below the district headquarters.) "PROPER SoP @ DC by CW 86-93." The handout calls 1773 a "proper attempt" at separation; the teacher corrects the weight of the word: the real, proper Separation of Powers at the level of the DC was done by Cornwallis 86-93 in 1793. In 1773 it was only the principle. Expect the exam to attach the DC's loss of judicial power to 1793 and Cornwallis 86-93 (this is Prelims 2010). 1773 versus 1793, do not mix.1773 (Hastings 73-85): separation attempted, overlap remained, 18 Mofussil courts.1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): the DC is stripped of all judicial powers, the 18 Mofussil courts are abolished and the district Diwani Adalats come back (the teacher's slide 19 note: "Mofussil courts ended, DA back"). 2.4.2 The Supreme Court (1774) The Regulating Act 1773 led to a Supreme Court in Calcutta in 1774, specifically to hear cases involving British subjects in Bengal, under British law. (British people, British judges, British law: a completely separate judicial track.) Supreme Courts followed in Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823). The Supreme Court was entirely separate from the Indian court hierarchy. Teacher's board: 1774, in yellow circle The 1774 picture on one board:SDA headed by the GG; SNA headed by Naib Nazim Md Reza Khan (reinstated 1774); Mofussil courts with a European judge assisted by Pandits and Maulvis; Nizamat courts with Kazi and Mufti under the European DC's supervision. The Supreme Court sits outside this ladder, only for Britishers. 2.4.3 Codification of laws 1775: a committee of 11 Pandits compiled Hindu law into a single coherent code so courts could interpret it uniformly. The English translation was published as the Gentoo Code (1776). ("Gentoo" comes from the Portuguese "Gentios," a derogatory term for Hindus, used because Hindus worshipped multiple Gods unlike monotheistic Christians.) 1778: a similar effort for Islamic law. Because of Mughal rule, Islamic law was already well organised, so the EIC simply translated the most authoritative existing Arabic legal manual, the Al-Hidayah, first into Persian by Indian scholars and then into English as The Hedaya (1791). The Code of 1781 made written orders compulsory and prescribed rules for court functioning. "WRITTEN LAW": this answers question 2 of slide 4 (written or discretion?). "ENGLISH WRITTEN": the Gentoo Code and the Hedaya are both the English written versions of Indian law, so British judges could use them. The Code of 1781 is boxed "in Bengal": it applied only in Bengal (see slide 22 below). 2.5 The Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (judiciary) Cornwallis 86-93 (GG 1786-1793) introduced the most systematic judicial reform of the early period. He is rightly called the father of civil services, but his influence on the judiciary was equally significant. 2.5.1 Why did Cornwallis 86-93 reform the judiciary? He had just introduced the Permanent Settlement of 1793 (PS1793), creating a new class of large zamindars as private property owners. For this to work, zamindars needed secure property rights:courts they could trust, and revenue officials who could not harass them. An officer who collected your tax should not also be the judge hearing your appeal against his own actions. So Cornwallis 86-93 properly implemented Separation of Powers at the level of the DC: the District Collector was stripped of all judicial powers and confined to revenue collection and administration. Teacher's board: why Cornwallis separated powers "Imagine": PS1793 has a sunset clause (on his board, applying it lands the zamindar's estate up for auction). Suppose the DC applies the sunset clause on a zamindar (Z) and his land goes up for auction. The zamindar files a case in the Diwani Adalat. What if the judge is the same DC? Then there is a conflict of interest, and security of property falls for the zamindar (he draws a sad face). That is why the DC could no longer be a judge. Beside it, in yellow: Cornwallis 86-93 = AUTHORITARIAN, therefore he removed Indians from all senior positions (the other side of the same reform). Prelims 2010 trap (handout, Section 2.5). "By a regulation in 1793, the DC was deprived of his judicial powers and made the collecting agent only. Why?" Correct: (c) absolute power in one person was undesirable (separation of powers; the post-PS1793 zamindar class needed independent courts). (a) efficiency of revenue collection is a partial truth, not the principal motivation. (b) "judicial power must be European-only, revenue can be Indian" is wrong: Cornwallis 86-93 in fact removed Indians from all senior positions, including revenue.(d) "judicial work demanded deep India knowledge" is a partial truth, not the principal motivation. Teacher's board: 1793 CW 86-93 CODE 2.5.2 In civil matters The 18 Mofussil courts were replaced by Diwani Adalats at the district level and City Courts for urban areas. Bengal was divided into four divisions: Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta and Dacca, and a Provincial Court of Appeal was set up in each. Appeals: district Diwani Adalats and City Courts, then the Provincial Court of Appeal, then the Sadar Diwani Adalat, shifted from Murshidabad to Calcutta. Personal laws of Hindus and Muslims continued in civil matters. PS1793 governed land revenue disputes. Per Charter Act 1793, all regulations for governing Bengal were codified, written orders made compulsory and laws printed in the vernaculars so people could know their rights. The Code of 1781 versus the Code of 1793: the difference is the ISSUING AUTHORITY. The 1781 code (by Hastings, applying only to Bengal) was issued by the GG (in Bengal), so a future GG could change it. The 1793 Code came through the Charter Act 1793, so it was issued by the British Parliament (the circled P) and carries more weight. Next to the Charter Act 1793 row he writes "By Br (P)": British Parliament. 2.5.3 In criminal matters Faujdari / Nizamat Adalats at the district level were abolished. Four Provincial Courts of Circuit were set up in the four divisions. A Court of Circuit is a court that physically moves around its division, hearing cases in different areas in rotation. This eliminated the need for a district-level criminal court. Appeals from the Courts of Circuit went to the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Islamic law continued in criminal matters, but with British legal modifications. This hybrid was Anglo-Muhammadan law. For about 70 years, until the Indian Penal Code 1860, courts applied it. The circle on slide 21: a Court of Circuit spends week 1 in district 1, week 2 in district 2, week 3 in district 3, week 4 in district 4, then returns to week 1. It is a travelling bench, so no district needs its own criminal court. He underlines Anglo-Muhammadan law and IPC 1860 and adds the three codes: CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861 (see Section 2.7). 2.5.4 Anglo-Muhammadan law in practice: three examples (handout only, no class notes) Handout only (no class notes). The slide (23) stops at the name "Anglo-Muhammadan law"; the three examples below come from the handout alone. A: weapon rule replaced by intent rule Whether a killing was capital murder depended on the weapon used: a sharp iron instrument (sword) meant murder; strangling, drowning or a heavy stone was often a lesser crime (the instrument was not "designed" to draw blood) He abolished this loophole: the intent of the accused decides, not the instrument. This matches the modern principle of mens rea B: the end of "blood money" (Diyat) Murder was largely a private dispute between families: the victim's heirs could pardon the killer for financial compensation (blood money, Diyat) Relatives could no longer pardon a murderer. This set the principle that a major crime is an offence against the State, not just a private injury C: abolition of mutilation The standard punishment for serious theft or dacoity was amputation of a hand or foot The EIC completely outlawed mutilation and replaced it with hard labour and rigorous imprisonment, typically 7 to 14 years 2.5.5 Personnel and a new profession: lawyers Cornwallis 86-93 was authoritarian. He removed Indians from all senior positions.All courts were headed by European officials. Kazis and Muftis were retained only as assistants, not judges. The office of Naib Nazim was abolished. One progressive change: lawyers were now permitted to appear in courts. Cornwallis 1793: Personnel and a New Profession This created a new professional class, the Indian lawyer, and, along with PS1793 (which made land a tradeable commodity), also a class of property dealers. "[NA ABOLISHED]": the Nizamat Adalat at district level is gone. "Cornwallis 86-93, father of: CS (civil services), property dealers, lawyer." One man, three offspring. Under the fork there is a short word that reads like "SHO" (the station house officer, which would be his police Daroga of Section 4.3): . 2.5.6 Why the new system increased litigation (class slide only, not in the handout) Lecture 20, slide 25 only (the handout does not carry this table). The slide gives three reasons litigation rose after PS1793, with no ink on it. 1. Separation of Powers (key reason) The DC lost all judicial and magisterial powers. Earlier the Collector could resolve revenue disputes swiftly and informally on the spot; after 1793 every such dispute had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats 2. Abolition of court fees Cornwallis 86-93 initially abolished court fees to make justice "accessible," which instantly flooded the courts with genuine and frivolous suits.Fees were reimposed just 2 years later, in 1795 3. A legal profession Formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) and a rigid hierarchy of appeals:cases were deliberately prolonged and appealed 2.6 Judicial system in Ryotwari areas The Bengal model of separated judicial and revenue functions worked in a zamindari system. In Ryotwari areas, where the ryot is recognised as the direct landowner, conditions were very different: A very large number of small landowners meant a very large number of land-related disputes. District courts were physically distant for poor ryots in villages. Judicial System in Ryotwari Areas Madras, 1814: the Bengal system was replaced on Munro's advice.Separation of judicial and revenue powers was ended. The European DC and his subordinates were given judicial powers so disputes could be resolved at the ground level. (Less paperwork, less travel, faster justice, at least in theory.) This led to greater Indianisation at the lower judiciary, because the DC's subordinates included Indian officials. The downside: enormous concentration of power in one official. The DC now collected taxes, maintained order and judged disputes, including disputes arising from his own tax collection decisions. Bombay, 1819: the same Ryotwari system was applied by Elphinstone, a follower of Munro's philosophy. Why Bengal separated and Madras merged: "WHR (where) the number of landowners is LESS" (the line points at "zamindari"): in a zamindari area there are few big landowners, so few disputes and a distant court is workable. In a ryotwari area the landowners are many, so the courts must come to the village. On the downside row he adds "+ his juniors": the DC's juniors (the subordinates, including Indians) also gain judicial powers. The Madras Torture Commission Report of 1855 is his example of what the concentrated power led to: "oppression by Mirasidars revealed." Learn the fact once, 1855, Madras Torture Commission, oppression exposed, and use it in either answer. 2.7 Charter Act 1833 (judicial impact) The Charter Act of 1833 made the GG of India the single central legislative authority for all of British India, and the laws passed were to apply equally to Indians and Britishers alike. (A major shift: one law for everyone, regardless of race.) One Law Member was added to the GG's Council: Thomas Macaulay was appointed, and a Law Commission (1834) was set up under him to codify all laws systematically. Codification was substantially complete by 1837, but full implementation came after 1857: Civil Procedure Code (CPC) 1859 Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860 Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) 1861 Subordinate judicial positions below the rank of District Judge were opened to Indians. Impact on the common Indian: justice became psychologically distant (new laws were western, complex and unfamiliar), physically distant for rural areas and financially distant (legal fees few could afford). The system was more systematic, but it served the educated and propertied far better than the poor. "Personal laws continued in personal matters": even with the IPC, CPC and CrPC, marriage and inheritance stayed under Hindu and Muslim personal law."Indianisation of the lower J": the opening of posts below District Judge is the lower judiciary's Indianisation (note how it follows the 1814 Madras Indianisation in Section 2.6). "Western Edu 1835": the new western, English-language law goes with western education from 1835 (Chapter 19: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture): the English-educated class is the one that could use the new courts. 2.8 Reforms by Bentinck 28-35 (GG 1828-33; GG of India 1833-35) Concept versus reality.In concept the polity has three equal organs: L (legislature), E (executive), J (judiciary).In reality the E is the top prestige:DC and senior civil servants want to be in E, and an inefficient officer is posted as a punishment to the Divisional Court. So the judiciary (J) was the dumping ground. This is the setup for why Bentinck 28-35 abolished those courts. Teacher's board: Bentinck 28-35, "Decs in (J)" (decisions in the judiciary) Teacher's board: Bentinck 28-35 Reforms Bentinck 28-35 abolished the divisional courts: both the Provincial Courts of Appeal (civil) and the Courts of Circuit (criminal) that Cornwallis 86-93 had created. Why: these courts had become parking grounds for inefficient officers (punishment postings for non-performers), which contributed to high pendency.High-ranking officers also meant high State expenditure, so the courts were ended as a fiscal-prudence measure. Transfer:judicial powers and pending cases went to District Judges. After Bentinck 28-35 the ladders are shorter: civil: District Diwani Adalat + City Courts go straight up to the SDA (the four Provincial Courts of Appeal are crossed out); criminal: Nizamat Adalat goes straight up to the SNA (the four Courts of Circuit are crossed out). He underlines "high State expenditure" on slide 30 and writes "86-93" (small, no name) beside "Cornwallis 86-93 had created": the courts he removed were Cornwallis 86-93's. Reforms by William Bentinck (GG 1828-33; GG of India 1833-35) 1835, language of the courts:Persian was replaced:vernaculars in the lower courts and English in the higher courts.Legal backing: Act XXIX of 1837. The removal caused anxiety among Muslim elites, because Persian education had been an important pathway to administrative careers. Courts for the Northwest Provinces: he created a Sadar Diwani Adalat and a Sadar Nizamat Adalat in the Northwest Provinces (the portion of Awadh annexed in 1801, given full province status in 1836), so people from this region did not have to travel to Bengal to file appeals. The NWP circle:1801 (the Awadh portion annexed) leads down to NWP 1836, a province with full status; the other oval is the Bengal Presidency, and the dotted line between them is written "Distance." Appeals to Calcutta meant a long journey, so (his inserted word) the NWP got its own two Sadar courts. Context on Persian (slide 31, typeset, no ink). Persian was introduced under the Delhi Sultanate in the 13th century. It got a major boost when Humayun 30-40, to win military support from Persia's Safavid dynasty to reclaim his throne from the Suri Dynasty (1540-55), accepted the condition of promoting Persian.Akbar 56-05, with finance minister Todar Mal, made Persian compulsory for all administrative records. 2.9 Indian High Courts Act 1861 and 2.10 the Federal Court (GOI Act 1935) The Indian High Courts Act 1861 led to High Courts in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta in 1862. The Calcutta High Court was created by merging three existing courts: the Sadar Diwani Adalat, the Sadar Nizamat Adalat and the Supreme Court at Calcutta. This finally ended the dual-track system of separate courts for Indians and the British. The GOI Act 1935, implemented from 1937, established a Federal Court, the direct ancestor of today's Supreme Court of India. It dealt with inter-governmental disputes (Centre versus Province, Province versus Province) and heard appeals from High Courts. Today's Supreme Court, set up under the Constitution of India 1950, continues this role with expanded jurisdiction. Because courts and revenue need officers, the question became who gets hired and how. Ask: what separates a service from mere employment, and what did Cornwallis 86-93 NOT introduce? 3.1 Issues in civil services, and what a "service" means The seven design questions for any civil service, as his board lists them: (1) nomination or examination? (2) if exam, by a specialised body like the UPSC or not? (3) syllabus: Indian or Western? (4) exam location: London, or India and London? (5) age limit: low or high? (6) organisation of the services (today IAS, IPS, IFS, IRS and more): one common exam or a separate exam for each service? (7) training: on the job or in a training institute? Read the rest of the chapter as the EIC's answers to these seven, in order. In any organisation officials may be simply employed, or organised into a service. A service means a pre-defined career path, fixed rules for pay, promotion and removal, and a clear structure of seniority and accountability: the difference between being an employee and being a member of a cadre. The history of the EIC's civil services is a move from a chaotic, patronage-based system to a structured, merit-based administrative cadre, with an extra tension: how many Indians would be allowed in? Teacher's board: "issues in CS" (in an oval) Without a service: "No career ladder" = "Total discretion," that is, total discretion in employment and in promotion. The boss alone decides who is hired and who is promoted. A service replaces discretion with rules. 3.2 Recruitment: from patronage to examination Initially EIC officials were recruited by nomination, not merit.Posts were either purchased or handed out through patronage. EIC Directors actively lobbied British Parliamentarians with offers of jobs for their sons. This bred corruption and incompetence. 3.3 Training Until 1800 Essentially on the job 1800-1806 Fort William College, Calcutta, set up by Wellesley 98-05 for training in Indian laws, customs and languages 1806-1858 Haileybury College, London (East India College) 1858 onwards British universities 3.4 Cornwallis 86-93: founder of civil services Cornwallis 86-93 brought the first proper structure to the civil services. He organised ("ORGanised") EIC employees into two tiers: Today's parallel Like today's Group A Like today's Group B Who Senior officers who signed a formal legal contract, a "covenant," with the EIC's Court of Directors in London before sailing to India Junior officers hired locally in India by the GG or provincial governors Pay and path High defined pay, clear career path Lower pay, less formal Access Under Cornwallis 86-93 reserved strictly for Europeans The space where Indians were allowed to serve: at first very low-level clerical roles, then Deputy Collectors and Deputy Magistrates by the 1830s-40s as the empire grew and needed cheaper local administrators "Organised employees into...": this is what the word "service" means (Section 3.1): from a pool of employees to ranked cadres. Beside the CCS access cell: Europeans-only = "Authoritarian" (the same Cornwallis 86-93 who removed Indians from all senior judicial posts). Beside the UCS: "Indians + British": the UCS was not Indians-only; it held both, which is why it is the space where Indians could enter. (b) Wellesley 98-05 is wrong: set up Fort William College 1800 for CCS training but did not create the service structure. Bentinck 28-35 went slightly further and encouraged recruitment of Indians to some senior positions. 3.6 Charter Act 1853: the exam opened to Indians The Charter Act of 1853 was a landmark: it mandated a Civil Service Examination for the CS and Indians were eligible to appear. 1854: a Select Committee of Parliament under Macaulay recommended replacing patronage-based recruitment with exam-based recruitment for a permanent civil service. This led to the Civil Services Commission (1854) in London, which held its first examination in 1855. Eligibility on paper did not mean access in practice: Age limit The maximum age ranged from 18 to 23,kept deliberately low.1859: the Crown cut the maximum entry age to 23. Then 22 in 1860, 21 in 1866, and 19 in 1876 (implemented 1878 so as not to hit aspirants already preparing) Syllabus Dominated by English Literature, designed to produce what Macaulay called "Brown Sahibs": Indians educated in English culture and values, culturally loyal to Britain Venue Held only in London For an Indian candidate Cost of travel to England; inferior preparation compared with British candidates; a syllabus that rewarded English cultural knowledge over Indian First Indians through 1864: Satyendranath Tagore (brother of Rabindranath Tagore) was the first Indian to clear the CCS exam.1867: four more Indians cleared it Why low age, English Literature and a London exam? "To prevent entry of Indians into CS." The age ladder itself he marks "not imp" (do not memorise every step). "Literature = source of values": English Literature on the syllabus carried English values, which is how the Brown Sahib is made. And the last row's point in his words: the exam tested "culture's knowledge," and western education in Britain was better than in India, so a Briton had the advantage. 3.7 The fight for Indianisation (1860 onwards) From 1860 the western-educated Indian middle class (WEMC), the very product of British educational policy, began demanding Indianisation of the civil services. Two core demands: Simultaneous examination in India (not just London). A higher maximum age limit. The British response was hostile.Post-1857 British administrators were insecure about Indian assertion and determined to keep Indians out of senior positions. Cornwallis 86-93 separated the judicial function from this officer (the DC/DM lost the power to be a judge), but the revenue and law-and-order functions stayed combined: DC (revenue) Collects land revenue, manages government land, maintains land records, collects various taxes The Mughal Diwani / Amalguzar function DM (law and order) Heads the district's criminal administration; coordinates with the SP to keep peace, prevent riots and issue executive orders such as Section 144 of the CrPC The Mughal Nizamat / Faujdari function Underlines on the DC / DM split:land revenue, government land, land records, taxes (the four jobs of the DC hat) and criminal administration and Faujdari (the DM hat). Underlining Faujdari and not Nizamat makes the DM the heir of the Mughal Faujdari function (district law and order), while the DC is the heir of the Diwani / Amalguzar function. This is the Section 2.2 ladder carried forward into today's district. Faujdar = SP, or DM = heir of Faujdari? Lecture 20 slide 8 says "Faujdar = like SP at DISTRICT" (Section 2.2), while slide 11 of Lecture 21 says the DM is the direct descendant of the Nizamat / Faujdari function. One consistent reading: the function (district law and order) passes to the DM as head, while the SP is the Faujdar's day-to-day counterpart. For an answer say "the DM inherits the Faujdari function; the Faujdar was like today's SP", and do not claim the DM is the Faujdar. 4.3.2 Result: the Daroga-Zamindar nexus A Daroga-Zamindar nexus quickly developed: zamindars bribed Darogas and kept private armed men (lathiyals). The nexus became the primary instrument of oppression of the rural poor in the early 1800s. The British blamed "Indian corruption" rather than the structural weaknesses of the system. 1799: Wellesley 98-05 restored police powers to zamindars, in effect admitting the Daroga system had not worked. 1802: the Daroga system was extended to Madras but was later abolished there too because of its failures. The resulting atrocities of revenue officials were exposed by the Madras Torture Commission report of 1855, which led to corrective measures. "Next: Gave Police Powers To DC's Juniors in MADRAS." He writes it between the 1802 and 1855 rows, so the board reads: the Daroga system was dropped in Madras, police powers then went to the DC's juniors (the Collector's subordinates, who were revenue officials), and the atrocities of revenue officials were exposed in 1855 by the Madras Torture Commission. It is the same "DC + his juniors" pattern he drew for the Ryotwari judicial system (Section 2.6, "+ his juniors"): in Madras the Collector's office ended up with revenue, police and judicial power at once. 4.4 The Police Act 1861 The Daroga system had failed. The British looked for a proven alternative and found it in the Irish Constabulary model: a centralised, hierarchical, quasi-military police force, effective in Ireland since 1787, designed as much for suppressing political agitation as for preventing ordinary crime. (The British were not primarily building a crime-prevention force; they were building a political control mechanism.) 4.4.1 Province-by-province road-test (pre-1861) Police Act 1861, the Irish Constabulary model, Lecture 21 slide 13 Sindh 1843 (annexed) Charles Napier, the military general who conquered Sindh, set up the Sindh Police on the Irish Constabulary model immediately after conquest Punjab 1849 Post-annexation Bombay 1853  Madras 1859  The 1st Police Commission (1860) was set up by Canning 56-62 under M.H. Court. It simply formalised what had already proved effective on the ground and borrowed heavily from the Sindh model when drafting the 1861 Police Act. A common UPSC trap: Charles Napier did NOT head the 1860 commission (many guidebooks wrongly say he did). Napier gave the blueprint (Sindh); M.H. Court's commission drew the national map using it. EACH Province, and the a/c chart. He underlines "EACH Province" and labels the idea "Concept of Provincial Police": the Act's novelty is a police force for every province. His chart: the IG is answerable (a/c, dotted) to the Governor / LG and the SP to the DM; the dotted arrows are the political accountability to civilian authority, overall a/c on the right. The solid arrows SI to SP to IG are the operational chain. The line SI to DM is crossed out: the Sub-Inspector no longer reports to the DC / DM as the Daroga did. He underlines the four exam points of the slide: Irish Constabulary model, 1st Police Commission (1860), M.H. Court, Sindh model (and the Napier trap is in the alert above). 4.4.2 The Police Act 1861 The Police Act, 1861 was passed in March 1861 by the GG's Council (as last restructured by the Charter Act 1853). (The Indian Councils Act 1861 came in August 1861 and created the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC); do not mix them.) It created the provincial police structure across all provinces: each Province to have its own police organisation, with a clear hierarchy: Inspector General (IG) The provincial police The Governor / Lieutenant Governor (LG) Superintendent of Police (SP) The district police The DC / DM Sub-Inspector (SI) The thana The SP (not to the DC as earlier) The Police Act 1861, provisions, Lecture 21 slide 15 Operational accountability ran upward through the police chain: SI, SP, IG.Political accountability ran to civilian authority: SP to DC/DM, IG to LG / Governor. This was only the organisational chart. In 1861 the British simply posted military officers or nominated European men into the senior posts: no formal cadre, no competitive exam, no unified service, just employees of provincial governments. The posts existed; the service did not yet. From 1857 onwards a "Police Raj" was created: Indians were excluded from all senior positions, and the emphasis was on effective policing, intelligence collection and political surveillance. Slide 15:"(not by Bn P)": the Police Act 1861 was passed by the GG's Council, not by the British Parliament (the contrast he keeps drawing with the Charter Act 1793, the 1919 Act and the 1935 Act). "Own" police organisation = own Resources and HR: the province gets its own money and its own staff. "Specialist" is underlined and linked to the circled Z and DC marked "non specialist": before 1861 the police work was done by non-specialists, the zamindar and the DC; now there is a specialist ladder (IG, SP, SI)."(not to DC as earlier)" is underlined: the SI reports to the SP. The bracket "e.g. Financial Control" sits beside the Accountability row (my reading: an example of how the civilian authority kept political control; the bracket's exact target is cramped:). Slide 16:"(IPS not created yet)" and IPS written over "cadre": the missing cadre is the future IPS (Section 4.4.3). "Police Raj" = "overuse of police"; and beside Emphasis: "ensure no repeat of 1857": intelligence and surveillance were meant to stop another revolt. 4.4.3 Formalisation into a structured cadre Formalisation into a structured cadre, 1893 to 1905, Lecture 21 slide 17 1893 First open competitive exam for senior police posts, held in London; top candidates became probationary Assistant Superintendents of Police under the Secretary of State for India 1902-03 Curzon 99-05 set up the 2nd Police Commission under Sir Andrew Fraser; report 1903. It organised superior police officers into one unified all-India cadre, the Imperial Police (IP) (informally the Indian Police); scheme implemented from about 1905 (Fraser's package) Provincial Police Service (PPS) created, with a new rank Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP) that accommodated Indians at officer level, always junior to the British IP.CID set up in every province, plus a central intelligence bureau, the Department of Criminal Intelligence (1903), forerunner of today's IB. But the IP itself stayed closed to Indians: Fraser did NOT recommend appointing Indians to it 1920 Direct entry into the IP officially opened to Indians (simultaneous exams in England and India from 1921), largely a result of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (GOI Act 1919) By 1931 Only 20% of SPs were Indians From 1939 More Indians posted as SP because British candidates were unavailable (recruited for World War II, 1939-45) 1948 The IP was administratively replaced by the Indian Police Service (IPS) by a Home Ministry resolution; statutory backing came from the All India Services Act, 1951 1861 built the structure, 1902-03 built the service, 1948-51 built the IPS. (Today's IPS is an All India Service under Article 312, with State police under State governments, directly inheriting the 1861 framework.) Slide 17: the door opened only at the junior end. He underlines Fraser, the 2nd Police Commission, the Imperial Police (IP), the Provincial Police Service, the DySP "but always junior to the British IP" and Fraser did "NOT recommend" appointing Indians to the IP: the package gave Indians a lower rank (PPS, DySP) and kept the top cadre closed, "preserving racial superiority at the top". He circles IPS in the 1902-03 cell: the Imperial Police created here is the ancestor of today's IPS (the 1948 step is on slide 18). His diagram (IB) DCI over CID1, CID2, CIDn shows the central Department of Criminal Intelligence (1903), forerunner of the IB, above a CID in every province.Slide 18: he underlines simultaneous exams, India from 1921, 20% of SPs were Indians, More Indians posted as SP, IPS via a Home Ministry resolution, All India Services Act 1951, and brackets "(* ICS exam in India: 1922)" beside the 1920 row: the police exam in India began in 1921, the ICS exam in India in 1922.

items.t: 5 · The three-pillar administrative legacy (handout and Lecture 21 slides 19 to 21)
items.x: Because each pillar moved only when pushed, the handout ends with one pattern. Ask: which two triggers drove reform, and what three legacies were left? The EIC's administrative evolution across judiciary, civil services and police shows a consistent pattern: structural improvement followed political convenience, not principle. Each major reform was triggered by a crisis (the Great Bengal Famine 1770, the 1857 revolt) or was a concession wrested by the Indian National Movement after sustained pressure. The British never voluntarily Indianised their administration beyond what was economically necessary (to reduce costs) or politically unavoidable (to manage nationalist pressure). They left behind, however inadvertently, a set of institutions that independent India would inherit, adapt and build upon:codified law, an organised civil service, a hierarchical police. Judiciary Diwani Adalats (civil; Pandits and Maulvis) plus Nizamat Adalats (criminal; Kazis, Muftis, Faujdars) Hastings 73-85's 1772 plan;1774 Supreme Court at Calcutta;Cornwallis 86-93 Code 1793 with Anglo-Muhammadan law Charter Act 1833 (Macaulay, Law Commission 1834) leading to CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861;High Courts Act 1861 (High Courts at Madras, Bombay, Calcutta 1862) GOI Act 1935: Federal Court (1937), then Supreme Court of India 1950; CPC, IPC and CrPC replaced in 2024 by BNS, BNSS and BSA Civil services Mansabdari nobility under Mughal patronage Cornwallis 86-93 (1793): founder of CCS plus UCS; salaries raised; seniority for promotion Charter 1853: exam mandated, Indians eligible (London only); ICS renamed by executive order 1892 (Lansdowne 88-94, per Aitchison 1887, NOT by ICA 1892) Lee Commission 1923 leading to PSC 1926;GOI 1935 Federal PSC (1937) then UPSC 1950 (Article 378);AIS under Article 312 Police Naib Nazim to Faujdars (rural) and Kotwals (towns), plus Zamindars (villages) Hastings 73-85's 1781 reforms;Cornwallis 86-93's Daroga System 1793 (failed through the Daroga-Zamindar nexus) Irish Constabulary road-test (Sindh 1843 Napier, Punjab 1849, Bombay 1853, Madras 1859); 1st Police Commission 1860 (M.H. Court) leading to the Police Act 1861 (March 1861) 2nd Police Commission 1902-03 (Fraser) leading to the Imperial Police (IP) cadre;1948 Home Ministry resolution leading to the IPS;AIS Act 1951 plus Article 312 The handout's scrambled table. In the PDF this summary table is broken (words split across cells; the last cell of the judiciary row is cut). The version above is rebuilt from the readable pieces; the one unclear part is the final words of the judiciary "modern legacy" cell, which read "CPC/IPC/CrPC replaced 2024 by BNS/BNSS/BS" and are cut off after "BS" [the handout page 193 is cut off here; Lecture 21 slide 20 prints the full set as BNS/BNSS/BSA, so the table above uses BSA]. The 2024 replacement appears only in this table and on Lecture 21 slide 20. Slides 19 to 21 carry no ink. Slide 19 is the typed pattern (reform followed political convenience, never voluntary Indianisation beyond cost or politics, and the inherited institutions); slides 20 and 21 are the matrix above in clean form, so the scrambled handout table can be checked against them.

items.t: 6 · The class PYQs and the Governor-General board (Lecture 21, slides 22 to 32)
items.x: Because the teacher then tested the chapter on real papers, the answers sit on the slides. Ask: why is Banerji the only one dismissed, why is Cornwallis 86-93 wrong for Ryotwari, and where do the reign-year codes come from? Slides 22 to 31 are four PYQs, each with a question slide and typed answer slides; slide 32 is a board of Governor-General and Viceroy tenures. The teacher's ink is only on the question slides (25, 27, 29) and on the board. Slides 22 to 24 and 26, 28, 30, 31 are typed. 6.1 Prelims 2010: why the DC lost his judicial powers (slides 22 to 24) No ink on these three slides. The answer is (c), exactly as in the alert in Section 2.5.1. Slide 24 gives the hook: "Tax-man can't be judge of his own tax: PS1793 zamindars needed clean courts, so Cornwallis split the hat," and why the others fail: (a) revenue efficiency was a side-benefit, not the principal motive; (b) wrong on facts, because Cornwallis 86-93 removed Indians from all senior positions; (d) "the DC lacked law training" is at best a partial truth, because the trigger was the conflict of interest after PS1793. 6.2 Prelims 2010: who created the CCS (slides 25 and 26) "1892" underlined beside the question. The question says the CCS "later came to be known as the ICS": the renaming is 1892, by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94 (Aitchison 1887), not ICA 1892; the creation is 1793, Cornwallis 86-93. Keep the two dates apart and the options sort themselves. Slide 26's reasons: (a) Hastings 73-85 ended the Dual Government and built the judicial plan of 1772-74 but did not create the CCS; (b) Wellesley 98-05 set up Fort William College (1800-1806) for training, and "the cadre structure pre-dated him by 7 years" (1793 to 1800); (d) Bentinck 28-35 opened the UCS to Indians under the Charter Act 1833, 40 years after Cornwallis 86-93. Its hook: "Cornwallis = Covenant: sign the contract in London, sail to India, draw senior pay." 6.3 Prelims 1999: the Indian leader dismissed from the ICS (slides 27 and 28) A tick on (b) Surendranath Banerji; circled F on Tagore, Dutt and Bose. The slide 28 reasons, which are the reasons for each F: Tagore (1864, the first Indian to clear the exam, Section 3.6) had a full ICS career and was not dismissed; R.C. Dutt (cleared 1869) retired honourably as a Divisional Commissioner;S.C. Bose cleared the exam in 1920 and resigned in 1921 in protest, and a resignation is not a dismissal.Banerji was among the four who cleared in 1867 and was dismissed in 1874 on a technical, age-related ground, a politically motivated removal that made him one of the earliest militant Moderates. The wider context (post-1857 insecurity, Indians kept out of senior posts) is Section 3.7. Slide only (not in the handout): the handout says only "1867: four more Indians cleared it". Banerji, Dutt and Bose, with the dates 1874, 1869, 1920 and 1921, come from slides 27 and 28 alone; use them for this question and do not mix them with the handout's table. 6.4 Prelims 2017: who introduced Ryotwari (slides 29 to 31) Three tags on three names.Cornwallis "86-93" = the Permanent Settlement 1793 in Bengal, the opposite (zamindari) system, so every option containing 1 is wrong. Alexander Read "1792 - Baramahal" = the early experiment. Munro "G (Ma) 1820-27" (I read it as Governor of Madras, as slide 30 says "later Governor of Madras") = the man who delivered the mature Ryotwari from 1820. Answer (c) 2 and 3 only. Slide 31's hook: "Ryotwari = Read drafted, Munro delivered: Madras 1820. Cornwallis stayed in Bengal with zamindars." Munro 1814 versus 1820: two different things. In Section 2.6 the Bengal judicial model was replaced in Madras in 1814 on Munro's advice (the DC regained judicial powers), and Bombay followed in 1819 under Elphinstone, "a follower of Munro's philosophy". The 1820 on this PYQ is the formal rollout of the Ryotwari revenue settlement in Madras (slide 30). Do not swap them; the settlement itself belongs to Chapter 16: Land Revenue Systems. 6.5 The Governor-General and Viceroy board (slide 32) The board is the source of the reign-year codes used in this notebook. It has no chapter content, only the list below, written as he writes it. Every code the chapter uses for a Governor-General or Viceroy matches it: Hastings 73-85, Cornwallis 86-93, Wellesley 98-05, Bentinck 28-35, Canning 56-62, Dufferin 84-88, Lansdowne 88-94, Curzon 99-05, Chelmsford 16-21. (Lytton 76-80, in the chapter from slide 6 of this lecture, and Ripon 80-84, from the handout, are not on the board.) W. HASTINGS 73-85 MINTO 05-10 CORNWALLIS 86-93 HARDINGE 10-16 SHORE 94-98 CHELMSFORD 16-21 WELLESLEY 98-05 READING 21-26 CORNWALLIS 86-93 (months) IRWIN 26-31 F. HASTINGS 13-23 WELLINGDON 31-36 BENTINCK 28-35 LINLITHGOW 36-43 DALHOUSIE 48-56 WAVELL 43-47 CANNING 56-62 (MAYO 69-72 written to its left) MTB 1947-48 DUFFERIN 84-88  LANSDOWNE 88-94  CURZON 99-05  Handwritten board, Lecture 21 slide 32: Governor-General and Viceroy tenures in two columns, no typed text Two Hastings, one code each. The board writes W. HASTINGS 73-85 (Warren, the Hastings of this chapter) and F. HASTINGS 13-23 (Francis). The code 73-85 belongs only to Warren Hastings; never put it on the other. Three oddities on the board: Cornwallis 86-93 appears a second time with "(months)" in brackets after Wellesley 98-05 (as written; what the bracket marks); MAYO 69-72 is written to the left and joined to Canning's row by a line, though he comes after Canning 56-62; and the right column spells WELLINGDON (31-36) and abbreviates Mountbatten as MTB 1947-48.

A trading company must run a state. Administration is the machinery by which a State carries out its policies, laws and schemes on the ground. When the EIC turned from a trading company into a Company State (1765-1858; the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function) it had to decide how much Indian machinery to keep and how much to replace. Three pillars carry the story: judiciary, civil services and police. The teacher calls the whole chapter the history of Public Administration in British India. The Mughal ladders of Bengal. Before 1772 Bengal had two separate hierarchies. In civil matters (Diwani) courts ran up to the Sadar Diwani Adalat, with Pandits and Maulvis judging personal law and the Zamindar's Kachari handling land revenue disputes. In criminal matters (Nizamat) Islamic law applied to everyone: the Kazi judged, the Mufti interpreted and the Faujdar, like today's SP, caught the accused and carried out the sentence. One man, two hats. After the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 the EIC held the Diwani and the Nawab kept the Nizamat: a Dual Government. Guided by Orientalism, the EIC let Muhammad Reza Khan head both and cared mainly about revenue. Revenue fell, law and order broke down, and the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed about one-third of Bengal. Hastings 73-85 steps in. In 1772 Hastings 73-85 ended the Dual Government. The British DC sat as judge in the civil courts, while in criminal courts the Kazi and Mufti stayed as judges under the DC's watch, because law and order was too sensitive to replace. The Regulating Act 1773 led to the Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774 for British subjects under British law, with Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823) to follow. Laws were written down too: the Gentoo Code (1776), the Hedaya (1791) and the Code of 1781. Cornwallis 86-93's Code of 1793. With the Permanent Settlement of 1793, zamindars became property owners and needed courts they could trust: if the DC auctioned an estate and then judged the owner's appeal, there was a conflict of interest. Cornwallis 86-93 stripped the DC of all judicial power (the Prelims 2010 answer), divided Bengal into four divisions with Provincial Courts of Appeal and Courts of Circuit, created Anglo-Muhammadan law, removed Indians from all senior posts and permitted lawyers. Ryotwari, Bentinck 28-35 and the codes. Courts clogged after 1793: the DC could no longer settle disputes on the spot, court fees were abolished (back in 1795), and lawyers prolonged cases. In Ryotwari areas, with many small landowners, Madras (1814, on Munro's advice) and Bombay (1819, Elphinstone) merged the DC's roles again. Bentinck 28-35 abolished the divisional courts, replaced Persian in 1835, and the Charter Act 1833's Law Commission under Macaulay led to the CPC 1859, IPC 1860 and CrPC 1861. High Courts came in 1862 and the Federal Court in 1937. From patronage to a service. A service means a career ladder with rules, not total discretion. Early EIC officials came by nomination and patronage, and Directors lobbied Parliamentarians with jobs for their sons. Cornwallis 86-93 organised them into the Covenanted Civil Service (senior, signed a covenant in London, Europeans only, like Group A) and the Uncovenanted (junior, hired locally, where Indians served, like Group B), with higher pay, curbed private trade and strict seniority; but entry stayed by nomination until the Charter Act 1853. The exam and its three locks. The Charter Act 1853 mandated an exam for the CCS and the first exam was held in London in 1855. Indians were eligible on paper, but the age limit was kept low, the syllabus was dominated by English Literature (to produce Macaulay's Brown Sahibs) and the venue was London. Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to clear it in 1864 and four more followed in 1867. The long fight for Indianisation. From 1860 the WEMC demanded a simultaneous exam in India and a higher age limit. The British answered with Lytton 76-80's lateral entry for loyal elite Indians (a Statutory Civil Services Act the teacher calls unimportant). Aitchison 1887 led to the three tiers ICS, PCS and Subordinate in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94; Islington (1912, report 1917) offered 25% yet refused a simultaneous exam, which the teacher marks as a CONTRADICTION; the GOI Act 1919 brought the exam to India in 1922, the PSC in 1926 and a 33% target; Lee (1923-24) set 20-40-40 and the PSC came in October 1926 with Ross Barker as first Chairman; the GOI Act 1935 gave the Federal PSC (1937), over 50% were Indianised by 1947, and Article 378 made it the UPSC in 1950. From Faujdar to Daroga. Under the Mughals the chain ran Naib Nazim, Faujdar, Kotwal, Zamindar. After the 1770 famine raised crime, Hastings 73-85 put English Magistrates in place of the Faujdars in 1781. Cornwallis 86-93 ended the zamindars' police powers in 1793: thanas of 30 square miles under an Indian Daroga, the DM supreme in his district. But a Daroga-Zamindar nexus of bribes and lathiyals oppressed the rural poor; Wellesley 98-05 restored the zamindars' powers in 1799, and the Madras trial of 1802 ended in the Torture Commission report of 1855. The Police Act 1861. The British turned to the Irish Constabulary model, a centralised, quasi-military force built as much for political control as for crime. It was road-tested in Sindh (1843, Charles Napier), Punjab (1849), Bombay (1853) and Madras (1859); M.H. Court's 1st Police Commission (1860), set up by Canning 56-62, borrowed from Sindh, and Napier did not head it. The Police Act (March 1861), passed by the GG's Council, set up the IG, SP and SI hierarchy (the SI reports to the SP, not the DC) but only posts, not a service. Fraser's commission (1902-03) created the Imperial Police cadre, closed to Indians; direct entry opened to Indians in 1920, yet only 20% of SPs were Indians by 1931; the IPS came in 1948 and the AIS Act in 1951. Crisis or pressure. Each major reform followed a crisis (the 1770 famine, the 1857 revolt) or a concession won by the Indian National Movement. The British Indianised only as far as cost or politics demanded. What they left behind, however inadvertently, was codified law, an organised civil service and a hierarchical police, which independent India inherited and adapted.

2025, 15 marks, 250 words: Phule's writings and efforts of social reform touched issues of almost all subaltern classes. Discuss Intro: Phule was the first reformer to attack caste, gender, class and economic exploitation together.Body: education (girls' school Pune 1848 with Savitribai; Hunter Commission 1882 memorandum); women (widow remarriage, against child marriage, infanticide prevention centre 1863); Dalits (Gulamgiri 1873, Satyashodhak Samaj 1873, Din Bandhu 1877); peasants (Cultivator's Whipcord 1881, night schools); workers (Bombay Millhands Association 1890 with Narayan Lokhande). Close: he spoke for the oppressed and organised them, bottom-up, unlike top-down upper-caste reformers 2021, 10 marks, 150 words: Trace the rise and growth of socio-religious reform movements with special reference to Young Bengal and Brahmo Samaj Intro: the shift from Orientalism after 1813, cultural nationalism and the Doctrine of Reason. Body: Young Bengal (Derozio, pure rationality, Society for Acquisition of General Knowledge 1838, failed for lack of faith engagement); Brahmo Samaj 1828 (monotheism, anti-Sati 1829, splits 1866 and 1878). Close: both stayed elite and urban; reason plus scripture worked better than reason alone 2019, 10 marks, 150 words: Examine the linkages between the 19th century "Indian Renaissance" and the emergence of national identity Intro: Europe's Renaissance chain and Bengal's parallel. Body: cultural nationalism (mild before 1857, strong after), the Doctrine of Reason turned on social practice and then on British rule, the Western Educated Middle Class. Close: from that class came the leaders of the Indian National Movement; Netaji called Vivekananda the spiritual father of the movement in Bengal 2017, 15 marks, 250 words: The women's question as part of 19th-century social reform: major issues and debates Intro: the British used women's status as the yardstick of civilisation, so reformers worked on women's issues. Body: Sati 1829, child marriage (IPC 1860, Age of Consent 1891, Rakhmabai), widows (1856 Act and its catch), infanticide (1870), polygamy, female education (Bethune 1849, Phule 1848, Vidyasagar's schools); debates: scripture versus logic, Tilak against Bhandarkar. Close: laws were top-down and the problem lay in society, so most reforms failed at scale

Story so far: the whole chapter is seven questions, from Renaissance to success and failure. Ask: where does each later section answer one of the seven? Teacher's outline of the chapter The chapter is seven questions. (1) Was there a Renaissance? (2) Why did it begin in Bengal? (3) Why in the 19th century? (4) What were the social issues? (5) What methods did reformers use: Press, People's movement, Laws (and for laws, the reformers "went to the British")? (6) The famous reformers. (7) Success or failure, and why? Everything below follows this order.

Because Europe's rebirth by reason changed religion, society, economy and polity, the Bengal reformers borrowed the same method. Ask: what did the reformers take from the past, and what did they use to fix it? The word Renaissance first named Western Europe's 14th-century intellectual rebirth: a conscious recovery of ancient learning, driven by reason and aimed at human welfare. 19th-century Bengal looked strikingly similar: the same problems: an oppressive priestly establishment misusing social power, no modern education,birth-based privilege and deep poverty; the same response: reformers reached back into ancient Indian scriptures to restore what was great, and used reason and rationality to remove what was not. The chain of consequences. The European Renaissance triggered a cascade: Reformation in religion, end of Feudalism in society, Capitalism in economy, Enlightenment in polity, and the Scientific and Industrial Revolutions. The Bengal Renaissance had a similar cascading effect: it fed a modern Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC), and from that class came the leaders of the Indian National Movement. Renaissance = re-birth of society, and it is the mother of Capitalism, Enlightenment and the Humanities. Before it (Lecture 21, slides 35 and 36) he drew Europe in the Dark Ages: education was theology; the Church taught "we are born to suffer", no happiness on earth; wealth was concentrated and no scope of being rich; no democracy. Then Venice and Genoa earned cash from trade, new towns in port areas grew, and cash became a source of power (against land). The theme turned to "Happiness of the Human", so each field changed: art (portrait painting), economy (capitalism: security of property, equality of opportunity, "right to be rich"), society (inter-personal relations, rights and obligations in marriage, and so social reforms), polity (fundamental rights, democracy, Enlightenment 17th-18th c), technology (medicine, machines, the Industrial Revolution 1750-1850, voyages of discovery 16th c) and psychology/philosophy.The method of the Renaissance is the "method of R": reason. Teacher's board: the Method of the Renaissance, "Like UPSC aspirant" The Renaissance method has two steps, "like a UPSC aspirant".Step 1: go back to the golden past (ancient Greek and Roman scriptures), copy-paste it to today's times, and realise it will not work.Step 2: do reason, logic, rationality. So: learn from the past, then find new solutions through the Doctrine of Logic/Reason/Rationality (DoL/R/R). He links this to the Constitution 1950: Scientific Temperament, which is a Fundamental Duty. Why "socio-religious reform" and not simply "social reform"? In India religion did not merely coexist with social practice, it determined it.Sati, child marriage, caste hierarchy, widow remarriage and polygamy were all justified by selective interpretations of religious texts. You could not touch the social practice without confronting the religious sanction behind it. Teacher's board: Social Reform splits into Socio-Religious Reforms versus Social Reform Socio-religious reformers use Logic AND Religion; pure social reformers use only Logic. Because the masses are deeply religious, a practice rooted in religion can only be changed by reforming or re-interpreting the religion. The Derozians are social reformers, not socio-religious reformers: they used only logic to convince people and the government. That is exactly why they failed (Section 7).

Because reformers had a method, they listed the evils it must tackle. Ask: which of these were never evil in themselves, only distorted? Reformers identified these major social ills: education, idolatry, priestcraft, child marriage, widow remarriage, female infanticide, polygamy, polytheism and casteism. A small mismatch. The handout's list has nine ills; the teacher's board (slide 34) draws ten, adding child sacrifice (Sagar Island 1803, Section 6). Learn ten. Not every item is evil in itself.Idol worship helps a worshipper concentrate spiritual energy; not all priests are negative:Ramakrishna Paramhansa himself was a temple priest.Polytheism is inherently pluralistic and so secular in character. Social ills arise when there is no genuine spirituality, when social power is misused, and when society is fragmented by divisions. The problem was never the practice itself but its distortion.

items.t: 3 · Why social reform began in the 19th century, and why in Bengal
items.x: Because the evils were old, something new must have started the reform. Ask: what did the British (Liberals, Evangelists, cultural nationalism) and Western education add? 3.1 The role of the British After 1813 the British moved away from Orientalism (which treated Indian culture and learning as worthy of respect and study) towards a new coalition of Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists, who actively supported Western education and social reform. The Evangelists also promoted conversion to Christianity, which created fear among Indians for the survival of their religion and pressure to reform from within. Why the government mattered: the government has L (legislative) and E (executive) power, and financial and military resources (MR); so if the Government wants, social reform becomes possible. After 1813 the British criticised Indian civilisation (Chapter 15), and the answer to that criticism was cultural nationalism. After 1857 the British ideology became "Dogs and Indians not allowed". 3.2 Cultural nationalism as a response As the British moved away from Orientalism they argued that the greatness of ancient India was a myth. Indian reformers pushed back with cultural pride: "we will prove you wrong by cleaning up what has gone wrong and recovering what was great." This cultural nationalism ran through all 19th-century reform: mild before 1857, far stronger after. Colonialism has three faces (Lecture 22, slide 7), political, economic and cultural, and each calls up a nationalism. The cultural nationalism goal: "by studying scripture we will prove that our ancient civilisation [Vedas, Shastras] does not support social ills and supports reason"; the ancient past was great; in the present, social reform makes Indian society great. Board: Socio-Religious Reformers The "Ctrl+F" method.Step 1: identify the logical, ideal practice. Step 2: open the scriptures (like a PDF), press Ctrl+F, search for LOGIC and get "50 results".Step 3:go to the people with those 50 results. The target population is deeply religious, so this has better chances than a pure social reformer's bare argument. (He uses the same picture for Roy on Sati: "choose logic, then Ctrl+F logic in scripture".) 3.3 Western education (1835 onwards) Reformers educated in Western thought met the Doctrine of Reason:no practice, however old or sacred-seeming, is beyond rational scrutiny. It became their primary tool against irrational and inhumane practices. The teacher's logic chain (Lecture 21, slide 39; the board also reads "UPSC syllabus minus anything which glorifies India"):shift from Orientalism to Liberalism (1813+), so the government was interested in social reform for the White Man's Burden (WMB);Western education (1835) produced a WEMC motivated by Reason (R) in India, and social reform was the first step; the WEMC became the leaders of social reform. 3.4 Why in Bengal Why Bengal? (Lecture 21, slide 40) It was the political headquarters (the Governor General sat here), so Western education progressed most here. Later he adds the education growth profile of the three presidency cities (Section 24).

items.t: 4 · Who led the reforms, over time
items.x: Because the government held the legislative and executive power, the early reformers asked for its help. Ask: why did British interest fall after 1857? First half of the 19th century (pre-1857) Western-educated men from upper castes, willing to seek the colonial government's help to pass reform laws Willing to assist: it fitted the White Man's Burden (WMB), the colonial belief that it was the "civilised" Englishman's duty to uplift "backward" peoples Second half (post-1857) More culturally nationalistic leaders, some without Western education at all (the teacher's examples: Dayanand and Vivekananda, who focused on the masses) Far less interested in reform and far more overtly racist about Indian civilisation. The 1857 Revolt shook British confidence and bred contempt Pre-1857 reformers: WEMC, gradualists, wanted British support (legislative and executive power), used the press as their tool, did not build a mass movement, made top-down reforms, and at first neglected the sensitive issues (women, caste). Post-1857 the British ideology is "very up racism and authoritarianism". Board: Why did British focus on social reform decline after 1857? "EIC business function ended in 1833, therefore only the political function matters, i.e Why British interest fell after 1857. The EIC's business function ended in 1833, so only the State's (territory, T) motive remained. Social reform was a secondary motive; the primary motive was empire plus the Drain, political and economic colonialism. The Revolt came from fear among Indians for their religion and customs, so the British gave up the secondary motive. Slide 10 adds the ideology after 1857: more racism and more authoritarianism, "Indians are beyond reform".

Because the reformers differed, the teacher sorts them by method, belief and goal. Ask: where does each man sit on the gradual or radical line? Three axes: method, beliefs, goals. (Add the first teacher cut: social versus socio-religious reformers, Section 1.) Sec 5, Classifying the Reformers, with teacher's dates 5.1 By method No mass movement attempted:Ram Mohan Roy (the teacher: he spoke complex Sanskritised Bangla prose, so he did not even try). Built mass movements:Keshab Chandra Sen (1860s), Swami Dayanand Saraswati (1870s), Swami Vivekananda (1880s). Pure rationality:Derozio and Young Bengal. They failed to create a mass movement because their target people were religious and pure reason without faith did not move them. Rationality plus scripture was more successful: Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Dayanand, Vivekananda. Mass-movement builders use the press AND go to the people (they change hearts, values and attitudes), and are usually radical.Those who use only the press and work among the elite are "armchair intellectuals", usually gradualist. A separate axis: who wants British help (the L and E authority) and who does not. 5.2 By beliefs Logic and rationality are the final authority (if reason and scripture conflict, choose reason): pre-1857 reformers, Roy and his contemporaries, with milder cultural nationalism and ease with Western frameworks. The Vedas are infallible:Dayanand, Ramakrishna, Vivekananda, the post-1857 camp, with stronger cultural nationalism. Their answer was to recover the pure original Vedic teaching. Beside the Ramakrishna line: "Upanishads = main" and "Rig = main Veda"; and in the margin "Vedas have test of rational thought" (Dayanand's claim that the Vedas stand the test of reason). 5.3 By goals Gradual reform:Roy, Debendranath Tagore, the Brahmo Samaj, the Prarthana Samaj. They avoided sensitive issues such as caste and marriage practices for fear of alienating the masses they wanted to uplift. Radical, immediate reform:Derozio's Young Bengal, Keshab Chandra Sen, Dayanand, Vivekananda, Vidyasagar, who took up even the most sensitive issues and wanted fast change. Gradualists do "holey-holey" (slow) reform, are not full-time reformers, do "easy first, tough reform later", and argue "society is not ready yet".Radicals work in mission mode, can be full-time reformers, and do "all together, tough first". Teacher's board: Types of Reformers (1) Social versus Socio-Religious; (2) Gradualists versus Radical Overlaps are normal. The same man sits in several boxes: Roy is no-mass-movement, rationality-plus-scripture, reason-as-final-authority and gradualist; Keshab is a radical mass-movement builder; Vidyasagar is radical and rationality-plus-scripture but not a mass-movement builder. Build the table yourself from the teacher's rule "10 basic Qs on XYZ".

Because the State held executive power, it could ban one cruel practice early. Ask: was this a social reform or an early executive act? In 1803, Wellesley 98-05 banned child sacrifice at Sagar Island (Sagar Dwip, where the Ganga meets the Bay of Bengal, a major Hindu pilgrimage site) in Bengal. An early sign that the colonial government would use executive power against specific social practices. A concept for the next section (Lecture 22, slide 14: Derozio was a Eurasian).Before the 1911 census: a person of mixed parentage was a "Eurasian"; a European living in India was an "Anglo-Indian" (Anglo living in India). From the 1911 census: mixed parentage = Anglo-Indian; Europeans = "Europeans in India".

items.t: 7 · Henry Vivian Derozio and Young Bengal (late 1820s to 1831)
items.x: Because logic alone was the first experiment, Young Bengal tried it. Ask: why did total faith in reason, with no religion, fail with a religious people? 7.1 Derozio Henry Vivian Derozio was a Eurasian teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta. He died suddenly in December 1831. In his active years (late 1820s to 1831) his followers were not called "Young Bengal": they were "Derozians", "Ultra-Reformers" or "the radicals"."Young Bengal" came later. (The label echoes Mazzini's "Young Italy", educated youth breaking from a tradition-bound older generation.) His method was "question everything": he pushed students to challenge orthodoxy (blind following of old practice) with reason, Western sciences and sometimes outright atheism. The formula (Lecture 22, slide 15): only logic, plus negating religion, plus radical reform = "viral" and "infamous". Under the death line the ink reads "by David Hare (Edu Reformer)": it seems to link Derozio's end with David Hare, the educational reformer. 7.2 What the Derozians did, and why they failed 1838: Young Bengal set up the Society for Acquisition of General Knowledge:Tarachand Chakravarty (President), Ramgopal Ghosh (Vice President). A forum to debate Western sciences and social reforms. No mass movement, no engagement with religious feeling. Why they failed:total faith in Western rationality plus complete disregard for religion created a gap with a religious people. They ate beef and drank wine, a public scandal: "great controversy but poor mass politics". Political demands (shared with Roy), ahead of their time:Separation of Powers, Freedom of the Press, Indianisation of the Civil Services, Trial by Jury (guilt decided by citizens, not one judge). These demands come from Western education, "modern polity". He adds dates for the services: Uncovenanted Civil Services open to Indians: 1833; Covenanted Civil Services: 1853 (the teacher's ink reads "UCS open to Indians: 1833" and "CCS: 1853"). Board: SoP (Separation of Powers), with two questions: which powers, at what level Separation of powers has two questions: which powers and at what level.Cornwallis 86-93 separated the J (judicial) and E (executive) powers at the District Collector (DC) level.The 1833 Charter added 1 legal member to the Governor General's council, "a grain of SoP";the 1853 Charter added 6 more, the "introduction of SoP" (separating legislative from executive work). At the Governor General's level there was no separation: he was boss of both L and E. (Detail in Chapters 17 and 18.)

Because Young Bengal failed, Roy joined reason to scripture. Ask: how did he use universalism, the Upanishads and the State together? 8.1 Who Roy was Roy is called the Father of Modern India. He was the first major figure to see that social reform could not be separated from religious reform, and the first to attempt a real synthesis of Indian tradition and Western modernity. The teacher brackets him as "[From Indian Society] [Initiator]". He was a scholar of the Vedas, Sanskrit, Persian literature and Christian scripture. He challenged the British claim of Christian superiority by engaging Christianity seriously. His position was universalism: all religions lead to the same God. For Hindus the Vedas were the supreme path, but he did not argue for conversion and did not treat Hinduism as the only road. He believed in cultural synthesis. (Rabindranath Tagore would later hold the same position.) He founded the Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1821) (with William Adam and Dwarkanath Tagore, as Section 23.5 and PYQ 18 note). Roy's synthesis: "Western culture, Western education without giving up Vedantic traditions"; it was a way of countering the Evangelists,proof of cultural nationalism, and of peaceful coexistence of Hinduism and Christianity.Cultural synthesis is "in line with" logic (the word after "in line with" is hard to read). Two ideas, two settings.Universalism is monotheism applied BETWEEN religions (all religions lead to God; all Gods are God). Monotheism applied WITHIN a religion (Hinduism) says God is one God and all Gods are one God: the Upanishads. Roy used both: universalism for Christianity and Hinduism, monotheism from the Upanishads for Hinduism. The RRR picture (Lecture 22, slide 20): an Indian scientist in Western dress, with no religious symbol, who still prays to his God before leaving home. That is Roy's synthesis in one image: modern outside, Vedantic inside. 8.2 Roy's beliefs His main concern was polytheism. From the Upanishads he argued that authentic Hinduism is monotheistic. He translated the Upanishads into Bengali to prove it. Brahmoism is defined by this monotheism. He also condemned idolatry, priestcraft, child marriage, the poor condition of widows, infanticide, casteism and polygamy. He used the Doctrine of Reason against three religious ideas: other-worldliness (heaven and hell as real places), the doctrine of Karma (present state fixed by a past life) and the doctrine of Incarnation (gods taking human birth). On Sati he argued that Sati is murder as per every Shastra. It was a scriptural argument because only that would move the British and orthodox Hindus.
