Beside Brahmoism the teacher bracketed "[within Hinduism]" and "[not a new religion outside Hindu]"; beside the list of evils a bracket "[= GG & BUT optional = polytheism]". His shortcut for Roy's method: "(1) choose logic, (2) Ctrl+F logic in scripture." 8.3 Roy on education For Roy rationality was supreme and the Vedas were not infallible (unlike Dayanand and Vivekananda after 1857). He wanted public money spent on Western education and Western sciences, not Indian classical learning. When the government proposed a Sanskrit College in Calcutta in 1824, he actively opposed it. Year 1791 (the teacher wrote 1791 on slide 50) 1824 Set up by Jonathan Duncan, under Cornwallis 86-93 Under Amherst 23-28, on the advice of the Orientalist faction of the General Committee of Public Instruction Purpose Train Pandits to administer Hindu law: a purely administrative need Better understanding of Hindu laws Later Not abolished by the English Education Act 1835 Roy opposed it.Vidyasagar became Principal in 1851, opened it to non-Brahmins and added Western sciences Roy "wants the West like the Industrial Revolution for GDP growth". He bracketed the 1813 Charter: Rs 1 lakh on education. Roy's advocacy of English education influenced Macaulay's Minute 1835 (Roy died 1833), which led to the English Education Act 1835. 8.4 Roy's method: use the State Roy was willing, strategically, to use British legislative and executive power. He worked with Bentinck 28-35,Thomas Macaulay and the philanthropist David Hare. The teacher notes (Lecture 22, slide 23) this cooperation was behind legislation for education and the Sati Abolition Act 1829. 8.5 Roy's administrative demands Beyond social reform Roy demanded Separation of Powers, Freedom of the Press, Indianisation of the Civil Services and Trial by Jury. Young Bengal made exactly the same demands: the emerging consensus of the WEMC.

Because Roy had a method, Sati became its great test. Ask: why did this law succeed when others stalled? 9.1 Sati defined, and its origin Sati was the practice by which a widow self-immolated on her husband's funeral pyre. The earliest firm epigraphic evidence is the Eran Pillar Inscription of Bhanugupta (510 CE) at Eran, in Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh: it records the wife of a chieftain named Goparaja performing the act after his death in battle (the handout says out of love and devotion). In Vedic times there was no Sati. The Rig Veda has a passage where a wife goes to the pyre but is called back by her family to the world of the living, and returns. Sec 9, Sati: Definition and Origins The post-Vedic Smritis supported it as a voluntary spiritual act, a sign of the wife's oneness of soul with her husband. Ancient times: the Rig Veda opposes Sati; the act was completely voluntary, no force, and (the teacher's gloss) it "gradually" split in two:Murder (relatives pressing for property, which he dates to the 1800s) and Suicide (done for self-respect). The teacher also underlined "epigraphic evidence" and Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh (the Eran site). 9.2 Why Sati persisted into the 19th century By the 19th century the original spiritual rationale had largely collapsed. What drove it was social pressure, greed and patriarchy: relatives did not want to share property with a childless widow; a widow was seen as an economic and social burden; Sati removed any perceived risk to caste "purity" or family honour from a widow's future conduct; society glorified the act as spiritual salvation, a powerful social pressure. So by the 19th century a "voluntary spiritual act" had become, in most cases, coerced suicide or outright murder, driven by inheritance greed and patriarchal control. 9.3 The scale of the problem Sati was never a pan-India phenomenon. It existed mainly in Bengal among upper castes, and historically in Vijayanagara (1336-1646) and Rajputana, where the related Jauhar (mass self-immolation by women to avoid capture and dishonour by victorious armies) had different origins in warrior-clan honour. What made the 19th century alarming:lower castes in Bengal began practising Sati as part of Sanskritisation. Board: Sanskritization Sanskritisation (Lecture 22, slide 25):when the lower caste (LC) copies the behaviour of the upper caste (UC).Why? When people perceive that a sub-group has true knowledge of religion and its rituals and practises them, that sub-group gets higher status. So imitating the upper caste is a tool for upward social mobility. On slide 26 his triangle puts UC at the top and LC below: the lower castes were climbing up by copying Sati. 9.4 How Sati was abolished (1829) Christian missionaries opposed Sati from 1813 but achieved nothing. The decisive campaign was Roy's. Bentinck 28-35 set a firm pre-condition: it had to be proven from Indian scriptures that Sati was not religiously sanctioned. (His Orientalist instinct: he would not override Indian tradition without Indian scriptural authority.) A formal scriptural debate followed: the Brahmo Samaj versus Radhakanta Deb, a prominent orthodox Hindu leader and, otherwise, an education reformer. The teacher dates the debate 1828.Roy won: Sati is murder as per the Shastras. 1829: the Bengal Sati Regulation (Regulation XVII), the 17th law of the year, made Sati punishable as culpable homicide. Radhakanta Deb founded the Dharma Sabha (1830) to oppose abolition and petitioned the Privy Council in London (the Crown's advisory body, here acting as the highest court of appeal for India). The petition was rejected. The Dharma Sabha's appeal to London is one of the earliest uses of the metropolitan legal system as a battleground for Indian policy; the same route was used in far bigger ways in the constitutional debates of the 20th century. Board: Success of Reforms When can a law succeed? Where there is a physical act plus physical evidence (a burning widow can be seen and proved).Two kinds of law:Enabling law (it permits something, such as the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856): the ultimate authority is the people, so law plays only a partial role.Disabling law (it criminalises something, such as Sati 1829): the ultimate authority is the administration, so the legislative and executive (L and E) role is bigger. That is why Sati ended and widow remarriage stalled.

Because Roy needed an organisation, the Brahmo Samaj of 1828 was born. Ask: who held it together, and who split it? Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828 as the organisational vehicle for his agenda. 10.1 What it stood for It worked against idolatry, priestcraft, polytheism and Sati. It did not at first focus on women's issues beyond Sati, or on caste: too sensitive; a strong stand risked losing members. On Karma and transmigration of the soul (past life, present life, next life) the Brahmo Samaj, unlike Roy personally, took no definitive stand, leaving it to members. Strong rejection would have closed the door on its Hindu middle-class audience. The Brahmo Samaj (1828): What It Stood For In practice it became a monotheistic religious movement of upper-caste, Western-educated Bengalis; it did not reach the masses. After Roy's death (1833), Debendranath Tagore (1817-1905), father of Rabindranath Tagore, gave it the organisational strength to survive. In 1860, Bijoy Krishna Goswami tried to reconcile Brahmoism with Vaishnavism to broaden its acceptance among Hindus. "Low-hanging fruits": easy reforms first, tough ones later. On karma he bracketed "[Re-Birth]" (transmigration = rebirth), and the reason for silence was "fear of having fewer members". His margin note "Dwarka, Deb, Rabindra" lists the Tagore line: Dwarkanath, Debendranath, Rabindranath. Roy was the "Steve Jobs", the idea man (RRR); Debendranath was the "Tim Cook", the organisational man (DBT). That is why Debendranath held the Brahmo Samaj together after 1833. 10.2 The Keshab Chandra Sen crisis and the splits of 1866 and 1878 The fault line was always gradualism versus radicalism, and it broke open with Keshab Chandra Sen (KCS) in the 1860s. Keshab was a radical; Debendranath a gradualist. Women Strong for women's rights, female education, widow remarriage, against child marriage Too sensitive to push publicly Caste Attacked the upper-caste character of the Brahmo Samaj, supported inter-caste marriage, challenged caste at its root Avoided it entirely Mass outreach Wanted to go beyond Calcutta's educated elite, to common Bengalis and beyond Bengal; launched missionary activity to make Brahmoism an alternative religion to Hinduism Did not want a break from Hinduism Keshab: mass movement, all-India movement, head-on on sensitive issues. Debendranath (DBT): fear of alienating Hindus. Keshab's slogan, as the teacher puts it: "Let's start a new religion" and so the split of 1866. 1866, the rupture: Keshab and followers wanted to distinguish themselves from Hinduism; Debendranath and followers wanted to stay within it. Keshab formed the Brahmo Samaj of India (1866). Debendranath formed the Adi Brahmo Samaj (1866): Adi = original, a statement that Roy's original vision was gradualist. Keshab's energy produced a legal result, the Brahmo Marriages Act 1872. The major drafting was done under Mayo 69-72 (Mayo was assassinated in February 1872 before it was formally passed). It gave legal validity to inter-caste marriages and widow remarriages, but only if the bride and groom first formally left Hinduism (a condition that limited its impact). Keshab also founded the Tabernacle of New Dispensation (Nababidhan), a syncretic body bringing together the truths of all major religions, and the Indian Reform Association (for women's education, temperance and wider social reform). Beside the Brahmo Marriages Act the teacher boxed "Mayo 69-72". On Nababidhan he bracketed "[Goal = Brahmoism = better than other religions]"; the Indian Reform Association is dated "1870, for social reform"; and the closing line: "BSoI 1866: for religion-related reforms [socio-religious reforms]" while the Reform Association is for social ones. 1878, the second split, inside Keshab's own Brahmo Samaj of India: Keshab married off his minor daughter, directly contradicting everything he had said on child marriage. His following fractured, and the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878) was formed. PYQ 2016 trap. The Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1821) is Roy's (the slide key says Roy, Dwarkanath Tagore and William Adam). Keshab = Tabernacle of New Dispensation + Indian Reform Association (the key gives the Tabernacle's foundation stone on 24 January 1868 and the IRA on 29 October 1870 with Keshab as President). PYQ 2012: Brahmo Samaj opposed idolatry and the need for a priestly class; it did not teach Vedic infallibility (the key adds that Debendranath treated the Upanishads as infallible and published parts as "Brahmo Dharma"). The teacher's "DS" note beside statement 3 is unclear. 10.3 Why the Brahmo Samaj failed The reasons were internal:ideological and organisational differences (gradualism versus radicalism, inside versus outside Hinduism); multiple splits that divided energy, membership and credibility; and an upper-caste, urban character with no mass reach. The teacher's one word for it: factionalism. 10.4 Akshay Kumar Dutt Akshay Kumar Dutt (the handout prints 1820-1866; the slide title prints 1820-1886) was a Brahmo Samajist who cited medical opinion against child marriage, an early use of science as a tool. He advocated courtship before marriage, equality and partnership within marriage, and the right to divorce by law and custom. "Only Logic": Akshay Kumar Dutt used science (medical opinion), not scripture. So by the teacher's scheme he is a pure social reformer, like the Derozians. Date conflict. Handout: 1820-1866; the slide's typed title: 1820-1886. Neither is the teacher's ink. Check your notebook; the dates are rarely tested.

Because Bengal's reform had reached the whole country, Maharashtra built its own bodies. Ask: how did the Prarthana Samaj copy the Brahmo Samaj? 11.1 The Paramhansa Mandali (1849) Maharashtra's first organised attempt was the Paramhansa Mandali (1849). It followed Young Bengal's path (reason, rejecting religious authority) and failed for the same reason: a religious society cannot be moved by reason alone. A link to Bengal-centrism: the English Education Act 1835 applied at all-India level (it implemented Macaulay's Minute) because of the Charter Act 1833, which turned the Governor General of Bengal into the Governor General of India. So a Bengal-based policy could reach Maharashtra. (See Chapter 17.) 11.2 The Prarthana Samaj (1867) The lasting effort of 1867 was the Prarthana Samaj, set up by Atmaram Pandurang with the active help of Keshab Chandra Sen, who wanted Brahmoism beyond Bengal. It is Brahmoism transplanted to Maharashtra. Members: Western-educated Marathi Brahmins, Gujarati merchants and Parsis (the same elite character that limited the 1828 Brahmo Samaj). Chief figure M.G. Ranade, assisted by R.G. Bhandarkar and K.T. Telang. Goals (teacher: "like KCS"): women's issues and caste, plus anti-idolatry, monotheism and opposition to priestly domination. Methods (teacher: "like DBT"):gradual, no break from Hinduism, slow reform from within: more acceptable to Hindu society, but it led to gradual irrelevance. When Dayanand's Arya Samaj arrived in 1875 (religious, radical, self-assertive, culturally nationalist) it drew away many who found the Prarthana Samaj too slow. The Prarthana Samaj opened branches in Gujarat, Karachi (the teacher adds: Sindh) and Madras. In Telugu-speaking areas of the Madras Presidency, Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu set up a society for widow remarriage. Reform in Madras was slow: Western education spread unevenly and casteism ran deep. Board: an arch sign, "Shadiyan hi Shadiyan, Dobara hi Dobara" (weddings and only remarriage) A joke-picture of how a widow-remarriage society could work, placed after Veeresalingam (Lecture 22, slide 40): a hoarding reading "Shadiyan hi Shadiyan, Dobara hi Dobara" (weddings, only second weddings), with a register of widows (the dead men's registry, "husbands who have died"), a register of potential grooms ready for widow remarriage, and press and advertisements to match them. It is the teacher's way of saying the societies were matchmaking bodies using the press. 11.3 M.G. Ranade (1842-1901) Mahadev Govind Ranade was the central intellectual force of organised social reform in Maharashtra. A student of Elphinstone College, Bombay, he became a judge of the Bombay High Court and a member of the Bombay Legislative Council. He edited Indu Prakash (an Anglo-Marathi weekly) with Bhandarkar. He is the Father of Indian Economics, a critic of British economic policy (the teacher links it to the Drain Theory), and one of the first to argue that the colonial State should promote industrialisation and welfare. His Essays on Indian Economics (1898) was the first systematic Indian analysis of the Indian economy. The British gave him the Companion of the Order of the Indian Empire (for his work on a committee on fiscal stability). He wrote Rise of Maratha Power, worked for female education, widow remarriage, against child marriage, and co-founded the Maharashtra Girls Education Society with Bhandarkar. (The teacher bracketed the Indian High Courts Act 1861 beside his judgeship: the court he sat on dates from that Act.) Organisations Ranade built: Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870): one of the earliest regional political bodies in India, on the rights of peasants in the Bombay Presidency; a precursor of the INC. Members: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Gopal Hari Deshmukh (the teacher adds P.M. Mehta and G.K. Gokhale as prominent names, read from his ink). The teacher calls it the first regional political party of WEMC Indians. Indian National Social Conference: first session held alongside the INC's Madras session in 1887.No scriptural debates: social reform argued on the Doctrine of Logic. The teacher calls it the all-India organisation for social reforms, where religion is not discussed. PYQ 1996 and PYQ 2012. The passage in PYQ 1996 (social and religious reform, "relied on legislation", Indian National Social Conference alongside the Congress) = Ranade, not Malabari or Vidyasagar. PYQ 2012: the Conference was formed because the Congress platform was for political topics only, so a separate social body was needed; it was all-India, not "Bengal groups" (the teacher: "not politics", "all India", "ORG for Reforms"). The slide key credits Ranade assisted by R. Raghunath Rao; the handout names Ranade alone: both agree on Ranade and 1887. 11.4 Gopal Hari Deshmukh, "Lokhitavadi" (1823-1892) Gopal Hari Deshmukh, pen name Lokhitavadi ("one who speaks for the welfare of the people"), held the most radical Maharashtra position: social reform is the first priority, above religion; if the scriptures conflict with social reform, change the religion, because religion is made by man, not the other way round. Roy used scripture for reform and Dayanand held the Vedas infallible; Lokhitavadi stood at the other end: human welfare beats religious authority. "Logic+ (logic over scripture)"; "like RRR [Logic versus Scriptures]" with a tick on Logic: he sits in the logic-first camp.

Because most reformers spoke about the oppressed, Phule spoke for them. Ask: how many groups did he organise at once? If most reformers spoke about the oppressed, Phule spoke for them and organised them. He is the first major reformer whose work addressed caste, gender, class and economic exploitation all at once. Education Memorandum to the Hunter Education Commission 1882:universal, practical primary education,State funded and run, targeted at lower castes and girls, with trained non-Brahmin teachers,mother-tongue instruction, nominal fees or scholarships, tighter inspection. In 1848 he opened India's first girls' school in Pune, with wife Savitribai Phule as the first female teacher (stones and dung were thrown at her on the way to school) Women Widow remarriage; against child marriage. 1863: an infanticide prevention centre: anonymous deliveries for pregnant widows, shelter for survivors of sexual assault, an orphanage Dalit rights 1873: Gulamgiri (Slavery) in Marathi: equates Shudras and Ati-Shudras with African American slaves, blames the priestly class, dedicated to the American abolitionists. In 1873 he founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (Truth-Seekers' Society) to challenge orthodoxy and caste; Din Bandhu newspaper (1877) Peasants Cultivator's Whipcord (1881): religion, bureaucracy and economic exploitation (moneylenders, high land revenue, ritual expenses) together grind down Shudra cultivators; festivals and rituals as instruments of economic extraction; he advocated self-reliance, land reforms, use of military labour for rural development; ran night schools for peasants Workers Night schools for labourers; co-founded the Bombay Millhands Association (1890) with Narayan Lokhande (main founder): an early effort for industrial workers' rights, not a formal trade union (no membership fees, rules or funds) Phule's parallel: both Shudras/Ati-Shudras under caste and African Americans under slavery were born into bondage with no exit, and in both the oppressor hid behind tradition and divine sanction. PYQ 1996 and 2016.Satya Shodhak Samaj = Jyotirao Phule, Pune, 1873, an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra (to improve the status of Shudra and untouchable castes, and the key adds: no priest needed to reach God). Not Tilak (1996) and not tribals in Bihar, temple entry in Gujarat or Punjab peasants (2016). The slides here are underlines only; no handwriting.

Because religion itself backed child marriage, it was harder than Sati. Ask: why did the age ladder (10, then 12) change so little on the ground? 13.1 Why child marriage was so hard to uproot Child marriage had explicit religious backing. The Garbhadhan ceremony prescribed marriage before puberty and consummation at puberty. So here reformers were arguing against a practice scripture itself sanctioned, not a distortion. Orthodox opposition was stronger, more principled and harder to beat than on Sati. "Harder than Sati, therefore religious sanction." 13.2 Legislative attempts Vidyasagar's efforts contributed to the Indian Penal Code 1860 under Canning 56-62: the minimum age of consummation = 10 years (Section 375 IPC 1860, the definition of statutory rape): a modest beginning. Akshay Kumar Dutt added the medical dimension. IPC 1860 at age 10 = "not a reform but a law to prevent violation of customary Hindu law." Because Garbhadhan put consummation at puberty, an age-10 floor only stopped the violation of the customary rule, it did not raise the marriage age. His laws board (Lecture 23, slide 7): Laws split into Civil and Criminal;Civil into Personal and Non-personal;inheritance is personal law, handled by personal law by default ("the State can make a law but, by default, personal law operates"). Three laws sit at the border: Sati Abolition Act 1829, IPC 1860 [age of consent 10], Age of Consent 1891 [12]. 13.3 The Rakhmabai case (1884-1888) Rakhmabai was married as an infant and lived apart from her husband for years. At 22, when he took her to court for denial of conjugal rights, she argued the marriage was invalid. The Rakhmabai Defence Committee, led by reformer Malabari (whose 1884 note on child marriage and enforced widowhood had already caused a storm), supported her; orthodox Hindus supported the husband.She lost (post-1857 orthodox opinion was strong enough to win in court). Then Queen Victoria herself overruled the decision and dissolved the marriage. The slide's underlines add: her husband Dadaji Bhikaji; Rakhmabai later qualified in medicine in England (1894) and was among the earliest practising female doctors, with Anandibai Joshi and Kadambini Ganguly. PYQ 2020 (Prelims). The Rakhmabai Case of 1884 is about (a) the Age of Consent debate and (b) the doctrine of Restitution of Conjugal Rights. It is not a case about women's right to education. Answer (b) 2 and 3. 13.4 The Age of Consent Act 1891 In 1890 the death of 11-year-old Phulmoni from sexual abuse by her husband forced the issue. Lansdowne 88-94 introduced the Age of Consent Bill 1891: minimum age of consummation 12. Passed in March 1891 as Act X (10) of 1891. Tilak: the British had no right to interfere in Indian custom and religion; reform must come from social movement, not colonial legislation. R.G. Bhandarkar of Poona Deccan College and the Prarthana Samaj: research showing the Dharmashastras permit marriage after puberty. Result: the reform failed on the ground;census data from the 1900s (the census ran every ten years from 1881) showed child marriage continued across all castes. The British were "not interested in initiating reform, but may act if pressure" (Lecture 23, slide 3): after the 11-year-old Phulmoni case they did the minimum (age 12). Bhandarkar's reply is "Logic + Religion" (logic plus the Dharmashastras): the scripture-based debate dominated socio-religious reform. On slide 5 the teacher draws the failure rule: no mass movement, therefore most reforms were failures; this is the "character" of the Bengal/Indian Renaissance. He applies it to the UCC (Uniform Civil Code): "best-case scenario = demand from among the minorities". (Reform that is not demanded from within fails.)

items.t: 14 · Female infanticide, and the Lex Loci Act 1850
items.x: Because law could stop killing but not hunger, infanticide split into two problems. Ask: where does the State end and society begin? Female infanticide in north and west India continued largely unabated. The reasons were structural: landowning high-caste men practised hypogamy (the handout's word; the teacher underlined "hypergamy": marrying women from lower castes, often several), which made finding grooms for the daughters of such marriages extremely hard;high dowry made it worse. Mayo 69-72 passed the Female Infanticide Act 1870, but law could not reach the root. Census data still showed high girl-child mortality: not direct infanticide but nutritional neglect (girls fed and cared for less, allowed to die), which could not be legislated away. Cause = dowry plus polygamy: the husband is upper caste (UC), the wife lower caste (LC). He adds the Brahmo Marriages Act 1872 beside the 1870 Act (both under Mayo 69-72). And the rule: until society changes, social reform will not succeed; the State (L and E) has limitations. Board: "Female Infanticide: infant girls killed; more role of (L)(E)" versus (circled vs) "Girl CHILD MORTALITY RATE [1yr-5yr]": malnutrition; more role of society, less  Two problems, two answers (Lecture 22, slide 29).Female infanticide (infant girls killed): more role for L and E (law). Girl child mortality, 1 to 5 years (malnutrition): more role for society and less for L and E, because "you cannot station a Havaldar in every home". The handout writes "hypogamy" and the slide underline reads "hypergamy" (the same idea in the teacher's version: higher-caste men marrying lower-caste women). Learn the meaning, not the spelling. The Lex Loci Act 1850 The Lex Loci Act 1850 (also the Caste Disabilities Removal Act 1850, and the handout's timeline also lists a Religious Disabilities Act 1850) protected the property and inheritance rights of converts. Before it, a Hindu who converted to Christianity (or any religion) forfeited ancestral property under traditional Hindu law. The Act overrode that: conversion no longer caused forfeiture. The State now stood for individual choice, not ancestral religious sanction. Two readings: it was called "the legal foundation of religious freedom in colonial India", but this is contested: orthodox Hindus and the WEMC saw a State tilt towards conversion (the strongest deterrent was gone); Christian missionaries saw a long-overdue protection of converts from predatory disinheritance. Both have evidence: the Act did weaken the orthodox hold on individual choice and made conversion materially safer. Beside the title: "1857 Revolt", "Ideology = evangelicalism", "disability = loss of inheritance on conversion", "fear of religion". The teacher ties this Act to the fear of religion that fed the 1857 Revolt; the orthodox Hindus and WEMC "opposed" it.

Because the home was the hardest ground, Vidyasagar fought on every front there. Ask: which of his battles succeeded and which did not? Born Ishwar Chandra Bandyopadhyay on 26 September 1820 in Bengal, he was a prodigy. He studied Sanskrit literature for years, moved to Calcutta young (a widow became his caregiver, which may have shaped his lifelong commitment to widows), passed the Hindu Law Committee examination and earned the title Vidyasagar ("ocean of knowledge") in 1839. He mastered English, Sanskrit and Bengali and used academic prize money to set up a school and print rare Sanskrit texts. His ideology: reason and rationalism are supreme. He said "I have no time to think about God": his energy went to social reform. He rejected other-worldliness. 15.1 The educator As Additional Secretary and then Principal of Sanskrit College (Calcutta, 1824), he threatened resignation if lower-caste students were not admitted and introduced Western sciences alongside Sanskrit. (The college Roy had opposed; Vidyasagar changed it from inside.) He wanted Western education and culture delivered in the vernacular, not only English, so that knowledge went beyond the elite. As Inspector of Schools in Bengal he set up 20 Model Schools and ended physical punishment. (Inspector = district level; the provincial head was the Director of Education, like SP and DGP in the police.) Vidyasagar: The Educator Female education is "the only true route to uplifting society". Between November 1857 and May 1858, in the middle of the Revolt, he opened 25 schools for girls with 1,300 girls enrolled at a time; attendance, books and transport free. He improved Sanskrit literature and made it accessible through Bengali. Tagore said his greatest contribution was to the Bengali language: the Father of Modern Bengali Prose. The teacher's label for his approach: Utilitarianism, "achieve maximum good or efficiency". And "Champion of women's issues":education, widow remarriage, child marriage, female infanticide, all arrows into one circle. "Father of modern Bangla prose": said RBT (Rabindranath Tagore). The teacher struck out "attendance" on the free list [read from the yellow cross-out]. 15.2 Widow remarriage His most celebrated battle: in 1855 he wrote a book on the miseries of widowhood and sent the government a petition with 1,000 signatures for a law allowing widow remarriage. Result: the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 26 July 1856; the first remarriage under it on 7 December 1856. He married his own son to a widow. Dalhousie 48-56 or Canning 56-62? The handout and the typed slide say the Act came "under Dalhousie 48-56". The teacher's ink says "Passed during Canning 56-62" and, in the margin, "Post in 1854 @ Charter 1853, by Dalhousie 48-56" (the first word and the meaning, probably that the process followed the 1853 Charter and was set going under Dalhousie 48-56, are not fully clear). So: Act passed 26 July 1856, Canning 56-62's year; the idea and groundwork Dalhousie 48-56's. For a Prelims code match, handout/typed key = Dalhousie 48-56; Canning 56-62 is safe only if the question says "passed". Bank item "under Lord Dalhousie" follows the handout. Vidyasagar: Widow Remarriage and Polygamy 15.3 Polygamy and the Bethune alert In 1855 he also petitioned the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal with 25,000 signatures for a ban on polygamy, and wrote two books against polygamy in 1871 and 1873. PYQ 2005 and 2021: Bethune School. The school (later Bethune Female School) was set up in 1849 by J.E. Drinkwater Bethune (Law Member of Dalhousie's Council and President of the Council of Education) under grants-in-aid.Vidyasagar was its Secretary (appointed by Bethune, December 1850, as the key to PYQ 2021 says), the key figure who built it. Bankim Chandra being the first graduate of Calcutta University is a separate fact often paired with Bethune. So PYQ 2005 statement 1 ("Vidyasagar founded" the Bethune School) is false on strict facts and the teacher marked it F with "DRINKWATER", yet UPSC's key (b) counts it true; PYQ 2021 asks for the Secretary = Vidyasagar.

items.t: 16 · Widow remarriage after the Act: why it failed
items.x: Because an enabling law leaves the choice to society, the 1856 Act stalled. Ask: what did the widow lose, and who won the scripture debate? The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856 was a landmark that did not solve the problem. The catch: on remarriage a widow lost her right to her deceased husband's property, enough to keep the law largely ineffective. Reform was scattered and always met organised orthodox resistance: Maharashtra:Vishnu Shastri Pandit formed a widow-remarriage society in 1866; orthodox rivals at once set up a counter-organisation. Phule worked among lower castes in Maharashtra for widow remarriage but failed. Madras:Veeresalingam Pantulu set up a society. Pandita Ramabai was a rare exception: a Brahmin woman who stayed unmarried long, finally married a man of a lower caste; after his death she went to England to study medicine,converted to Christianity (criticised even by reformers), and in the USA raised money for a widow home in Bombay. She opposed the new role model of the "educated but obedient wife". The result was failure. Post-1857 orthodox Hindus had stronger social support and won the scripture-based debate, proving "to most people's satisfaction" that Hinduism did not allow widow remarriage. The damage spread downward: even lower castes, who had traditionally allowed widow remarriage, stopped it to align with upper-caste norms (the handout: "Sanskritisation working in reverse", adopting upper-caste restrictions, not only customs). By 1900, only 38 widow remarriages had taken place in Maharashtra. The reform worked only in Haryana, where it was already accepted. "Pre-1857 reformers never went to the masses, therefore leadership of the masses was taken by the orthodox." That is the vacuum the second-wave reformers found. The women's reform Acts at a glance (1829 to 1929) 1829 Sati abolition (Regulation XVII) Bentinck 28-35, via Roy; Sati = culpable homicide 1850 Lex Loci Act (and a Religious Disabilities Act 1850) Converts keep ancestral property 1856 Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (26 July) Dalhousie 48-56 (handout) / passed in Canning 56-62's year (teacher); via Vidyasagar; the widow lost the husband's property 1860 IPC: age of consent 10 (the figure calls it "Age of Consent Act 1860") Canning 56-62; via Vidyasagar 1870 Female Infanticide Act Mayo 69-72 1872 Native (Brahmo) Marriages Act Mayo 69-72; inter-caste and widow marriage if the couple leaves Hinduism 1891 Age of Consent Act (Act X) Lansdowne 88-94; age 12 1929 Sharda Act (Child Marriage Restraint) Age 14 for girls, 18 for boys; Harbilas Sarda (handout figure only; no class slide) Order trap. The handout's one-line arc runs "...Age of Consent 1860, Female Infanticide 1870, Native Marriages 1872, Age of Consent 1891, Sharda 1929", but the arrows in the handout's flow chart run 1872 before 1870. Use the dates: 1870, then 1872.

items.t: 17 · Character and failures of early 19th-century reform
items.x: Because the same pattern repeated, the chapter now states the character of early reform. Ask: which failures were about people and which about method? 17.1 What defined these movements Led by Western-educated upper castes:anti-priest in orientation but upper-caste in composition. The primary focus was women, partly from conviction and partly because the British had begun using the status of women as the benchmark of a civilisation. Scriptures were central to every argument: reformers used them, orthodox Hindus used them, and even the British insisted on scriptural justification before acting (recall Bentinck 28-35's pre-condition). Cultural nationalism throughout: reformers sought modernity within Indian traditions rather than adopt British culture as superior. Why women, and why men reformers (Lecture 23, slide 17): before the 1800s the criterion of civilisation was language and literature, but in the 1800s it was the status of women."That's why" the issues were women's issues and most reformers were men. His pitch rule: "Be like our ancestors = pitch; be like the British is not a pitch." On slide 14 the board reads "most issues = women issues, but [most] reformers are men, therefore failure" [the word before "reformers" is unclear: check your notebook]. 17.2 Why they failed Why Early Reform Failed (contd.) No mass movement Western-educated reformers did not try. Roy wrote complex Sanskritised Bengali prose the common person could not follow. The Prarthana Samaj had only 72 members. Small bodies, elite language Top-down, not bottom-up Reform came by British legislative and executive authority, not demand from below. The teacher's triangle: reform the UC and the LC will follow British involvement bred distrust Using British authority frightened people that their religion was under threat, pushing them to orthodox leaders Gradualism Slowed everything, letting orthodox resistance consolidate No women in leadership Women-centred reforms, yet no major reform body was led by a woman. The teacher: "agent of change should be from the group you want to change" Upper-caste leadership only Lower castes did not associate with movements led by those who gained from caste Silence on caste The central structural issue of Indian society was largely avoided Post-1857 shift When second-wave reformers tried to build mass movements, orthodox sections had already captured the masses' leadership Rival orthodox bodies out-mobilised Dharma Sabha against the Brahmo Samaj on Sati; the counter-society against Vishnu Shastri Pandit on widow remarriage Orthodox won the scripture debate On widow remarriage; even lower castes followed Post-1875 Hindu Revivalism A positive face (assertion of Indian traditions, radical reform from within) and a negative face (communal tension, Hindu supremacy over other religions) Hindu revivalism "by default" had two faces.+ve: social reforms, cultural nationalism,no communalism, examples SDS and SV (Swami Dayanand Saraswati and Swami Vivekananda). -ve:"only the Hindu God is the true God",aggressive reconversion (Shuddhi),aggressive cow protection movement, ending in communal tensions. He also struck out "Out-mobilised" on the slide's row label. Reformer organisations at a glance. See the handout grid in Section 19 (after Arya Samaj), which lists the Brahmo Samaj 1828, Young Bengal, Paramhansa Mandali 1849, Prarthana Samaj 1867, Deoband 1867, Satya Shodhak Samaj 1873, Arya Samaj 1875, Theosophical Society 1875, Aligarh 1875, Ahmadiya 1889, Ramakrishna Mission 1897 and SNDP 1903, plus the later Self-Respect Movement 1925.

Because the early reformers did not reach the masses, a second wave came after 1857. Ask: how is the Arya Samaj different from the Brahmo Samaj? 18.1 Swami Dayanand Saraswati His original name was Mool Shankar, from Gujarat. He never married. He left home and spent 20 years travelling in search of spiritual truth. His journey ended in Mathura, where Swami Virajananda directed him to learn directly from the Vedas. Virajananda gave him a task, to spread Vedic knowledge, and a new name: Rishi Dayanand (later Maharishi). 18.2 His beliefs and Satyarth Prakash His foundation: the Vedas are the ultimate, infallible source of all true knowledge; everything after (rituals, idol worship, caste hierarchy, priestly domination) was corruption. The answer was Back to the Vedas, not Western modernity. He wrote it out in Satyarth Prakash (The Light of Meaning of Truth, 1875),deliberately in Hindi, not Sanskrit, to reach the masses. It is the foundational text of the Arya Samaj. It attacks idol worship, polytheism, animal sacrifice, untouchability, child marriage and birth-based caste; it also critically examines Christianity, Islam, Jainism and Buddhism, arguing that Vedic Hinduism is superior to all. He stressed the Doctrine of Reason, with the claim that the Vedas alone contain scientific truths, so Hinduism is not backward, it is ahead. Beside the title: "ARYA Samaj 1875". Beside "Vedic Hinduism is superior to all": "[BUT on ground, no communalism)" (on the ground the Arya Samaj, he says, did not begin as communal). On the margin of the Vivekananda slides he contrasts "vs SDS" (Dayanand): Hinduism = superior, and idols and rituals rejected. 18.3 Founded 10 April 1875, Bombay The Arya Samaj ("Society of the Nobles") was founded on 10 April 1875 in Bombay (the teacher underlined Bombay). Motto: "Krinvanto Vishvam Aryam", "Make this world noble." Its ten tenets cover God, the Vedas, dharma, truth, righteous conduct, physical and social good, love and justice, knowledge over ignorance, collective welfare and individual freedom within social rules. "Not imp" (Lecture 23, slide 22) beside the ten tenets. 18.4 What the Arya Samaj did Attacked ills from within the Vedic framework: idolatry, polytheism, priestcraft, rituals, birth-based caste, child marriage; supported widow remarriage, inter-caste marriage and female education. Caste: discarded birth-based caste and denounced untouchability; upheld the Varnashram system by profession, not birth: Brahmans scholars, Kshatriyas protectors, Vaishyas traders, Shudras in service, changeable with profession, not hereditary, not hierarchical. (Dayanand proposed a meritocratic alternative, not a defence of caste.) Women: "an educated man needs an educated wife"; widow-remarriage programmes in the 1880s. Shuddhi: bringing back those converted (voluntarily or not) to Islam or Christianity. Under Dayanand it was for those who came forward, not a forced reconversion. Gurukuls to teach Vedic knowledge and train spreaders. Projected Hinduism as a "religion of the book" like Islam and Christianity: the Vedas as Shruti (that which is heard) and Apaurusheya (not of human origin, eternal cosmic truths). Swarajya: a country free of foreign influence, an aggressive, self-assertive answer to British criticism. On the Swarajya slide he wrote "CULTURE" above the table with a curved line to "free of foreign influence": Dayanand's swarajya is cultural (freedom from foreign cultural influence), not yet political. 18.5 Successes and failures The Arya Samaj failed in east and west India (the teacher: competition from the Brahmo Samaj of India 1866 in Bengal and the Prarthana Samaj 1867 in Maharashtra) but succeeded most in Punjab and the North-West Provinces, especially after Dayanand's death in 1883, when it became both more popular and more aggressive. Why Punjab: late-19th-century Punjab was a region of intense religious competition (Hinduism, Sikhism, Islam, Christian missionaries), and the Samaj's assertive, organised, scriptural approach suited it. After his death the disciples set up the Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) College Trust and Management Society: the first DAV High School at Lahore on 1 June 1886,Lala Hans Raj headmaster (Shaheed Bhagat Singh studied at DAV School, Lahore). The teacher: the DAV is Western education plus the Vedas. Though never directly in the independence struggle, Dayanand's teachings influenced Lala Lajpat Rai, V.D. Savarkar, Madam Cama, Ram Prasad Bismil, M.G. Ranade, Madan Lal Dhingra and Subhas Chandra Bose (the handout's list). PYQ 2001 (Prelims). (i) Arya Samaj was founded in 1875,not 1835. (ii) Lala Lajpat Rai followed the Arya Samaj; he did not oppose its Vedic appeal. (iii) Under K. Hedgewar, the RSS (1925) was partly inspired by the Arya Samaj's organisational model; be careful with the chain of influence. With statement 3 (Keshab's Brahmo Samaj for women's education) and 4 (Vinoba's Sarvodaya Samaj for refugees) true, the answer is (d).

Because pride can turn aggressive, revivalism had two faces. Ask: which reactions did the negative face provoke? Post-1857, reform and revivalism split into two streams. Positive revivalism: a more confident assertion of Indian traditions against British criticism: Dayanand, Ramakrishna, Vivekananda attacked social ills from within the tradition. Negative revivalism (intensified after Dayanand's death in 1883): under leaders like Pandit Lekh Ram and Pandit Guru Dutt the Arya Samaj became militant: Vedas preached with missionary zeal and an aggressive Shuddhi to reconvert from Islam, Sikhism and Christianity. In response the Singh Sabha movement among Sikhs intensified and Muslims launched Tanzim and Tabligh. The Cow Protection Movement led to the Cow Killing Riots of 1893. He wrote "1873" just above Singh Sabha (the date of the Sikh body). The same +ve and -ve boards appear in Section 17.2. Deoband, the Theosophical Society, the Ahmadiya and the Self-Respect Movement appear only in the handout grid; they are not taught in the class slides of this chapter. Adyar (Madras) is the Theosophical Society's headquarters from 1882 (see the Madanapalle trap in Section 21).

Because the educated found their jobs hollow, Ramakrishna offered undiluted tradition. Ask: why did Vivekananda win more mass acceptance than Dayanand? 20.1 Ramakrishna Paramhansa A temple priest, not a Western-educated reformer, writer or debater. He believed in meditation, renunciation and monotheism; Western ideas and education left him untouched. He did not criticise colonial rule, but his pure focus on Hinduism was an implicit rejection of Western values and culture. His appeal to educated Bengalis is revealing. They held clerical jobs under British administration, which he called Chakri (the grinding routine of office work), and found them spiritually hollow. Reformism by the 1870s felt like an admission that Indians were uncivilised. Ramakrishna offered not reform, not self-criticism, but the spiritual richness of their own tradition, undiluted. He argued that Chakri left no time for spiritualism, and that this absence was the real source of the educated middle class's dissatisfaction. Under the Chakri row he wrote "1833: UCS open to Indian", meaning that jobs in the Uncovenanted Civil Services opened to Indians in 1833 produced the clerks who found Chakri hollow. 20.2 Swami Vivekananda Ramakrishna's most famous disciple, a different kind of figure: intellectual, activist, globally engaged. Universalism, genuine: a Christian could become a better Christian by studying Vedanta. No conversion, no aggression: spread the values, not the label. The teacher: vs SDS (Dayanand): Dayanand held that Hinduism was superior; Vivekananda believed in the superiority of Hindu philosophy but not as a negative revivalist. On the Upanishads: "Spirit = curiosity = Q and A": the Doctrine of Reason. He had faith in the glory of Hindu civilisation but admitted degeneration in recent times, without blaming a particular religion. "Service of Jiva is worship of Shiva": social service is spiritual; he popularised Daridra Narayan (God in the poor); he thought existing reform too elitist; real work meant going to the masses through service. Ramakrishna Mission (1897): two aims: spread Vedanta and undertake social service; an army of followers carrying the message of Vedanta, the Upanishads, Buddha and Jesus. Also akhadas and gymnasiums: Indian masculinity of physical strength and mental spirituality is superior to the Western; Indians were not "feminine", differently strong. Idols and rituals: he accepted them as legitimate aids to religious feeling (the teacher again: vs SDS), which gave him far greater mass acceptance. 1893: Parliament of Religions, Chicago: Western materialism and Indian spiritualism must come together; he became internationally famous. No political message, nationalism purely cultural; Netaji Bose called him the spiritual father of the Indian National Movement in Bengal. After his death (1902) revivalists selectively used him: Vedic supremacy, some rituals, Hindu glory, and recast "recent degeneration" as degeneration under Muslim and Christian rule. Today the Mission runs schools, dispensaries, hospitals and relief work. Sister Nivedita (Margaret Noble), Vivekananda's Irish disciple: nurtured cultural nationalism; worked for women's education (the Nivedita School at Calcutta, 1898); saw independence as a spiritual necessity; gave secret support and guidance to revolutionary groups in Bengal, especially the Anushilan Samiti, bridging spiritual revival and militancy. Wrote The Master as I Saw Him (1910); lived in India until her death in 1911.

Because culture needed symbols, Bankim gave India Bharat Mata and Bande Mataram. Ask: how is Anandmath different from Jana Gana Mana? He held that without religious revival there could be no revival of India, yet his was a Hindu secular outlook: religion as a cultural and nationalist force, not a communal one. He portrayed Krishna as a modern politician and nation-builder and promoted rational Hinduism, not orthodox Hinduism. (The teacher's ink: under "religious revival" "Do Logic"; under "rational Hinduism" "values".) His novel Anandamath (1882) gave India Bharat Mata (Mother India as a goddess) and Bande Mataram, the anthem of the National Movement. He was the first graduate of Calcutta University (founded 1857; handout sections 24.8 and 24.9 add that Joddu Nath Bose was the other of the first two graduates in 1858). A related note on the National Anthem:Rabindranath Tagore composed Jana Gana Mana in Bengali and himself translated it into English at Madanapalle (Andhra Pradesh) in 1919, where it was also set to music. Bande Mataram is from Anandmath (1882); the two have distinct origins. PYQ 2021 (Prelims): Madanapalle = Tagore translated Jana Gana Mana into English (1919),not the Theosophical Society headquarters, which is at Adyar (Madras) from 1882. (The slide key adds that Margaret Cousins composed the tune; the answer is (c).) Dates of novels and arts (handout flow chart, Section 25).Durgesh Nandini 1865 (Bankim, the first Bengali novel; PYQ 1996 answer (b)) comes after Neel Darpan 1860 (Dinabandhu Mitra, indigo planters' tyranny), so Neeldarpan is earliest in PYQ 2018 against Arya Samaj 1875, Anandmath 1882 and Satyendranath Tagore in the ICS (the teacher's ink 1864, the key 1863).

Because Muslims had their own questions, Sir Syed chose modern education without surrender of faith. Ask: where did his social and political positions diverge? The most significant Muslim social reformer of the 19th century. On social questions he was modern: supported widow remarriage; opposed triple talaq, polygamy, purdah and child marriage; wanted Western and female education, all without abandoning the core beliefs of Islam: "modernisation without surrender of faith". The teacher notes "(* like RRR)", the same synthesis as Roy. But his political theory divided. India was not one nation but a summation of Quams. The Hindu Quam and the Muslim Quam were separate: he wanted unity between Quams but insisted on separateness. The Muslim Quam, as the community that had ruled India before the British, deserved special status, and Western education was essential to win it. The teacher's label: "Father of the 2-nation theory". The handout traces the logic "planted in the 1870s and 1880s" through the Muslim League (1906) to Partition in 1947. 1875:Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, Aligarh (later Aligarh Muslim University): the heart of the Aligarh Movement, unity and educational strength within the Muslim Quam. The teacher: Western education without giving up the core of Islam. 1886: the Mohammadan Educational Congress, set up as a rival to the INC, which he viewed as a Hindu organisation. Jamia Millia Islamia (1920): set up at Aligarh by a breakaway faction at AMU. When Gandhi called, in the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22), for students to leave British-supported institutions, AMU stayed pro-British; the breakaway group founded Jamia: anti-colonial Islamic activism, pro-independence, led by Western-educated radical nationalists. Founding leaders: Abdul Majid Khwaja, Maulana Mehmud Hasan, Maulana Md Ali, Hakim Ajmal Khan and Dr Mukhtar Ahmed Ansari (who later headed the All-Party Conference that produced the Nehru Report in August 1928).

Because Kerala's caste was the most severe, a lower-caste ascetic built parallel institutions. Ask: why was this method different from petitions and debates? Born 1856 in Travancore (Kerala) into the Ezhava community, a lower caste in one of the most casteist societies in India. Ezhavas were denied temple entry, barred from public roads near upper-caste homes, and from many kinds of education and employment. He became a wandering ascetic, studied Sanskrit, Tamil and Malayalam and Advaita Vedanta (all existence as one consciousness), and from it drew his social vision: caste is philosophically incoherent. Slogan: "One Religion, One Caste, One God for Mankind." Work and method:institutional, like Phule more than Roy or Vivekananda. He built and consecrated temples open to all castes. The first: Aruvippuram, 1888, a Shiva idol; to upper-caste critics: "This is not a Brahmin's Shiva. This is an Ezhava's Shiva." (All without leaving Hinduism, converting, or legislation.) He set up temples, schools and ashrams open to all, and founded the Shri Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam (SNDP) in 1903 for the upliftment of Ezhavas and lower castes. Gandhi: visited him at Sivagiri in 1925 and called him one of the greatest men he had met; both opposed untouchability but by different methods (Gandhi inside the Congress framework, the Guru from within the community, in Kerala where the problem was acutest). Three responses to caste failure:Gandhi's assimilationist approach, Narayana Guru's reformist-institutionalist work inside Advaita Vedanta, and Ambedkar's exit through conversion to Buddhism. Significance: (1) reform reaching south India seriously, led by a lower-caste ascetic, not Western-educated upper-caste men; (2) a new method:parallel institutions instead of petitions or debates: "creating facts on the ground"; (3) an argument orthodox Hinduism could not dismiss: he held it to its own highest standard.

Because reform needed readers and thinkers, the government's school policy shaped everything above. Ask: for whom was each education policy designed? No class-slide gap here. This whole section follows Lecture 23 (slides 39 to 57) and Lecture 24a (slides 1 to 15), so the teacher's ink sits beside the facts. The lecture runs Orientalism and Macaulay first, then Adam, Wood, the universities, and finally the commissions to 1944, while the handout order is the same. 24.1 Why Western education came so late Western education reforms did not arrive until after 1813, because of Orientalism: the dominant British view in the late 18th and early 19th century was that Indians should be governed the Indian way, working within Indian literature, languages and laws; "reform could wait." In England, Edmund Burke (1729-1797), whose critique of the EIC led to Pitt's India Act of 1784, believed Indians were not ready for Western-style reforms or education. In India the two leading Orientalists were William Jones and Warren Hastings 73-85. He wrote "1835" under the title (the date when Western education became policy) and ticked two items: the dominant Orientalism and Edmund Burke. 24.2 The key Orientalists William Jones (judge at the Calcutta Supreme Court, 1783-94), a scholar of ancient Greek, Roman and Persian literature, was mesmerised by Sanskrit. He argued that Sanskrit epics and poetry were of greater literary stature than anything in Greek, Roman or English literature, a claim that raised the prestige of Indian civilisation abroad more than almost any other act of the era. With Warren Hastings 73-85 he began the codification of Hindu and Islamic laws into English, in 1775 and 1778 (handout). He founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784) for Oriental research. (Dwarkanath Tagore, grandfather of Rabindranath and father of Debendranath, was a member.) Warren Hastings 73-85 set up the Calcutta Madrasa (1781) for Arabic, Persian and Islamic law, to understand Indian legal systems and train Indians to help the EIC rule "the Indian way." The Sanskrit College, Calcutta (1824) followed for Hindu law (the one Roy opposed, Vidyasagar transformed). Wellesley 98-05 set up Fort William College, Calcutta (1800) to train newly arrived British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs. (William Carey taught Bengali and Sanskrit there.) "not imp" beside the heading and beside the Jones row (Lecture 23, slide 40). Slide versus handout on Jones's codification. The handout dates the codification to 1775 (Hindu) and 1778 (Islamic). The typed slide says Jones proposed it to Cornwallis 86-93 in 1788 to remove reliance on Pandits and Maulvis, and lists Halhed's Gentoo Laws (1776, via Persian) replaced by the Manusmriti (1794, from Sanskrit) and Al-Sirajiyyah (1792) supplementing The Hedaya (1791). The teacher marked the slide "not imp". Learn the institutions (below), not these dates. PYQ 2018 and 2021: whose college?Benaras Sanskrit College (1791): Jonathan Duncan, not William Jones (teacher: "x ?"). Calcutta Madrasa (1781): Warren Hastings 73-85 (tick, with his code 73-85). Fort William College (1800): Richard Wellesley 98-05 the Governor General, not Arthur Wellesley (teacher: "Arthur" circled, "RICHARD", 98-05, cross). PYQ 2021: Wellesley 98-05 set it up to train British civilians (the answer slide notes William Carey was a teacher, not the reason). The teacher's ink "1800-06" beside Fort William College is unexplained; the handout gives 1800. 24.3 Who pushed for Western education David Hare (a Calcutta watchmaker) was a remarkable reformer: Championed Western education in English with Roy and Radhakanta Deb. Co-founded the Calcutta School Book Society (1817) with Radhakanta Deb (elementary schools, textbooks in English and Bengali). Co-founded Hindu College, Calcutta (1817) with Sir Edward Hyde East (Chief Justice, Calcutta Supreme Court) and Roy (later Presidency College, where Derozio taught). Founded Hare School (1818). He visited Hindu College daily. Died of cholera in 1842; Christian missionaries refused him a burial site as a "non-believer." Thousands joined his funeral procession. Slide 41 right margin: "# Books, # Schools-Colleges, # Teachers" (what the pushers built). On slide 42 he wrote "6:50 pm" (a time note, not a fact). "not imp" beside the "Who Pushed" heading (slide 43) and beside Charles Grant (slide 44). He pointed to Metcalfe: "Liberator of the Press". Handout versus slide on Hindu College and Hare's burial. The handout says Roy co-founded Hindu College and that Hare was buried within the grounds of Presidency College. The slide says Roy backed the initiative but withdrew before it opened, and that Hare was buried at College Square near Hare School. The slide also adds that the college's higher section became Presidency College in 1855 and its school section Hindu School. For PYQ 2009 use: Hindu College, 1817: Edward Hyde East, David Hare, Raja Ram Mohan Roy (answer (d)). Distractors: Derozio taught there (not a founder); Vidyasagar was Principal of Sanskrit College;Keshab had no role; Alexander Duff came in 1830 and founded the General Assembly's Institution (later Scottish Church College). John Malcolm (Governor of Bombay 1827-30) favoured radical reform and Western education and sciences, driven by the Doctrine of Reason and Humanism. A cohort of liberal administrators: Thomas Munro (Governor of Madras 1820-27); Elphinstone (Governor of Bombay 1819-27, twice refused the Governor General's post to finish his book); Charles Metcalfe (GG 1835-36), whose liberation of the press brought conflict with the Court of Directors and resignation in 1838. (The slide groups these four as "conservatives/paternalists" who preferred gradual change; it names James Mill and Bentinck 28-35 as the radicals.) Charles Grant, an evangelist, was both a Member of Parliament and a director of the EIC: he presided over the Charter Act 1813, which legalised missionary entry and set Rs 1 lakh a year on education (the slide: from surplus revenues, for literature, learned Indians and scientific knowledge, with the medium left open; it adds that he campaigned with William Wilberforce). He wanted English-medium Western education so Indians would know the laws against EIC official corruption, and believed spreading Christianity would create political stability through a common religion. 24.4 Macaulay's Minute (1835): the decision and the reasons The Anglicist-Orientalist debate was settled by Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (1835), implemented through the English Education Act 1835. It chose Western education in English and was the main policy framework until Wood's Despatch 1854. It was the product of Roy's advocacy (he died in 1833), Bentinck 28-35's support and Macaulay's drafting. The board settles the debate (1813-35) on two questions: Syllabus (Indian or Western; Western wins) and Medium (Vernacular or English; English wins). Western syllabus brings Western values and the glorification of the British, producing Brown Sahibs: brown in skin colour, British from inside (taste, values), and the result is political stability."imp" is written beside the Decision and Reasons slide (Lecture 23, slide 48). Teacher's board: "MACAULAY'S minute on Indian's education" ("Indian's" boxed; it means education of Indians, not an Indian syllabus), leading "to Policy", which is implem Macaulay's famous line: "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia." Official Fulfil the White Man's Burden by giving Western sciences and humanities; empower Indians against corruption of EIC officials Real Cut the cost of administration (Macaulay's Law Commission 1834 was framing Western-style laws, and needed Western-educated Indians in the lower bureaucracy); create Brown Sahibs: Indians "Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals and intellect", loyal, glorifying British culture, and a domestic market for British goods Teacher's board: Reasons for Macaulay's Minute (1 to 3) Six reasons, as the teacher numbered them (slides 46 and 47):(1) Political stability: Western education is costly, so only the rich (city-living, upper-caste, landed class, the traditional leaders of the masses, who moved to cities after the Permanent Settlement 1793) can afford it; they become pro-British leaders while the poor followers are not led by anyone else. (2) Administration: the Charter Act 1833 brought Western-like laws (Law Commission 1834 under Macaulay) and Uncovenanted Civil Services open to Indians, which lowers fiscal expenditure (Indians in lower posts), so Western education was needed. (3) Ideological:Liberals (Macaulay) "give the best to India, and the best is the West", for the WMB.(4) Personalities:Roy + Bentinck 28-35 + Macaulay.(5) Administration (again): Western education to reduce corruption through an understanding of rights in Western-like laws. (6) Economy:create a market for British exports through the Western values and taste of Brown Sahibs. Why elite Indians supported it: access to government jobs, legal practice, medical practice, teaching and journalism; and a genuine belief that Western sciences could modernise and industrialise India. Downward Filtration Theory: the British would not build mass education infrastructure. They would educate only the urban elite, who would pass education downward to the masses at no extra State cost.High fees blocked the urban poor;rural areas got nothing (an urban-rural divide). Beside "genuine belief": "cute Brown Sahib believes in WMB" (he calls the educated elite "cute Brown Sahibs", believers in the White Man's Burden themselves), and "we will educate elites in cities who then [do the] mass education" with a circled "Gap" under "mass education suffered". 24.5 William Adam's reports on vernacular education (1835-38) Adam's three reports are the most critical documentary evidence of indigenous education before Macaulay's Minute 1835 and Wood's Despatch 1854 dismantled it. Context.Bentinck 28-35 appointed William Adam (a Scottish missionary who had co-founded the Calcutta Unitarian Committee with Roy in 1821) to survey indigenous education in Bengal and Bihar. The three reports (1835-38) fall in the same window in which Macaulay's Minute settled the debate; they describe the system that policy then bypassed. Findings. Massive scale: over 1,00,000 pathshalas in Bengal and Bihar alone, almost every village. It contradicts the colonial claim that "India was illiterate before the British." Caste inclusivity: children of all castes (except the lowest or untouchables) often sat together; poor agrarian families could attend. Trap: "Adam concluded the indigenous system was rigid and excluded lower castes" is false. Extreme flexibility (most often tested):no fixed fee (paid in kind, rice or grain, or cash by ability); no printed books or fixed syllabus (oral instruction, slate practice, local texts); no separate buildings (banyan trees, temples, mosques, the teacher's home); no annual exams or timetables (continuous personal assessment); suspended during harvest. Curriculum: strictly functional: basic literacy, arithmetic, accounts for daily agrarian and commercial life, exactly what Macaulay dismissed as "useless". Impact. India had no "education vacuum" waiting to be filled; a functioning mass-scale vernacular system existed, starved of funds and destroyed by the shift to English-medium administrative education. (Wood's Despatch later proposed "vernacular primary schools" as a State innovation, which is hollow against Adam; its real innovation was grants-in-aid and an inspectorate.) 24.6 The English Education Act 1835: key features Goal: promote European literature and science among Indians (the slide: among urban elite Indians). Medium: all education funds to be used for English education alone. Cut-off:no more government money for printing Oriental works;no new stipends for students entering Oriental institutions. Existing institutions (Calcutta Madrasa 1781, Benaras Sanskrit College 1791) were not abolished. (The teacher wrote 1781 and 1791 under them.) 24.7 Subsequent milestones (1844 to 1856) 1844 English compulsory for government jobs: a serious blow to vernacular languages 1847 Roorkee Engineering College (university in 1949; IIT Roorkee in 2001) 1849 Bethune School for Women by J.E. Drinkwater Bethune (Law Member of Dalhousie's Council, President of the Council of Education): female education under grants-in-aid (non-returnable State funding); Vidyasagar was closely associated and served as its Secretary 1851 Vidyasagar Principal of Sanskrit College, Calcutta under Dalhousie 48-56: opened to non-Brahmins, added mathematics and English literature 1856 Vidyasagar Inspector of Schools (Bengal) under Dalhousie 48-56; same year the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act "PVT sector = ABSENT; Govt job = MAJOR attraction" (so English became the ticket to work). This repeats Section 7.2's separation-of-powers board. 24.8 Wood's Despatch (1854) Why Wood's Despatch? "British India = large (even Punjab annexed 1849), therefore administration" needs a pyramid with a "huge number of lower staff": an ARMY OF CLERKS (the UCS gives "semi-senior" clerks), so mass basic education was needed. The Wood's Despatch of 1854, called the "Magna Carta of English Education in India", was a set of directions sent from London by Charles Wood,President of the Board of Control (1784), to Dalhousie 48-56. It was the most comprehensive education policy the British had issued and a shift from Macaulay's Downward Filtration. What it directed: Language ladder: Western education for the masses in vernaculars at the elementary level;vernaculars plus English at high school (classes 9 and 10);English at college. (Today: elementary = classes 1-8; secondary = 9-10; senior secondary = 11-12.) Education Departments in provincial governments, closer to the field. Teacher Training programmes. Continued support for female education. Universities in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta (departments for law, engineering, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic). Grants-in-aid (in the PYQ lists); a Director of Education in each province and an Inspector of Schools at district level. Real goals: Admin A cheap supply of clerks to cut administrative cost Culture Spread Western culture among the masses, plus "moral development and intellectual growth" (Prelims 2002: this was the despatch's stated aim) Economy Enlarge the market for British goods Polity Glorify British rule among the masses for political stability "WESTERN syllabus" above the ladder (the content is Western even when the medium is vernacular). On the goals slide: beside "moral development" he wrote "ethics: Western values >>> Indian values." PYQ 2002 (aim) and PYQ 2018 (three statements).Aim as stated = (b) spread of Western culture (the teacher ticked it "T"); employment was the "real reason" (his bracket on (a)); (c) is F because the ladder starts in vernaculars; (d) "scientific research in traditional education" is F (the teacher's ink "ended in 1835", the stem says "traditional"). PYQ 2018: grants-in-aid T, universities T, English at all levels F: answer (a) 1 and 2. Impact: Dalhousie 48-56 supported it and laid the groundwork; the three universities (Madras, Bombay, Calcutta) were officially established in 1857 under Canning 56-62 (Dalhousie left in 1856). Two more followed: Panjab University, Lahore (1882) and Allahabad University (1887), taking the total to five by the close of the 19th century. Bankim Chandra Chatterjee and Joddu Nath Bose were the first two graduates of Calcutta University in 1858. Result: failure: female education neglected, high fees blocked the masses, mass infrastructure never built. 1870: the subject of Education was transferred to the Provinces. Dalhousie 48-56's vernacular push: more elementary schools in Bengal and Bihar, and backing for technical education (efficient labour, good consumers, cheaper administration). 24.9 Universities and the education architecture Wood's Despatch laid the groundwork for the three Presidency universities; Dalhousie left India in 1856, and they opened in 1857 under Canning 56-62.Roorkee (1847) gained standing in Dalhousie 48-56's time (later Thomason College, then a university in 1949, then IIT Roorkee in 2001). The Despatch also set the spine of governance: a Director of Education at each provincial level and an Inspector of Schools at the district level, a structure that survived into independent India. > teacher (Lecture 24a, slide 4): "Education growth profile": the cities in the order their Western education grew: (1) Calcutta, (2) Bombay, (3) Madras, with years written beside (they read 1699, 1687, 1639, the last possibly 1632; the unclear digits are best checked against your notebook). PYQ 1996 (order of landmarks) and PYQ 1996 (education policy).Hindu College 1817 → Adam's reports 1835-38 → Wood's Despatch 1854 → University of Calcutta 1857: answer (a) 1, 3, 4, 2 (the teacher's ink beside Hindu College reads "David Hare (1830s)", which clashes with the 1817 in the handout and the key; both put it first). Macaulay's Minute 1835 → Wood's Despatch 1854 → Hunter 1882 → Sargent 1944: (a) 2 1 4 3. The handout adds the full order: Macaulay → Wood → Hunter → Sargent. 24.10 Why the British pulled back from higher education after 1870 In 1870 the State cut funding for higher education in Bengal, officially to fund mass vernacular education. The real reasons: WEMC Indians were writing increasingly nationalist articles in the press, and the Anglo-Indian press called college-educated Indians seditious.Brown Sahibness had begun to wane within 35 years of the English Education Act: the Doctrine of Reason was turned against British rule. By 1904 Curzon 99-05 called universities "factories of sedition." The White Man's Burden was looking farcical. 1882: under Ripon 80-84, education became a free enterprise: private institutions could open schools and colleges with State aid and less control; higher education grew rapidly, but only richer sections benefited. "Peak of Brown Sahib = 35 years [1835-70]" (slide 2). Western education has three results: in polity a desire for democracy, which includes the desire for Indians' participation in government and administration; in economy a desire for the Industrial Revolution; in societysocial reforms.In the short term: Brown Sahibness, hence British political stability. In the long term: an ever-growing, stronger INM. Slide 3: INM method 1857-1905: "Pen / Press" (the nationalist press), and a note that activities that destabilise the colonial State are "sedition" before 1947, which is nationalism (but not after 1947). Slide 1 classifies the WEMC as three branches: Youth, Capitalists (merchants, manufacturers) and Professionals (government jobs, lawyers boxed, doctors, engineers, press); the INM was led by the WEMC. 24.11 The Hunter Commission (1882-83) Set up by Ripon 80-84 to assess progress since Wood's Despatch, the Hunter / Indian Education Commission found primary and secondary education in serious trouble, worsened by the 1870 transfer to cash-strapped Provinces. Recommendations: Transfer education to Municipalities (urban) and District Boards (rural), both just empowered by Ripon 80-84's Local Self Government Resolution of 1882. Focus on mass education in vernaculars. Strengthen female education, especially outside Madras, Bombay and Calcutta. Divide secondary education (classes 9 and 10) into literary and vocational streams. A special fund for mass education for Backward communities (rejected). He brackets the District Boards as "(* District Panchayat)", marks the vernacular item "[Primary]", and links literary and vocational to "IIT" and "ITI" (the vocational stream's later forms). Slide 6 adds the pattern of control: the subject of education went to the Provinces in 1870, to the Local Bodies in 1882, back to the Provinces in 1919.Phule's Hunter memorandum (1882) is in Section 12. 24.12 Curzon's attack on the universities Curzon 99-05: "universities are factories of sedition." Based on the Raleigh Commission Report (1902) he passed the Indian Universities Act 1904: Universities under direct government control (it could veto or amend Senate regulations). Fewer fellows, shorter tenures, most fellows government nominees. Stricter affiliation of private colleges (a direct attack on nationalist and Swadeshi institutions). Rs 5 lakh a year for education. He also set up the Indian Agricultural Research Institute at Pusa, Bihar (1905), funded by Henry Phipps, a family friend. 24.13 The Sadler Commission (1917-19), and Gokhale's compulsory education Bill Named after Dr Michael Sadler: College entry after class 12 instead of class 10. Strengthen secondary education (classes 9 and 10). Universities to be residential, autonomous and unitary, not scattered affiliated colleges (Sadler is credited with the concept of the modern university campus system). Under Chelmsford 16-21,seven new universities were set up, including Osmania University in the princely State of Hyderabad. The Government of India Act 1919 formally gave education to the Provinces. "not imp"; "Campus system" under the title. He also circled "1861 to 1919" and joined it to the Imperial Legislative Council (the Council that existed from 1861 to 1919, Chapter 25). English only after class 8. Handicraft skilling in the regular curriculum. Free and compulsory education in vernaculars for 7 years, ages 7 to 14 (slide key). Source conflict on the age. He wrote "[Primary]" beside the access row, and beside "school-community contact": "motivation to the poor to pursue education (+) creates empathy among WEMC kids/youth." Macaulay versus Wardha.1835 Macaulay: English-medium, elite-focused, top-down, designed to create Brown Sahibs for colonial stability. 1937 Wardha: vernacular, activity-based, community-rooted, to create citizens, designed for self-governance. 24.16 The Sargent Plan (1944) The last major educational despatch of the British era, officially the Report of the Central Advisory Board of Education on Post-War Educational Development in India: the most comprehensive but unimplemented blueprint. Goal: bring Indian education up to contemporary England's standard, in a phased plan of 40 years for 100% literacy. Structure (John Sargent, the GoI's Educational Advisor):pre-primary 3-6;basic elementary, universal and free, 6-14 (junior basic 6-11, senior basic 11-14; inspired by Gandhi's Wardha Scheme of Basic Education); high school 11-17, selected students only, in academic and technical-vocational streams; university degree standardised to 3 years. Adult illiteracy to be liquidated in 20 years; one of the first British reports to provide for the differently-abled; a big expansion of teacher training, physical education and compulsory medical inspection. Criticism: Indian leaders furiously rejected the 40-year timeline (waiting till 1984 for basic literacy was an insult); and no funds were allocated. "not imp" beside both Sargent slides. 24.17 The overall impact of Western education By 1921: 92% illiteracy, and only 2% of women literate. A culture of public debate through the press created civil society. A passion for Western sciences among educated Indians (Roy and others saw it as the only route to modernisation).
