Europe's rebirth, Bengal's mirror. The Renaissance was Western Europe's 14th-century rebirth, driven by reason and aimed at human welfare, and it set off the Reformation, the end of feudalism, capitalism, the Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution. 19th-century Bengal looked similar: an oppressive priestly establishment, no modern education, birth-based privilege and poverty. The response was the same too: reach back to the scriptures for what was great and use reason to remove what was not. The Raj opens the door. After 1813 the British moved from Orientalism to Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists, who backed Western education and reform, while Evangelist conversion frightened Indians into reforming from within. The British called ancient India a myth, and cultural nationalism was the reply. Western education (1835) gave the Doctrine of Reason, and Bengal led because the Governor General sat there. Logic alone, or logic plus scripture? In India religion determined social practice, and the masses were deeply religious, so a reformer had to reform or reinterpret religion. Derozio's Young Bengal used only logic, ate beef and drank wine, and won a great controversy but poor mass politics. The socio-religious reformers used the Ctrl+F method: find the logic in the scripture and show it to the people. Roy, the bridge. Roy, the Father of Modern India, held universalism and found monotheism in the Upanishads; he used the Doctrine of Reason against other-worldliness, Karma and Incarnation. He opposed the Sanskrit College of 1824, wanted Western sciences, and worked with Bentinck 28-35, Macaulay and David Hare. His political demands, shared with Young Bengal, were Separation of Powers, a free Press, Indianisation and Trial by jury. Sati: the first law. By the 19th century Sati was driven by property, burden, honour and glory, and lower castes in Bengal had begun to copy it through Sanskritisation. Bentinck 28-35 demanded scriptural proof, so in 1828 the Brahmo Samaj beat Radhakanta Deb in debate, and in 1829 Regulation XVII made Sati culpable homicide. Radhakanta Deb's Dharma Sabha appealed to the Privy Council in 1830 and lost. The Brahmo Samaj splits. The Brahmo Samaj (1828) took the low-hanging fruits first and stayed an upper-caste, urban body; after Roy's death in 1833 Debendranath Tagore, the organisation man, held it together. Keshab Chandra Sen wanted a mass, all-India movement and a new religion, so 1866 gave the Brahmo Samaj of India and the Adi Brahmo Samaj; he also drove the Brahmo Marriages Act 1872. In 1878 he married off his minor daughter and the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj split away. Maharashtra and the voice from below. The Paramhansa Mandali (1849) copied Young Bengal and failed the same way; the Prarthana Samaj (1867) of Atmaram Pandurang, Ranade, Bhandarkar and Telang was Brahmoism for Maharashtra, with Keshab's help. Ranade also built the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha and the National Social Conference (1887). Phule opened a girls' school in Pune (1848), wrote Gulamgiri and founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873): he spoke for the oppressed and organised them. The home front: marriage, age, infants. Child marriage had religious sanction in the Garbhadhan ceremony, so the IPC 1860 set only age 10 and the Rakhmabai case (1884) split opinion. After the death of 11-year-old Phulmoni, Lansdowne 88-94 raised the age to 12 in 1891; Tilak said reform must come from society, Bhandarkar showed the Dharmashastras allow marriage after puberty, and census data showed the practice went on. The Female Infanticide Act 1870 could not reach dowry and hypergamy, nor the nutritional neglect of girls. Vidyasagar's war on widowhood. Vidyasagar changed Sanskrit College from within, opened 25 girls' schools in 1857-58, and sent a petition with 1,000 signatures; the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act came on 26 July 1856 and he married his own son to a widow. But a widow lost her husband's property on remarriage, orthodox Hindus won the scripture debate after 1857, and Maharashtra saw only 38 widow remarriages by 1900. Early reform failed because it was elite, top-down, gradual and silent on caste. Pride, revival and other answers. Dayanand's Arya Samaj (1875) said the Vedas were infallible, rejected idols and rose in Punjab, while Ramakrishna and Vivekananda offered spiritual pride and Vivekananda accepted idols and won the masses. Revivalism had a positive face and a negative one (aggressive Shuddhi, cow protection and communal tension). Sir Syed built Aligarh (1875) on modernisation without surrender of faith, and Narayana Guru consecrated an Ezhava's Shiva at Aruvippuram in 1888. Schools: from Orientalism to Sargent. Orientalists (Warren Hastings 73-85, Jones, Wellesley 98-05) governed the Indian way until Macaulay's Minute settled the debate in 1835 for a Western syllabus in English, making Brown Sahibs and a downward filtration that never reached the masses. Wood's Despatch 1854 gave the vernacular-to-English ladder, grants-in-aid and three universities (1857), then came Hunter 1882, Curzon's Act 1904, Sadler, Hartog, Wardha 1937 and the unfunded Sargent Plan 1944. By 1921 only about 8% were Western educated and 92% were illiterate. The press and the educated eight per cent. The press began in 1780 with Hicky's Bengal Gazette, shut down in 1782 by Warren Hastings 73-85, and then ran a cycle of repression (1799, 1823, 1878, 1908-10) and concession (Metcalfe 1835, Ripon 80-84's repeal in 1882). Indian-run papers carried reform and then nationalism, and the WEMC's method from 1857 to 1905 was pen and press. The Doctrine of Reason that was meant to make Brown Sahibs ended by making the leaders of the Indian National Movement.

Because the WEMC chose reform, the bottom of the order spoke first, in defiance. Ask: why are these revolts called the pre-history of modern nationalism? The Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC) responded to British rule largely through socio-religious reform movements. They believed in the benevolence of British rule, that the British would modernise India, and many benefited from the new economy and jobs British rule created. But peasants and tribals, the people at the very bottom of the new colonial order,responded first: not with petitions but with defiance, often with violence. INM leaders later called these pre-1857 revolts the "pre-history of modern nationalism." That does not mean they were failures: they were the first draft of a political resistance that would, over a century, become the Indian National Movement. The 1857 revolt was in many ways the culmination of a hundred years of such small and big rebellions. To understand 1857, first understand what drove peasants and tribals to revolt again and again. Western = Medicine, Law, Admin. The WEMC got its jobs from the new Western professions: medicine, law and administration (ADMIN underlined). And the pre-British era jobs that the new system replaced: Mansabdars, Faujdars, Amalguzars, Amils, Pundits, Maulvis, Kazis, Muftis (military and revenue officers and the religious-legal class). Reading: the old job-holders lost their positions while the new Western-educated class gained, so the old elite had a grievance of its own. "Pre-history" = "unwritten history" (the teacher's gloss: these revolts are the part of the story that the standard nationalist history did not write). And the verdict in his words: "NOT 100% MODERN BUT anti-colonial." Board: definitions Who is a peasant and who is a tribal? A cultivator who farms for food security is poor: a ryot or peasant. A cultivator who farms for profit is rich: a farmer. The basis of the word "peasant" is OCCUPATION (cultivation). A tribal is one who lives away from the mainstream, in hills, forests, deserts or islands (hills and forests underlined), and is not part of the majority population of the plains. Therefore the tribals traditionally enjoyed autonomy in three ways: political (the tribal chief), economic (forest resources) and socio-cultural (their own way of life). The dotted line: the land revenue systems of the plains were not applied by Indian kings to these areas. That is what the British changed.

Because the peasant's security was land revenue, every British system squeezed him in its own way. Ask: which system, which villain, which loss? 2.1 Why did the ryot have so many grievances? The British introduced not one but several land revenue (LR) systems, and each squeezed the peasant in its own way. Farming System of 1772 (Bengal) LR collection was auctioned to the highest bidder, a revenue farmer (the teacher: ijaradar). He extracted as much rent as he could, with the support of British officials, since collection happened under the District Collector's supervision. The peasant had no protection Permanent Settlement 1793 (PS1793) Replaced the revenue farmer with the zamindar as permanent owner. For the ryot it was not an improvement: the zamindar charged high rents, imposed illegal extra cesses called abwabs, and evicted at will. The ryot had no occupancy rights (no security of tenure), and British law was on the zamindar's side since all legal rights in land were vested in him Rent Act of 1859 Meant to correct this: a ryot who cultivated the same plot continuously for over twelve years earned occupancy right (not to be arbitrarily evicted). But its implementation in Bengal was ineffective and the exploitation continued Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas The oppression came directly from the British government through high LR demands. If the ryot could not pay, his land was auctioned; this drove him to the moneylender; high interest led to deeper indebtedness; default meant losing land to the moneylender. The peasant went from cultivator with land to labourer on someone else's field Board: Peasant Revolts Any revolt in Bengal: read it by period.Before 1772: high LR.1772-1793: higher LR plus the revenue farmer (ijaradar, FS1772), and the British government pro-revenue-farmer (RF circled): "legal right to collect LR."1793-1859: higher rents + illegal abwabs + lack of occupancy rights + the zamindar (Z circled) + the British government: therefore the PS1793 Act gave all rights to the zamindar and, practically, none to the tenant ryots.1859-85: higher rents + illegal abwabs + lack of occupancy rights, because of the loophole in the Rent Act 1859.Revolt in "SCAM-B" (post 1801): higher LR + higher-interest loans: British government [LR] + moneylender [loan] + landlessness.Mahalwari: "C, U, P": the circle splits in two halves, zamindari-like issues (A) and ryotwari-like issues (B). The full story of the experiments is in Chapter 16: Land Revenue Systems. 2.2 Contract farming: the indigo system European indigo planters forced ryots to cultivate indigo on a portion of their land. The handout dates it in Bengal until 1860, and later in Bihar until 1918. The ryot was made to take a loan from the planter at the outset, then sold the indigo back to the planter at a price far below market rate. He was perpetually in debt. Indigo exhausted the soil, reducing the productivity of the land he used for food crops. Board: "(4) Contract Farming [Indigo cultivation] [Bengal, Bihar; Till 1863, L 1863-1918]" If he refused, the planter's Indian agents, local British officials and courts came down on him. There was no escape. Date conflict: indigo in Bengal. The handout says Bengal until 1860, Bihar until 1918. The teacher's board (slide 1) writes "Bengal, Bihar: Till 1863, then 1863-1918." Two models on the board.Ordinary system: State, then LR, from the zamindar (Z, the landowner), who takes rent from the ryot (tenant).Indigo model: the zamindar still pays LR to the State, but now the European planter takes the land on lease (lease amount to the zamindar) and collects rent from the ryots (the planter becomes the middle landlord), and in addition there is a contract between the planter and the ryot: the ryot must grow indigo on a part (one quadrant) of his plot. So the ryot faces both rent and contract. Board: the indigo debt trap as a flow The indigo debt trap (the teacher's board) Planter gives a loan (the board says low-interest) to the ryot at the start Ryot buys equipment and indigo seeds from the planter Ryot sells the indigo to the planter and gets a price that is not remunerative Inability to pay: the rent and the loan Soil productivity falls (indigo exhausts the soil; the quadrant turns Banjar, fallow land) Debt trap: the ryot is forced to grow indigo by taking more loan,else eviction, plus oppression by the planter's Indian agents Why it is a debt trap by design. The first loan binds the ryot to the planter for inputs and for sale. The price he receives is not remunerative, so he cannot pay rent and loan, so he must borrow again from the planter. Meanwhile soil productivity falls and the plot turns Banjar (barren). The handout's own line: "the same structural logic as modern-day bonded labour." The handout does not mention that the planter's first loan was low-interest; that word is on the teacher's board. The handout stresses the below-market price and the debt. Both agree on the trap. (The fractions are the teacher's board only; the handout says "a portion of their land.") The Bengal revolt is in Chapter 22 and Champaran in Chapter 37. 2.3 What role did religion play? Religion played a dual role: grievance and organiser. As a grievance: (1) Christian missionaries were converting people; (2) the British ended revenue-free and rent-free land tenures held by temples, mosques and religious institutions; (3) social reform laws were seen as interference in religion: the Sati Abolition Act 1829, the Lex Loci Act 1850 (inheritance even after conversion to another religion) and the Hindu Widow Remarriages Act 1856. As an organiser: pre-1857 India had no political parties, no newspapers with mass reach, no formal organisations. (The handout's parallel: the INC, BJP and RSS do today the work that religion did then: leadership, coordination, unity.) A revolting religious sect already had a leader, a philosophy, a sense of community and the habit of collective action. Religion filled the organisational vacuum. Board: "# Religion Role in Pre-1857 Revolts" Grievance, four points:taxation on the lands of temples and mosques;ending revenue-free or rent-free tenures of religious sects, temples and mosques; 1813+ (circled): Christian missionaries could enter for conversion (the 1813 Charter, see Section 3); and social reforms created fear of religion.Organiser:unity among followers comes from religion and the leader comes from the religious class; he defines the Goal, the Plan, the Programme and the Voice/slogans. When economic grievances of followers exist, a social leader, i.e. a religious one (L circled), takes up the political role.

Because the tribal also lived by forest and chief, the British reach into the forest hurt him doubly. Ask: how did LR enter the forest, and what did the Act of 1878 take? 3.1 What was different about the tribal experience? Tribals lived in forests and hills, away from the plains. Two things gave their life its shape: tribal autonomy (in civil and criminal matters they governed themselves by their own customary law) and their relationship with the forest (home, livelihood, identity). British rule destroyed both. Tribal livelihood = three lives.Cultivation (the tribal as a ryot or peasant), hunting (hunters), and gathering forest produce (gatherers), with barter trade with plains people.Today the major forest produce is timber; the minor is bamboo, tendu patta, sal, honey and so on.Law = tribal law, and L, E, J (legislative, executive, judicial) = the tribal chief: all three powers sat with him, which is the political autonomy."Don't get confused if the phrase 'Peasant Revolt' is used for a tribal revolt": many tribals were cultivating, so a tribal revolt can be called a peasant revolt in some books; keep the two kinds apart by the leader and the grievance (forest and autonomy for tribals). How the British pushed LR into the forests: four routes (the primary British concern was extraction of land revenue): Board: "# TRIBALS", "# enjoyed autonomy" 1. Zamindars from the plains were made legal owners of tribal land. 2. Tribal lands were farmed out to revenue farmers. 3. In some cases the tribal chief was recognised as a zamindar, with the same exploitative powers. 4. In others tribal ryots were made individual landowners, breaking up the collective, community-based relationship with their land. High LR demands and the British insistence on cash payment (instead of produce) brought in moneylenders:indebtedness, then loss of land. (The handout's explanation: a subsistence farmer who grows grain but must pay in rupees has to sell in the market first, exposing him to price swings and middlemen at every step.) Board: "# TRIBALS" The "both LR systems" on tribal land: the British used both the ryotwari idea (cultivator = landowner) and the zamindari idea (big person = landowner) and also the contract of LR, that is auction, of the right to collect LR (the revenue farmer). That matches the handout's four routes. Two dates:1853+ Railways (railway lines through forests, Section 3.2) and the 1813 Charter, which ended the EIC's monopoly over business with India and legalised the entry of missionaries (for conversion). The teacher adds that by 1813 the Industrial Revolution (1750-1850 in England) was mature and progressing, hence the pressure to open India to British business. Board: "TRIBALS GRIEVANCES" The big tribal grievances circle: outsiders from the plains and from Britain pushed in, band by band. From the top: Laws (Forests Act 1878, the ban on hunting and Jhum, the tax on toddy under the Abkari system), then Christian missionaries, then the British state's laws and officials (they hurt autonomy), then British businesses (mining, rail-road, timber; with railways, ships and forced labour), then merchants (for trading forest resources), then zamindars and lenders (the British insisted on cash payment of LR), then revenue farmers (Farming System), then ryot = landowner and tribal chief = landowner (the ownership changes), then zamindar = owner. His reading in one line: tribal life, hit in the political, socio-cultural and economic ways, was "turned upside down by outsiders," both Indian (from the plains) and British. 3.2 The ban on Jhum and hunting The British banned Jhum cultivation (slash-and-burn or shifting cultivation) because they wanted settled peasant communities paying land revenue regularly. For hill tribals Jhum was their way of life. The ban on Jhum and on hunting criminalised their way of existing. The Chenchus of Hyderabad were pushed to the edge of extinction. Why ban Jhum, Podu (the Andhra word), shifting or slash-and-burn cultivation, and why ban hunting?Answer: the British wanted settled peasant communities, paying LR regularly, for ease of LR collection. A shifting cultivator or a hunter has no fixed field to assess and tax. 3.3 The Indian Forests Act 1878 The Indian Forests Act 1878, passed under Lytton 76-80, divided all forests into three categories. The British called it "scientific forestry;" in practice it was legal dispossession. Why they needed it: the railway boom of the 1870s needed enormous supplies of durable timber (teak, sal, deodar); each mile of track needed roughly 2,000 wooden sleepers. The state wanted absolute control over the best forests. Board: "Lytton 76-80: Indian Forest Act 1878 Reserved Forests Everything prohibited unless specifically permitted. The most commercially valuable forests. All traditional rights legally extinguished: no grazing, no firewood, no Jhum. Purpose: unhindered commercial timber extraction by the government and contractors "Tribals not allowed": loss of home (land) Protected Forests Everything permitted unless specifically prohibited. Commercial potential but too much local use to close at once. The state could declare tree species state property and close sections at any time. A transitional category: many were later upgraded to Reserved "Tribals can't sell forest produce": loss of forest rights and resources Village Forests Assigned to specific village communities. Very few were created. Strict colonial rules on cattle, wood and species; access could be revoked. The British never left any forest truly in local hands "Open to all in practice" (the teacher's gloss) The legal masterstroke: before the British, forests were common property resources managed by the communities. The 1878 Act turned customary rights into privileges granted by the mercy of the colonial state; a privilege can be taxed, restricted or revoked. Overnight, gathering firewood, grazing a cow or clearing a small patch made millions of forest dwellers trespassers on their own ancestral land. Beyond the Act:land acquisition for railway and road construction and commercial timber displaced tribals from their homes, and they were often forced into unpaid labour on the very projects that dispossessed them. Reserved = loss of home (land); Protected = loss of forest rights and resources; Village Forests = open to all in practice. Compare the handout: Village Forests were few and tightly controlled, so check which wording your teacher used before answering; the teacher's "open to all in practice" is his shorthand, not the handout's meaning. See the alert below. Possible mismatch on Village Forests. The handout says village forests were very few and heavily controlled by the colonial state (access revocable). The teacher's board says "open to all in practice." The two can be reconciled only as: on paper assigned to villages, in practice not truly local (handout) versus usable by people in practice (teacher).  for what he said aloud. For Prelims, remember the order and the rule of each category (Reserved: all prohibited unless permitted; Protected: all permitted unless prohibited). Today: the Forest Rights Act 2006 gives the right to forest lands and forest resources to STs and other traditional forest dwellers in 5th Scheduled areas (Central and East India). The 6th Schedule gives autonomy in the North East tribal areas.MFP = Minor Forest Produce = non-timber forest produce. (The handout adds: the FRA 2006 "attempts to begin correcting what this Act did.") 3.4 The Abkari system On the Abkari slide (Lecture 25, slide 21) he underlined "Abkari (Excise) Administration," "auctioned," "criminalised," "2nd only to LR," and "Christian missionaries." (Not shown as a figure here: the words are in the table below.) Before British rule, brewing local liquor from palm sap (toddy) or mahua flowers was a customary right, lightly regulated or untaxed. These drinks were tied to religious rituals, festivals and daily nutrition. The colonial state, through the Abkari (Excise) Administration, claimed a monopoly over the manufacture and sale of all intoxicating liquors and drugs. It auctioned the right to tap palm trees and sell liquor to the highest-bidding contractors; the contractors raised prices steeply to recover their investment. Brewing without a licence was criminalised, so tribals had to buy back their own drinks at inflated prices. Excise duties became one of the largest sources of provincial revenue: second only to land revenue in many areas. Note: this grievance later fed the temperance and anti-liquor strand of the INM: Gandhi's call to picket liquor shops in the NCM and CDM. After 1813, the entry of Christian missionaries added a religious grievance to the economic and cultural one.

Because the grievances differed by class, the revolts differ by who led them. Ask: elite or peasant at the head? Board of terms: "Uprising / Rebellion / Revolt / Ulugulan / Hool" Words used for these events:uprising, rebellion, revolt, Ulugulan (Munda), Hool (Santhal) all mean a rising. Mutiny = when followers revolt against their leader (a type of revolt): the Sepoy Mutiny, employees mutinying, and the teacher's example of white (British) political groups in India revolting against their own government, non-violently.Revolution = a huge change in a short time (small triangle on a short base); the Industrial Revolution (100 years) is a big result over a long base (big triangle on a 100-year base). Revolt = an attempt at revolution = usually violent but not always: e.g. the Indigo Revolt 1859. (Lecture 25, slide 23, yellow ink.) Revolutions (French Revolution 1789 and the other one he writes as "ARGS-83") were quick. BUT the Indian National Movement was not: the reason is Purna Swaraj (complete independence) and the span 1857-1947 = 90 years. The INM was gradual, step by step:goals became more radical, the method went from pen, to protests, to guns. Sec 4 Two Kinds of Uprisings There were two distinct kinds: 4.1 Civil Uprisings: led by the elite (a Raja, a zamindar, a mansabdar). Peasants participated, but the leadership and cause were primarily those of the dispossessed elite.The 1857 revolt is the biggest example of this kind. 4.2 Peasant Revolts: led by the peasants themselves. "Peasant Revolts" is the umbrella term (the broad word used for everything in the chapter); under it come two kinds: Civil Uprising and Peasant Revolts (peasant-led). He writes "TRADITIONAL" above "Who led it" and ties it to Civil Uprisings: civil uprisings are led by traditional elites. (On the Chapter 21 title slide he writes the same idea: "common ppl led by TRADITIONAL elites" for 1857.)

Because the elite lost status, land or autonomy, they rose first, and peasants joined. Ask: what exactly did each lose? 5.1 to 5.6: Chait Singh, Bishnupur and Birbhum, Wazir Ali, Poligars, Bundelas, Veluthampi 5.1 1778-81: Raja Chait Singh of Benaras Benaras was annexed by the EIC through the Treaty of Faizabad 1775. Chait Singh was a big zamindar with the title of Raja and the loyalty of his people, with his own military and fort. His estates were seized for non-payment of land revenue and he revolted. (PS1793 later formally brought Benaras into the Bengal-BOB-North Madras-Benaras settlement) 5.2 1789: Bishnupur and Birbhum, Bengal Local zamindars and their ryots oppressed by the LR demands (the handout: of the Permanent Settlement's precursors) rose against the EIC's revenue machinery. Minor in scale but frequent UPSC distractors: know the name and date (the PYQ 2006 wrong option C) 5.3 1799: Nawab Wazir Ali 97-98 The deposed Nawab of Awadh (ruled only 1797-98) revolted with peasant support. The slide adds: he was deposed by John Shore 93-98 in return for a promise of a Rs 76 lakh annual subsidy by his uncle Sadat Ali Khan II (under ToA 1765); the peasants joined because of high LR oppression 5.4 1799-1805: Poligar Revolts Poligars = traditionally autonomous local chiefs in South India. British Rule of Law and equality before law hurt their elevated social status (the same grievance as the taluqdars in 1857: loss of privilege backed by customary law). The Ryotwari settlement took away their lands; high LR on peasants brought popular participation. Revolted and crushed 5.5 Post-2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05): Bundela chiefs The Subordinate (Subsidiary) Alliance imposed a British Resident on the Maratha states. Bundela chiefs, suffering Resident interference, revolted with peasant support 5.6 1809: Dewan Veluthampi of Travancore After the Subsidiary Alliance of 1805, the British Resident interfered in Travancore's internal affairs. Veluthampi, the Dewan, revolted with Nair troops and peasants. Crushed Poligar = Local chief; autonomous traditionally; private army and forts; landed magnate. That is his shorthand for what the Poligars lost (status and privilege) when British Rule of Law came. The teacher also wrote "Bundelas" above the typed words "Maratha states" and struck those words out: the Resident was imposed on the Bundela chiefs' area. And the handout's key point for the whole section: civil uprisings are driven by the loss of the elite's privilege, and peasants join because LR also hurts them. Slide versus handout on Wazir Ali: the handout says only that he "revolted with peasant support." The slide adds the Rs 76 lakh subsidy,John Shore 93-98, and uncle Sadat Ali Khan II, and writes the dates Wazir Ali 97-98. These are additions, not contradictions. Keep the extra detail from the slide; the exam-level fact is 1799, deposed Nawab of Awadh, peasant support. 5.7 The Paika Rebellion (1817) Who: the Paikas were the traditional landed militia of Odisha, a warrior class rooted in the feudal order. Leaders and goal:feudal aristocrats, chiefly Bakshi Jagabandhu (military commander of the Raja of Khurda) and marginalised zamindars. The goal was to restore lost hereditary privileges, authority and rent-free estates. Multi-class support: despite elite leadership, massive grassroots support from ordinary peasants, salt makers and the tribal Kondhs of Ghumusar: a true multi-class uprising. EIC provocations (after conquering Odisha, 1803): stripped the Paikas of their rent-free land tenures (jagirs); imposed extortionate short-term settlements demanding revenue strictly in silver (Sicca) rather than the traditional cowrie shells;banned local sea-salt production to create a monopoly that sent prices soaring; and dethroned the revered Raja of Khurda, uniting elite loyalists and the masses. Course: rebels destroyed British symbols of authority (police stations, courts, salt monopoly offices), briefly captured Puri, forced the EIC forces to retreat and proclaimed the Raja of Khurda as sovereign. Crushed: the British declared martial law and crushed the core uprising with overwhelming force by 1818.Bakshi Jagabandhu led a jungle guerrilla war until he surrendered on negotiated terms in 1825. Verdict: one of the most formidable pre-1857 armed uprisings; because of its scale and multi-class participation, it is debated in modern historiography as a candidate for India's true "First War of Independence." "(Like Rajputs)": the Paikas were a warrior class, like the Rajputs (hereditary soldiers on rent-free land). And the underlined verdict with his note: "First War of Independence" [instead of the 1857 Revolt]: the Paika Rebellion is the candidate for the title that the books give to 1857. The five things he underlined: Bakshi Jagabandhu, marginalised zamindars, salt makers, banned sea-salt, dethroned Raja.

Because the peasants led themselves here, their targets were exact: revenue farmer, grain, prison, court. Ask: whom did they hit, and why? 6.1 The 1783 Rangpur Rebellion, North Bengal Grievance: the Farming System of 1772 unleashed revenue farmers on the peasantry; Debi Singh and Gobinda Singh were particularly oppressive and British officials colluded. This came on top of the Great Bengal Famine of 1770, which had broken the economic spine of the peasantry. Action: they looted the grain stores of Debi Singh and Gobinda Singh, attacked prisons and freed imprisoned ryots, and attacked local courts. They were not blindly violent: they hit the revenue farmer, his grain stores, the prison and the court. Own government: for a time they ran their own government, funded by self-imposed taxes. Result:crushed by the EIC. "Peasant = Leader Revolt": Rangpur is the textbook peasant-led revolt, so the peasant is the leader. (Compare Section 4: civil uprisings are led by elites.) 6.2 Mysore 1830-31 Background: the Wodeyar dynasty was restored to Mysore in 1799 after the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War. But the Subsidiary Alliance of 1799 required a heavy annual subsidy to the British, so the Wodeyar government imposed high land revenue demands. Revolt: the peasants revolted against both the Wodeyar administration and British agents. Result: the EIC crushed it, as was its obligation under the SA 1799, which required the British to protect the ruler.

Because religion supplies leader and unity, an economic grievance became a faith movement. Ask: who is the leader, and what is the slogan or symbol? 7.1 The Sanyasi and Fakir Rebellion (1760-1850s) Gomastas, 1757+: before, the ryot and artisan sold to the domestic (Indian) trader. After 1757, they were squeezed past him through Gomastas (Indian agents) straight to EIC officers, so the domestic trader (the sad face) lost his trade. This is the "EIC monopoly over domestic trade" in the Sanyasi grievance list, and it links to Chapter 10 (Gomastas and private domestic trade after Plassey). Sec 7.1 Sanyasi and Fakir Rebellion (1760-1850s) Board (yellow): "Ryot" and "Artisan" with arrows to "Domestic Trader" (sad face), and large curved arrows from each, labelled "Gomastas", to "eic officers"; circled "1757 Place and scale:North Bengal and Bihar; ran across nearly a century (1760 to the 1850s),peaking around 1800 with about 50,000 members. Two groups, two faiths: the Dasnami Sanyasis (peasants and small traders) and the Madari Fakirs (peasants who held revenue-free or rent-free land tenures, now ended by the EIC). Hindu and Muslim respectively, they cooperated: common ground in their religious philosophies and, more importantly, identical economic grievances. Grievances:high land revenue;high rents after PS1793; the EIC's monopoly over domestic trade in Bengal. (Echo: Mir Qasim 60-63 tried to end internal duties before Buxar 1764 because EIC agents were strangling local merchants: the same squeeze now hurt the Sanyasi traders.) Result: finally crushed by the British. Anandamath:Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novel Anandamath (1882) was inspired by this revolt; its song Vande Mataram became the anthem of the INM. (Prelims 2006.) The curve: the revolt starts around the 1750s (1760), rises through 1772 and 1793, peaks at about 1800 with 50,000 participants, and falls away by the 1850s. The peak sits on 1793/1800, right after PS1793 raised rents. The teacher also lined up Dasnami Sanyasis with Madari Fakirs (the two faiths). 7.2 The Pagal Panthi Revolt (1823-33), East Bengal Leaders:Karim Shah, and after him Tipu Shah. Grievance: against zamindars: high rents, illegal abwabs, denial of occupancy rights. Action: Tipu Shah promised lower rents once the zamindars and the British were defeated: a political programme delivered through religious leadership. Result: crushed by the EIC. "(Religion providing leader)": beside the leaders row he notes that religion provided the leader (the point from Section 2.3). He underlined East Bengal, Karim Shah, Tipu Shah and zamindars. 7.3 Titu Mir of 24 Parganas (1831) Who: Titu Mir belonged to the Wahabi sect and taught the reformist philosophy of Shah Waliullah of Delhi. His followers were poor peasants who adopted a distinct physical identity (a unique beard and dress), itself a marker of resistance. Grievance: a tax on beards levied by the local zamindar; oppression by indigo planters, zamindars and British officials. Action: the followers set up their own government with self-imposed taxes and built the famous bamboo fort at Narkelberia village. Sec 7.3 Titu Mir of 24 Parganas (1831) Result:crushed by the EIC army. The circle labelled "Followers": the followers' land lay under zamindars (Z) of two kinds: one half under a zamindar who has not leased lands to planters (so only the zamindar's rent and beard tax hurt), the other half under a zamindar who leased lands to the planter (so the indigo planter hurt as well). Either way the poor peasant followers were squeezed. Reading note on slide 35: the letter on the board that I read as "Z" (zamindar, the same glyph the teacher uses for the zamindar on slides 1 and 93) could also be a fraction ("half"). The meaning above fits the table's grievance row (zamindars plus indigo planters).  for the exact figure he drew. 7.4 The Faraizi Movement (1830s, revived 1870s), Bengal Leaders:father-son line: Haji Shariatullah (1830s), Dudu Mian (mid-century), Naya Mian (1870s). Belief: the Quran is the only true source of Islamic law; purge Islam of un-Islamic beliefs and practices: a return to the faith in its original form. Grievance: oppression by indigo planters, zamindars and British officials. Slogan (Dudu Mian):"land belongs to God, therefore any rent or tax on land is ungodly." Fighting a sin is a far more powerful mobilising argument than fighting an economic injustice. Sec 7.4 Faraizi Movement Parallel state: their own government, courts, and taxes. Result: crushed by the British. W.W. Hunter, The Indian Musalmans: argued British neglect of Muslims had contributed to the Faraizi movement and that the British should favour Muslims for the sake of political stability; a discontented community is dangerous. This had long-term consequences for British policy on Hindu-Muslim relations. "*voice" beside "The slogan": the slogan is the movement's voice (the "voice" point of modern politics in Section 9). He underlined Hunter's argument that the British should favour Muslims for political stability and circled "DnR" (see the alert below). Unreadable ink on slide 36: the circled "DnR" at the right is not explained on the slide (it might refer to the leaders Dudu and Naya, but the R does not match a name in the table).  for what he said. Treat the leaders as Haji Shariatullah, Dudu Mian, Naya Mian (all three underlined). 7.5 Moplah / Mopilla revolts in Malabar (1840, 1870s, 1921) Three groups, one land:Moplahs (Muslim ryots of the Malabar coast), Janmies (members of Brahmin princely families, historically big landlords) and supervisors who collected LR for the Janmies. The land's earnings were shared among all three, each with a customary right. How British rule broke this:Malabar was annexed after the Third Anglo-Mysore War (1789-92). The British LR system recognised only the Janmies as legal owners. The Moplahs lost all customary rights overnight and became exploited tenants, while the Janmies were backed by British law. (British Orientalists gave ideological cover: Lord Parshuram had gifted all the land to the Janmies.) Character: violent, and communal in colour because oppressor and oppressed had different religious identities. The same dynamic returns in 1921 during the Non-Cooperation Movement (see Chapter 38 and the NCM chapters). Result: crushed by the EIC army. On the slide (Lecture 25, slide 37) he underlined "(1840, 1870s, 1921)," "Moplahs = Muslim ryots" and "Janmies." Nothing else is written in ink; the same slide is not a PYQ slide, but note that the PYQ 2020 option (b) "Mappila Rebellion 1921" is a trap for the Ulgulan question (Section 10.1). Handout Prelims 2006 alert sits under the Moplah row, but the question is about Anandamath = Sanyasi rebellion (Section 7.1). The slide order puts the PYQ after Moplah (Lecture 25, slide 38), which is why it appears there.

Because forest and autonomy were taken, the tribals rose in a chain, ending in the Santhal Hool. Ask: what triggered each, and how did the British answer? 8.1 to 8.3: Pahariya, Bhil, Ramosi 8.1 Pahariya Revolt (1778), Rajmahal Hills: the Pahariyas were among the earliest tribals to resist. When the EIC extended revenue collection and administration into the Rajmahal Hills, these hunter-gatherers and shifting cultivators revolted against the destruction of their autonomy and livelihood. The British used military force and a policy of containment, pushing them further into the hills. 8.2 Bhil Revolts (1818-31), Western India: the Bhils of the Khandesh and Rajputana hills revolted repeatedly. Annexation of Maratha territories after the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1818) brought their homelands under direct EIC control; new LR demands, plains-based moneylenders and curtailed forest rights provoked the risings. Suppressed militarily, but the British also raised the Bhil Corps (a locally recruited force) as a pacification strategy. 8.3 Ramosi Uprising (1822), Western Ghats near Pune: the Ramosis had been watchmen and guards under the Maratha state and lost their customary occupations and status after the British takeover. A localised but violent rising, put down by force. Slide 39 (Lecture 25) underlines "hunter-gatherers and shifting cultivators," "further into the hills," "new LR demands," "plains-based moneylenders," "curtailment of traditional forest rights," the "Bhil Corps ... pacification strategy" and "Ramosi Uprising (1822)," "watchmen and guards," "under the Maratha state," "lost their customary occupations and status." So for each: Pahariya = containment; Bhil = recruit them (Bhil Corps); Ramosi = job lost with the Maratha state. 8.4 to 8.6: Kol, Kandh, Khasi 8.4 Kol Uprising 1831-32, Chhota Nagpur and Singhbhum The Kols' tribal autonomy was destroyed. The Raja of Chhotanagpur farmed out tribal lands to merchants and moneylenders, outsiders called Suds. The Kols lost customary land rights. Action: they targeted the property of the Suds, not their lives: again, the tribals knew their oppressors.Crushed by the army 8.5 Kandh Uprising 1837-56, Odisha (Ghumsar/Kalahandi) Leader: Chakra Bisoi. The British banned human sacrifice, tied to the Kandhs' religious ritual of Meriah. To the British a humanitarian intervention; to the Kandhs an attack on their religion and autonomy.Prolonged resistance, eventually crushed 8.6 Khasi Uprising 1829-33 Leader: U Tirot Sing. The British built the Brahmaputra Valley-Sylhet Road, bringing an influx of outsiders (British businesses, their Indian agents, British officials) into Khasi territory: loss of Khasi land and disruption of their way of life. Crushed "in Bangladesh": he points at Sylhet (the end of the Brahmaputra Valley-Sylhet Road) to say Sylhet is in Bangladesh today, so do not look for it inside India on the map. He underlined the Kol's "action" (property, not lives), and the Khasi leader U Tirot Sing, the Suds, and Meriah by name. 8.7 The Santhal Hool (1855-56) Homeland: the Santhals called it Damini-i-koh, "the skirts of the hills" (Rajmahal Hills, Jharkhand). The British opened it up for settlement, bringing non-Santhal zamindars and moneylenders, whom the Santhals called Dikus (outsiders).Railway and road construction further devoured Santhal land. Leaders: the brothers Sido Murmu and Kanhu Murmu. Action: (1) in 1855 the Santhals gave the British a formal prior warning, a public declaration of revolt: political action, not mere violence; (2) they rose with bows and arrows against the "unholy trinity": the British, the zamindars and the moneylenders, to win back their fatherland from the Dikus; (3) British authority in the region collapsed; (4) the British retaliated with organised military force,burning villages and killing about 50,000 Santhals. Sec 8.7 Santhal Hool 1855-56: Cause, Course, Outcome as eight boxes Result: crushed with extreme ferocity, but with a real political impact: a separate administrative unit, the Santhal Parganas, was created with protections for tribal culture and identity, and restrictions on transfer of Santhal land to non-tribals were imposed there: an early protective land law acknowledging the Diku problem. (Prelims 2018.) Cross-reference: Bankim's Bharat Mata idea in Anandamath (1882) drew on the same emotional idea of a fatherland to be reclaimed; the Santhals had said it in their own idiom three decades earlier. Land Loss (Acquisition): from the railway and road box the teacher draws an arrow to "Land Loss: Acquisition" (land acquisition for railways and roads is the economic cause). He underlined the 1855 prior warning (political action), bows and arrows, the brothers' names, the unholy trinity and about 50,000 killed. Prelims 1998 answer (d) 2, 4, 1, 3. Santhal (1855) then Mutiny (1857) then Indigo (1859) then Deccan Riot (1875). The two traps: putting the Mutiny first (the Santhal rising came before it) and reversing Indigo and Deccan. Prelims 2018 answer (c) Both 1 and 2: Santhal Parganas created, and land transfer to non-Santhals restricted. Handout-figure extras. The handout figure spells the leaders "Sidhu and Kanho" (the PYQ answer slide also writes "Sidhu and Kanho") and says the Santhal Parganas were carved out of "Bhagalpur, Bihar to Orissa," a semi-autonomous unit. That geography is not in the handout text or the class slides, so keep it as a handout-figure detail only. The text and the teacher write Sido and Kanhu Murmu. Mismatch between the handout figure and the handout text. The figure lists "Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908; Beth Begari banned" as the outcome of Birsa's revolt, and the Kol Revolt as "1831" (the text and slide say 1831-32). The Tenancy Act and Beth Begari are not mentioned anywhere in the handout text or class slides of this chapter; treat them as a handout-figure fact to check in your own notebook. Also the figure reorders the boxes (Khasi after Kandh); the class slide 51 keeps Khasi 1829-33 before Kol. Use the dates, not the box order.

items.t: 9 · Understanding the character of pre-1857 revolts
items.x: Because the revolts were many and scattered, the question is what they add up to. Ask: modern nationalism, or its pre-history? 9.1 Were these revolts modern nationalism? No. Modern nationalism rests on a specific idea of the Nation and a specific idea of Politics. The handout's model is the French Revolution's Liberty, Equality, Fraternity: a modern nation is one where citizens feel united as one people (Fraternity/Unity),equal before the law (Equality), and collectively supreme (the national interest, not that of any king, caste or class, is paramount: Liberty/Sovereignty). Modern politics needs: a united leadership; a clear ideology and goal; a plan (long-term) and a programme (short-term); a mouthpiece (newspaper, website) to articulate ideology and justify actions; and an organisational structure through which directions reach every follower. Two halves of "modern INM": the idea (modern nation = ideology) and the method (modern politics).Nation = the sum of people, and three words: one (fraternity), equal (equality), supreme (liberty): the modern meaning given by the French Revolution 1789.Consequences:Polity (democracy, republic, fundamental rights, DPSPs, right to equality), Economy (capitalism: equality of opportunity, right to property, LPG; socialism: land reforms, redistribution of wealth, welfare state), Society (feminism because 50% of the nation is female; anti-casteism; no discrimination on religion or language). Modern politics (the method of the INM):A ideology, B goals, C plan (long-term), D programme (short-term: "what today?"), E organisation, strong united leadership, G money (the rupee sign), and "voice" to carry all of A to E and G (fasts, yatras, symbols, flags, slogans, poems, songs, plays and films, graffiti, memes, press, social media, radio, television). Board: "modern Nation [ideology]" (left), "Modern INM", "modern Politics [method of INM]" (right) The teacher's board has A, B, C, D, E and G; there is no letter F (leadership sits between E and G without a circled letter). "mmp" is circled beside the title on slides 44 to 47; it most likely abbreviates "modern nation, modern politics," but  for what he meant. Where the pre-1857 revolts fell short: 1. Not all-India movements: no unity across regions. 2. No coordination with each other. 3. Only local leaders: nobody thought of India first and their region second. 4. Lacked proper planning. 5. Their goal was not democracy in any modern sense. On the same board he also writes the point that calling Hitler an "extreme" nationalist brings a bad name to nationalism (slide 92): the teacher asks "Why not" call him a "pseudo-nationalist" instead, with a fragment "100%." underlined under the Hitler line. The reading: real nationalism is the fraternity-equality-liberty idea above; a leader who denies equality is not a nationalist at all.  for the exact wording he gave around "100%". 9.2 Then why "pre-history of modern nationalism"? Because they were unmistakably political: not apolitical, not merely criminal, not merely religious. They had: Ideology: they wanted to restore the moral order British rule had disturbed. Their vocabulary was not rights, democracy, colonialism or "No Taxation Without Representation," but immoral rule implies oppression, which implies denial of economic, cultural and political rights:different language, same moral architecture. Organisation:religion provided unity, leadership and the habit of collective action, especially when a whole sect revolted. Many set up their own governments, courts and taxes: a functioning parallel state, however temporary. Programme:meetings were held, plans were made. Political awareness: the Rangpur peasants hit grain stores, prison and courts; the Kols targeted property, not lives; the Santhals said "We have always hunted game in these forests. Now we hunt our oppressors." They knew exactly what instrument oppressed them. Political symbolism:public marches and meetings (not secret); the Santhal warning of 1855;Birsa Munda's uprising timed for Christmas 1899; the Santhal idea of the fatherland that must be reclaimed. Crimes are committed secretly. Politics is done in public. These revolts were public: that is why INM leaders called them the pre-history of modern nationalism. (Teacher: not 100% modern but anti-colonial.)

Because the old grievances lived on after 1857, two more tribal risings follow. Ask: where does religion, and where does Gandhi, enter? 10.1 Munda Ulugulan (1899-1900), Chhota Nagpur Leader:Birsa Munda. Grievances:loss of lands to outsiders;oppression by British officials;missionary activities of Christian missionaries in tribal areas. Role of religion: people believed Birsa had supernatural healing powers and that British bullets would turn to water when fired at him. (A recurring feature where people face a vastly stronger enemy: it makes resistance feel possible; religion gave courage where reason might have said surrender.) Political symbolism: he chose Christmas of 1899 to launch the Ulugulan: a deliberate rising against British power on the most sacred day of the religion the missionaries were using to erode Munda identity. Result: crushed by the British. (Prelims 2020: 'Ulgulan' = the Great Tumult = Birsa Munda's revolt 1899-1900.) He wrote "POST 1857" above the title: the last tribal revolt in the chapter is after the Revolt of 1857, which is why the chapter's title splits Pre-1857 and Post-1857. Underlined: loss of lands to outsiders and missionary activities. (The same word list on slide 22: Ulugulan = the Munda word, Hool = the Santhal word, both meaning rising.) 10.2 The Rampa Rebellion / Fituri, Andhra Grievances (Rampa Hills of Andhra): 1. Commercial exploitation of forests. 2. Land acquisition for road construction. 3. Loss of lands to moneylenders and merchants. 4. Prohibition of Podu cultivation (shifting cultivation, the Jhum equivalent). 5. Restriction on use of forest resources. 6. Tax on toddy (the Abkari system at work). Leadership: the Muttadars, local estate holders, roughly poligars or taluqdars: the same pattern as civil uprisings: elite leaders with popular participation. First phase:crushed by 1880 (the 1870s start). Second phase (Gandhian overlap): in 1920 the Rampa tribals' movement merged into the Non-Cooperation Movement; their civil disobedience was violation of forest laws, in Andhra under Alluri Sitarama Raju. After NCM withdrawal (1922): Raju concluded India could be liberated only by force and re-initiated the Fituri (the violent rebellion). Captured and executed in 1924. The intersection: a pure tribal economic revolt in the 1870s,merges with Gandhi's mass movement in 1920, then after Gandhi's withdrawal produces a leader who draws the opposite lesson. Raju becomes a revolutionary martyr in the Andhra tradition. He underlined Muttadars and Civil Uprisings: Rampa is the tribal revolt with elite (muttadar) leadership, so it blends two kinds from Section 4. He also underlined the 1920 merger, "violation of forest laws" as civil disobedience, "after NCM withdrawal (1922)," "re-initiated the Fituri," "captured and executed in 1924." Date wobble on Rampa: the handout says first phase crushed by 1880, started in the 1870s; the map slide (Lecture 25, slide 25) writes "Rampa (Andhra) 1879/1922." They are consistent: 1879 as the rising's first year and 1922 as the Fituri's restart after NCM. For Prelims the safe reading is 1870s start, crushed by 1880; 1920 merger; 1922 Fituri; 1924 execution.

Chait Singh's revolt begins (to 1781) ★ 1783 Rangpur Rebellion: Debi Singh and Gobinda Singh targeted ★ 1789 Bishnupur and Birbhum revolts (distractors) 1793 Permanent Settlement: zamindar as owner, abwabs, no occupancy right ★ 1799 Wazir Ali 97-98 revolts; Santhal Parganas ★ 1856 Hindu Widow Remarriages Act 1857 Revolt of 1857 (the culmination); Mutiny of the Sepoys ★ 1859 Indigo Revolt (Bengal Ryoti system); Rent Act 1859 ★ 1870s Rampa Rebellion begins (first phase crushed by 1880); Faraizi revived under Naya Mian 1875 Deccan Riot (Prelims 1998 chronology) 1878 Indian Forests Act under Lytton 76-80: Reserved, Protected, Village ★ 1882 Anandamath by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (inspired by the Sanyasi Rebellion) 1899 Birsa Munda launches the Ulugulan on Christmas (to 1900) ★ 1917 Gandhi's Champaran Satyagraha (Tinkathia, Bihar) 1920 Rampa tribals merge into the Non-Cooperation Movement 1922 NCM withdrawn; Alluri Sitarama Raju re-initiates the Fituri 1924 Alluri Sitarama Raju captured and executed 2006 Forest Rights Act (today's correction of the 1878 Act)

The bottom of the order moves first. The Western Educated Middle Class believes in the benevolence of British rule and answers it with socio-religious reform. Peasants and tribals, at the very bottom of the new colonial order, answer with defiance and often violence. The teacher's one-line logic: the common man wants security, economic, physical and socio-cultural. The peasant's squeeze. The Farming System of 1772 auctions land revenue to a revenue farmer (ijaradar). PS1793 makes the zamindar owner, with high rents, illegal abwabs and no occupancy right. The Rent Act 1859 promises occupancy after over twelve years but is ineffective in Bengal. In Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas the road is auction, moneylender, then landlessness. The indigo trap. The European planter gives a loan at the start, sells inputs to the ryot and buys the indigo back at a price below market. The ryot cannot pay rent and loan, the soil is exhausted, and he must borrow and grow indigo again, or face eviction. The teacher's two systems: Bengal Ryoti (a quadrant of the plot, Indigo Revolt 1859) and Bihar Tinkathia (3/20th, Champaran Satyagraha 1917). Religion adds fuel. As a grievance: temple and mosque lands are taxed, revenue-free tenures end, missionaries may enter after 1813, and Sati 1829, Lex Loci 1850 and Widow Remarriage 1856 are seen as interference. As an organiser: with no parties or newspapers, a sect already has a leader, a philosophy and unity. The tribal's world turned upside down. Tribals lived by cultivation, hunting and gathering, under their own tribal law and chief. The British pushed land revenue in through four routes (zamindars as owners, revenue farmers, the chief made a zamindar, ryots made individual owners), demanded cash, and banned Jhum and hunting because they wanted settled peasants paying LR regularly. The forest is fenced (1878). Under Lytton 76-80 the Indian Forests Act 1878 splits forests into Reserved, Protected and Village, driven by the railway need for timber (about 2,000 sleepers a mile). Customary rights become privileges, and millions become trespassers on ancestral land. The Abkari system adds an auctioned liquor monopoly, second only to land revenue. The elites rise: civil uprisings. Raja Chait Singh of Benaras (1778-81) loses his estates for unpaid LR. Wazir Ali 97-98, the Poligars, the Bundelas and Veluthampi (1809) each lose status, land or autonomy to British rule or its Resident. The Paikas of Odisha (1817) draw multi-class support and are debated as a candidate for the true First War of Independence. Peasants lead: Rangpur and Mysore. In 1783 the Rangpur peasants, hurt by the Farming System and the 1770 famine, loot the grain stores of Debi Singh and Gobinda Singh, free prisoners, attack courts and run their own government. In Mysore (1830-31) peasants rise against the Wodeyars and British agents because the SA 1799 subsidy forced high LR. Religion leads. Dasnami Sanyasis and Madari Fakirs (1760-1850s, peak about 1800 with 50,000) inspire Anandamath. Karim and Tipu Shah lead the Pagal Panthis. Titu Mir builds a bamboo fort, the Faraizi (Dudu Mian) say land belongs to God, and the Moplahs lose rights because the British recognise only the Janmies. The tribals rise, ending in the Hool. Pahariya 1778, Bhil 1818-31, Ramosi 1822, Khasi 1829-33, Kol 1831-32 and Kandh 1837-56 each rise against loss of land, forest rights or religion. The Santhals (1855-56) give a public prior warning, rise with bows and arrows against the unholy trinity of British, zamindars and moneylenders, and about 50,000 are killed. The Santhal Parganas follow, with a bar on land transfer to non-Santhals. After 1857: Birsa and Rampa. Birsa Munda's Ulugulan (1899-1900) begins on Christmas 1899, with a belief that British bullets turn to water. The Rampa revolt, led first by Muttadars and crushed by 1880, merges into the NCM in 1920. After 1922 Alluri Sitarama Raju restarts the Fituri and is executed in 1924. The verdict. They were not all-India, not coordinated, with local leaders, no plan and no democratic goal, so not modern nationalism. But they had ideology, organisation, programme, awareness and symbolism, and crimes hide while politics shows. Hence the pre-history of modern nationalism, and the culmination of a hundred years before 1857.

The remark is about the Hindu-Muslim unity of purpose of 1857, which is why divide and rule became central after 1857 Section 6.3 Prelims 2005 Kunwar Singh belonged to: (a) Bihar (b) Madhya Pradesh (c) Rajasthan (d) Uttar Pradesh (a) Bihar. Kunwar Singh = Jagdishpur, Bihar, a Zamindar who lost his lands under the sunset clause of PS 1793. (The slide's explanation: Rajputana's hotspot was Kota; UP's leaders were Hazrat Mahal and Lakshmi Bai) Section 4.1 (vi) Prelims 2005 Which territory was not affected by the Revolt: (a) Jhansi (b) Chittor (c) Jagdishpur (d) Lucknow (b) Chittor.
