Jhansi (Lakshmi Bai), Jagdishpur (Kunwar Singh), Lucknow (Hazrat Mahal) were major theatres Section 6.2 (ii) and the map in Section 4 Prelims 2006 Who was betrayed by a 'friend', captured and put to death by the British: (a) Nana Sahib (b) Kunwar Singh (c) Khan Bahadur Khan (d) Tantia Tope (d) Tantia Tope, betrayed by his associate Man Singh, hanged April 1859. (The slide's explanation adds: Nana Sahib escaped to Nepal; Kunwar Singh died of wounds in April 1858) Section 4.1 (viii) Prelims 2006 Governor-General of India during the Sepoy Mutiny: (a) Lord Canning (b) Lord Bentinck (c) Lord Hardinge (d) Lord Lytton (a) Lord Canning 56-62. The teacher wrote the reign-years beside every option: Canning 56-62, Bentinck 28-35, Hardinge 10-16, Lytton 76-80. Only Canning's span covers 1857. He became the first Viceroy in 1858 (same man, two titles) Section 7.1

Story so far: the Company State of the last chapters is about to be shaken. Hold the formula: sepoy mutiny plus civil rebellion, led by traditional elites. Chapter 21 title slide: The Revolt of 1857 The whole chapter in one line.1857 = Sepoy Mutiny (+) Civil Uprising, and the civil part was common people led by traditional elites (dispossessed rajas, Mansabdars, taluqdars). Marked imp for both PRE and Mains. The handout page for this chapter ends with the index of the next chapter (What Changed After 1857, the Indigo Revolt 1859-63, Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873, Maharashtra, Punjab). That belongs to Chapter 22: Peasant Revolts After 1857.

Because the revolt had two streams, the story must too: one begins in the barracks of the Bengal Army, the other in the villages. Ask: why the Bengal Army and not Bombay or Madras? A two-stream definition (Lecture 25, slide 64). The handout says the Revolt of 1857 was not simply a military mutiny: it was a sepoy mutiny combined with a civil rebellion, two streams that flowed together. Defining the Revolt of 1857 Sepoy Mutiny Sepoys of the Bengal Army The largest of the three armies (Bengal, with Bombay and Madras smaller) Civil Rebellion Dispossessed elites, taluqdars, peasants All believed that religion was under threat, even those who did not take part Formula 1857 Revolt = Sepoy Mutiny + Civil Rebellion Teacher ticks this Why the Bengal Army and not the others? The teacher's board stacks reasons: it was the largest army [Bo, Ma = Bombay and Madras were smaller]; the ratio of Indians to British was very high (the handout says the British-to-Indian ratio was lowest there); most sepoys were upper caste (UC), so caste homogeneity, so caste unity; and a commonality of grievances with the villages they came from. He also writes that even non-participants agreed that religion was under threat. Two PYQ alerts sit under this heading in the handout (Prelims 1998: the WEMC opposed the revolt; Prelims 2005: Chittor was not affected). The slides use them under "Arguments Against It Being a War of Independence," so they are worked in Section 6.2 below.

Because the grievances had piled up, one rebel's shot was enough. Follow the dates: Barrackpur, Meerut, Delhi. The Opening Shots, a flow of seven boxes The opening shots of 1857 29 March 1857: Mangal Pandey, sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry (BNI), Barrackpur near Calcutta, fires at European officers; his fellow sepoys refuse to arrest him 8 April 1857: Mangal Pandey hanged 22 April 1857:Jemadar Ishwari Prasad (who refused to restrain Pandey) hanged; the 34th BNI disbanded as collective punishment 10 May 1857: sepoys at Meerut mutiny 11 May 1857: they march to Delhi and proclaim Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 (1837-1857, last Mughal emperor) Emperor of Hindustan By end of May: the revolt spreads across the North-West Provinces and Awadh; the civil population joins in 11 May to 20 September 1857 in Delhi, and broadly until spring 1858: British rule collapses across a large swathe of north and central India The banner: for the first time in a century, the British monopoly over organised violence in India was broken. The violence on both sides was enormous. The handout and the slide print the emperor as "Zafar3757" and the province as "NWP1836." These are PDF artefacts. They read Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 (the teacher writes "37-57" on slide 6) and NWP 1836 (his board on Lecture 26a, slide 2).

Because the sepoy was a peasant in uniform, every wound of pay, caste, Awadh and land was his own. Ask: which was the cause and which only the trigger? 3.1 Service-related grievances Racism. Indian sepoys earned far less than European soldiers, got smaller pensions, and faced routine slurs: they were called "Suar" (pigs). The highest rank an Indian could reach was Subedar, worth only 60 to 70 rupees a month. Economic. To offset high war expenditure, the British cut sepoy salaries and abolished the allowance for serving outside one's home region in 1856. That allowance mattered doubly: losing it was an economic blow and, for many upper-caste men, a religious insult, since serving far from home or crossing water was seen as causing loss of caste. 3.2 Socio-religious grievances Early on, the British recruited upper castes and respected caste customs: ruling the Indian army the Indian way. This was the ideology of Orientalism: to govern India, work within Indian traditions, at least initially. As the empire expanded and the army became more heterogeneous, respecting caste customs became inconvenient. The British now wanted a uniform army culture where loyalty ran to the employer, not to caste or religion. i) Caste privileges were reduced: food restrictions, religious symbols, and the right to refuse service in polluting regions were curtailed. ii) Sepoys were forced to serve in Burma, Sindh or Afghanistan, risking loss of caste; those who refused were dismissed or punished. iii) Christian missionaries in cantonments since the Charter Act 1813 created anxiety about forced conversion. iv) The rumours.Cow and pig bone dust in flour; and the new Enfield rifle cartridges (which replaced the Brown Bess musket) were greased with cow and pig fat and had to be bitten before loading. Whether true or not, the rumours landed on fertile ground: the fear that the British were engineering a loss of Hindu and Muslim identity to make conversion easier. The teacher underlines every step of the story on slide 67 (Orientalism, then expansion, then recruitment from other castes, then uniform culture, then forced service abroad, then loss of caste, then punishment, then missionaries, then 1813, then the cartridge rumours). No handwriting: the underlines tell you the whole chain is examinable. 3.3 Political grievance: Awadh The single largest source of recruits for the Bengal Army was Awadh. Nearly every family there had a member in the British Indian Army. The annexation of Awadh in 1856 felt like a personal betrayal: their loyalty had cost them their homeland. Teacher's board: "Bengal Army was Dominated by Sepoys from Awadh (+) Some from Bihar", with the upper-caste bracket "[ UC: Brahmin, Bhumihars, etc]" The Bengal Army was dominated by sepoys from Awadh, plus some from Bihar, and the upper castes among them were Brahmins, Bhumihars, etc. He adds a starred rule, written as "Bor DnR": do not keep sepoys from a State in the army of that State. Then his peasant logic: the first livelihood of anyone from a peasant family is being a peasant; poor peasants use family labour;step 2 is that he became a sepoy of the EIC army. Therefore sepoy = peasant IN uniform (he writes IN large). Yellow reminder: in any agrarian economy the masses are peasants (his AGRI triangle sits inside the GDP circle). Teacher's board: UNDIVIDED AWADH, an oval split into 1801 (left) and 1856 (right) Undivided Awadh was taken in two bites.1801: the Doab, Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand (the left half). 1856: the rest (the right half). The land revenue system differs: Mahalwari 1822 in the 1801 half; Summary Settlement (with no detailed field survey) in the half annexed in 1856. Names: the 1801 land was the Ceded Districts, renamed NWP 1836; then 1877 "NWP and Oudh";1902 "UP of Agra and Oudh";1937 = United Provinces. 3.4 Agrarian grievances i)Summary settlements in Awadh fixed LR without proper field surveys, so demands were unreasonable. ii) Peasants unable to pay: lands auctioned by the government, or lost to moneylenders through debt. iii)New British courts backed moneylenders, completing the dispossession. iv) The sepoy was a peasant in uniform: these wounds were his family's wounds. 3.5 The trigger versus the cause The greased cartridge was merely the trigger. The revolt began in the Bengal Army because upper-caste identity had been most carefully preserved there, and the ratio of British to Indian soldiers was lowest in that army. Bombay and Madras armies were heterogeneous, so there was less caste-based unity. Why the Sepoys Mutinied (contd.), with the teacher's ink Three board notes on one slide. (1) The Awadh annexation of 1856 was on the ground of MALADMINISTRATION ("also": it came on top of the grievances above). (2) "Now he removed his [uniform] to be peasant again": the sepoy peeled off the uniform and went back to being a peasant. (3) Fyi: the rumour of cartridges having cow and pig fat was just a TRIGGER and there were MULTIPLE reasons for the 1857 Revolt. Trap: Awadh was NOT annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse. The teacher's board says 1856: maladministration. (Jhansi, by contrast, went by the Doctrine of Lapse: Section 4.1.) A practice question in the Question bank phrases Awadh's annexation as "under the Doctrine of Lapse": teacher and handout win; the bank's wording is wrong on that point. Also, a practice statement says the Bengal Army had the "highest ratio of British to Indian soldiers": the handout says the lowest.

Because the same policies ruined the elites, the taluqdars and the peasants, they found leaders in the dispossessed. Ask: who lost what, and who led from where? 4.1 Feudal elites and dispossessed rulers The whole civil rebellion on one board.Civil rebellion = North and Central India. It splits into LEADERS and FOLLOWERS.Leaders = ex-rajas and Mansabdars, who lost status through annexation and Doctrine of Lapse, on three fronts: political, economic (no jagirs, no Khalisa land) and social (British rule of law, equality before law).Zamindars (Taluqdars) lost status too: economic (Mahalwari: they lost milkiyat, ownership), social (equality before law) and political (their private army and forts, which he crosses out because they were disbanded). Followers = peasants and artisans. Peasants: already done (see the agrarian grievances): higher LR, the Rs lender, loss of lands; the lender is the "villain of 1857," with the British beside him. Artisans: the Industrial Revolution (1750-1850) in Britain, and the Indian economy exposed to industrialising Britain through the Charter Act 1813. Teacher's board: "# Br Manufactured Goods" with two branches: "Cheaper in Rs (*MRP)" and "Later Better in Quality also", circled "vs" "Indian Handicrafts". Teacher's board: "1857 REVOLT = Sepoy MUTINY (+) Civil Rebellion" with a bracket over the mutiny "Bengal Army = Sov Why the artisans were ruined:British manufactured goods were cheaper in rupees (the MRP, starred) and later better in quality too, against Indian handicrafts. Hence the destruction of Indian industry that the rebels also complain about (Section 6.3). Annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse and other policies stripped ruling families of power, and with each fallen ruler the entire dependent court aristocracy fell too. These displaced elites had both motive and, often, remaining private resources to lead a rebellion. Nana Sahib Kanpur Adopted son of Baji Rao II 96-18 (1796-1818), denied pension after annexation. Teacher: Baji Rao II 96-18 went to Bithur (Kanpur) with a pension after the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War 1817-19. Tantia Tope was his deputy Begum Hazrat Mahal Lucknow Led the revolt at Lucknow. Wife of the deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah (Awadh annexed on grounds of maladministration) Khan Bahadur Khan Rohilla Bareilly Rohilla leader; Rohilkhand annexed when half of Awadh was annexed (1801) Rani Lakshmi Bai Jhansi Jhansi annexed on grounds of Doctrine of Lapse (the teacher writes 1854 beside it). Fought fiercely; died in battle at Gwalior on 17-18 June 1858; one of the most celebrated symbols of the revolt Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah Faizabad Fiery religious leader who rallied both Hindu and Muslim support; one of the most formidable rebel commanders in Awadh Kunwar Singh Jagdishpur, Bihar Zamindar who lost lands under the sunset clause of the Permanent Settlement Act 1793 (forfeiture of zamindari rights on non-payment of LR by a fixed deadline: a harsh, inflexible rule that destroyed many old landed families). Brother Amar Singh also active. Guerrilla warfare (slide) Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 Delhi Canning 56-62 announced in 1856 that Mughals would be called only "Princes" and would vacate the Red Fort. After Delhi fell he was captured, tried, exiled to Rangoon (Burma), and died in 1862: the last Mughal emperor, a prisoner far from the empire his ancestors had built Tantia Tope central India Nana Sahib's ablest commander, the revolt's greatest guerrilla fighter. After Kanpur and Jhansi fell he refused to surrender, waged a long guerrilla campaign across central India, was betrayed by his associate Man Singh, captured and hanged in April 1859 Feudal Elites and Dispossessed Rulers, leaders continued (typed) He dots under the exam words: Amar Singh, guerrilla warfare, Doctrine of Lapse, guerrilla fighter, central India, "betrayed by friend," Man Singh. The strip "Awadh | Bihar | Bengal" with Orissa below and Delhi at the corner is a location aid beside Kunwar Singh. Prelims 2005 and 2006 are on this slide.Kunwar Singh = Bihar (Jagdishpur), not UP or MP. Tantia Tope = the one betrayed by a "friend" (Man Singh) and hanged April 1859; not Nana Sahib, Kunwar Singh or Khan Bahadur Khan. The slide's answer note says Nana Sahib escaped to Nepal and Kunwar Singh died of wounds in April 1858 (from the slide only, not the handout text). Centres of the Revolt of 1857, a map of India with red dots (Meerut, Delhi, Bareilly, Lucknow, Faizabad, Gwalior, Kota, Jhansi, Kanpur, Jagdishpur, Barrackpur, Calcutta)  No ink on the map slide, but it is the one picture that ties every leader to a centre. Main revolt zone: NWP and Awadh. Kota in Rajputana is the exception inside loyal Rajputana (Section 6.2). Use it for the "which place was not affected" Prelims trap (Chittor is not on the map). The handout's flowchart adds four names that the handout text does not:Azimullah Khan (with Nana Sahib and Tantia Tope at Kanpur), Bakht Khan (at Delhi), Birjis Qadr (with Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow) and the dates 20 September 1857 (Delhi recaptured) and April 1858 (Jhansi falls). They are from the handout figure only. 4.2 Taluqdars and big landowners The Mahalwari settlement in the North-West Provinces (half of Awadh had been under SA since 1801) and in Awadh (annexed 1856) transferred land rights to actual cultivators in many cases, stripping Taluqdars of their personal estates. The British also disbanded private forts and armies. Then rule of law, equality before the law, removed their social superiority. Having lost economically, militarily and socially, Taluqdars threw their lot in with the peasants. 4.3 Peasants High LR led to debt to moneylenders, then loss of land through government auctions and moneylender takeovers. Traditional occupancy rights were gone.British courts sided with moneylenders. So peasant anger in 1857 was directed both at the British government and at the moneylenders: both were seen as oppressors. 4.4 Religion: a fear shared across society The whole rural society shared a fear that its religion was under threat. The fear was not invented: i) Since 1813,Christian missionaries had operated in India, at times under police protection. ii)Socio-religious reforms, however well-intentioned, escalated anxiety: a) Sati Abolition Act, 1829; b) Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856; c) Removal of Caste and Religious Disabilities Act, 1850, also called the Lex Loci Act (Latin for "law of the place"): it gave inheritance rights to those who converted to another religion, so it incentivised conversion to Christianity. iii) The British had started taxing revenue-free lands of mosques, temples and religious sects: Hindus and Muslims both felt the threat. Why the Civil Population Rebelled (typed table: Taluqdars, Peasants, Religion, Immoral British Rule) iv)Pundits and Maulvis gave the resentment a voice and spread it among the people. A shared moral conviction across communities: British rule had disrupted the right political, economic, social and religious order.The goal of 1857 was to restore what had been lost. Three board lines on slide 9. (1) Conversions threaten the "order," which he circles and links to WAY of Life. (2) Commodification of land leads to landlessness, which did NOT exist in pre-British times. (3) Doctrine of Lapse and annexation lead to loss of status of the traditional elites. So the "disrupted order" is: religious/way of life, economic (land as a commodity), political (elites). The handout's cause flowchart is wider than its text. It adds, from the figure only: the General Service Enlistment Act 1856 (the foreign-service rule behind the sepoys' loss-of-caste fear) and the label Enfield P-53 for the rifle. It also lists the Mughal "Princes" demotion and the Charter Act 1853 exam bar as causes. Treat these as handout-figure facts.

Because the rebels had no money, no command and went all to Delhi, the flame went out. Ask: which reasons are about resources, which about organisation, which about unity? Teacher's board The teacher's war-victory formula (a board that compares what decided past wars). 1st Battle of Panipat 1526: TECHNOLOGY. For 1857: railways and the telegraph network (+) against primitive weapons in the hands of the civil population.3rd Battle of Panipat 1761: alliance, numbers, unity (here: SA (+) British Royal military (+)). 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63: military + rupees (ryots not militarily trained), and manufacturing: control over ammunition and arms (+) we were poor.By the 1770s the Marathas (Ma, circled) began winning: tactics + geography + leadership. (Read as the factors tech, unity, military + money, tactics + geography + leadership; the Marathas label is .) The fan on the right is the "who stayed out" list (it feeds Section 6.2): those who did not lose milkiyat,kings whose kingdoms were not annexed, the WEMC who benefited from new jobs, the Bombay and Madras armies (sad face), Punjab (canals of the 1850s, farmers happy),Bengal (zamindars were the big landlords of the British),Madras (the Madras Torture Commission 1856 gave relief; the spelling is) and Bombay (Ryotwari + cotton as a cash crop; good surveys: the Bombay Survey System, the Wingate settlement). Top line: on Swadharma we won (the Nov 1858 Proclamation); on Swaraj we lost. Teacher's board: circled "TACTICS" Tactics, in three moves. (1) No single military commander-in-chief, so no unified army, and no coordination between multiple armies. (2) The mistake: sepoys going to Delhi. All the energy was concentrated in Delhi;defeat of Delhi = defeat of the sepoy mutiny = defeat of the 1857 Revolt, because the sepoy = the military of the revolt. (3) Revolts were geographically localised with no efficient communication and no control of the telegraph network: so in his circle of four revolt centres, when the British attacked centre 1, help from centre 2 did not come, and the army was not unified. The handout lists eight reasons: 5.1 Rebels had no financial resources. 5.2 Peasant fighters lacked modern weapons and training. 5.3 The British had superior leadership, a centralised bureaucracy, a professional army, and a functioning telegraph and communication network. 5.4No effective central command on the Indian side: multiple regional leaders, no coordination. 5.5 A tactical error: rebel energy concentrated on Delhi. When Delhi fell, the symbolic heart of the revolt fell with it. 5.6 The uprising was fragmented and localised: the British defeated rebel groups one at a time. 5.7 The whole Indian Army did not revolt.Bombay and Madras regiments stayed quiet;Punjabi and Gurkha soldiers actively helped the British. (The Bengal Army was the largest, so roughly half the Indian army mutinied, but the other half held, and that was enough.) 5.8 Civil rebellion was confined to north and central India; minor participation elsewhere. The typed slide labels each reason by theme: Money; Tech and Army; Leadership, Org and Army; Org; Tactics; Org; Army and Lack of Unity; Lack of Unity. Three themes carry the answer: resources, organisation, unity.

Because the revolt was this large, historians argue over its name. Ask: is it a mutiny, a war of independence, or more than a mutiny without modern nationalism? This is the most contested question about 1857, and it has no simple answer. War of Independence, Three Positions (typed table: Colonial; V.D 6.1 Three positions Colonial view Primarily a sepoy mutiny. The civil rebellion was just lawless elements exploiting disorder V.D. Savarkar (1909 book) and Karl Marx Savarkar's book The Indian War of Independence: fought for Swadharma and Swaraj.Karl Marx also saw it as a nationalist revolt (the slide words it "anti-colonial revolt") Mainstream historical view Far more than a mutiny, but modern nationalism was absent, so it cannot be called a proper war of independence in the modern sense Marx's wording differs. The handout says Marx saw 1857 as a nationalist revolt; the teacher's slide says an anti-colonial revolt. Both mean Marx sided with the rebels against British rule. Use the handout's wording in exams (the Question bank's practice question uses "nationalist uprising"). Modern nationalism requires: the nation as the sum of equal people who feel a common identity; power vested in the people (democracy and republic, not monarchy); Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. By this standard, 1857 falls short. His line of positions: a line with Colonial at one end and 100% Nationalist at the other; "OUR POSITION" is the circled 1, a little nearer the nationalist end. Independence of whom? Answer: of the people = the nation. So independence is independence to the Nation; the nation is supreme; the goal is democracy. A "random link" beside Savarkar: Hind Swaraj (1909) (the same year as Savarkar's book). Under "1857 falls short" he asks "modern political methods?" and draws a cross with modern Nation | modern politics, then writes "70% marks to 1857 revolt" (what the 70% refers to is ; it reads as his score for how much of the modern tests 1857 meets). 6.2 Arguments against it being a war of independence i) Whole India did not participate: only north and central India was mainly active. a) Ryotwari areas (Sindh, Coorg, Assam, Madras, Bombay: "Scam B"): ryots had become landowners under British rule. b) Punjab: middle-class peasants benefited from canal construction. c) Bengal: Zamindars had benefited from the Permanent Settlement of 1793. ii) Those who benefited from British rule stayed out. a) WEMC believed in British rule as a force for modernisation and had gained jobs and status under it. b) Princes whose territories were not annexed largely stayed loyal, and some actively aided the British, for example Rajput Kings. However, Rajputana did witness upheaval: sepoy mutinies and mass revolt, the most famous being Kota, led by Lala Jaidayal and Mehrab Khan. The rebels completely took over the city and held their own King hostage in his palace for six months. They killed the British Political Agent Major Charles Burton. The British could reconquer the city only in 1858. iii)Taluqdars who had retained their land stayed out. iv)The whole Indian Army did not revolt. v) The revolt was spontaneous: no planning, no manifesto, no coordination. (Modern political movements need organised planning and coordination, which itself embodies Fraternity.) vi) The goal was not a modern republic or democracy; it was to restore the old order, the rule of monarchs and feudal lords. The "who stayed out" fan from the board on slide 10 (Section 5) is exactly this list: those who did not lose milkiyat, kings not annexed, WEMC with new jobs, Bombay and Madras armies, Punjab canals, Bengal landlords, Madras, Bombay. Learn the reason each region stayed out: Ryotwari (ryots became owners), canals, the 1793 Permanent Settlement, jobs. PYQ 1, Prelims 1998: the educated middle class in India (a) opposed the revolt of 1857 [circled T] (b) supported it [circled F] (c) remained neutral [circled F] (d) fough Prelims 1998 (the WEMC). The WEMC opposed the revolt. He splits it: ideologically = tick (they opposed it in thought), militarily = cross (they did not fight against it). So their stance was overall not neutral, only militarily neutral. That is why (c) neutral is wrong and (a) opposed is right. PYQ 2, Prelims 2000: "In this instance we could not play off the Mohammedans against the Hindus." Aitchison's remark related to (a) Revolt of 1857 [circled T] (b) Champar Prelims 2000 (Aitchison).(a) 1857 is the answer. He marks (b) NA, and (d) F (with "QIM 1942-45," the first letters are ; it points to the 1942 movement). (c) Khilafat and NCM is circled T (it too showed Hindu-Muslim unity), but is a mismatch with Aitchison. He then makes a random link: the Aitchison "Report," which divided services into AIS, PCS and SUB CS (All-India, Provincial and Subordinate civil services; the expansions are as read from his letters). Prelims 1998 and Prelims 2005 (Chittor). WEMC = opposed (not supported, not neutral). Chittor = Rajputana = loyal princes = NOT affected. Jhansi, Jagdishpur and Lucknow are major theatres. Kota is the exception inside Rajputana (do not confuse it with Chittor). 6.3 Arguments that it was much more than a mutiny Modern nationalism was absent, yes. But something more than narrow self-interest was present: i) Common enemy and common hatred: against annexations, high LR, loss of land, oppression by moneylenders and EIC officials, destruction of Indian industry. ii) The sepoys' own declarations went far beyond personal grievances: high LR, increased Chowkidari tax, rising unemployment of artisans and learned men, toll taxes on public roads, and the declining status of the Indian ruling class. They were, in effect, speaking for all Indians. iii) Hindu-Muslim unity: a shared belief that Hindustan belonged to Hindus and Muslims alike. Aitchison: "In this instance we could not play off the Mohammedans against the Hindus." This unity is why divide and rule became central to post-1857 policy. iv) The rebels wanted the British out of all of Hindustan, not just their own area. (Fighting for your village is self-interest; fighting to free the whole country is fraternity, an embryonic national consciousness.) v)Regional leaders did communicate with each other, however imperfectly. vi) The rebels did not seek a return to 17th-century centralised Mughal rule. They envisioned the 18th-century decentralised setup: real power at the provincial level, the Mughal emperor a symbolic weak centre (an early instinct towards federalism). A movement of the masses, not just elites: vii) In many cases elites were pushed into leadership:Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, Nana Sahib and the Rani of Jhansi took up roles partly because circumstances compelled them. viii)Peasants and artisans in many regions continued fighting after their Taluqdar leaders had surrendered. ix) The sepoy was a peasant in uniform: when he removed that uniform, the initiative returned to where it had always come from: the common people. Prelims 2000: "could not play off the Mohammedans against the Hindus" = the Revolt of 1857 (Hindu-Muslim unity of purpose), not Champaran 1917, Khilafat and NCM 1919-22 or the 1942 movement. The slide's reasoning: Khilafat and NCM showed unity about 60 years later; 1942 about 90 years after.

Because the Company had failed, the Crown took over and rebuilt the state. Ask: which door did it close, and who knocked loudest afterwards? Teacher's board: boxed "Impact of Revolt" with five branches The five-branch board for the Mains question "impact of the revolt."Ideology: racism up, authoritarianism up. Polity:GOI Act 1858 ended the Company State and began direct rule of the British State; the Proclamation of Nov 1858; and the Mughal empire ended legally.Civil Services: the same exam (1853 Act), first held in 1855, now in London with a lower age limit;Indianisation resisted now. He also notes UCS 1833 (sad face) and CCS 1853 (smiley). Next to it: Police Act 1861.Army:Peel Commission.Society: the Nov 1858 Proclamation shelved social reform and cut conversions. 7.1 Political impact: end of the EIC The EIC was blamed in Britain for mismanaging Indian affairs. Pressure mounted to end a peculiar arrangement of absentee sovereignty: real sovereign power was British, but Britain was absent as the actual ruler and governed through an agent, the EIC, creating a dangerous gap between real authority and day-to-day governance. The Government of India Act, 1858 (Act for Better Government of India, 1858) ended EIC rule: i)Queen Victoria declared sovereign of India: direct Crown rule over British India, paramountcy over Indian princes. (The title Kaiser-i-Hind, Empress of India, came later through the Royal Titles Act, 1876 and was proclaimed at the Delhi Durbar of 1877. Victoria had used it informally since 1858.); ii) A Secretary of State for India, a full Cabinet member, replaced the President of the Board of Control as the top authority in Britain on Indian affairs. iii) On 1 November 1858 Queen Victoria issued a proclamation promising religious tolerance and governance in accordance with India's own traditions and customs.Socio-religious reforms and the promotion of Christianity were shelved. On the Proclamation row:"No more annexations."British India = 63% of the territory of India. (Same figure as the 63% territory in Chapter 10.) The Proclamation is the Swadharma victory on his war board: "we won." Why 1857 is a Watershed, Political: End of the EIC (typed) PYQ 6, Prelims 2006: Who was the Governor-General of India during the Sepoy Mutiny? Teacher's yellow reign-years: (a) Lord Canning 56-62, (b) Lord Bentinck 28-35, (c) Lor PYQ 6 (Prelims 2006). The teacher does not mark T or F. He writes the reign-years beside each option, so you can see by the dates alone that only Canning 56-62 covers 1857.Bentinck 28-35 is two decades earlier; Lytton 76-80 is two decades later. (Hardinge 10-16 is his code: see the alert in the Exam lens.) 7.2 Ideological impact: racism, authoritarianism and the unintended birth of modern nationalism Post-1857, British attitudes hardened: Indians were now seen as racially inferior, incapable of self-governance and beyond reform. The British became more autocratic and unwilling to give Indians any senior role in bureaucracy, police or military. This backfired. The Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC), educated in British institutions and believing in British liberalism, had wanted a share in governance. They were shut out. That frustration became the seed of the modern nationalism-based INM that began developing in the second half of the 19th century. Watershed, Ideological: Birth of Modern Nationalism, three stacked boxes with arrows (The British, in trying to lock the door, inadvertently created the very class that would eventually break it down.) Two ticks on the board: the first box ("Racism and Authoritarianism") and the second (WEMC, with a sad face). The sad face is the point: a class that had stood with the British in 1857 (Prelims 1998) was shut out afterwards, and turned to modern nationalism. 7.3 Administrative impact: policing 1857 made clear how vulnerable the British were without effective policing and intelligence. The 1st Police Commission (1860), set up by Canning 56-62 under M.H. Court, led to the Police Act, 1861, passed in March 1861. It created a proper provincial police structure with a clear chain of command, for the first time:Inspector General (reporting to the Governor/LG) to Superintendent of Police (district level) to Sub-Inspector (the thana). Watershed, Policing: Chain of Command From 1857 onward a "Police Raj" was effectively created, with Indians excluded from all positions of importance. The police chain of command (Police Act 1861) Governor / Lieutenant Governor (LG/G) the provincial head (the teacher's tag) Inspector General reports to the Governor/LG Superintendent of Police district level (the teacher's tag: DC/DM) Sub-Inspector at the thana He tags the top and middle of the chain:LG/G beside the Inspector General (who reports up to the Governor/Lieutenant Governor) and DC/DM beside the Superintendent of Police (the district officers: Collector and Magistrate). A long line from DC/DM runs down to the Sub-Inspector box and ends in a cross. 7.4 Administrative impact: civil services i) The exam was introduced under Charter Act 1853, but now it would not be held simultaneously in India. ii) Maximum age of eligibility deliberately set at 19 to 23, low enough that most Indian candidates would be too old before they were ready. (Indian students typically finished their education later than British ones: a quiet but effective barrier.) iii)Statutory Civil Service (1870, implemented 1878 by Lytton 76-80): Indians could be nominated to certain posts reserved for Covenanted Civil Service (CCS) officers, but only loyal, hand-picked elites.Co-option, not inclusion. Date conflict on the Statutory Civil Service. The handout says 1870 (Act), implemented 1878 by Lytton 76-80; the typed slide says rules of 1879 under the GOI Act 1870.Handout wins: 1870 and 1878. Note the slide's 1879 if the question uses it. Also, the handout's flowchart (page 238) attaches the civil-service age cap to Lytton 76-80, whereas the handout text and the slide tie the age cap to the post-1857 policy; treat Lytton 76-80 as the Statutory Civil Service man. The handout's aftermath flowchart adds the Indian Councils Act 1861 beside the Police Act 1861 (see Chapter 25: Indian Councils Act 1861), says the Proclamation kept Princely States preserved and no more Lapse (matching the teacher's "no more annexations"), and ends with divide and rule intensified, communal policies, economic exploitation deepens. These are handout-figure facts.

items.t: 8 · Changes in the army: the Peel Commission
items.x: Because the revolt was at its core a military mutiny, the last and deepest reform was the army: a coup-proof design. Teacher's board: circled "PEEL", "BACKGROUND" The Peel Commission's background, as he reads it. (1) Lack of unity between the armies: the three armies were regional (Bombay, Madras, Bengal); each separate. (2) No caste-based unity (the cross reads as "no": the new army must not have it). (3) No very low ratio of British to Indians (the cross again: the ratio must not be very low). (4) Reward those who stayed loyal:Punjab, the princes, the zamindars. (The circled "cont" from Madras is .) The British understood that 1857 was, at its core, a military mutiny. Preventing another one required a complete restructuring of the army, not minor adjustments. The Crown appointed the Royal Commission on the Reorganisation of the Indian Army in July 1858. It submitted its report in March 1859. It is popularly known as the Peel Commission, after its head Major-General Jonathan Peel, who also served as Secretary of State for War (1858-59) in the British Cabinet. (Jonathan Peel was the younger brother of Sir Robert Peel, the British Prime Minister who created the modern London police force. The Peel family had a hand in restructuring both Indian policing and the Indian army after 1857.) The Commission's goal: a "coup-proof" colonial army, one in which no future Bengal Army-style mutiny would ever be possible. Its recommendations were implemented through a combination of legislation and executive military orders over the following years. He underlines the answer words on slide 23: the Royal Commission, Jonathan Peel, the goal (prevent a repeat of 1857), the European Forces (India) Act 1860 (twice for the year), abolishing the EIC's European army, ratios 1:2 and 1:3, Indians barred from artillery, the deliberate mix of castes, religions and ethnicities. The rupee mark beside "without a bounty" points to the money cause of the White Mutiny. How the recommendations were implemented 8.1 European Forces (India) Act, 1860. The major legislative outcome. It abolished the EIC's separate European army and formally merged those soldiers into the regular British Crown Army. This triggered a brief "White Mutiny" among EIC European soldiers, who resisted the transfer without a financial bounty. 8.2 Fixed ratios of British to Indian soldiers, through executive War Office directives:Bengal Army (where the mutiny had been worst) 1 British for every 2 Indian (1:2);Madras and Bombay Armies 1:3. 8.3 Indian artillery monopoly broken. The British took complete and exclusive control of the artillery; Indians were barred from artillery units and heavy weapons. (Control of artillery = control of the most decisive firepower; no Indian artillery meant no Indian capacity for a conventional offensive war.) 8.4 "Divide and rule" regiments.Deliberate mix of castes, religions and ethnicities in each regiment; no single group could dominate or form a bloc; inter-regional interaction between army units discouraged (pan-India unity among regiments had been the British nightmare in 1857). Changes in the Army, Peel Commission (contd.) (typed rows 8.5 Martial Races, 8.6 Loyalty to "the salt", 8.7 Standing army, 8.8 Senior positions, 8.9 Civilian finance cont 8.5 Martial Races. Recruitment based on the idea of "martial races":Jats, Rajputs, Sikhs, Gurkhas and others described as naturally loyal, courageous, good fighters, but, in the British framing, incapable of independent leadership (ideal soldiers, never officers; a theory as much about control as capability). Regions that stayed loyal in 1857 were heavily favoured. 8.6 A culture of loyalty to "the salt" (namak ka haq) and to one's community's honour, actively promoted. 8.7 A large permanent standing army maintained to counter future revolts. 8.8Minimum or no Indians in senior military positions. 8.9Financial control of the army under civilian authority: the military could not independently mobilise resources. 8.10 The army was actively deployed against INM activities and peasant revolts; sepoys kept in barracks to minimise political exposure to the growing INM. 8.9 = "checks and balance" (civilian finance control over the military). The zig-zag drawing at the top right with a sad face and the words "#1 Navy = Br" is ; it appears to say the Navy stayed a British preserve, but the sketch is not legible enough to read as fact. The hinge. 1857 was the hinge. The EIC's improvised governance ended; the Crown took direct charge with a restructured army, new police and redesigned civil services, all built to prevent recurrence. The reforms were more efficient and more repressive, planting the WEMC that would later demand independence. (The teacher's summary slide, Lecture 26a slide 25: Company State replaced by Crown Rule; Indians excluded from senior civil services in practice; high racism and authoritarianism prompted the WEMC to begin the modern INM, demanding rights and a constitutional regime; by 1929 these demands escalate into Purna Swaraj.)

1750-1850 The teacher's board: Industrial Revolution in Britain (the artisan's ruin) 1801 Half of Awadh (Doab, Gorakhpur, Rohilkhand) ceded to the British under a Subsidiary Alliance 1813 Charter Act 1813: Christian missionaries in cantonments; Indian economy exposed to industrial Britain ★ 1817-19 Third Anglo-Maratha War: Baji Rao II 96-18 sent to Bithur (Kanpur) with a pension (teacher's ink) 1822 Mahalwari settlement in the 1801 half of Awadh (teacher's board) 1829 Sati Abolition Act 1836 Ceded Districts renamed NWP 1836 1850 Removal of Caste and Religious Disabilities Act (Lex Loci Act) ★ 1853 Charter Act 1853: the civil services exam introduced (the teacher: first exam 1855) 1854 Jhansi annexed on the Doctrine of Lapse (the teacher's ink) 1856 Awadh annexed (maladministration); sepoys' allowance abolished; Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act; Canning 56-62 announces Mughals will be "Princes" ★ 1857 29 March: Mangal Pandey fires at Barrackpur; 8 April hanged; 22 April Ishwari Prasad hanged, 34th BNI disbanded ★ 1857 10 May: Meerut mutiny; 11 May: Delhi, Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 proclaimed Emperor of Hindustan ★ 1857 20 September: Delhi recaptured by the British (handout figure); Zafar exiled to Rangoon 1858 17-18 June: Rani Lakshmi Bai dies in battle at Gwalior; Kota reconquered by the British ★ 1858 July: Royal Commission on the Reorganisation of the Indian Army (Peel Commission) appointed ★ 1858 GOI Act 1858 ends the EIC; Queen Victoria sovereign; Secretary of State for India ★ 1858 1 November: Queen Victoria's Proclamation (religious tolerance; no more annexations) ★ 1859 March: Peel Commission report; April: Tantia Tope hanged after betrayal by Man Singh ★ 1860 1st Police Commission (Canning 56-62, M.H. Court); European Forces (India) Act 1860 (White Mutiny) ★ 1861 Police Act, passed in March 1861 ★ 1862 Bahadur Shah Zafar dies at Rangoon 1870 Government of India Act 1870: Statutory Civil Service (implemented 1878 by Lytton 76-80; the slide says 1879) 1876 Royal Titles Act: Kaiser-i-Hind, Empress of India 1877 Delhi Durbar proclaims the title; the Awadh-and-Agra region is called "NWP and Oudh" (teacher's board) 1902 "UP of Agra and Oudh" (teacher's board) 1909 V.D. Savarkar's book The Indian War of Independence; Hind Swaraj (the teacher's random link) 1929 The teacher: the WEMC's demands escalate into Purna Swaraj 1937 "United Provinces" (teacher's board)

A village in uniform. The Bengal Army is the largest of the three armies, filled with upper-caste sepoys from Awadh and some from Bihar, and Indians far outnumber the British in it. The sepoy is a peasant in uniform: he is paid less than a European, is called Suar, and cannot rise beyond Subedar at 60 to 70 rupees a month. 1856: four blows. To offset war costs the British cut sepoy pay and abolish the allowance for serving outside the home region, a loss of money and of caste. Awadh, the biggest recruiting ground, is annexed on grounds of maladministration and feels like personal betrayal. The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act is passed, and Canning 56-62 announces that the Mughals will be only 'Princes'. The fat on the cartridge. The new Enfield rifle replaces the Brown Bess, and its cartridge, greased with cow and pig fat, must be bitten before loading. With rumours of cow and pig bone dust in flour, and missionaries in cantonments since the Charter Act 1813, sepoys fear a plot against Hindu and Muslim identity. The teacher is clear: the cartridge was only the trigger. Barrackpur to Delhi. On 29 March 1857 Mangal Pandey of the 34th BNI fires at European officers; he is hanged on 8 April and Jemadar Ishwari Prasad on 22 April, and the 34th BNI is disbanded. On 10 May Meerut mutinies and on 11 May the sepoys reach Delhi and proclaim Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 Emperor of Hindustan. Delhi is held until 20 September, and for the first time in a century the British monopoly of organised violence is broken. The village joins. Annexation and the Doctrine of Lapse have stripped rulers and their courts; Mahalwari, disbanded forts and equality before law have stripped the taluqdars of estates, arms and status; high land revenue, moneylenders and courts that side with lenders have ruined the peasants. Cheaper British goods ruin the artisans. Above all, the whole countryside fears for its religion: missionaries 1813, Sati 1829, Lex Loci 1850, Widows 1856. Lamps in eight hands. Nana Sahib rises at Kanpur, Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, Khan Bahadur Khan at Bareilly, Lakshmi Bai at Jhansi, Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah at Faizabad, Kunwar Singh at Jagdishpur in Bihar and Zafar at Delhi, with Tantia Tope as the great guerrilla. Lakshmi Bai dies at Gwalior in June 1858; Tantia Tope is betrayed by Man Singh and hanged in April 1859; Zafar is exiled to Rangoon and dies in 1862. Why the flame went out. The rebels have no money, weapons or training, and no central command. The teacher's board shows the mistake: all the sepoys go to Delhi, so the fall of Delhi is the fall of the sepoy mutiny and of the revolt. The revolts are local, with no control of the telegraph; Bombay and Madras stay quiet and Punjabis and Gurkhas help the British. Mutiny, war or more? The colonial view says sepoy mutiny; Savarkar (1909) and Marx say war of independence; mainstream historians say far more than a mutiny but without modern nationalism. Against the war: Scam B areas, Punjab, Bengal, the WEMC, loyal princes (Kota the exception), no manifesto, an old-order goal. For more than a mutiny: a common enemy, Hindu-Muslim unity (Aitchison), a federal vision, a mass movement. The Crown takes over. The GOI Act 1858 ends the EIC: Queen Victoria is sovereign and a Cabinet-rank Secretary of State replaces the President of the Board of Control. The Proclamation of 1 November 1858 promises tolerance and shelves social reform; the teacher adds no more annexations, with British India holding 63% of the territory. Britain now sees Indians as racially inferior and more authoritarian rule follows. A Police Raj and a shut door. Canning 56-62's 1st Police Commission of 1860 leads to the Police Act of March 1861: Inspector General, Superintendent of Police, Sub-Inspector, with Indians excluded from important posts. The civil services exam is no longer held simultaneously in India, the age cap is 19 to 23, and the Statutory Civil Service of Lytton 76-80 admits only hand-picked elites: co-option, not inclusion. The coup-proof army. The Peel Commission (appointed July 1858, report March 1859) leads to the European Forces (India) Act 1860, ratios of 1:2 in Bengal and 1:3 in Madras and Bombay, and an Indian ban on artillery. Regiments mix castes and religions, recruitment favours martial races, loyalty to the salt is taught, and the army is kept in barracks and used against peasant revolts and the INM. The door that made its own key. The WEMC, schooled in British liberalism, had wanted a share in governance and was locked out. That frustration became the seed of the modern nationalism-based INM, and by 1929 its demands would escalate into Purna Swaraj. 1857 was the hinge: more efficient and more repressive reforms that planted what would later demand independence.

Prelims 2020 Indigo cultivation in India declined by the beginning of the 20th century because of (a) peasant resistance to the oppressive conduct of planters (b) its unprofitability in the world market because of new inventions (c) national leaders' opposition to the cultivation of indigo (d) Government control over the planters (b). The death blow was chemistry, not resistance: BASF (Germany) made synthetic indigo in 1897, cheaper and more consistent, and demand for natural indigo collapsed. (a) The Indigo Revolt 1859-63 ended forced cultivation in Bengal but did not cause the early-20th-century decline. (c) Leaders' opposition is the Champaran Satyagraha 1917 and the Champaran Agrarian Act 1918, after the decline had begun. (d) The Indigo Commission 1860 dealt with contract terms, decades earlier. The slide's tick beside (b) and the crosses are typed, not handwritten Section 2.5 (Result) Mains No Mains PYQ is shown on the class slides for this chapter Practice questions built from the notes are in section 7 and in the flash cards (the "rehearsal" view of these revolts; the WEMC's role) Sections 2.4, 6 and 7

Story so far: the English once beheaded a king for taxing without consent, and the educated Indian carries that idea to the peasant. Keep the teacher's frame: mainstream society, WEMC, FRs, NTWR, Democracy. Chapter 22 title slide with the teacher's frame Where the chapter sits. The teacher places these revolts among the plains and mainstream society (as against the tribal uprisings of Chapter 20; the exact words are slightly unclear). The new actor is the WEMC, and what the WEMC brings is Western polity = Enlightenment ideas:Fundamental Rights (FRs), NTWR (No Taxation Without Representation) and Democracy. His English history behind it: in 1688 the principle was settled that the King cannot rule without the consent of (P) (the circled P reads as Parliament, going by the Civil War sequence next to it), against the idea of the King's own supremacy. Democracy is rooted in NTWR:Charles I levied taxes without that consent, which led to the English Civil War 1642-51 and Charles I was beheaded. Then the two lines that tie it to India: "Peasants = Masses" and "Nation = sum of people = one" (people underlined): a nation is the sum of all its people, so the peasants (the masses) have to be inside it.

Because 1857 failed as a war, resistance changed its tools. Ask: what do the peasants now use (law, organisation) and who joins them (the WEMC)? What Changed After 1857 at Peasant Revolts The Revolt of 1857 was a turning point not just in British policy but also in the character of Indian resistance. The peasant revolts after 1857 differed from earlier uprisings in two ways: First, peasants now had a greater awareness of British laws and institutions. They did not just pick up weapons: they filed court cases and they organised themselves. They used the legal system that colonial rule had imposed on them as a tool against that very rule. Second, the Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC) began to take up peasant causes.English-educated lawyers, writers, journalists and reformers spoke for the ryot in English newspapers, in courts and in public associations. The peasant was no longer alone. Two hooks on slide 40. (1) Beside "awareness of British laws and institutions" he wrote "Whenever this word, then think about State structure" with L-L, L-E, L-J under it (the three organs of the State: law-making, law-executing, law-judging; this is his rule shorthand from Chapter 8; the exact letters are slightly unclear). So "British laws and institutions" = the courts and the legal order the peasant learnt to use. (2) "no ORG name in PRE 1857 revolts": before 1857 the revolts had no named organisation; after 1857 they do (the Pabna Agrarian Leagues, the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, the Lahore Indian Association and others below). Then, starred, "Recall Modern Politics": the pre-1857 revolts had no clear ideology (goals), no plan (programme), no organisation, were not united and strong, and had no voice of the whole people. Those are exactly the things that appear in the post-1857 revolts: "Elements of Modern Politics appear." Board only: Modern method The modern method is a ladder, and violence is not the first step.Step (1): exhaust the non-violent (NV) methods:courts (by the Government of India's own law), the press, and peaceful protests.Step (2): violent protests.Step (3): revolutionary methods, with the star "Bhagat Singh = Modern Nationalist" (a revolutionary can still be modern if he came to arms after the first steps). Versus (v/s):the 1857 revolts were not "modern nationalists", and the teacher asks "?" because they "wanted Monarchy = feudal elements." This is why the post-1857 peasants, who went to court first, are called the start of modern politics. Do not confuse "modern" with "non-violent". The teacher's point is the order (non-violent methods exhausted first) and the goal (rights, representation, democracy, a nation of all people). The 1857 rebels wanted to restore monarchy (feudal elements), which is why he marks them as not modern nationalists.

Because the new tools needed a first test, Bengal's indigo ryots go first. Follow the chain: contract, trap, squeeze, court, voice, end. 2.1 Context: how did indigo cultivation begin? In 1788 the East India Company (EIC) began promoting Indigo cultivation in Bengal by giving loans to ten European planters. The EIC could have given the same loans to local zamindars but chose European planters: preferential treatment from day one. The teacher dates this under Cornwallis 86-93 (his board: "CW 86-93" under "Origin 1788"): 1788 falls inside those years. Two systems, and the money chain of the second.Nij: the planter buys land directly and cultivates indigo himself; this was expensive and complicated (buying large tracts, organising labour, arranging bullocks and ploughs). The scribble beside Nij reads like "Nij = Ryt" (the exact words are unclear). Ryoti (Bengal): the planter leases land from zamindars and contracts with ryots. His drawing shows who pays whom: the ryot pays rent to the European planter, the planter pays a lease amount to the zamindar (the circled Z; across this chapter the teacher's circled Z means the zamindar), and the zamindar pays Land Revenue (LR) to the State. The circle cut into four with "Indigo" in one quarter is the 25% condition: one quarter of the ryot's land goes to indigo. Indigo Revolt (1859-63): Two Cultivation Systems The planters moved from Nij to Ryoti because Nij was costly and complicated.After the Permanent Settlement of 1793 zamindars were large landowners and land had become a commodity that could be sold, rented, leased or mortgaged, so a planter could simply lease land from a zamindar. Under the Ryoti system the planter signed contracts with tenant ryots with three key conditions: (i) The ryot had to grow indigo on at least 25% of the land he occupied. (ii) The planter gave loans at low interest and also sold indigo seeds and seed drills to the ryot. (iii) The planter then purchased the cultivated indigo from the ryot. On paper this looked like a commercial arrangement.In practice, it was a trap. Who farms The planter himself Tenant ryots under contract Land Bought directly by the planter Leased from zamindars Problem or condition Costly and complicated: large tracts, labour, bullocks, ploughs 25% of occupied land under indigo; low-interest loans, seeds and seed drills; planter buys the crop Where (the shift away from it is why Ryoti spread) Bengal (teacher's note) 2.2 What were the grievances of the ryots? The ryots had real and compounding grievances: Indigo destroyed soil fertility. Once a plot was used for indigo, its productivity for food crops fell sharply, hurting the ryot's overall income. The price the planter paid was not remunerative.Low fertility plus low prices meant the ryot was perpetually in debt, even though the loan rates were low. To pay back one loan, the ryot took another. Since he could not repay, the planter had grounds to remove him from his occupied land (during the lease, the planter was effectively the de-facto zamindar for that ryot). The cycle of debt kept the ryot tied to indigo "not by force of arms, but by force of finance." Then came two triggers: An international trigger:indigo prices on global markets fell, partly due to a financial crisis on the Stock Exchange (a crisis in financial markets caused a general slowdown in the British economy: people lost money, their buying power fell and demand for goods, including indigo, dropped). Planters then offered the ryots even less.The squeeze became unbearable. An administrative trigger: a sympathetic Lieutenant Governor of Bengal directed District Collectors to take the side of ryots in disputes, on the ground that forced cultivation was against the spirit of capitalism and free-market economics. (The post of Lieutenant Governor of Bengal was created in 1854 to reduce the Governor-General's workload, a change made possible by the Charter Act of 1853.) 2.3 What did the ryots do? The ryots responded with a sophisticated, multi-pronged campaign: (i) They refused to accept new loans and refused to cultivate indigo. (ii) They organised a social boycott of the Indian agents of the planters. This was effectively Non-Cooperation, decades before Mahatma Gandhi. Board only: Indigo, the ryots' actions (iii) When planters went to court to enforce contracts, ryots began a no-rent campaign. (Again, Non-Cooperation before Gandhi's era.) (iv) When planters attempted eviction, ryots went to court to enforce their occupancy rights under the Rent Act of 1859. (After the Permanent Settlement of 1793 the ryot was a tenant, and the Rent Act gave him certain legal protections.) His board, in order, and the point inside it.(1) Ryots refuse to grow indigo. (2) The planter files court cases against the ryots: the starred note "Contract = legal" means the planter's cases were legally sound, so going to court did not save the ryots. (3) The ryots reply with a no-rent campaign (boxed). (4) The planter tries eviction. (5) The ryots organise themselves (circled "ORGANIZED") and file court cases (circled "COURT") using the Rent ACT 1859 (the biggest oval on the slide). So both sides used the law, and the ryots won ground only when they were organised and used a law that protected tenants. The social boycott in the handout is not on his board but is in the handout's list. 2.4 The role of the Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC) The handout opens this section with a bracket: "The spirit of Fraternity at work here: a key element of Modern Nationalism."The educated class standing up for the oppressed peasant was a new phenomenon in Indian public life. The slide title repeats it: "(spirit of Fraternity)." The WEMC played a decisive role in amplifying the ryots' cause: 1860: Neel Darpan (Blue Mirror). The playwright DeenBandhu Mitra wrote this powerful play depicting the oppression of ryots by indigo planters. It created enormous public awareness. The Bengali poet Michael Madhusudhan Datta translated Neel Darpan into English, and the Christian missionary James Long published it, bringing the issue to the attention of audiences in England. Indigo: The WEMC Steps In (spirit of Fraternity) The planters filed a case of libel (maan-haani) against Long. He was convicted, fined Rs 1,000 (paid by Kaliprasanna Sinha) and sentenced to one month's imprisonment. Hindu Patriot (English) and Somprakash (Bengali) published strong editorials in favour of the ryots. Even the British Indian Association (1851), an organisation of educated zamindars, supported the ryots. Their motivation was partly self-interest: they resented the dominance of European planters over the rural economy. Voice. Beside the press the teacher starred "voice" and, on the right, wrote "Recall Modern Politics: E -> voice" (education brings voice): the WEMC gave the peasants the voice that pre-1857 revolts lacked. For the press he adds a tip: "use the name to guess the language of the newspaper":Hindu Patriot is an English name, so an English paper; Somprakash is an Indian-language name, so Bengali. Beside the British Indian Association he writes "1851 -> ORG of edu" with the circled Z: an organisation of educated zamindars. Under "libel" he wrote the Hindi word for defamation (maan-haani, as in the handout). 2.5 Result The Indigo Commission (1860) was set up. It ruled that ryots must honour existing contracts but were free to refuse future ones. By 1863 indigo cultivation had largely shifted from Bengal to Bihar, where it operated as the Tinkathia System: essentially the same as the Ryoti System, but here the ryot was forced to grow indigo on 3/20th (three-twentieths) of the land he occupied. The long-term death blow to natural indigo came not from peasant resistance but from chemistry. Indigo Revolt: Result In 1897 the German company BASF developed synthetic indigo,cheaper and more consistent than the natural product. As synthetic indigo flooded global markets, demand for natural indigo collapsed, destroying whatever economic logic remained in the plantation system. (Prelims 2020.) The Bihar chapter closed only in 1917, when Mahatma Gandhi (MG) launched the Champaran Satyagraha, leading to the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918, which brought the Tinkathia System to its end. Two underlines and one value-addition. He underlined "by 1863" and "3/20th of occupied land" (the Tinkathia share) and wrote "From" above "Bengal -> Bihar" (indigo moved from Bengal to Bihar). Then, bottom right, a WWI (1914-19) note: Germany versus Britain; German (synthetic) dye was not available; so demand for natural indigo went up; so planters had a "short window to earn rupees." That is, the war gave natural indigo a brief revival before the decline; the 1897 BASF blow is the long-term cause. Prelims 2020: answer (b) unprofitability in the world market because of new inventions. The trap is picking (a) peasant resistance because this chapter is about the revolt. The revolt ended forced cultivation in Bengal and shifted indigo to Bihar, but the early-20th-century decline was BASF's synthetic indigo of 1897. (c) belongs to Champaran 1917-18; (d) the Indigo Commission 1860 only settled contract terms. Tinkathia (3/20th) against Ryoti (25%).25% is 5/20, so Bihar's 3/20th is a smaller share of the ryot's land than Bengal's quarter, though both were forced. The handout calls Tinkathia "essentially the same as the Ryoti System".

Because the Rent Act 1859 gave rights that zamindars then broke, a new villain appears. Ask: why does the WEMC split here but not in indigo? Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal The ryots of Pabna district in Bengal had a different grievance. The Rent Act of 1859 had granted them occupancy rights, the right not to be arbitrarily evicted. But zamindars were routinely violating these rights. On top of that, rents were being raised illegally, and illegal extra cesses called Abwabs were being collected. A different villain, and an extra trick. The teacher heads the slide "Ryot vs Indian Z": in Indigo the enemy was a European planter; in Pabna it is an Indian zamindar (circled Z). He adds a (+) point: zamindars evicted tenants before 12 years to prevent the occupancy right from arising (this is why the twelve years in the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885, below, matters). Above the title: "L ORG [* e.g. LoN 1920]" (a League is an organisation; his example is the League of Nations of 1920; the reading is slightly unclear). The ryots organised themselves into Agrarian Leagues, a formal structure of collective action. They pooled money to fight their cases in court. A leader called Ishan Chandra Roy then replicated the movement in neighbouring districts. (Organisation and legal awareness: the two new features of post-1857 revolts, clearly on display here.) Beside Organisation the teacher starred "Modern Politics": an organisation with a name (the Agrarian League) is exactly what the pre-1857 revolts did not have. He underlined Ishan Chandra Roy. The WEMC was divided on this issue: For the zamindars Hindu Patriot (English) and Amrita Bazar Patrika (Bengali and English) For the ryots Bengalee (English), edited by Surendra Nath Bannerjea (SNB); and the Anglo-Indian press The Anglo-Indian press also sided with the ryots because here it was an Indian landlord under attack, not a peasant defying a European. Why the WEMC split: follow the money. His board: 1835: Western education = costly.Only rich parents could send their kids to schools and colleges.Who is rich? The zamindar.Zamindar -> son -> WEMC.Therefore: selfish interest >> larger interest (the arrow from this bracket goes to the "WEMC divided" row). So the WEMC members who were zamindars' sons backed the zamindars (Hindu Patriot, Amrita Bazar Patrika); SNB's Bengalee backed the ryots. Beside Amrita Bazar Patrika he wrote "1878" (the year the paper turned to English; see Chapter 19). Hindu Patriot changed sides. In the Indigo Revolt (section 2.4) Hindu Patriot ran strong editorials for the ryots; in Pabna it is for the zamindars. The teacher's reason for the split is "selfish interest >> larger interest": the enemy in Indigo was a European planter (even the zamindars' British Indian Association resented the planters), in Pabna it is an Indian landlord (the class many WEMC members came from). Anglo-Indian against Eurasian (a terminology trap), on slide 49: before the 1911 Census "Anglo-Indian" meant a European living in India and "Eurasian" meant a person of mixed British-Indian descent. The 1911 Census flipped this: "Anglo-Indian" came to mean a person of mixed descent, and "Eurasian" fell out of use. In the Pabna passage the "Anglo-Indian press" is therefore the European-run press in India (as it was in the 1870s). 3.1 Result: the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 No extra ink on the result slide (slide 50). It is typed and carries the steps below. Governor-General Ripon 80-84 (the handout writes "Ripon (1880-84)") set up a Rent Commission in 1880, which led to the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885. This Act gave occupancy rights to ryots who had cultivated different plots of land in the same village continuously for more than twelve years. The Act was properly implemented and finally brought genuine relief to Bengal's ryots. From Pabna to the Bengal Tenancy Act Rent Act 1859: gives tenants occupancy rights (no arbitrary eviction) Zamindars violate them: illegal rent rises, Abwabs, evictions before 12 years 1873:Agrarian Leagues in Pabna pool money for court cases; Ishan Chandra Roy spreads it WEMC divided: Hindu Patriot and Amrita Bazar Patrika for zamindars; Bengalee (SNB) and the Anglo-Indian press for ryots 1880:Ripon 80-84 sets up a Rent Commission 1885: Bengal Tenancy Act: occupancy rights after more than 12 years in the same village; properly implemented, real relief Code for Ripon. The handout writes "Governor-General Ripon (1880-84)" and does not use a code. The teacher's code for Ripon (80-84) is the one written on his slides in Chapter 14; it is used here and agrees with the handout's years.

Because land revenue and debt weigh on the Deccan, the revolt there is about bonds. Ask: what do the ryots burn, and why? 4.1 1873-74: the no-tax campaign In 1873-74 ryots in Maharashtra launched a no-tax campaign against a hike in Land Revenue (LR). This was direct, organised resistance to colonial fiscal policy. Why the hike? On the same slide (Lecture 26, slide 53) he wrote that Land Revenue goes up after 30 years in the Ryotwari system in Bombay: the periodic revision is the source of the hike of 1873-74 (the exact wording of the bracket is slightly unclear). 4.2 Bombay Deccan Riots (1875) Maharashtra: Two No-Tax Campaigns Board only: Cotton, the US Civil War and the Bombay Deccan A cotton boom and bust behind the riots (not in the handout).1861-65 US Civil War:supply of raw cotton from the US fell (the US supplied Britain), so the price of cotton rose (underlined), so demand for Indian raw cotton rose (a circled plus), so the ryot was happy (the smiley face). When the civil war ended (underlined), the arrows are read as supply from the US up, price down, demand for Indian cotton down (the three arrows) and the ryot was sad (the sad face). The funnel marks the Bombay Deccan as the raw-cotton region feeding Britain. Boom borrowing followed by bust is the setting for the debt that exploded in 1875. Reading of slide 51. The three small arrows after "Civil war ended" (up, down, down) and the funnel sketch are not labelled in full. The reading above (US supply up, price down, demand for Indian cotton down) is the natural reverse of the boom column beside it. Check your notebook. Bombay Deccan Riots (1875) The grievances:high Land Revenue under the Ryotwari system,oppression by moneylenders, and loss of land. Background: the Limitation Law of 1859 in Bombay. It ruled that interest on a loan could be applied only for three years, regardless of when the ryot repaid. Moneylenders found a workaround: they made the ryot sign a fresh debt bond after three years, with the accumulated interest now added to the principal. The debt could never truly be paid down. The arithmetic on the right margin:Rs 100 = loan; three years' interest = the new principal (the fresh bond starts again from the bigger sum). Each bond is bigger than the last, so the debt grows even though the law limits interest to three years. Action: the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870), associated with Ranade (M.G.), collected 17,000 signatures on powers-of-attorney to represent ryots. It successfully convinced the government to declare that confiscation of land should be the last resort in recovering Land Revenue arrears. Why this body matters: "Regional / for all ppl / ORG" and "= 1st Regional Pol Party of WEMC": the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was a regional organisation for all the people (that is what "Sarvajanik" says), and the first regional political party of the WEMC. Compare the Lahore Indian Association in section 5.2, which he also calls a "Regional Pol Party of WEMC". Retaliation:moneylenders refused to extend any further loans, leaving ryots unable even to pay their Land Revenue. Violence broke out. The ryots did not attack moneylenders' lives. They burned debt bonds. (An awareness of the instrument of oppression, not just its wielder.) Under "burned debt bonds" he wrote "L Proof of Loans": the debt bond is the proof of the loan, so destroying it destroys the moneylender's claim. Result: the Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act of 1879 was passed. It gave protection against loss of land due to indebtedness and regulated interest rates. From the cotton boom to the Relief Act 1861-65: US Civil War; cotton price and demand for Indian cotton rise; the ryot is happy (teacher's board) After the war: prices and demand fall; high Land Revenue under Ryotwari and the Limitation Law 1859 workaround trap the ryot in debt 1870:Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (Ranade): 17,000 signatures; land confiscation to be the last resort Moneylenders refuse loans; ryots cannot pay Land Revenue 1875: Bombay Deccan Riots: ryots burn debt bonds, not lives 1879: Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act: protection against land loss, regulated interest 4.3 1896-97: the second no-tax campaign In 1896-97 another no-tax campaign broke out because the government refused to grant any remission (a one-time reduction) in Land Revenue despite widespread crop failure. "In Ryotwari, lower LR if bad harvest." In the Ryotwari system a bad harvest was supposed to bring lower Land Revenue (a remission). The refusal in 1896-97 therefore broke the logic of the system itself. The dotted line on slide 53 joins "refused any remission" to this note.

Because Punjab sent soldiers to the Army, even a canal bill carries 1857 in its shadow. Ask: what made the British withdraw? 5.1 Kuka Revolt (1871-72) "Not imp" (the transcription reads "nor imp") is written beside the Kuka Revolt title. Learn it lightly: who (Baba Ram Singh, Namdhari), what (reformist sect, cow protection, no rituals), end (exile to Burma, 1872). Leader:Baba Ram Singh, head of the Namdhari Sect. The Namdharis were a reformist Sikh sect with a distinct identity. They sought to purify Sikhism through social reform. They believed in a living Guru and in the Guru Granth Sahib as the holy book. They upheld strict equality of status for women. They rejected rituals, relying only on the chanting of mantras, hence the name "Kuka" (reciter). They were anti-priestly and strongly pro-cow protection. The revolt began as violence against cow slaughterers and priests, and then turned against the British.Baba Ram Singh was exiled to Burma in 1872. 5.2 Punjab Canal Colony agitations (1907) In west Punjab, from 1885 to 1940, the British built canals in semi-desert areas to convert them into fertile lands for land revenue income. These areas were called Canal Colonies, and lands were allocated to farmers from other parts of Punjab at no or nominal cost, on the condition that they bring the land under cultivation and pay water rates and land revenue. Some lands were given as reward for civil and military service, while some large plots were sold to large investors. In 1907 the British government introduced a bill that would allow the government to: Board only: Canal colony, water rates, leadership Control inheritance of land in the canal colonies, and Increase water rates and fines for violations of canal colony regulations. Three organisations mobilised the peasantry: the Lahore Indian Association (1877), the Arya Samaj (1875) and the Singh Sabha (1873). A no-tax campaign began, which later escalated into riots. Leadership: religion and politics. His brace puts Singh Sabha (1873) and Arya Samaj (1875) under "Role of Religion" and the Lahore Indian Association under "Regional Pol Party of WEMC" (the same label he gave the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha). So the leadership of the Canal Colony agitation was both religious bodies and a WEMC political body. His drawing shows the canal feeding the fields and a box "Water rates [up]": the colonists' fields depend on the canal, so a rise in water rates hits every farmer. Year of the Lahore Indian Association: handout 1877, teacher 1878. The handout and the typed slide (slide 56) say Lahore Indian Association (1877); on his board (slide 55) the teacher wrote "Lahore Indian Association 1878." Both are on the pages of the chapter. The handout's 1877 is kept in the facts and in the quiz; know that the teacher's board says 1878, and check your notebook. The British response was twofold:repression, and then quiet withdrawal of the bill. The reason: post-1857 the Indian Army was heavily recruited from Punjab, particularly from the Sikh community.Disaffection among Punjab's peasantry could spread to the army, the way it did in the 1857 revolt. "Fear of 1857 Repeat." The British gave way in 1907 not out of kindness but out of fear that peasant anger would reach the Army, which was recruited heavily from Punjab and from Sikhs. He underlined "Post-1857 the Indian Army was heavily recruited from Punjab." This is the Prelims-style "why" question of the chapter. Board only: Punjab, Mahalwari, zamindar = landowner In Punjab a "zamindar" is not rich (slide 48). He writes: Mahalwari, therefore most landowners = ryots, not super rich.Z (zamindar) = landowner = ryot here (underlined "here"); Zamin = land, Dar = holder ("owner in the British era"). Post 1947 there was land redistribution from the rich to the poor, so "landowner or Z = not rich." The opening joke ("Baap Z, from where do I take a car?": if my father is a zamindar, where is the car?) makes the same point. This is why the Punjab canal-colony farmers appear as peasants in this chapter even though they own land; the same word zamindar means a large landlord in Bengal (Permanent Settlement) and a landowning peasant in Punjab (Mahalwari). The small economic sketch on the left (Agri circle to Service circle with Industrial and Agri wedges) is a sketch of the economy's structure shifting from agriculture to services; its words are not fully legible. System Permanent Settlement 1793: zamindars became large landowners, land a commodity Mahalwari: most landowners are ryots, not super rich (teacher) Who is the zamindar A big landlord (leases to planters, demands rent from ryots) A landowner = ryot here (Zamin = land, Dar = holder) Revolt in this chapter Indigo, Pabna: ryot against planter or zamindar Canal Colony 1907: farmers against government rules

items.t: 6 · A thread running through all these revolts
items.x: Because every region ticked the same boxes, the chapter closes on the pattern. Remember ROLE: rehearsal, organised, law, educated. Look across Bengal, Maharashtra and Punjab and a pattern emerges. In each case: Peasants were not reacting with blind rage. They were organising: forming leagues, pooling resources, filing cases. They were using the tools of the colonial legal system against colonial exploitation. Sections of the WEMC (journalists, lawyers, reformers) were lending their voice. This is not yet the Indian National Movement. But it is the soil in which that movement would grow. Think of these revolts as the rehearsal. The INM later perfected the methods (non-cooperation, no-tax, boycott, legal challenge) that peasants were discovering through trial and error in these decades. Non-cooperation Indigo: refusing loans and cultivation; social boycott of the planters' Indian agents (decades before Gandhi) No-tax (no-rent) Indigo: no-rent campaign; Maharashtra 1873-74 and 1896-97;Punjab 1907 no-tax campaign Boycott Indigo: social boycott of the planters' agents Legal challenge Rent Act 1859 in court (Indigo); Agrarian Leagues pooling money for cases (Pabna); 17,000 powers-of-attorney (Poona Sarvajanik Sabha) The thread, in his words from slide 57 (dashed underlines only): "Peasants organised," "colonial legal system," "WEMC." Those three underlined phrases are the whole chapter: organisation, law, educated leadership. No Mains PYQ on the slides for this chapter, so the two practice answers below come only from the notes (the question bank's 5 Mains practice questions are on the Question bank page).

items.t: 7 · Mains answer skeletons (practice, from the notes)
items.x: Because the idea matters more than the detail, practise the two skeletons: the rehearsal, and the WEMC. These two are practice questions (the notes' own forecast; no Mains PYQ is on the class slides). The skeletons use only this chapter's facts. Q1. "The peasant revolts after 1857 were the rehearsal for the methods the Indian National Movement later perfected." Examine (15 marks, 250 words). Intro: after 1857 resistance changed: peasants used British law and organised, and the WEMC took up their cause. These revolts are the soil in which the INM would grow, not yet the INM. Body:non-cooperation (Indigo ryots refused loans and cultivation and boycotted the planters' agents, before Gandhi); no-tax (no-rent in Indigo; Maharashtra 1873-74 and 1896-97; Punjab 1907); boycott (Indigo social boycott); legal challenge (Rent Act 1859 occupancy rights; Pabna leagues pooling money; Poona Sarvajanik Sabha's 17,000 powers-of-attorney); relief laws (Commission 1860, Deccan Act 1879, Tenancy Act 1885). Closing: the INM did not invent these methods; it scaled them (Champaran 1917, Non-Cooperation 1920 on the slide-58 timeline). Add the teacher's modern method ladder (court, then protest, then revolution) and the note that they were regional (the Sabha and the Lahore Association are "regional political parties of the WEMC"). Q2. "The WEMC's entry into peasant causes was a new phenomenon." Examine its role and limits (15 marks, 250 words). Intro:fraternity at work: the educated class stood up for the oppressed peasant; the teacher's "voice." Body:Indigo: Neel Darpan 1860 (Mitra), Datta's translation, Long's libel conviction (Rs 1,000, one month), Hindu Patriot and Somprakash editorials, British Indian Association 1851. Pabna: the WEMC split (Hindu Patriot and Amrita Bazar Patrika for zamindars; Bengalee under SNB and the Anglo-Indian press for ryots) because education was costly, so WEMC members were zamindars' sons (selfish interest >> larger interest). Deccan: the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (Ranade, 17,000 signatures), the first regional political party of the WEMC. Closing: the WEMC gave the peasants voice and organisation, but its class interests limited it; both help explain why the movement later needed a mass base.
