1857 changes the way of resisting. After 1857 the peasants did not just pick up weapons: they filed court cases and organised themselves, using the colonial legal system against colonial rule. The Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC) began to speak for the ryot in newspapers, courts and associations. The teacher's ladder says modern politics tries non-violent methods first: courts, press, peaceful protest. 1788: a trap that looked like a contract. The EIC began promoting indigo in Bengal in 1788 with loans to ten European planters, preferring them to zamindars. Nij farming (the planter buys land) was costly, so planters moved to the Ryoti system: lease land from zamindars, then contract with ryots to grow indigo on at least 25% of their land, with low-interest loans, seeds and seed drills, and the planter buying the crop. The squeeze. Indigo ruined the soil, the price was not remunerative, and the ryot borrowed one loan to repay another, tied by force of finance. A Stock Exchange crisis then cut global indigo prices, and a sympathetic Lieutenant Governor of Bengal told Collectors to side with ryots against forced cultivation. The ryots go to court. They refused new loans and indigo, boycotted the planters' Indian agents, and began a no-rent campaign when planters sued (the teacher: the contract was legal). When planters tried eviction, the ryots organised and went to court under the Rent Act of 1859. This was Non-Cooperation decades before Gandhi. The educated join. DeenBandhu Mitra's play Neel Darpan (1860) shocked the public; Michael Madhusudhan Datta translated it and James Long published it, and for that Long was convicted of libel, fined Rs 1,000 (paid by Kaliprasanna Sinha) and jailed a month. Hindu Patriot and Somprakash ran editorials, and the British Indian Association (1851) of educated zamindars backed the ryots, partly from self-interest. Indigo ends slowly. The Indigo Commission (1860) said honour old contracts, refuse new ones. By 1863 indigo moved to Bihar as Tinkathia (3/20th of land). The long-term death blow was BASF's synthetic indigo in 1897 (Prelims 2020), with a short WWI revival, and Champaran (1917) and the Act of 1918 ended Tinkathia. Pabna, 1873: a league and a split. Zamindars violated the occupancy rights of the Rent Act 1859, raised rents illegally and collected Abwabs. The ryots formed Agrarian Leagues, pooled money for court, and Ishan Chandra Roy spread them. The WEMC split: Hindu Patriot and Amrita Bazar Patrika for the zamindars, Bengalee (SNB) and the Anglo-Indian press for the ryots. Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission (1880) led to the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885: occupancy rights after more than twelve years. The Deccan's bond trap. No-tax came in 1873-74 against a Land Revenue hike. The Limitation Law 1859 allowed interest for three years only, so moneylenders made a fresh bond with the interest added to the principal. The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) gathered 17,000 signatures; moneylenders refused loans; in 1875 the ryots burned debt bonds, not lives. The Relief Act came in 1879, and a second no-tax campaign in 1896-97 over refused remission. Punjab: a sect and a canal bill. The Namdhari (Kuka) sect under Baba Ram Singh turned from violence against cow slaughterers and priests to violence against the British, and he was exiled to Burma in 1872 (the teacher: not imp). In 1907 a bill to control inheritance and raise water rates in the canal colonies brought the Lahore Indian Association, the Arya Samaj and the Singh Sabha into a no-tax campaign. The British repressed, then quietly withdrew it, fearing the Army, recruited heavily from Punjab, might follow. The rehearsal. Across Bengal, Maharashtra and Punjab, peasants organised, used the colonial legal system and found the WEMC lending its voice. It was not yet the national movement but the soil in which it would grow: non-cooperation, no-tax, boycott and legal challenge were all rehearsed here before Champaran (1917) and Non-Cooperation (1920).

Story so far: nothing yet. Keep the whole chapter in one line: petition, provoke, organise, converge. Ask: what is the INC, and who spoke before it? Chapter 23 title slide with the teacher's board What INC means, letter by letter: I = Indian; N = Nation = Pol (polity, written with "one" and a partly unclear "equal supreme"); C = ORG (organisation).A political party = an ORG whose motive is power over the State. Here the State is the colonial State. So the INC = the Indian people's ORG = a political party, and it was the first all-India political party, in 1885. The teacher's "Early" (boxed in the title) points to what came before it: not all India, but regional political bodies:Bombay (1870, circled), Calcutta (1876), Punjab (1877), Madras (1884). The year box "1857-85" is the span of the chapter. Two motives for a State. For the colonial State the teacher writes "motive: Loot, Dominate colony." For a nation State (circled V1) the motive is "welfare of nation" (circled T). The box on the right reuses the State structure of Chapter 1 (its section on power, State and sovereignty, which also tabulates a political party's motive as power over the State): a symbolic sovereign ("Sym Sov") over L, E, J (legislative, executive, judicial), and ministers working through CS and MS (read as civil servants and military servants, as in Chapter 1). The "Recall" table (Modern Nation: eco, Pol, Social; Modern Politics: a row of short labels ending in ORG, L, Z, voice) is beyond ORG (circled and underlined). Teacher's board: priority and the two kinds of ORG Of, By, For. The landed-class associations were OF, BY and FOR the landed class. Because Western education was costly, it is understandable that they were "of" and "by" the educated landed class, BUT "for" the landed class and not for the people = Sad. The regional WEMC organisations (post-1870) were of and by the WEMC class, but FOR the people: and "people" = landed + WEMC + peasants + workers = the masses. Then, beyond the dotted line, comes the all-India INC of 1885 (next chapter). The starred note: "Link ideology of modern Nationalism" (the people-for-all idea is the modern nation concept). The ladder of methods (the teacher's "radicalness" board) Teacher's board: "Radicalness of methods in INM (1857-1947) = Political Domain" Conservatives Minimum change Same method as the moderates (press, petitions, prayers); the teacher links them to the social reformers (his initials RRR, ICV, DBT, MG Ranade) No street protests; no involvement of the masses Moderates Bigger but gradual change Press, Petitions, Prayers = 3P; they also use FIR, court cases, elections Street protest Annie Besant and Madan Mohan Malviya (the teacher: "no name by books") Gradual 3P; go to the people; what is written in the press is told in layman's language No street protests MG Larger Non-violent, extra-constitutional: press and street protests No FIR, no court cases, no elections: no use of the grievance redressal mechanisms of the colonial State Extremists Faster Violent protests if peaceful methods fail; press, 3P, elections, FIR, court cases Nothing is ruled out Revolutionaries Immediate and fundamental Press and guns Constitutional limits The handout (Section 3) gives the same ladder in one line:conservatives want very little change; moderates gradual reform; extremists faster change; revolutionaries immediate and fundamental transformation. The teacher's board adds the middle group the books do not name (Annie Besant and Madan Mohan Malviya) and MG (his shorthand for Mahatma Gandhi) as the group that left the colonial redressal channels. RRR and DBT are the teacher's shorthand for Roy and Debendranath Tagore in Chapter 19; ICV is initials only on this slide. Teacher's board: Conservatives = Landed Class; a bracket for Moderates = WEMC, Extremists, MG, Revolutionaries; a circle labelled "1921 Census" over "Indian Pop", with an Conservatives = Landed class. The bracket groups Moderates, Extremists, MG and Revolutionaries with "Moderates = WEMC" written on the first line. The circle is the Indian population in the 1921 census, and the small segment marked 8% is labelled WEMC: the educated sliver that led the movement (the handout's 1921 figure is 8% overall literacy, Section 5).

items.t: 1 · How the Indian National Movement began
items.x: Because the INC came late, the story opens before it: who spoke first? Ask: why was the first voice not the educated middle class? The Indian National Movement (INM) was, in its mature form, led by the Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC). But the first organised political voice in modern India was not theirs. It belonged to a different group: the educated landed class. Their regional associations were the earliest formal platforms for putting Indian political demands. Who led the INM and where did it begin? Mature INM = WEMC. First organised voice = educated landed class, through regional associations (Section 2).

Because the educated landed class had voice and money, it formed the first bodies (1851-52). Ask: what trigger sent three bodies to petition at once, and what does 'all-Indian' mean? The first major voluntary organisation in India was the British Indian Association [BrIA 1851], set up in Calcutta in 1851. Radhakanta Deb was its first president. Its members came from educated men of the landed class. It was also the first all-Indian organisation in character, unlike Dwarkanath Tagore's Landholders' Society (1838), which had included many non-official Anglo-Indians. (Before 1911, "Anglo-Indian" meant a European settled in India, not a person of mixed parentage.) The same period saw the Bombay Association (1852) and the Madras Native Association (1852). All three were educated, landed and conservative. The immediate reason for all three: the British Parliament was deliberating on the Charter Act of 1853 and Indian elites wanted to put their demands before it. "All-Indian" is not "all India." The teacher brackets BrIA 1851 as "[only Bengal]" and "all-Indian" as "[no Br Person in it]": it was all-Indian in membership (no Briton in it), unlike the Landholders' Society (1838), which he tags "L ORG" (read as a landed ORG) with its non-official Anglo-Indians underlined. The "imp" brace sets "1st all-Indian" against "1st all India [INC 1885]": the BrIA is the first all-Indian ORG (Indians only), the INC the first all-India ORG (the whole territory). On the Bombay row he adds "Dadabhai Naoroji in BoA 1852" (Naoroji was in the Bombay Association of 1852; the same man appears in the 1876 revival, Section 13). The handout's flow chart (shown in Section 13) adds that BrIA 1851 had Debendranath Tagore as secretary and the Hindu Patriot (Harish Ch. Mukherjee) as its voice; the Madras Native Association (1852) was Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty's body, the first political body in Madras. PYQ 7, Prelims 2017: associations and founders Prelims 2017: answer (b) 1 and 3 only.Pair 1 is correct: Radhakanta Deb was the first president of the British Indian Association (1851); the teacher also wrote "Dharma Sabha 1830" beside it (the digits of the year are). Pair 3 is correct:Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association (1876).Pair 2 is the trap: the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884) was founded by M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Anandacharlu, not by Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty, who is linked to the Madras Native Association (1852).

Because they were landlords, they asked politely and for themselves. Ask: why did three petitions, called 'un-British', get nothing? Their Demands and Why None Were Met (Conservatives) The three associations sent separate petitions, not a joint one. They were not yet a single national fraternity, but three regional lobbies. Their grievances fell into two kinds: Common grievances:high taxes,expensive and incompetent administration,neglect of education and public works. Elite personal interests: opposition to the salt and opium monopolies. They did not oppose British rule itself. They opposed what they called "un-British" rule: British governance was, by definition, just and fair, and exploitation was a departure from that standard. This is "Brown Sahib" thinking: the phrase "un-British" assumes British rule is good by default. They were not calling colonialism wrong; they were calling exploitation un-British. No demands were met. These conservatives had too much to lose: the colonial land revenue systems had directly benefited them, and their social standing depended on British patronage. Framework to carry forward: conservatives want very little change; moderates gradual reform; extremists faster change; revolutionaries immediate and fundamental transformation (the teacher's ladder, Section 0). Why the petitions failed, in his words."Factionalism," "no unity" (three separate petitions). Beside the first row he links the regional lobbies to "Salaries of (CS)" (CS circled; read as civil servants' salaries, the costly administration of the common grievances:). "1835 Policy: only elite" points to neglect of education (the 1835 Downward Filtration Theory, Section 5). On public works he writes "INFRA you see as soon as you step out of home (7)" against "In Home: electricity, water, sanitation, gas" (public works = the infrastructure outside the home). Elite interests = "[Selfish]" (the salt and opium monopolies were "of Govt."). On un-British: "You are Br BUT WHY are you not behaving like British." Bottom right: "PS 1793 and other LR systems created Landed class (+); Br Police protected LLO; (-ve) they owed their status and security of life and property to British."

items.t: 4 · The INM after 1857: a product of colonial policy
items.x: Because the landlords failed, the movement needed a new class and new tools, and the Raj itself supplied both. Ask: which colonial policies were the tools and which the villain? Teacher's board: "# FYQs # Factors behind Rise of INM"; "# INM was Product of Colonial Policies" A deep irony: the British built many of the very tools that would later be used against them. The growth of the INM after 1857 was in large part a consequence of colonial policies themselves. FYQ board: "Factors behind rise of INM" (FYQs underlined) and "INM was a product of colonial policies." Colonial policies were GOOD or BAD (= the villain).GOOD = Press, Railways, Post and Telegraph, Western Education: "we got" the tools of the INM, modern by default:ideas of modern polity (including fundamental rights and the welfare State), the vocabulary of modern politics,methods of modern politics (a modern press, organisations), the press as a voice to demands, and better communication (leader to leader, leader to people, and people to people). BAD = authoritarian and racist policies = anger, motivation, energy for the INM. His rule: "Stronger the villain, stronger the hero; rise of villain = rise of hero." Teacher's board: what makes a CLASS, "when": (1) number of members rising, AND (2) consciousness among members of Common Problems and Solutions, AND (3) members are ORGAN A class exists "when" three things are true, joined by AND:(1) the number of members rises;(2) consciousness among members of common problems and solutions;(3) the members are organised (he draws a small hierarchy: one circle over a row of three, one of which has another row of three below). This is why the WEMC became a class only when it was numerous, aware of common problems and solutions, and organised (Sections 5 and 13).

Because the Raj taught the educated, it created its own critics. Ask: why was the movement uneven, and who was left out? Factor 1: Western Education The rapid expansion of Western higher education after 1857 created a new group: a politically conscious WEMC. (It is specifically higher education that matters: colleges and universities are where people develop political ideology and a sense of public affairs; primary schooling alone does not produce political movements.) The British meant this class to be loyal "Brown Sahibs." But as the WEMC realised the British had no genuine intention of sharing power,admiration turned to criticism, and criticism turned into a demand for Indian rights. Western education did not spread evenly, so the INM grew unevenly. The Downward Filtration Theory (1835) had focused education only on the elites of the Presidency Towns. Mass education stayed neglected, shown by the Census of 1921: only 8% overall literacy and 2% female literacy, despite Wood's Dispatch (1854) and the Hunter Commission (1882-83) both calling for wider expansion. So early INM leadership was dominated by upper-caste (UC) Marathis, Tamilians and Bengalis of the Presidency Towns. Muslims were comparatively under-represented in early Western-educated politics: partly from a wish to preserve Persian literary culture, partly from the conservative influence of the Ulamas. "It's in college that the first exposure to politics happens" (a dotted line to "higher"). Admiration "of Br Rule" turned to demand "for Indian rights." The teacher also notes "1857: 3 universities {M, B, C}" (Madras, Bombay, Calcutta) and "Post 1857: rising authoritarianism, racism" (the reason admiration soured). His starred pair: the 1882 Hunter Education Commission and the 1921 census, 8% (circled). On Muslims he writes "insecurity @ Persian literary culture + getting HURT" (the "or" signs between them are). Teacher's board: "Level of Western EDU, also Level of (modern) INM", a descending green bar chart: Calcutta city (tallest), Bombay city, Madras city, Rest of Br India (lo The bar chart:level of Western education (and so the level of modern INM): Calcutta city highest, then Bombay city, then Madras city, and the rest of British India lowest.Profile of INM leaders till 1920:from M, B, C; rich; upper-caste Hindus; Bangla, Marathi, Tamil speakers. His line: uneven growth of Western education leads to uneven growth of the INM. Why Persian Was Embedded in Muslim Culture Persian was not just a language: it was a cultural identity. The Mughal court used Persian as its official language. (The teacher adds: the Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) also promoted Persian.) Humayun 30-40 took help from the Safavid Dynasty of Persia (Shia) to reclaim power from the Suri Dynasty (1540-55). The Nawabs of Awadh were Shia.Golconda and Bijapur were Shia-ruled until Aurangzeb 58-07 annexed them in 1686 and 1687 respectively. For many educated Muslims, abandoning Persian meant abandoning something precious. Beside the Awadh line (a curve from the Suri line points there) the teacher wrote "Sadat Khan 22-39," the Nawab of Awadh of the Chapter 3 successor states. His insert: Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) promoted Persian.

Because the WEMC now had readers, the press carried its voice. Ask: how does a regional leader become a national one? Factors 2 and 3: Press, Railways and Telegraphs By 1875, India had over 400 newspapers in English and vernacular languages, with a combined readership of more than 1.5 lakh. The press was the primary tool of the WEMC. It built inter-regional awareness, spread nationalist ideas, and helped regional leaders grow into national ones. When a regional leader begins writing and speaking on all-India issues (the budget, civil services, famine), he gradually becomes a national leader. The press was the engine of that change. "Regional + all India": the press turns a regional leader into an all-India leader (his small circle with an arrow to a big circle). He adds "Census: 1901: 30 cr population" (the scale of all India; the exact point he makes with it is not written). "Hearts mind of a leader [Emotions and Awareness]": read as the press shaping a leader's emotions and awareness.

Because distances shrank, leaders could meet. Ask: what did railways and the telegraph add to the press? From the 1850s,railways and the electric telegraph physically and communicatively connected distant parts of India. Leaders from Bombay, Bengal, Madras and Punjab could now meet, correspond and coordinate. The infrastructure of empire became, unintentionally, the infrastructure of anti-colonial politics. Under railways: "ALL india LEADERSHIP" and "Ppl to Ppl contact" (the slide 13 ink above): railways gave an all-India leadership and people-to-people contact.

Because the Raj kept insulting the educated, anger grew. Ask: which provocations are dated and which is a result? "If Western education was the slow fire that built the INM, British racism was the accelerant." Every act of racial discrimination reminded Indians of their subordinate status and added recruits to the movement. It is the biggest single contributor to the movement's growth. (Like a film villain, it gives the hero a reason to rise.) Factor 4: British Racism and Authoritarianism (the accelerant) 8.1 1850: the Black Acts (Bethune's Bills) Before 1850, a European charged with a crime in the mofussil (rural areas outside the Presidency Towns) could be tried only by the Supreme Court in a Presidency Town (Calcutta, Bombay or Madras). That bypassed the local Company courts where Indian judges (Sadr Amins, Munsifs) sat. This made justice for ordinary Indians nearly impossible: witnesses and complainants had to travel to a Presidency Town at great cost. The Black Acts ended this privilege and brought Europeans in the mofussil under the criminal jurisdiction of the ordinary district courts, where Indians served as judges. Europeans protested so fiercely in the press that it is called the "white rebellion," and the Acts had to be suspended. Recall: the Charter Act of 1833 had promised racial equality. The Black Acts tried to act on that promise. The same principle returned in the Ilbert Bill of 1883 (Section 12). The "white rebellion" was by the Anglo-Indian (European) press ("ANGLO INDIAN" written above it). The starred note links the lower judiciary (J) opened to Indians in 1833 to the Sadr Amins and Munsifs, and "State's" over the courts; his first letters "UCs" are . What it hurt: "This hurts Brown Sahib mentality and the WMB narrative" (WMB read as the White Man's Burden narrative:). And: "Br negated opinion, petition of WEMC [= Authoritarian]" (the British overrode WEMC opinion and petitions: that is the authoritarian side). 8.2 1850: the Lex Loci Act The Lex Loci Act (Removal of Religious/Caste Disabilities Act) gave the right of inheritance to converts from any religion to any other. It was passed despite Indian opposition and was widely seen as a tool to promote conversion to Christianity. 8.3 1868: Income Tax First introduced in 1860, then withdrawn under press pressure, then re-introduced in 1868, even as famines swept different parts of India through the 1860s and 70s. The WEMC answered with a sharp slogan: "No Taxation Without Representation." The worst famine of the period was the Great Madras Famine of 1876-78, caused by two consecutive years of drought. About one crore Indians died. The slogan was raised "in Press," in the 1860s-70s. On the famine he adds "[Cannibalism also Reported]." And the lesson of the Income Tax: "Got to know Govt's priorities in India" (tax during famine showed what the Government put first). 8.4 1870: education cuts in Bengal The Anglo-Indian press had been calling the WEMC "seditious." The colonial response was not to engage with the criticism, but to cut higher-education spending in Bengal, while military spending and high taxes continued as before. 8.5 Cultural nationalism hardens into political nationalism British racism also deepened cultural nationalism. The extremist leaders Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal (Lal-Bal-Pal) and Aurobindo later used it to strengthen political nationalism. Recall the cultural nationalism of the period: Arya Samaj 1875, Swami Vivekananda, Bankim Chandra Chatterjee (Chapter 19). His closing line under the table: "All are post 1857. Why? Because of rising racism post 1857."

Because Lytton 76-80 antagonised every section in four years, the educated turned bitter. Ask: which of his six measures hit the press, the services and the treasury? Viceroy Lytton 76-80 managed to antagonise practically every section of educated Indian opinion in just four years. (The slide numbers the measures in a different order from the handout; this chapter follows the handout's numbering and gives the slide's year where it differs.) The Lytton Years (1876-80), antagonising everyone 9.1 1876: ICS age cut from 21 to 19 Since the examination was held only in London, lowering the age made it near-impossible for Indians to compete. The demand for an examination centre in India was rejected outright. (The ICS exam was set up by the Charter Act 1853 and first held in 1855. A simultaneous exam in India was accepted only under the GOI Act 1919, and the first India-based exam was held in 1922.) He corrects the wording to "simultaneous exam in India" and writes CCS over "ICS" (the abbreviation the slide itself uses in the Statutory Civil Service row). Underlined: GOI Act 1919, first held 1922."76-80" under the title is Lytton's term. 9.2 1878: the Statutory Civil Services Act A new service category was created, but entry was by nomination, not examination.Only loyalists were nominated. Think of it as colonial "lateral entry": designed to look inclusive while making sure loyalists got in. Date conflict. The handout writes 1878 (Statutory Civil Services Act); the slide's table writes 1879 (Statutory Civil Service) and adds that these were "Lytton 76-80's rules under the GOI Act 1870" (the slide types it as "Lytton7680's"): provincial governments nominated Indians to CCS-reserved posts, subject to approval by the Government of India and the Secretary of State; nomination, not the exam held in England; a service distinct from the CCS. For Prelims remember 1878-79 and the method (nomination); the question bank's own statement uses 1878. The teacher's ink: "ONLY LOYALISTS were chosen; 1%; WEMC opposed it." 9.3 1877: the Delhi Durbar An enormous and expensive imperial spectacle, held while the Great Madras Famine was killing people across south India. Queen Victoria was crowned Kaisar-i-Hind (Empress of Hindustan). The WEMC press was scathing. There was also a three-year press campaign, 1877-80, by the WEMC demanding Indianisation of the Civil Services; the Durbar added fuel to it. The campaign is underlined and marked "(failed)"; below it "WAS neglected," i.e. the demand for Indianisation was neglected. The word "Queen" is overwritten on the slide (). 9.4 1878: the Vernacular Press Act It targeted the vernacular press, which had grown sharply critical of British policy. Printers and publishers had to deposit a security bond, forfeited if they published anything "objectionable" (in practice, anything anti-British). The British Liberal MP Gladstone criticised the Act publicly from London. The most dramatic response came from the Amrita Bazar Patrika, which converted itself overnight from a Bengali newspaper to an English one, placing itself outside the Act's reach. "Vernacular Press Act = Financial Surgical STRIKE" (a strike on the press through a money bond). On Gladstone: "Br (MP)," "PM in 1880," "4 Time PM" (he was only an MP in 1878, and became Prime Minister in 1880: see Ripon, Section 10). The Lytton Years (1876-80), contd 9.5 1878: the Arms Act Indians required a licence to own arms; Europeans and Eurasians were exempt. B.C. Pal launched press campaigns against this openly discriminatory law. "Europeans & Eurasians = Anglo Indians" (his gloss on the exempt group, matching the handout's note on the old meaning of "Anglo-Indian"). 9.6 1878-80: the Second Afghan War Lytton fought a costly campaign in Afghanistan, driven by fear of Russian influence, when the Indian treasury was already stretched by famine relief. The treaty that ended the war shaped the modern borders of Afghanistan. The First Afghan War of 1838-42 was fought for exactly the same reason (fear of Russian expansion) and was an expensive disaster. The British learned very little. "Lytton's Afghan Adventure = Unnecessary [no real threat]." And: "The same rupees could have been used for famine relief." The scribble over "while famine relief" on the slide is; the handout says the famine relief costs had already stretched the treasury. The handout's chart adds two small facts that are not in the handout text or the slides: the Royal Titles Act of 1876 (before the Durbar) and the name "Gagging Act" for the Vernacular Press Act (the same label used in Chapter 19). It also says the Factory Act capped under-12s at 9 hours and calls the European agitation the "White Mutiny." The slide numbering (9.4 Arms Act, 9.5 Statutory Civil Service) differs from the handout (9.5 Arms Act, 9.2 Statutory Civil Services); the content is the same.

Because Gladstone's Liberals won in 1880, a liberal Viceroy followed Lytton. Ask: which Lytton measure did Ripon undo, and which did he only amend? Ripon's Interlude (1880-84), the liberal contrast When Gladstone's Liberal Party won the 1880 British elections, he sent a reformist Viceroy, Lord Ripon 80-84. The contrast with Lytton 76-80 was stark. "Ripon 80-84 = Liberal, sent by Liberal PM Gladstone, BUT faced opposition from the rest of the British civil service in India, because they are racists and authoritarian." (The opposition to Ripon 80-84 from Europeans in India recurs in 10.5 and in the Ilbert Bill, Section 12.) 10.1 1880: the Rent Commission Set up by Ripon 80-84, it eventually led to the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885. Recall the pressure of the Pabna Agrarian Leagues of 1873 for fair implementation of the Rent Act of 1859 in Bengal. Over "Rent Act of 1859" he writes "amendments in": the 1885 Act is amendments in the Rent Act of 1859. 10.2 1881: the Factories Act Child labour was banned for children under 7.Working hours were capped for children under 12.Four monthly holidays were mandated. Moderate Indian leaders opposed this Act: it would hurt Indian capitalists, who were already struggling against competition from cheaper British manufactured goods. (A reminder that "Indian interests" were not one unified position.) Prelims 2007: the first Factory Act (women and children) = Ripon's time. The slide's answer note: under-7s barred; under-12s capped at 9 hours. Prelims 2007: answer (c) Ripon 80-84. The teacher's trick: write 1881 over the question and the reign years beside each option.1881 falls only inside Ripon 80-84: Lytton 76-80 ended in 1880, Bentinck 28-35 was long before, Canning 56-62 was earlier. Why moderates opposed it: the Act "will raise costs of operations."Industrial Revolution (IR) came by capitalism:Britain (1750-1850), France (1870+), Germany (1870+) (with FDI by Britain, written beside Germany), Japan (1868+), USA (1865+) all did IR via capitalism."For WEMC, India will do IR only when Indian capitalists are STRONG, and then pro-worker laws can be made." The double hurt:(a) the Government is not pro Indian capitalist; (b) the Government is raising the costs of business (and British businesses in India are rich and can bear the costs). On the right: FACTORIES (machines) came by FDI by Britain and by some Indians.IR is read here as the Industrial Revolution (his shorthand): for the exact wording of the "IR" lines. 10.3 to 10.5: Press, arms, ICS 1882: Vernacular Press Act repealed. 1882: Arms Act amended. Now everyone, including Europeans, needed a licence. A liberal gesture, but Ripon amended, not repealed, the Act: a reformer, but still a colonial ruler (the teacher: "working for LLO"). 1882: ICS age limit raised back to 21. Ripon also pushed for a simultaneous exam in India;Europeans in India strongly opposed it and the proposal failed.

Because Ripon wanted to train Indians in self-government, local bodies were elected. Ask: what did the government still control? Local Self-Government (1882), Ripon's key reform Ripon's most significant reform was the Local Self-Government Resolution/Act of 1882. The stated goal was to train Indians in the practice of self-government. Rural:elected District Boards across British India. Members were to be elected by land revenue payers and rent payers, not nominated by officials. Urban: municipalities were strengthened: at least two-thirds of members elected, and the chairperson a non-official member. Charge: local bodies were given health, education, sanitation, roads and communications, with autonomy in day-to-day functioning. The government kept the power to inspect and dissolve a local body (regulation, not total control). The Hunter Education Commission (1882-83) followed: it recommended transfer of education to local bodies and a focus on mass education in vernacular languages, especially female education.Implementation remained poor. "Ripon 80-84 = Father of L&G" (read as Local Self-Government). "Students should recognise Local Government versus Local SELF-Government. Key word = 'Self'.""Now" elected:land-revenue payers = landowners; rent payers = tenants. His ladder: Centre, Provinces, Local Bodies (boxed) = LSG = i.e. democracy at the third level, via power to local bodies, which needs two things: economic: funds; political: autonomy in decisions. Compare with today: Local Self-Government is now a constitutional right under Part IX (Panchayati Raj) and Part IX-A (Municipalities), inserted by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments of 1992. Ripon's 1882 Act was the colonial seedling; the 1992 amendments made it a constitutional tree.

Because Europeans would not accept Indian judges over Britons, the bill was watered down. Ask: why did this episode radicalise the WEMC most? The single episode that most sharply exposed British racial attitudes and most decisively radicalised the WEMC was the Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883-84. The Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883-84) Drafted by Law Member C.P. Ilbert, the bill proposed to extend the jurisdiction of Indian district judges to try cases involving Britons in the mofussil (rural) areas. It would end an existing privilege: a Briton in rural India could not be tried before an Indian judge. The European community's reaction was immediate and furious: they organised, lobbied and protested, and the bill had to be withdrawn and amended. The final version required a mixed jury in any case involving a Briton. For the WEMC this settled any remaining doubt: the British would not treat Indians as equals in courts, in civil services or in political life. The controversy triggered massive press campaigns across the country and is rightly called a major milestone in the growth of Indian political consciousness. Europeans protested "in Press" (arrow to "protested"); the WEMC campaigned "in favour of the Ilbert Bill ... (use of Press)." The exam line: "Where was the maximum use of the press by the WEMC before 1885? Ans: Here (the Ilbert Bill)." He also notes "Indian HC Act 1861: HCs in 1862 {M, B, C}" (the High Courts at Madras, Bombay, Calcutta) beside the courts theme; why he places it here is not written. Prelims 2003: answer (a): to bring Indians and Europeans on par in the criminal jurisdiction of courts. The distractors are the other Lytton-era laws:(b) the Vernacular Press Act (1878);(c) the rejected ICS-in-India demand; (d) the Arms Act (1878), where the teacher wrote 1878. PYQ 6, Prelims 2013: the Ilbert Bill controversy Prelims 2013: answer (c): removal of the disqualifications imposed on Indian magistrates with regard to the trial of Europeans.(a) arms restrictions = the Arms Act 1878;(b) restrictions on Indian-language newspapers = the Vernacular Press Act, 1878;(d) a cotton cloth duty has nothing to do with it; the teacher wrote "WWI 1914-19" beside it.

Because the landlords had failed and the WEMC was angry, a new kind of body appeared from 1870. Ask: which four bodies, which founders, and which year for the Commons petition? From 1870 a new kind of Indian political organisation appeared: led not by conservative landlords but by young, politically minded professionals of the WEMC. They challenged the older landed-class bodies and gradually replaced them as the principal voice of Indian opinion. The handout's chart adds names the handout text does not give: Bengal British India Society 1843, East India Association 1866 (London, Dadabhai Naoroji), the Bombay Presidency Association 1885 (Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang, Badruddin Tyabji),Ananda Mohan Bose with SNB, and that the Indian Association was originally the Bharat Sabha. Use them as extra detail; the Prelims questions in this chapter need the four bodies below. WEMC-Led Associations (Post-1870) 13.1 Bombay The old Bombay Association of 1852 was briefly revived in 1876 when Dadabhai Naoroji and Naoroji Ferdunji returned from London. But the younger generation was not satisfied with its conservative outlook. The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) was set up by M.G. Ranade. It brought together Telang (K.T.) and Mehta (P.M.), and later Gokhale (G.K.) and Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Its aim was to represent all sections of society: a significant departure from the landlord focus of the earlier bodies. In 1875 the Sabha sent a petition to the British House of Commons demanding direct Indian representation: one of the earliest such demands addressed to the Imperial Parliament itself. "Of and By WEMC, BUT For all people [* the modern nation concept]" (the same Of-By-For idea as slide 3). "P.M." is written above the Poona line (the handout's P.M. Mehta). After the 1875 petition: "Indians should vote in elections of Br (P)" (P circled, read as Parliament): direct representation meant Indians voting in British elections. Prelims 2002: answer (d) The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha. The teacher wrote the founding year beside each option: the Indian Association was founded only in 1876 (SNB) and the Madras Mahajan Sabha in 1884, so neither could petition in 1875; only the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870, M.G. Ranade) existed. (a) a "Deccan Association" petition is not recorded in the chapter. 13.2 Bengal Surendranath Banerjee (SNB) founded the Indian Association (1876) with the explicit goal of "representing the people." SNB had actually passed the ICS examination but was not selected, because of an age dispute (a difference between the English calendar and the Hindu calendar). Personal injustice became political fuel. "Not selected" or "dismissed"? The handout (13.2) and slide 22 say SNB passed the ICS but was denied over an age dispute; the handout's Prelims 1999 alert and the slide answer say he was dismissed from the ICS (slide: entered the ICS in 1869 and dismissed in 1874 over a minor procedural lapse). The teacher's ink on the PYQ slide is "(Age) Dismiss."For the exam, use "dismissed" (answer (b)). In a Mains line: "an age and calendar dispute cost him the service, and that injustice became political fuel." PYQ 2, Prelims 1999: the leader dismissed from the ICS Prelims 1999: answer (b) Surendranath Banerji. The teacher's ink gives the exit of all four:Satyendranath Tagore = 1864, the first (never dismissed); Banerji = (age) dismissed (the slide: entered 1869, dismissed 1874; he went on to found the Indian Association, 1876); R.C. Dutt = retired (Drain Theory); S.C. Bose = resigned (AIR 4, first attempt, six months' preparation; the slide: 1921, to join the movement). 13.3 Punjab The Lahore Indian Association (1877) was set up by Sardar Dyal Singh Majithia when SNB toured Punjab. Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh were prominent leaders there, not founders. 13.4 Madras After the Madras Native Association closed in 1862, political activity in Madras went into a lull, before the Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884) revived it. Its founders were M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer (the legendary nationalist journalist who also founded The Hindu) and P. Anandacharlu. PYQ 1, Prelims 1996: event chronology Prelims 1996: answer (c) A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1.1883 = first session of the National Conference at Calcutta (the Indian Association; the teacher: "1st attempt by SNB to set up an all India ORG"); 1906 = Muslim League founded at Dacca;1927 = All India States People's Conference;1932 = Communal Award announced from Whitehall (August). The wrong options swap A and B or C and D. By 1870 an organised INM under WEMC leadership had begun.Pre-1870: WEMC was politically active but without formal organisation.Post-1870: active and organised. The shift matters: organised movements are qualitatively different from individual opinion-making. Through the 1870s-90s there was a phase of coexistence and gradual transition as WEMC bodies steadily replaced the older conservative associations of the landed class.

Because these bodies were organised, they acted. Ask: what did they do beyond talking? What These New Associations Did The WEMC associations were not merely talking shops. They took on concrete roles. 14.1 Leadership of peasants: for example the Indigo Revolt (1859-63), the Bombay Deccan Riots (1875) and the Punjab Canal Colony Agitations (1907). 14.2 Famine relief: the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha organised relief during the famines of the 1870s and held arbitration courts for cheaper dispute resolution, since fighting cases in colonial courts was prohibitive for ordinary people. 14.3 Labour rights: they protested the Plantation Labour and Inland Emigration Act (1859), which gave planters the power to arrest workers who tried to leave their contracts: effectively serfdom. 14.4 Political demands:representation in Legislative Councils (set up by the Indian Councils Act of 1861); separation of powers between Legislature, Executive and Judiciary; reduction in Home Charges;extension of the Permanent Settlement of 1793 (PS 1793) to other areas. Later, they also used British institutions, especially the Legislative Councils, after the Indian Councils Act of 1892 let more Indians in, as platforms for criticising British policy from within. "Breaching" under "left their contracts" (the offence was breaching the contract). "# 17000 signs on Power of Attorney" is tied by a dotted line to the table's header; its context is . On the PS 1793 demand: "[Selfish: Landowner = (2) in PS 1793 + believed in Capitalism (* Cornwallis 86-93, his "CW86-93")]" (the circled 2 is). Read: asking for the PS 1793 to be extended was a selfish demand, because landowners were a beneficiary of it, in the capitalist logic of Cornwallis 86-93.

Because all five roots were now in place, one body could unite them. Ask: which five roots, and what is the next chapter's INC? The Roots of the INC (1885) This was the foundation. Out of this soil, Western education, a free press, racial provocation, organised WEMC associations, railways and telegraphs, the Indian National Congress would emerge in 1885. The handout page then ends with the index of the next chapter (the INC 1885 and the English political reformers: Chapter 24).

1833 Charter Act: racial-equality promise, revisited by the Black Acts and the Ilbert Bill 1835 Downward Filtration Theory: education for Presidency Town elites 1838 Dwarkanath Tagore's Landholders' Society (many non-official Anglo-Indians) 1850 Black Acts (Bethune's Bills); Lex Loci Act ★ 1851 British Indian Association, Calcutta; Radhakanta Deb first president ★ 1852 Bombay Association and Madras Native Association ★ 1853 Charter Act (the trigger for the 1851-52 petitions); the ICS exam set up 1854 Wood's Dispatch 1855 First ICS exam (in London) 1857 Three universities (Madras, Bombay, Calcutta) 1859 Plantation Labour and Inland Emigration Act; Indigo Revolt 1859-63 1860 Income Tax introduced, then withdrawn 1861 Indian Councils Act (Legislative Councils); Indian High Courts Act 1862 Madras Native Association closed; High Courts at Madras, Bombay, Calcutta 1868 Income Tax re-introduced: "No Taxation Without Representation" ★ 1870 Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (Ranade); education cuts in Bengal ★ 1873 Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1875 Poona Sarvajanik Sabha petitions the House of Commons; Deccan Riots; 400+ newspapers ★ 1876 ICS age cut 21 to 19; Indian Association (SNB); Great Madras Famine 1876-78 ★ 1877 Delhi Durbar (Kaisar-i-Hind); Lahore Indian Association; press campaign 1877-80 ★ 1878 Vernacular Press Act, Arms Act; Second Afghan War 1878-80; Statutory Civil Service (slide: 1879) ★ 1880 Ripon 80-84 arrives; Rent Commission 1881 Factories Act: under 7 banned ★ 1882 Local Self-Government; VPA repealed; Arms Act amended; ICS age back to 21; Hunter Commission 1882-83 ★ 1883 Ilbert Bill; first National Conference at Calcutta (Indian Association) ★ 1884 Madras Mahajan Sabha; Ilbert Bill compromise (mixed jury) ★ 1885 INC at Bombay; Bengal Tenancy Act ★ 1907 Punjab Canal Colony Agitations 1919 GOI Act: simultaneous ICS exam accepted 1921 Census: 8% literacy, 2% female 1922 First India-based ICS exam 1992 73rd and 74th Amendments: Part IX and IX-A

The landlords petition (1851-52). The first organised political voice is not the middle class but the educated landed class. The British Indian Association (BrIA 1851) is set up in Calcutta with Radhakanta Deb as first president; the Bombay Association and the Madras Native Association follow in 1852. All three petition because Parliament is discussing the Charter Act of 1853, and they send three separate petitions, not one. They never oppose British rule: they call exploitation 'un-British'. Nothing is granted. These conservatives have too much to lose: land revenue systems like the Permanent Settlement of 1793 created the landed class, the police protect them, and their status and security depend on the British. The teacher's board puts it as Of, By, For: their bodies were of, by and for the landed class, not for the people. The Raj builds a class (after 1857). Higher Western education after 1857 creates a politically conscious Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC), meant to be loyal Brown Sahibs. When it sees no real intent to share power, admiration turns into criticism and then a demand for Indian rights. But education is uneven (the Downward Filtration Theory of 1835 favoured Presidency Town elites; 1921 literacy is only 8%, female 2%), so the movement starts in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. The tools: press, rails, wires. By 1875 India has over 400 newspapers and more than 1.5 lakh readers; the press turns regional leaders into national ones. From the 1850s railways and the telegraph let leaders from Bombay, Bengal, Madras and Punjab meet and coordinate. The infrastructure of empire becomes the infrastructure of anti-colonial politics. The villain does its work. The 1850 Black Acts try to put Europeans in the mofussil under Indian judges and are suspended after a 'white rebellion'. The Lex Loci Act 1850 protects converts' inheritance over Indian opposition. Income Tax (1860, withdrawn, 1868) arrives during famines and draws 'No Taxation Without Representation'. In 1870 Bengal's higher-education budget is cut while military spending continues. Lytton antagonises everyone (76-80). Lytton 76-80 cuts the ICS age from 21 to 19 (1876, exam only in London), holds the Delhi Durbar (1877) during the Great Madras Famine, passes the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act (1878), creates the nomination-based Statutory Civil Service, and fights the Second Afghan War (1878-80). The Amrita Bazar Patrika turns English overnight to escape the press law. Ripon, the liberal contrast (80-84). Gladstone's Liberals win in 1880 and send Ripon 80-84. The Rent Commission (1880) leads to the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885; the Factories Act 1881 bans labour under 7; the Vernacular Press Act is repealed and the Arms Act amended (1882); the ICS age goes back to 21. His key reform is Local Self-Government 1882: elected District Boards and municipalities with two-thirds elected. But Europeans in India oppose the simultaneous exam and it fails. The Ilbert Bill (1883-84). Law Member C.P. Ilbert proposes that Indian district judges may try Britons in the mofussil. Europeans organise, lobby and protest, and the bill is withdrawn and amended to need a mixed jury. For the WEMC the last doubt is gone: the British will not treat Indians as equals. Its press campaigns are the biggest use of the press before 1885. The WEMC organises (1870 onwards). The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870, Ranade) petitions the House of Commons in 1875 for direct Indian representation. Surendranath Banerjee, who lost his ICS career over an age dispute, founds the Indian Association (1876); the Lahore Indian Association follows in 1877 and the Madras Mahajan Sabha in 1884. These bodies are of and by the WEMC but for all the people. More than talking shops. The new associations lead peasants (Indigo Revolt 1859-63, Bombay Deccan Riots 1875, Punjab Canal Colony 1907), run famine relief and arbitration courts, protest the Plantation Labour Act of 1859 (serfdom), and demand Council seats, separation of powers, lower Home Charges and an extended Permanent Settlement. After the Indian Councils Act of 1892 they use the Councils themselves. Five roots, one Congress (1885). Western education, a free press, racial provocation, organised WEMC associations, and railways and telegraphs all converge on the Indian National Congress at Bombay in 1885: the first all-India political party and the all-India culmination of the regional bodies.

Prelims 1998 "The Congress is tottering to its fall and one of my great ambitions while in India is to assist it to a peaceful demise." Attributed to: (a) Lord Dufferin 84-88 (b) Lord Curzon 99-05 (c) Lord Lytton 76-80 (d) None of these (b) Lord Curzon 99-05. Teacher's ink: (a) Dufferin 84-88 [INC formed] F; (b) Curzon 99-05 ticked; (c) Lytton 76-80 [INC 1885] F; (d) X, F. Theodore Beck - Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College, Aligarh; 2. Ilbert Bill - Lord Ripon; 3. Pherozeshah Mehta - Indian National Congress; 4. Badruddin Tyabji - Muslim League. Khan", "Br funded (AMU)"; Ilbert Bill 1883-84, Ripon 80-84, T; Mehta INC, T; Tyabji 1887, 1st Muslim Pres, League 1906, F; (a) X, (d) ticked Section 1 Prelims 2000 Four statements on the INC: 1. Sarojini Naidu was the first woman President; 2. C.R. Das was in prison when he functioned as President; 3. The first Britisher President was A.O. Hume; 4. Alfred Webb was President in 1894. Codes: (a) 1 and 3 (b) 2 and 4 (c) 2, 3 and 4 (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 (b) 2 and 4. St. 1 false (Besant 1917 was first; Naidu 1925 the 2nd woman, 1st Indian woman, the teacher's ink). St. 2 true (Gaya 1922). St. 3 false: teacher writes "Never" (Hume was never President; the first Britisher was Yule 1888). St. 4 true Section 2.2 Prelims 2004 1. First session of the INC was held in Calcutta; 2. Second session was under Dadabhai Naoroji; 3. INC and Muslim League both met at Lucknow in 1916 and concluded the Lucknow Pact. Codes: (a) 1 and 2 (b) Only 2 (c) 2 and 3 (d) Only 3 (c) 2 and 3. St. 1 false: teacher writes BOMBAY. St. 2 true: teacher writes CALCUTTA beside it. St. 3 true (circled T) Section 2.3 Prelims 2008 Where was the first session of the INC held in December 1885? (a) Ahmedabad (b) Bombay (c) Calcutta (d) Delhi (b) Bombay. Calcutta is the classic trap: it hosted the 2nd session (1886). No ink on the slide Section 2.3 Prelims 2011 The purpose for which Sir William Wedderburn and WS Caine set up the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893: (a) agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons (b) campaign for entry of Indians into the Imperial Judiciary (c) discussion on India's Independence in the British Parliament (d) agitate for entry of eminent Indians into the British Parliament (a). It was a pressure group of sympathetic British MPs raising Indian reforms in the Commons. The first woman President of the INC was Sarojini Naidu; 2. The first Muslim President was Badruddin Tyabji. Codes: (a) Only 1 (b) Only 2 (c) Both (d) Neither (b) Only 2. Story so far: the whole chapter is one question, who really founded the INC and why. Ask: where do the Presidents, the debate and the English friends each answer it? The chapter on one line. The INC was founded in Bombay in December 1885; its founder was A.O. Hume, a retired civil servant and Liberal; the Safety Valve Theory says the British used it to let off steam, but the evidence is thin; the better reading is that earlier all-India efforts already existed and Indians used Hume as a Lightning Conductor. The English friends (Hume, Wedderburn, Jardine, Yule, Webb) are the people-list UPSC asks. The handout figure adds facts that are not in the handout text: Hume as an ex-ICS Scottish ornithologist and General Secretary till 1892; the venue Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay on 28 December 1885 with 72 delegates; Bonnerjee as a Bengali lawyer; and the INC's four objectives (close ties among workers, dissolve race, creed and province barriers, record conclusions, a programme for the next year). Learn them as handout-figure facts; the slides do not repeat them. The handout page for this chapter ends with the index of the next chapter (the Indian Councils Act 1861); that belongs to Chapter 25.

items.t: 1 · The foundation of the INC: what the handout flags (Sec. 1)
items.x: Because UPSC tests the founding facts first, the handout opens with two alerts. Ask: what is the Tyabji trap and who was the first woman President? Section 1 of the handout is two alerts, both PYQs. They are worked fully here because they are the most-asked facts of the chapter. PYQ 2, Prelims 1998: correctly matched pairs 1. Theodore Beck - MAO College, Aligarh Correct Beck was the 1st Principal of the MAO College, Aligarh. The teacher adds "+ Sir S.A. Khan" and notes the college was British-funded (AMU) 2. Ilbert Bill - Lord Ripon Correct The Ilbert Bill (1883-84) came in Ripon 80-84's viceroyalty 3. Pherozeshah Mehta - INC Correct Mehta was an INC founder-member 4. Badruddin Tyabji - Muslim League Wrong Tyabji was the 1st Muslim President of the INC (Madras 1887) and died in August 1906, before the Muslim League was founded (December 1906, Dacca) Prelims 1998: answer (d) 1, 2 and 3. The commonly picked wrong options include the false pair 4: (a) 1, 2, 3 and 4; (b) 2 and 4 (drops the correct pairs 1 and 3); (c) 1, 3 and 4. Trap: Tyabji is the INC's man, not the League's. Prelims 2015: answer (b) Only 2. Statement 1 is false: Annie Besant was the 1st woman President (Calcutta 1917); Sarojini Naidu was the 2nd (Kanpur 1925). Statement 2 is true: Tyabji, Madras 1887. Wrong options: (a) Only 1; (c) Both; (d) Neither.

Because the founding raises the question of who did it, Hume enters. Ask: what makes the INC the 1st all India ORG but not an all Indian one? 2.1 Founding facts and the founder The Birth of the INC Founded Bombay, December 1885 1st President Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee (W.C. Bonnerjee) A.O. Hume Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant who toured India in the early 1880s and persuaded political leaders in Bombay, Madras and Calcutta to gather for a common conference. Credited with the most active role in bringing it together The man most active in bringing the leaders of the three Presidencies together was A.O. Hume. The next question is the famous one: what motivated Hume? That is the Safety Valve Theory (Section 3). The INC was the 1st all-India organisation, but not an "all-Indian" one. The board reads "1st all India ORG" and "not an all Indian ORG" (the letters "ian" are circled): it covered all of India, but it was not made of Indians alone, because its founder was a Briton: "Founder = A.O. Hume." (The earlier bodies in Section 4 are, in his word on slide 43, attempts at an all-India organisation; the INC is the first that worked.) Rule: the President is not from the region of the session. The teacher underlines "not" beside the 1st President row. The first case is in the handout figure: Bonnerjee, a Bengali lawyer, presided at the Bombay session. The same rule fits Yule 1888, whose Agency House was in Calcutta, presiding at Allahabad. Hume in three words: LIBERAL, Retd ICS, genuine belief in WMB.Liberal means he believed in representative governance, like his British Liberal tradition. Retd ICS is underlined on ICS (the handout calls him a retired British civil servant; the handout figure says ex-ICS). He wanted a strong opposition party, so that the accountability of the British Government of India can be ensured, giving good governance and a responsive government (responsive to the people's problems). items.t: 3 · The INC as a British "Safety Valve": the debate
items.x: Because Hume was British, a story says the British planned it. Ask: what are the three flaws (Babus, Archive, Home Rule)? The Safety Valve Theory - The Debate 3.1 What does the Safety Valve Theory say? The theory says Hume founded the INC not out of genuine sympathy for Indians but as a deliberate British strategy: a platform where the educated Indian elite could air grievances peacefully, so preventing a violent mass uprising against British rule. Origin: a biography of Hume written by William Wedderburn in 1913. Per Wedderburn, in 1878 Hume came across seven volumes of secret reports compiled by religious gurus. They allegedly described a conspiracy by the lower classes to overthrow British rule. Alarmed, Hume met Viceroy Dufferin 84-88 (Lord Dufferin, Viceroy 1884-1888). Together they brought educated Indians together to form the INC as a "safety valve" to vent grievances and prevent revolt. R.P. Dutt, the noted (communist) historian, also supported this reading. "Think: whistle, lid, cooker." The teacher's picture: Indians are the steam inside a pressure cooker; the burner under it is British oppression; the whistle (the safety valve) lets the steam out so the lid does not blow. The ink beside the pot reads "By Rule" (the pot of Indians is under British rule) and the flame is labelled "OPPRESSION". That is the theory's logic: the INC = the whistle on the British cooker. He then dismisses it for the exam: "never in exam, always on YouTube." A date puzzle in the handout. The handout says Hume found the seven volumes in 1878 and then met Dufferin 84-88, who became Viceroy only in 1884. The meeting therefore came years after the reports; the PYQ-answer slide (slide 50) places the meeting in 1885. Use: reports 1878, meeting with Dufferin 84-88 (1884-88 term), INC December 1885. 3.2 Why is the Safety Valve Theory wrong? The theory does not hold up, for three reasons: (i) The seven volumes were never found in any archive. There is no reference anywhere except in Wedderburn's biography, written by a close personal friend of Hume, nearly four decades after the events. (ii) Dufferin 84-88 did not take Hume seriously. Far from being a co-conspirator, he hated the Moderates and did not see them as leaders of the Indian masses. He called them a "microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest," hardly the language of a man who thought they could prevent a mass revolt. (iii) Dufferin 84-88 did not welcome the INC. He quietly asked the Governor of Bombay to be alert about it. He feared it would grow into something like the Irish Home Rule League. (The Irish Home Rule League, led by figures like Charles Parnell in the 1870s-80s, demanded Irish self-governance within the British Empire. It became a powerful political force that consistently embarrassed and pressured the British government. Dufferin 84-88's comparison was a warning, not a compliment.) So the man the theory names as co-designer actually viewed the INC with suspicion. The entire theory rests on a single unverifiable source, written by a friend, about events he did not witness. The teacher's own marker for the exam is "never in exam"; the question bank still holds practice questions on the theory (they are handout-built, not real PYQs). Learn the three flaws in one pass and move on.

items.t: 4 · Would the INC have formed even without Hume? The debate
items.x: Because the safety valve fails, the real history is the earlier effort. Ask: which bodies already existed before 1885, and what was Hume's real use? Yes, and this is the more important point. Political activity among Indians was rising steadily before 1885, across all three Presidencies and beyond. The pre-1885 regional associations had pushed issue after issue and none of their demands had been met. The logical next step was an all-India organisation. 4.1 What were the pre-1885 associations doing? Pre-1885 Campaigns and Protests Lex Loci Act Protests against the Lex Loci Act of 1850 Income Tax 1868 Nationwide protests against the Income Tax of 1868 Civil Services 1877-80 A campaign (1877) for Indianisation of the Civil Services Afghan War and VPA 1878 Campaigns against the Afghan War (1878-80) and the Vernacular Press Act (VPA 1878) Ilbert Bill controversy Active support for the Ilbert Bill (1883-84) Volunteer Corps A demand for the right to join units that were restricted to Europeans only Appeal to British voters In 1885, an appeal to British voters to vote for pro-Indian candidates (the teacher: led by Dadabhai Naoroji) The lead actor in many of these agitations was the Indian Association (1876) of Surendranath Banerjea, editor of Bengalee and one of the most prominent political voices of the era. The Indian Association was a permanent organisational body. Banerjea used it to launch the Indian National Conference (1883), a periodic gathering bringing delegates from across British India. The Conference met in 1883 and 1885, then merged into the INC in 1886. The Indian Association itself continued as a separate body. But Banerjea was not alone: associations in other parts of India were equally active. The Indian Association = a "Regional Political Party." On the slide he strikes through "body" and writes "Regional Political Party": a permanent, regional political organisation (Bengal), unlike the Conference, which he labels "ATTEMPT all India ORG" (an attempt at an all-India organisation). So: Indian Association 1876 = regional party; Indian National Conference 1883 = attempt at an all-India body; INC 1885 = the 1st all-India ORG that lasted. He also links the 1885 appeal to British voters to Dadabhai Naoroji. 4.2 Were efforts for an all-India body already underway? All-India Efforts Already Underway British India Association 1851: tried to open branches in Bombay and Madras to submit a joint petition to London during the Charter renewal of 1853 Native Press Association 1877:journalists invited to the Imperial Darbar formed it, an all-India body; they elected Surendranath Banerjea President and resolved to meet annually National Conference 1883: the Indian Association held it at Calcutta; another was scheduled for 1885. It ran on nearly identical tracks to the INC, so the 1886 merger was natural, not forced Theosophical Society 1884:delegates from across India gathered at its annual convention in Madras National Fund 1885: established for political campaigns, both inside India and in London Verdict The machinery was already being built. The 1885 conference was the natural culmination of decades of organised political work, not a sudden British invention "Native Press Association is not a political party." He writes "not-equal POL PARTY" under it: it was an all-India body of journalists, not a party. He underlines Surendranath Banerjea (President of the NPA, and the man behind the Indian Association). Beside the National Fund he writes: "we went to Britain and appealed to British voters to vote for pro-[Democracy in India] candidates" (the National Fund paid for political campaigns in India and in London, which fits the 1885 appeal on slide 43). Slide note: the first words of that line ("Br &") are . 4.3 Then why did Wedderburn write what he wrote? Wedderburn was Hume's close friend. He wanted to portray Hume, a Briton working for Indian political rights, as a patriot: a man who sacrificed his career to save the British Empire from its own folly. The Safety Valve narrative made Hume look prescient and heroic. But it was a story written for a friend's legacy, not as history. 4.4 So what was Hume's real usefulness? His actual contribution was more practical than mythological. Mediator: he helped bridge differences among the regional organisations that were competing for leadership of a future national body. Getting Bombay, Calcutta and Madras to sit together was not simple; Hume helped make it happen. Protective cover:Gokhale put it plainly in 1913: the British would never have allowed an all-India organisation to be formed under the leadership of an Indian. A British founder gave the INC protective cover in its early years. The two readings: if the British thought they were using the INC as a safety valve,Indians were using Hume as a lightning conductor, to channel the energy of political organisation past the British reflex to shut it down. Who uses whom The British use the INC Indians use Hume Purpose Vent grievances and prevent revolt Channel the energy of political organisation past the British reflex to shut it down Source Wedderburn's 1913 biography (R.P. Dutt agreed) Gokhale, 1913 Handout verdict Wrong: unverifiable, a friend's story The better reading

items.t: 5 · Key English figures behind the INC
items.x: Because Hume was not alone, the handout names his English friends. Ask: who was the first non-Indian President, and who set up the 1893 committee? 5.1 A.O. Hume: the founder Hume's motivations were reformist, even if the Safety Valve story distorts them. As Secretary of the Department of Revenue, Agriculture and Commerce in 1871, he worked under Viceroy Mayo 69-72 (Lord Mayo, 1869-1872) to improve agricultural yields. He opposed Viceroy Lytton 76-80's heavy expenditure on the Afghan War (1878-80) and was dismissed from his post for it. He supported Ripon 80-84's reforms, especially the Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882. He was a Liberal in the British political tradition, someone who believed in representative governance. He wanted the INC to function like "His Majesty's Opposition": a formal, legitimate channel of political dissent, the way an opposition party functions in a democracy. In 1885 he also published a direct appeal to British voters to elect pro-Indian candidates to Parliament. He served as the General Secretary of the INC (the handout figure: till 1892): not its President, but arguably its most active organiser in the early years. Hume = LIBERAL, Retd ICS (slide 40). The Liberal label explains why he backed Ripon 80-84 and wanted an opposition party; the "Retd ICS" label explains why a retired civil servant knew how to get the leaders of the three Presidencies together. The 1885 appeal to British voters is on slide 43 (led by Dadabhai Naoroji), and slide 44 links it to the National Fund (see Section 4.2). 5.2 William Wedderburn: the co-founder who became a biographer William Wedderburn, a retired civil servant who had been ex-Secretary to the Bombay Government, was a co-founder of the INC in 1885. He became the 2nd non-Indian President of the INC, serving in 1889 and again in 1910. Like Hume, he supported Ripon 80-84's reforms. He favoured Cooperative Banks to provide cheap loans to farmers. His pro-Indian positions cost him: he was denied a judgeship at the Bombay High Court. (High Courts were established under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861 and began functioning from 1862.) Later, as a Member of Parliament in Britain, he supported INC demands through the 1890s, in close partnership with Gopal Krishna Gokhale. With W.S. Caine he set up the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893 (Prelims 2011). Prelims 2011: answer (a) To agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons. The Indian Parliamentary Committee (Wedderburn and Caine, 1893) was a pressure group of sympathetic British MPs that raised and pressed Indian political reforms in the Commons.(b) the judiciary was never its brief (Wedderburn's own record cost him a Bombay High Court judgeship); (c) in 1893 the language was reform within British rule, not independence; (d) it was a group of sympathetic MPs, not a vehicle for sending Indians into Parliament. Wrong options commonly picked: (b), (c), (d). Five green underlines, one idea: the question's William Wedderburn, WS Caine and Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893, and the answer's Indian political reforms and House of Commons. On slide 41 he calls Wedderburn "Retd ICS" and "Hume's follower" (retired, same Liberal line, backed Ripon 80-84). 5.3 Justice John Jardine: the Liberal lawyer John Jardine was also a co-founder of the INC in 1885. He had served as Chief Secretary of Bombay and as a Judge of the Bombay High Court. He later became an MP (1906-1918) and was a Liberal. 5.4 George Yule: the merchant President George Yule was the 1st non-Indian President of the INC, presiding over the Allahabad Session in 1888. He was a merchant and businessman: founder of the Agency House "Andrew Yule and Company" in Calcutta. He also served as President of the Indian Chamber of Commerce. The fact that a man of his economic standing was willing to preside over the INC in 1888 was itself politically significant. He also had the distinction of having killed 400 tigers, which says something about the social world of such colonial figures. What it was A British trading and financial firm in colonial India: a cross between a private bank, an investment firm and a business management company What it did Raised capital, extended credit and financed trade (bank-like, though not banks in the formal sense); and acted as agents running enterprises:tea plantations, jute mills, coal mines, shipping companies Today's words NBFC + private equity firm + holding company Managing agency system One firm controlling and managing many businesses for a fee or a share of profits; a dominant feature of the colonial economy Examples Andrew Yule and Company, Jardine Henderson, Bird and Company End Abolished in independent India in 1970: it concentrated enormous economic power in a few, mostly British, hands and was seen as a vehicle of economic drain and monopoly 5.5 Alfred Webb: the Irish friend Alfred Webb was an Irish politician who served as an MP in the 1890s and was the 3rd non-Indian President of the INC, presiding over the Madras Session of 1894. He was invited personally by Dadabhai Naoroji, with whom he shared a close friendship. He was strongly opposed to racism (he supported Britain's first anti-racist journal) and opposed the opium trade into China. His Irish background (Ireland had been under British control for centuries and was still fighting for Home Rule while Webb presided in 1894) likely shaped his sympathy for people under imperial rule. 5.6 The English friends of the INC at a glance A.O. Caine John Jardine Co-founder; Liberal lawyer Chief Secretary of Bombay, Judge of the Bombay High Court;MP 1906-1918 George Yule Merchant President 1st non-Indian President (Allahabad 1888); Andrew Yule and Company (Agency House); President, Indian Chamber of Commerce; 400 tigers Alfred Webb Irish friend 3rd non-Indian President (Madras 1894); Irish MP in the 1890s; invited by Naoroji; against racism and the opium trade From regional bodies to the INC Before 1885: regional associations campaign on Lex Loci 1850, Income Tax 1868, Civil Services, Afghan War and VPA 1878, Ilbert Bill 1883-84, Volunteer Corps;none of their demands is met Attempts at an all-India body:BIA 1851, Native Press Association 1877, Indian National Conference 1883, Theosophical convention 1884, National Fund 1885 Regional rivalry: Bombay, Calcutta and Madras compete for leadership of a future national body Hume the mediator: a Liberal retired civil servant helps the three Presidencies sit together December 1885, Bombay: the INC is founded; Bonnerjee is President 1886: the Indian National Conference merges into the INC; the Indian Association continues as a regional body Hume as lightning conductor: a British founder gives protective cover against the British reflex to shut it down Source Wedderburn's 1913 biography; R.P.
