Small bodies, big complaints. Long before 1885 regional associations protested the Lex Loci Act 1850 and the Income Tax of 1868, campaigned for Indianisation of the Civil Services (1877), against the Afghan War and the Vernacular Press Act (1878), for the Ilbert Bill (1883-84), and demanded the right to join the Volunteer Corps. None of their demands was met. The first attempts. The British India Association (1851) tried branches in Bombay and Madras for a joint petition on the Charter renewal of 1853; journalists at the Imperial Darbar formed the Native Press Association (1877) with Banerjea as President; the Indian Association (1876) launched the Indian National Conference (1883); Madras hosted the Theosophical Society convention (1884); a National Fund followed in 1885. The retired civil servant. A.O. Hume, a Liberal retired British civil servant, had worked under Mayo 69-72 (1871), was dismissed for opposing Lytton 76-80's Afghan War spending, and backed Ripon 80-84's reforms. He wanted the INC to be 'His Majesty's Opposition': a strong opposition party so that the government is accountable, with good governance and a responsive government. Bombay, December 1885. The INC was founded in Bombay in December 1885 with W.C. Bonnerjee as 1st President. The teacher calls it the 1st all India ORG but not an all Indian one, since its founder was a Briton; and the President is not from the region of the session. Hume served as General Secretary, never as President. Presidents and Firsts. Naoroji 1886 (Calcutta), Tyabji 1887 (1st Muslim, Madras), Yule 1888 (1st non-Indian, Allahabad), Wedderburn 1889 and 1910, Webb 1894, Besant 1917 (1st woman), Das 1922 (from prison, Gaya), Naidu 1925 (2nd woman). Calcutta hosted the 2nd session, not the 1st; Tyabji died in August 1906, before the League of December 1906. The Safety Valve story. Wedderburn's 1913 biography says Hume received seven volumes of secret reports in 1878 describing a conspiracy of the masses, met Dufferin 84-88, and together they founded the INC as a safety valve; R.P. Dutt agreed. The teacher draws a pressure cooker: Indians as steam, oppression as flame, the INC as the whistle. Why the story fails. The seven volumes were never found in any archive; the only source is a friend's book written nearly four decades later. Dufferin 84-88 called the Moderates a 'microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest', and quietly told the Governor of Bombay to be alert, fearing an Irish Home Rule League. The teacher: never in exam, always on YouTube. The bridge and the umbrella. Wedderburn wrote to make his friend Hume a patriot. Hume's real usefulness was practical: a mediator who got Bombay, Calcutta and Madras to sit together, and, as Gokhale put it in 1913, a British founder gave protective cover because the British would never allow an all-India body under an Indian leader. If the British used the INC as a safety valve, Indians used Hume as a lightning conductor. The English friends. Wedderburn (co-founder, 2nd non-Indian President 1889 and 1910, MP, with W.S. Caine set up the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893 for reforms in the Commons); Jardine (Judge, MP 1906-1918); Yule (1st non-Indian President, Andrew Yule and Company, an Agency House, 400 tigers); Webb (Irish MP, Madras 1894, invited by Naoroji, against racism and the opium trade). What UPSC asked. Curzon 99-05 made the 'peaceful demise' remark (1998); the 1998 pairs trap is Tyabji and the Muslim League; 2000 asked Naidu, Das, Hume, Webb; 2004 and 2008 asked the first session (Bombay); 2011 the Wedderburn and Caine committee; 2015 the first woman and first Muslim Presidents. The teacher writes Mains - No Q, PRELIMS ticked.

Prelims 2002 Which Act of British India strengthened the Viceroy's authority over his executive council by substituting the "portfolio" or departmental system for corporate functioning? (a) Indian Councils Act, 1861 (b) Government of India Act, 1858 (c) Indian Councils Act, 1892 (d) Indian Councils Act, 1909 (a) ICA 1861 is correct. The Act gave legal recognition to the Portfolio System that Canning56-62 had introduced in 1859: departments allotted to individual VEC members, whose decisions were final, subject to the Viceroy's veto. (b) GOI Act 1858 moved rule from the Company to the Crown (control in London), not the working of the council. (c) ICA 1892 and (d) ICA 1909 grew the legislative outer ring, not executive working. Trap: introduced 1859, legal 1861 Section 3 (the Portfolio System) and Section 7 (the alert)

Story so far: ICA 1861 is the working Constitution of British India, and the teacher's first verdict is 'not a democracy'. Ask: who is the Top Boss? Chapter 25 title slide: Indian Councils Act, 1861 (ICA 1861) = Constitution of Br India ICA 1861 is the working Constitution of British India (CoBrI). A Constitution's primary purpose is to create the State structure and to define the functions and responsibilities of the State functionaries. The Constitution of British India (CoBrI) runs from the Regulating Act 1773 to the GOI Act 1935, and ICA 1861 is its centrepiece. It "may not be an ideal Constitution [* CoI = our Constitution of India]", and "the Moderates wanted an ideal CoI" (see Chapter 26). The line "by Br (P)" (P circled) shows it was made by the British for British India, which by his figures (as on the Chapter 10 board) held 63% of the territory and 78% of the population. What the circled P stands for, and the exact percentages (written quickly), are .

items.t: 1 · Core philosophy: despotism controlled from home
items.x: Because the top boss sits in London, the Government of India is a despotism controlled from home. Ask: which two laws rebuilt the State in 1861, and which arms did each cover? Teacher's board: "If ICA 1861 served as CoBrI (Constitution of Br India)" arrow to "Democracy?" then a circled "No": "(Statement of Top Boss = [circle] PM of Br / SoS for Charles Wood, the Secretary of State for India, said the Government of India must be a "despotism controlled from home." Despotism is simply a dictatorship."Home" meant Britain. The dictator at the top of the chain was the Secretary of State for India himself, sitting in London. This one line captures the fundamental feature of British Indian governance, and it remained the operating principle right until 1947. If ICA 1861 is the Constitution of British India, is it a democracy? No (circled). The "Statement of Top Boss" is the circled stack PM of Britain, then SoS for India, then Viceroy and GG. He tells you to "Recall: GOI Act 1858" (the Act that made the SoS the top boss: see Chapter 17). On the EIC administration chapter he adds that books credit the GG, but the real legal decision was the SoS for India's ("Legal" and "SoS for India" underlined). His conclusion: "This proves that no intent of sharing power with Indians." The words he scribbles above this ("yes ... of MAX age for CSExam", with a crossed word) are ; they refer back to the EIC administration chapter (Chapter 18). Core Philosophy slide "L = Br": the legislature (L) is British. The top boss line runs from the President of the Board of Control (1784) down, through the GOI Act 1858, to the SoS for India = Top Boss. So the head of the chain was a British minister, not a person answerable to Indians. The ICA 1861 was, at its core, a comprehensive restructuring of the British Indian State. The British thought in terms of three arms of the State: Legislature and Executive: restructured by the ICA 1861. Judiciary: reorganised at the same time by the Indian High Courts Act 1861. Two laws, one year: the whole State machinery overhauled in 1861. The three arms by letters: ICA 1861 = L and E (both circled); the Indian High Courts Act 1861 = J (circled). These are the same L, E, J letters he uses for "rule" in Chapter 8 and Chapter 10.

items.t: 2 · What the Act did to the Legislature and the Executive
items.x: Because the British wanted a law-making body without sharing power, they made the executive wear a second hat. Ask: why are the ILC and the VEC 'not really two bodies'? Teacher's board: "Layman Terms: ICA 1861 created [boxed] ILC, VEC (Centre) / PLCs, GECs (Provinces)", with the expansions at right: Imperial Legislative Council for law m Out of the Governor-General's Council, the ICA 1861 effectively created two bodies: the Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC) for day-to-day executive functions, and; the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) for law-making. Both operated under the authority of the Viceroy/Governor-General. At the province level, a parallel structure: Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) and Governor's Executive Councils (GECs). In layman terms ICA 1861 created four bodies: ILC and VEC at the Centre; PLCs and GECs in the Provinces."By law," ILC and VEC are not really two separate bodies.VEC = E (executive) = Cabinet; its members are today's ministers.ILC = the VEC opens the doors of its room and the additional members join (so ILC = VEC + additional members). The blank he leaves in quote marks: "Pre 1858 called Legal ''"; the word he means for the pre-1858 additional members is the legal members of 1833 and 1853 (Section 3), but the exact wording is . However, be precise: the ICA 1861 did not create two separate, independent institutions. It was simpler and cleverer: the VEC was expanded by adding "additional members" for law-making sessions. These additional members (other British officials and a handful of nominated non-officials) formed an outer ring, brought in only when laws were being made. So the same council wore two hats: 2.1) Day-to-day executive work: it was the VEC. 2.2) Making laws: it became the ILC (= VEC + Additional Members). Every VEC member was automatically part of the ILC. The design guaranteed the British executive a built-in official majority in every legislative vote. "Official" = Bureaucrat [PRO Br]: an official is a bureaucrat, and bureaucrats are PRO-British. That is why a council with an official majority can never go against the Raj. The expanded-council model, 1861 to 1919 ICA 1861:VEC (executive) and ILC = VEC + Additional Members; official majority ensured ICA 1909 (Morley-Minto): the outer ring grows and gains marginal new powers for non-officials GOI Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford): the VEC-ILC model is abolished and replaced by a bicameral Central Legislature: the Council of State (CoS) and the Central Legislative Assembly (CLA), structurally distinct from the VEC The handout page ends with the index of the next chapter ("Moderates' Ideology, Demands, Weaknesses, Goals and Methods"); that belongs to Chapter 26, not here. Slide 8 (typed boxes of this model) adds nothing beyond the flow above and is not reproduced.

items.t: 3 · The Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC): its evolution and the 1861 changes
items.x: Because an executive council needs working departments, the Portfolio System was made law and the council grew. Ask: why a Finance Member in 1861 and Public Works in 1874? Teacher's board: Evolution of the Governor-General's Council Understanding the VEC means tracing it backward before seeing what 1861 changed. 1833: the composition shifted from the 1793 status (GG + 3 Councillors + C-I-C, the extraordinary member) because a Law Member was added for law-making. 3.1) 1833 Executive meetings of the GG's Council = GG + 3 + C-I-C (extraordinary member appointed by the Court of Directors, CoD). 3.2) 1833 Legislative meetings = VEC + 1 legal member. 1853: the composition shifted further: the Law Member was elevated to ordinary executive member and 6 legal members were added for law-making. 3.3) 1853 Executive meetings = GG + 3 + C-I-C (extraordinary, appointed by the CoD) + the 1 Legal Member of 1833 elevated to Executive Member. 3.4) 1853 Legislative meetings = VEC + 6 legal members. The council's history in his formulas:1773 = GG + 4C; 1784 = GG + C1 + C2 + C-I-C; 1793 = GG + (C1 + C2 + C3) + C-I-C, the C-I-C "extra-ordinary, appointed by CoD"; 1813 = no change; 1833 = split into an E meeting and an L meeting (L = E + 1 legal member), "grain of SoP"; 1853 = E: GG + 4C + C-I-C, L: E + 6, "SoP introduced"; 1858 = no change, but the GG's Council = the Viceroy's Council.SoP: 1833 gave the grain, 1853 introduced it by splitting the executive meeting from the legislative one. Handout and board count the same council in different ways; they agree. The handout writes 1853 as GG + 3 + C-I-C + 1 Legal Member elevated; the board writes it as GG + [4C] + C-I-C (3 + the elevated law member = 4). Likewise the handout's 1833 "GG + 3 + CIC" is the board's "GG + (C1 + C2 + C3) + C-I-C". Use either; they are the same body. The ICA 1861 gave legal recognition to the Portfolio System, introduced by Canning56-62 in 1859: allocating specific departments (what we call ministries today) to individual VEC members, whose decisions on their portfolios were final, subject to the Viceroy's veto. This formalised cabinet-style administration at the centre. Portfolio System = Ministry System. In those times a ministry was called a Department, for example (his example) "SVP was minister of States Dept" in 1947. Underlined: it was introduced by Canning56-62 in 1859 and gave cabinet-style administration at the centre. Prelims 2002 trap: introduced 1859, recognised 1861. The 1859 practice was in-house; the ICA 1861 is the Act that wrote it into law. Do not pick 1858 (Crown takeover), 1892 or 1909 (legislative ring). A 5th Ordinary Member was added constitutionally in 1861 to handle Finance, effectively a Finance Minister. This was a direct result of the 1857 revolt, which left the British Indian economy heavily in debt. The Act formally expanded the Executive Council to 5 members, institutionalising the Finance Member (a practice begun in 1859 with James Wilson, who died in 1860, before the Act was passed). The post came in 1859; constitutional backing came in 1861. James Wilson introduced income tax in 1860. Later income tax was withdrawn under pressure from the western-educated middle class (WEMC), and re-introduced in 1868. So the VEC was now: GG + 5 ordinary/regular members + C-I-C (extraordinary member, appointed by the Secretary of State for India). The 5 ordinary members each ran one portfolio:Home, Revenue, Finance, Law, and Military. (The Military Member here is the ordinary administrative Military Member, not the C-I-C.) Why the C-I-C is not an ordinary member, or even an automatic ex-officio member: the Crown wanted deliberate checks and balances over the armed forces. Administrative Military Member (ordinary, in the VEC): handled paperwork, that is logistics, the defence budget, administrative orders for the Military Department. Operational C-I-C (extraordinary): supreme field command over the actual army, "the man giving battle orders". The picture: the Military Member ran the office, the C-I-C ran the battlefield. The Crown did not want one man wearing both hats, because that would concentrate too much power in one office. By the 1870s, massive investment in railways, canals and infrastructure needed its own dedicated portfolio, so a 6th Ordinary Member was added in 1874 for Public Works. Updated cabinet: 6 Ordinary Members (Home, Revenue, Finance, Law, Military and Public Works). In today's terms: the Ordinary Military Member = the Defence Minister; the C-I-C = the CDS. His closing formulas on the board: VEC = GG + C-I-C + (C1 to C6) and ILC = VEC + 6 to 12 additional members. He writes "1861" over the 5-member cabinet and "1874" under it for the 6th. On the summary slide he adds "1874: C6" beside the executive row (slide 20).

Because the ring of additional members was nominated, the British could afford half non-officials. Ask: how does 7 beat 6, and why did the elites get the seats? Whenever a question mentions the Indian Councils Acts (1861, 1892, 1909), split the government into two boxes in your mind: the Executive Council (VEC) and the Legislative Council (ILC) = VEC plus the "additional members" (a mix of officials and non-officials). Teacher's board: "1861: (VEC) circled: [GG + 4C + CIC] + C5 (Finance)" with ( 1858) over the bracket and ( 1861) over C5 Under the ICA 1861,6 to 12 additional law members could be nominated by the Viceroy for the ILC, of which half must be non-officers. So ILC = VEC + 6 to 12 = (GG + 4 + 1 finance member added in 1861) + 6 to 12.Earlier, all were officers. This introduced "a grain of representation in governance": a non-officer lawmaker could be an Indian, a tiny element of popular and representative governance, because law-making is an integral part of governance. The board's arithmetic:VEC in 1861 = [GG + 4C + CIC] (as it stood in 1858) + C5 Finance (added 1861).ILC = VEC + 6 to 12 additional members, of which half must be non-officials, that is 3 to 6. He crosses out "Indians" and writes "Non-officials, not unofficial".Case of 6 additional:officials = 10 (the 7 of the VEC plus 3 officers), non-officials = 3 (a politician, a civil-society person or a businessman). Therefore a majority of officers is guaranteed. Non-official is not the same as Indian. The teacher strikes "Indians" and writes "non-officials" (and "not unofficial"). The handout says a non-officer lawmaker could be an Indian, and on slide 13 he adds that the non-officers who joined were Anglo-Indian and Indian.Do not write "half the members were Indians" in an answer. "1861: 1st time non-officers can be lawmakers"; "no elections: elections 1st time in ICA 1909." So 1861 = first non-officers (all nominated);1909 = first elections (see Chapter 31). Why was this safe for the British? The official majority was guaranteed. The VEC alone (GG + 5 + CIC = 7) already outnumbered or matched even the maximum possible non-officials (6 out of 12 additional members). The British could afford the gesture because the math was rigged. In 1862, 3 Indians were nominated to the ILC: the Raja of Banaras, the Maharaja of Patiala, and Dinkar Rao of Gwalior (knighted in 1877 as Sir Dinkar Rao). All were elites, some from Princely States. The British logic: since the elite Indians had stayed loyal during 1857, their cooperation should be rewarded and secured. By having elite cooperation in law-making, they could do Divide and Rule, the same logic as the Permanent Settlement of 1793 and the 'Brown Sahib' policy of 1835:co-opt the elites, exploit the masses. Until ICA 1892, only 45 Indians were nominated in total, mainly Zamindars and moneylenders from the British Indian Association (BrIA, 1851),British businessmen and some Rulers of Princely States. A deliberate selection of loyalists. The Legislature (ILC), contd "Goal = reward those loyal in 1857." The logic is "co-opt the elites" (the same as the Permanent Settlement 1793 and the Brown Sahib policy 1835). India = British India, ruled by the British, and 565 Princely States (PS), ruled by Indian princes; the nominees came from both. A non-officer = one who is not a bureaucrat or soldier = a non-State actor; the ones who now joined the ILC were Anglo-Indian and Indian."[31 yrs]" under "Until ICA 1892" is the gap 1861 to 1892. And the telling point, underlined: "notice: Nationalistic WEMC missing": the Western Educated Middle Class, the nationalist voice, was not among those chosen (see Chapter 23). Teacher's board: "Legislature" splits into "Officers (sad face): never fights election, ALWAYS Nominated" and "Non-officers (smiley)", which splits into "Nominated (sad f The Legislature tree: officers (sad: never fight an election, always nominated) against non-officers (smiley); non-officers can be nominated (sad) or elected (smiley); elected can be indirect (sad) or direct (smiley)."Towards Democracy": 1861 (1st time non-officers) to 1892 to 1909 (1st proper indirect election) to 1919 (1st time direct elections, and 1st time an elected MAJORITY) to 1935 to 1950. ICA 1861 sits at the first rung of that ladder. Compare the later Acts: Chapter 28, Chapter 31, Chapter 34. The teacher's "Towards Democracy" ladder 1861 (ICA 1861): first time non-officers in the legislature (all nominated) 1892: the next step (see Chapter 28) 1909 (Morley-Minto): first proper indirect election 1919 (GOI Act): first direct elections; first time an elected majority 1935, then 1950: the ladder continues to the Constitution of India

Because the ILC was only a consultative add-on, it stood at the bottom of the ladder of powers. Ask: which rungs needed 'Viceroy, may I?' and which were barred? Teacher's board: "Powers of any Legislature": Discussion; Asking Questions, Discuss Ans, Supplementary Q; Resolution [(L) tells (E) whats Desired by (L)] [* Think Your Ne The powers of any Legislature, in increasing order of significance:discussion, then questions + discuss answers + ask supplementary questions, then pass resolutions, then passing bills, then discussing and passing the Budget (voting on individual items and on the Budget as a whole), then creating the Executive, then dismissing the Executive, then amending and drafting the Constitution. The ILC's status was at the very bottom of this ladder. A resolution is the Legislature (L) telling the Executive (E) what the Legislature desires. His hook, exactly as written: "Think Your New Yr Resolution."Bills: introduce and pass, or reject.Budget: discuss, vote and pass.Create the Executive / destroy the Executive.Draft and amend the Constitution at the top. 5.1) Discussion Only with the Viceroy's prior approval 1 5.2) Ask questions to the Executive NOT allowed 2 5.3) Bring and pass resolutions NOT allowed 3 5.4) Introduce bills Only with the Viceroy's prior approval 4 5.5) Budget discussion or vote NOT allowed 5 5.6) Veto The Viceroy held absolute veto over all bills (his power) 5.7) Ordinance power The Viceroy could make law by executive order, valid for 6 months, bypassing the Legislature (his power) "ILC is not equal to a modern P (Parliament)" with a sad face. Discussion and Introduce Bills are underlined: even those two needed the Viceroy's prior approval. Everything above them was NOT allowed. The ILC was not a modern Parliament in any meaningful sense:small membership, entirely nominated (no elections), and no control whatsoever over the Executive. It was a consultative add-on to the Viceroy's own council: useful to the British because it looked like participation while delivering none. Ordinance = law made by the Executive, bypassing the Legislature.

Because the 1833 centralisation had gone too far, 1861 gave some law-making back. Ask: why did NWP and Punjab wait? At the Province Level (typed table) The provincial provisions mirrored the arrangement at the Centre.PLCs and GECs were created. Under the ICA 1861, each PLC = Governor (or Lt Governor) + Executive Council members + additional members nominated for law-making (the same formula as ILC = VEC + additional members). The bigger change was in the relationship between the Centre and the provinces.Centralisation had peaked in 1833, when the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras were taken away and concentrated at the centre.ICA 1861 began reversing that: it restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras, and; it proposed new PLCs for Bengal, Punjab and the North-Western Provinces (NWP). "Charter 1833 took away (L) powers" (the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras): the Charter Act of 1833 is the peak of centralisation (see Chapter 17). ICA 1861 restores them: "Decentralisation begins." On the long arc he adds "e.g. GG" with a line to "Centralisation" and "GG(Be) to GG(I)": the Governor General of Bengal became the Governor General of India (in 1833), the example of centralisation in a single title. Why Bengal needed a fresh PLC (handout only, no slide). The handout adds why Bengal needed a fresh PLC: Bengal's provincial council had evolved into the GG(India)'s Council by 1833, became the Viceroy's/GG's Council in 1858, and was rebranded as ILC and VEC in 1861. So the old Bengal body had moved up to the Centre, and Bengal needed a new one of its own. The long arc:centralisation began 1773, peaked 1833, and decentralisation began 1861, finally peaking with Provincial Autonomy under the GOI Act 1935. Teacher's board "Power": Centre against Provinces The power split between Centre and Provinces. His definitions: Unitary = Centre at least 75%, Provinces at most 25%.Federal = about 50% each. For British India: 1833: Centre 100%, Provinces 0%. 1861: Centre 90%, Provinces 10%. So 1861 moved only 10 points from the Centre, and by his own definition it is still unitary. The board's rows look as if 1833 is "Unitary" and 1861 is "Federal"; do not read it that way. The words "Unitary" and "Federal" are the definitions (at least 75% against about 50%), and the dated figures are 100/0 (1833) and 90/10 (1861), which is nowhere near 50/50. The handout summary (8.11) says "Not federal" and the title of the next slide (19) has the teacher's sad face on "Federalism". Use: ICA 1861 = decentralisation, but not federal. New PLCs were set up in: 6.1) Bengal: 1862. 6.2) NWP: 1886. (NWP was the half of Awadh annexed in the 1801 Subsidiary Alliance as permanent payment of subsidy, where Mahalwari was first applied in 1822; given province status in 1836 but without a legislature and under a Lt Governor.) Why the delay? Memories of 1857 were still raw, and the British were cautious about loosening their executive grip. 6.3) Punjab: 1897. (Annexed in 1849.) Why the delay? A frontier province: the British preferred strong executive control to the slower deliberation of a legislative body. Beside this list he writes "not imp". Learn the three years lightly (1862, 1886, 1897), and do not spend time on the NWP background.

items.t: 7 · True federalism: just a small beginning
items.x: Because the Viceroy kept five keys, decentralisation was not federalism. Ask: which Act ended each key, and what is the parallel in the Constitution of India? The Viceroy's Powers over the Provinces (typed table) Even as some power was decentralised, executive control stayed tightly centralised. The Viceroy's powers over provinces under ICA 1861: 7.1) Nomination of non-officers to the PLC The Governor nominated PLC non-officials, but no nomination was valid until the Viceroy formally sanctioned it: "giving with one hand and taking with the other" Ended by ICA 1892, shifting more real power to the Governors none given 7.2) Rule-making He framed the rules for the functioning of the ILC, PLCs, VEC and GECs Ended only by GOI 1935 (Provincial Autonomy) none given 7.3) Bill approval His approval was needed before certain bills could even be introduced Relaxed by GOI 1919, and further by GOI 1935 (subjects divided between Centre and Provinces) Article 304: the President's recommendation for certain State bills 7.4) One country, one budget No separate provincial budget: only one budget for British India Ended by GOI 1919, which separated the provincial budget from the central budget for the first time Article 202: every State Legislature has its own State budget 7.5) State reorganisation He could create new provinces and appoint Lieutenant-Governors Under GOI 1935 the power shifted from the Viceroy to the Crown (effectively the British PM) Articles 3, 4 and 155 of the COI 1950 "Federalism" with a sad face against the title. He underlines: no nomination valid until the Viceroy sanctions (7.1), approval before certain bills can be introduced (7.3), no separate provincial budget and "Ended by GOI 1919" (7.4), Articles 3, 4 (7.5) and the shift "from the Viceroy to the Crown" under GOI 1935 (7.5). Below 7.5 he writes something that starts "Provincial" and has "OR" above it: . Prelims 2002 (UPSC tested this). The question and answer are in the Exam lens: (A) Indian Councils Act, 1861 is correct. (B) GOI Act 1858 ✗, (C) ICA 1892 ✗, (D) ICA 1909 ✗. The students who err are those who confuse the topic.

items.t: 8 · ICA 1861 at a glance (the handout's summary)
items.x: Because the whole chapter points one way, the summary says: nominated, no elections, no responsible government. Ask: what is the teacher's test of a fully responsible government? 8.1 Philosophy Despotism controlled from home (Charles Wood) 8.2 Executive (VEC) GG + 5 ordinary members + CIC (extraordinary); the 6th ordinary member in 1874 (teacher's ink) 8.3 Legislature (ILC) VEC + 6 to 12 additional members (half non-official) 8.4 Portfolio System Given legal recognition (introduced by Canning56-62 in 1859) 8.5 First Indians (1862) Raja of Banaras, Maharaja of Patiala, Dinkar Rao of Gwalior 8.6 Provincial bodies PLCs and GECs created; Bombay and Madras legislative powers restored 8.7 New PLCs Bengal 1862, NWP 1886, Punjab 1897 8.8 Legislature powers Minimal: no questions, no resolutions, no budget discussion, no vote 8.9 Viceroy powers Absolute veto, ordinance (6 months), prior approval for bills 8.10 Election method All members nominated: no elections 8.11 Federalism Not federal: decentralisation from the 1833 peak; the Centre made the budget 8.12 Nature of government Despotism: no responsible government anywhere "Fully responsible government: every minister has to be an MP or MLA first." Applied here (our reading of the handout facts): the VEC members were appointed, the ILC was nominated, and it could not question or dismiss them, so the ICA 1861 fails the test. (Compare rungs 6 and 7 of the ladder in Section 5.)

1773 Regulating Act: GG's council = GG + 4C; centralisation begins 1784 GG + C1 + C2 + C-I-C (President of the Board of Control, 1784) 1793 GG + 3C + C-I-C, the C-I-C extraordinary, appointed by the CoD 1813 No change in the council's composition 1833 Executive meeting and legislative meeting split; legislative = VEC + 1 legal member; Bombay and Madras legislative powers taken away: centralisation peaks ★ 1851 British Indian Association (BrIA) founded 1853 Law Member elevated to executive member; legislative = VEC + 6 legal members; separation of powers introduced 1857 The revolt leaves the Indian economy heavily in debt 1858 GOI Act 1858: SoS for India the Top Boss; GG's Council = Viceroy's Council ★ 1859 Portfolio System introduced by Canning56-62; James Wilson first Finance Member ★ 1860 James Wilson introduces income tax and dies 1861 Indian Councils Act 1861 (ILC = VEC + 6 to 12 additional; 5th Ordinary Member for Finance; portfolio system legalised); Indian High Courts Act 1861 ★ 1862 First 3 Indians in the ILC; Bengal PLC set up ★ 1868 Income tax re-introduced 1874 6th Ordinary Member added: Public Works ★ 1877 Dinkar Rao knighted as Sir Dinkar Rao 1886 NWP PLC set up (not imp, teacher) 1892 ICA 1892: Viceroy's sanction on PLC nominations ended; only 45 Indians nominated 1861 to 1892 1897 Punjab PLC set up (not imp, teacher) 1909 ICA 1909: first proper indirect election; outer ring gains marginal powers 1919 GOI Act 1919: VEC-ILC model abolished (CoS + CLA); first direct elections; provincial budget separated ★ 1935 GOI Act 1935: Provincial Autonomy; rule-making and State reorganisation power shift 1947 End of the despotism "controlled from home"

The despot at home. After 1857 and the Crown takeover of 1858, the Secretary of State for India sits at the top of the chain in London. Charles Wood calls the Government of India a 'despotism controlled from home', and this stays the operating principle until 1947. The teacher: the Constitution of British India runs from the Regulating Act 1773 to the GOI Act 1935, and it is not a democracy. Two laws, one year. In 1861 the State is overhauled: the ICA 1861 restructures the Legislature and the Executive (L and E), and the Indian High Courts Act 1861 reorganises the Judiciary (J). Out of the Governor-General's Council come the VEC for executive work and the ILC for law-making. One room, two hats. The VEC expands by adding 6 to 12 additional members for law-making: the VEC opens the doors of its room and the additional members join, and the room becomes the ILC. Every VEC member sits in the ILC, so the executive keeps an official majority. The same pattern appears in the provinces as PLCs and GECs. The cabinet takes shape. Canning56-62 starts the Portfolio System in 1859 (departments allotted to individual members, decisions final subject to the Viceroy's veto) and the ICA 1861 makes it law. The 1857 debt brings a 5th ordinary member for Finance (James Wilson, income tax 1860, he dies 1860; the tax returns in 1868), so the VEC is GG + 5 + C-I-C. The C-I-C stays extraordinary so that one man does not hold both the office and the battlefield; a 6th member for Public Works comes in 1874. A grain of representation. Of the 6 to 12 additional members the Viceroy nominates, half must be non-officials: for the first time non-officers can be lawmakers, and in 1862 three Indians join (the Raja of Banaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Dinkar Rao of Gwalior). The goal is to reward those loyal in 1857 and co-opt the elites. Only 45 Indians are nominated until 1892. Seven beats six. The VEC alone (GG + 5 + C-I-C = 7) matches or outnumbers the most non-officials possible (6). In the teacher's case of 6 additional members, officials are 10 (7 + 3) against 3 non-officials. The majority of officers is guaranteed, and 'official' means bureaucrat, PRO-British. A legislature at the bottom of the ladder. Of the ladder of legislative powers (discussion, questions, resolutions, bills, budget, create the Executive, dismiss it, amend the Constitution) the ILC has almost none: discussion and introducing bills only with the Viceroy's prior approval, no questions, no resolutions, no budget vote. The Viceroy holds an absolute veto and a 6-month ordinance. It is 'not a modern Parliament', all nominated, no elections. The first small step back. The Charter Act 1833 had taken the law-making of Bombay and Madras to the Centre. The ICA 1861 restores it and proposes PLCs for Bengal, Punjab and the NWP (Bengal 1862, NWP 1886, Punjab 1897, the delays due to raw 1857 memories and a frontier province). On the teacher's board the Centre's share falls only from 100% (1833) to 90% (1861). BRASS: the Viceroy keeps the keys. The Viceroy needs to sanction the Governor's nominations (ended by ICA 1892), frames the rules for all councils (ended only by GOI 1935), must approve certain bills before introduction (relaxed 1919 and 1935), keeps a single budget for all of British India (ended by GOI 1919) and can create provinces and appoint Lt Governors (to the Crown under GOI 1935). Giving with one hand and taking with the other. The long road to democracy. The arc runs: centralisation began 1773, peaked 1833, decentralisation began 1861, Provincial Autonomy in 1935. The ladder of elections runs 1861 non-officers, 1909 first proper indirect election, 1919 first direct elections and elected majority. The expanded-council model lasts until GOI 1919 (CoS and CLA). The teacher's test of responsible government is that every minister is an MP or MLA first; the ICA 1861 fails it, and the Moderates ask for an ideal Constitution.

Prelims 2000 Assertion (A): the basic weakness of the early nationalist movement lay in its narrow social base. Reason (R): it fought for the narrow interests of the social groups which joined it. Options: (a) both true, R explains A (b) both true, R does not explain A (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true (c) A is true, but R is false. A is true: uneven representation and the total exclusion of non-elites is the early INC's most serious structural weakness. R is false: its members were elites, but its demands went well beyond elite interests (lower Land Revenue, end of the Salt Tax, repeal of the Arms Act 1878, trial by jury). The teacher's ink: "T" circled on A, "False" over R's "narrow interests", and on the right: the INC did not take up inter-religious issues (neither for H nor for M), the 1886 RULE: Indian vs Indian issues won't pick up, Indian vs British issues picked up Section 3.3 (the 1886 rule) and Section 2 (what the demands were) Mains (the year is not given in the bank) Why did the Moderates fail to carry conviction with the nation about their proclaimed ideology and political goals by the end of the nineteenth century? (10 marks, 150 words) A cause-chain on the teacher's "Reasons for Failures = weakness" board: weak claim of representing Indians, no trust in the masses, weak demands, weak methods (3P, gradual, part-time politicians). Skeleton below Section 3 (the whole of it) and Section 4 Mains PYQ skeleton: why the Moderates failed to carry conviction (from the notes only) Intro: the Moderates (Utilitarian and Liberal, firm believers in Rule of Law) wanted Limited Self-Government within British rule by petitions, resolutions, the press and debate, and by 1900 their programme had produced none of its 11 demands. Body (the teacher's four power factors):(1) Weak claim to represent Indians: upper-caste Western-educated middle class from Madras, Bombay and Calcutta; Hindus 90%, Muslims about 6.5% (census: 20%); Bombay alone about half the members; peasants, workers, women and lower castes absent; so less pressure on the British.(2) No trust in the masses: they were not Western-educated and would not understand modern politics; involvement would raise the chance of violence; so no mass base.(3) Weak demands: limited self-government, and class-coloured demands (no anti-Zamindar stand, PS 1793, Punjab Land Alienation Bill 1900 opposed, Indian capitalists over labour). (4) Weak methods:3P (Prayer, Petitions, Protests in the press), gradual, part-time politicians, a 3-day annual drama; called the "Strategy of Mendicancy." Closing: a movement that neither represented the people nor threatened to unleash them carried no real pressure; the British could ignore a few hundred professionals. Fair verdict (Gokhale 1913): they were building the institutions and culture of politics for a country with no national organisation.

Because the opponent was a foreign State, the Moderates wanted to limit its power with laws and a constitution. Ask: which two Western traditions and which kind of methods followed from that? 1.1 Why the Moderates wanted to limit the State: the class board In the West the State was an indigenous monarchy (the teacher writes Britain and France), so democracy grew gradually: the power of the Monarch went down and the power of Parliament went up. The nature of that State was monarchy, so limiting the monarchy meant limiting the power of the State. He adds how:Britain did it without a written Constitution, France with a Constitution: both ended with a limited State.In India (and the USA) the opponent was the imperialism of a foreign power.Step 1 for the Moderates = limit the power of the colonial State. The instrument = a Good Constitution, and so constitutional development. So the Moderates' ideology centres on constitutions, laws and rights. 1.2 Two Western traditions: Utilitarianism and Liberalism Teacher's board: Development of Democracy in the West versus India and USA Teacher's board: "Till now student knows" a bracket splitting into Orientalism, Authoritarianism, Racism, [Liberalism] boxed and [Utilitarianism] boxed, with a line to ev The Moderates were shaped by two Western philosophical traditions: Utilitarianism The right action is the one that produces the greatest good for the greatest number; belief in laws and good governance as the mechanism for change Faith in laws as the tool of reform Liberalism Stresses individual rights, rule of law and constitutional governance Faith in constitutional government and rights Together  The conviction that gradual constitutional reform is the right way to reform On the board he lists the "isms" the student already knows from Chapter 15: Orientalism, Authoritarianism, Racism, Liberalism and Utilitarianism, with evangelicalism (Christianise India) joined on at the end. He boxes only Liberalism and Utilitarianism as the Moderates' two. Utilitarianism = Good Laws, Rule of Law + efficiency.Liberalism = opposed to Authoritarianism, and he adds a circled plus: it means "Give Best To India" in Polity, Eco(nomy) and Society. On the ideology tree (Lecture 28, slide 27) he writes beside Utilitarianism "Good Laws / Rule of Law / Law = Agent of Good Change [the delta sign]" and beside Liberalism the bracket [anti-Colonialism]. The line labelled "linked" joins Utilitarianism to Constitutionalism. 1.3 Constitutionalism From the isms grew the Moderates' belief in Constitutionalism: a legitimate State should provide Responsible Government, protect the rights of citizens, and operate under the Rule of Law. Teacher's ideology tree (Think of Constitutionalism as the values reflected in our Preamble, the Basic Structure doctrine and the Directive Principles of State Policy.) Constitutionalism = limiting the power of the State via a Constitution. He adds a personal reading: when it is said that the "primary" purpose of the COI is to limit the power of the (Nation) State, "for me: this shows distrust." For India after COI 1950 he draws the line between Nation and Nation State, and concludes: Constitutionalism = Ideal Democracy with Rule of Law, where limiting the power of the State is automatically covered. The values are the ones in the Preamble + FRs + Basic Structure + DPSP (he marks them with a query arc). He also hangs Secularism and National Unity and Constitutional methods from the same Ideology tree. 1.4 Two terms the teacher defines: Responsible Government and Constitutional methods Responsible Government = part of Constitutionalism = the accountability of the Executive (E). It is operationalised as E responsible to the Legislature (L) / Parliament. The test: a Minister has to be an MP or MLA first. If yes, then Parliament (P) is the mother of the Executive (E).A child is always accountable to its mother, including elimination (the no-confidence motion). He draws the Executive as a segment inside the circle of Parliament. He also leaves a question for himself: "what should I make of it when the INC demanded immediate Responsible Government?" (the board gives no answer; check your notebook). Teacher's board: (2) Constitutional methods = use of Grievance Redressal mechanisms provided by State, e.g Teacher's board: (1) Definitions of imp Terms The Moderates believed in Constitutional Methods: they would use only the institutions and mechanisms that the State itself provided to redress grievances. Today's equivalents: fighting elections, using the Legislature, approaching the Judiciary; filing RTI applications, using CPGRAMS, writing to Citizen Charters; sending petitions to the government. Constitutional methods = use of the grievance-redressal mechanisms provided by the State (the State = L, E, J): FIR, Court case, RTI, CPGRAMS, NOTA, fight elections, Citizen Charter. The topic belongs to Good Governance (Public Administration). His Methods map has three parts: (1) Constitutional [non-violent, legal];(1.2) Extra-constitutional, which splits into 1.2.1 not unconstitutional and not illegal and 1.2.2 unconstitutional and illegal (which can be violent or non-violent); (2) Protests:violent ones were not by Mahatma Gandhi, peaceful ones were by him;(3) MG methods = non-violent extra-constitutional mass struggle [Satyagraha]:Non-Cooperation (not illegal, not unconstitutional: e.g. boycott of British goods, elections) and Civil Disobedience (illegal, unconstitutional). Teacher's board, white chalk: boxed "For a civil servant, PROTESTS shall" leading to "# Shame # incompetency?" (Genuine PROTESTS = failure of Civil Servant) and "# STRICT A civil-servant lens on protests: for a civil servant, genuine protests are a source of shame and a sign of the servant's own failure (incompetency?), while protests that are not genuine and cause law-and-order problems call for strict action. And a heroes' flip:pre-1947 heroes = Revolutionaries, Extremists, Mahatma Gandhi (MG) (with a surprised face: against the colonial State); post-1947 heroes = Moderates, with the board's "therefore" pointing to the Nation State. 1.5 Did the Moderates oppose British rule? The Moderates knew British rule was exploitative: they were not naive. But they believed in the Providence of British Rule: if sufficiently pressurised, the British could be made to modernise India. Their goal was therefore not independence but Limited Self-Government: a greater Indian share in governance within British rule. Why so limited? Because they believed the masses, without widespread Western education, were not yet ready for full self-rule. Their ultimate long-term vision (rarely stated loudly): Self-Government like Canada or Australia, with full British citizenship. They sought not the removal of British rule but the removal of "Un-British Rule" (Surendranath Banerjea): the gap between Britain's own stated liberal values and its actual conduct in India. The first President of the INC, W.C. Bonnerjee, declared that the INC was "loyal to the British and well-wishers of the British." He underlines "Providence of British Rule", "if", "pressurised" and "the British could be made to modernise India" (the whole faith rests on the if), the Canada or Australia vision, the "loyal and well-wishers" line, and the words national unity, Capitalism and Industrialisation on British lines. Beside "Un-British Rule" the typed slide adds the bracket [Dadabhai Naoroji's book = Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901)], which he also underlines. 1.6 What "Limited Self-Government" means: Sovereignty and Swaraj boards Sovereignty has three parts:(A) symbolic sovereignty (powerless), and the power to do L, E, J on (B) external sovereign functions [D, C, FA] and (C) domestic sovereign functions [Home, Finance etc]. He adds the note "ChatGPT sovereignty = B + C" (it reads as: the popular definition counts only the real powers, B and C, and leaves out the symbolic part, A). D, C, FA are Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs (see Chapter 1). Teacher's board: Swaraj [Swa = People, Raj = Govt] (Self Govt) Teacher's board: Sovereignty Swaraj = Swa (People) + Raj (Government) = Self-Government. He lays out four meanings, numbered on the board: (3) Limited Self-Government (the Moderates): the symbolic sovereign is British,external functions stay British, and domestic affairs are a partnership between Indians and British, "so:so" (about half and half). (2) Swaraj / SG within the British empire:(a) symbolic sovereign British, external British, domestic significantly with Indians (75% or more with Indians);(b) Dominion Status = when domestic is 100% with Indians.(1) Purna Swaraj:symbolic sovereign Indian,external Indian and domestic Indian.(4) Philosophical:Bhagat Singh = end of class oppression;MG's Swaraj = self-rule of each individual, no L, E, J, a stateless society = enlightened anarchism. Teacher's board: 15 Aug 1947 (Special Dominion Status), with "Books Simply Say: Dominion Status on 15 Aug 1947" 15 August 1947 = a "Special Dominion Status": the symbolic sovereign is still British, but external and domestic functions are Indian (both I). "Books simply say: Dominion Status on 15 Aug 1947." 26 January 1950: the symbolic sovereign also becomes Indian (I), external and domestic stay Indian. 1.7 Secular, pro-industry, pro-capitalism The Moderates were secular in orientation and actively promoted national unity. They believed in Capitalism and Industrialisation on British lines as the path to Indian prosperity. Teacher's board: "Why Moderates Believed in Capitalism?" Before 1929, all examples of IR (circled) via Capitalists (pvt Sector) Why did the Moderates believe in capitalism?Before 1929, all examples of IR (industrial revolution) came via capitalists (the private sector). And Japan from 1868 onwards went through its IR as "State aided Capitalism." So the examples he cites for industrialisation all run through capitalism. ("IR" is read as industrial revolution; the board writes only "IR".)

Because they believed in pressing the State by constitutional means, they made concrete demands. Ask: how many were political, how many economic, and how many were met? The handout says "Not a single one was met. The result of two decades of petitions and prayers was, in practice, zero." The teacher's heading on the slide splits the demands into POL (political) and economic (a tick before POL). 2.1 Governance and legislative reform (the political demands) What "Limited Self-Government" meant in practice (map of Lecture 29, slide 1): the symbolic sovereign and external functions stay British; the domestic field is a partnership. Inside the domestic field, by power: L (legislature): the Moderates wanted indirect elections, an elected majority and a powerful L.E (executive) = British ministers, which splits into CS (civil services) and Ms (ministers): the books focus on these.J (judiciary): the books are quiet, but Indianisation can be considered a demand under it. The starred tree: the legislature = officers + non-officers; the non-officers are nominated or elected; the elected are chosen indirectly or directly (the Moderates' demand lives in the elected, indirect end). 2.1 Abolish the India Council The 15-member advisory body sitting in London around the Secretary of State. Logic: lobbying one Secretary of State is easier than lobbying fifteen members of a Council 2.2 Expand the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) and the Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) With at least 50% indirectly elected members 2.3 Greater powers to the ILC and PLCs Meaningful legislative authority, not just advisory roles 2.4 Indianisation of the Civil and Military Services Hold the Civil Services examination simultaneously in India and Britain and raise the age limit to 23. This would make administration more responsive, less expensive and less racist. The demand for Indians at officer rank in the military was similarly rejected (the British could not imagine taking orders from Indians) Teacher's board: Moderates LTD SG Military aside (handout and slide): only after the 1st Round Table Conference of 1931 did Indian officer appointments begin in the military services, which led to the Indian Military Academy at Dehradun in 1932, though the British were careful in selection. Indian officers were recruited in real numbers only during World War 2, in response to INM demands. Moderates' Demands: Governance and Legislative Reform Ink on the governance table: (1) India Council: arrow up to 1858 and BoC 1784 (the Council of India, from 1858, stands where the Board of Control 1784 stood, with members of a SoS for India; see Chapter 17). (2) 2.2: he underlines "at least 50% indirectly elected members." (3) 2.3: he inserts "genuine" before "legislative": the demand is for genuine legislative authority. (4) A starred note: "1877-80: Press campaign on Indianization of CS" (the last letters are cut off at the slide edge). (5) 2.4: he underlines simultaneous exam in India and Britain and age limit 23, and writes MILITARY over "Officer-rank". (6) In the right margin, the starting point:ICA 1861: ILC = Viceroy's Executive Council + 6 to 12 additional members, of whom half must be non-officials, who can be Indian or Anglo-Indian (see Chapter 25). Teacher's board: LONDON, boxed "SoS for India" with a line down to "India Council" (15 members, underlined), starred bracket "Prez BoC 1784" and "(BoC 1784)" with B circl Two maps for the first four demands.Left (London): the SoS for India with the India Council of 15 members above the Viceroy and GG in India; a star notes the President of the BoC 1784 (it reads as the post the SoS stands in for; see Chapter 17). Right (the legislature): officers versus non-officers; non-officers are nominated or elected; elected are indirect or direct. His white loop takes in non-officers, the elected and nominated junction, and "Indirect", with Direct left outside: the Moderates' demand (at least 50% indirectly elected) sits in that loop. 2.2 Economic and social demands "GUESSED: demands from previous chapters." His own list of Moderate economic demands, which you can guess from the earlier chapters:IR of India (industrial revolution, as in Chapter 27's theme); government support for the private sector of India [capitalists];tariffs that raise Indian exports of finished goods [machine-made] and lower British exports to India ("FG" is read as finished goods); lower taxes [Land Revenue + Income Tax (1860, 1868)];lower expenditure on the large standing army;end of the government monopoly on salt and opium;extend PS 1793;spread of Western education to the masses;better public works. A circled "@BD" sits beside the taxes line (not expanded on the board: check your notebook). 2.5 Decrease and share Military Expenditure The Indian Army was used for British imperial adventures that had nothing to do with India, like the Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901) in China.Partially met, but no significant change 2.6 A Volunteer Army Recruitment open to all, not restricted by the "Martial Races" doctrine. (Today India has a volunteer army: anyone can apply.) The British rejected it, fearing disaffection, especially if Marathas and Bengalis joined in large numbers 2.7 Trial by Jury The right to be judged by a jury of peers rather than by colonial officers 2.8 Repeal of the Arms Act 1878 It had disarmed ordinary Indians. Framed as a Right to Bear Arms for self-defence, not as a call to violence 2.9 Decrease Land Revenue and end the Salt Tax The Salt Tax is the same tax Gandhi attacked in the Salt March 1930; a grievance for decades 2.10 Extend the Permanent Settlement of 1793 (PS 1793) outside Bengal So that Land Revenue could not be arbitrarily increased. Partly a principled demand, partly self-interested (see Section 3.4) 2.11 End the exploitation of Indentured Labourers in Assam Tea Plantations Workers bound to plantations under harsh contracts  Outcome No demands were met Teacher's board: Moderate Economic Demands, with the word G U E S S E D down the left and "Demands From Previous Chapters" Ink on the economic table:2.5: underlines the Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901) in China.2.6: adds "of Peel Commission" (the Martial Races doctrine is of the Peel Commission; the notes give no more, check your notebook). 2.7: the bracket [*RRR + Derozians] (starred): the demand for trial by jury was raised earlier by RRR and the Derozians (in Chapter 19 the trial-by-jury demand belongs to Roy and Young Bengal, so "RRR" reads as Roy; check your notebook). 2.8: underlines "Right to Bear Arms for self-defence."2.9: writes [GST] under the salt tax (an analogy he does not spell out on the slide). 2.11: underlines Indentured Labourers, links it to the word CONTRACT, and underlines Assam Tea Plantations and contracts.Outcome: underlines "petitions and prayers." "Not a single demand was met" versus 2.5 "partially met." The handout says no demands were met (outcome) yet it also says the military-expenditure demand was "partially met but no significant change occurred." Learn it as: none met in any real sense; the military-expenditure one was only nominally touched.

items.t: 3 · Weaknesses of the Moderates and the INC
items.x: Because none of the demands was met, the chapter turns to why. Ask: who was in the INC, who was left out, and whose interests shaped its politics? 3.0 The teacher's frame: why they failed "Moderates = politicians," so judge them on power factors. Four reasons for failure (weakness): (1) a weak claim that the INC represents Indians: it was UC WEMC (upper-caste Western-educated middle class) from M, B, C (Madras, Bombay, Calcutta), which means less pressure on the British.(2) Masses' support? The Moderates had no trust in the masses: the masses were not Western-educated, so they would not understand modern polity demands, and involvement would raise the chance of violence.(3) Weak demands, shown by a bargaining story: a mother negotiating with a shopkeeper (the first word reads "Link" or "Like"; the numbers on the board are Rs 500 and Rs 2000, with the settlement at Rs 1000); it reads as: if your opening demand is small, the settlement is small (the board does not spell the lesson out; check your notebook). (4) Weak methods: 3P = Prayer, Petitions, Protests in the press;gradual; and part-time politicians, starred with "3 DAY annual DRAMA." 3.1 Uneven representation and the exclusion of non-elites The most serious structural weakness of the early INC was uneven representation and the total exclusion of non-elites. It was dominated by Western-educated professionals: lawyers, doctors, merchants and bankers, journalists, teachers, social reformers and landowners. Most members came from the three Presidencies (Bombay, Madras, Calcutta); the rest of India was hugely underrepresented. Even within the Presidencies, Bombay was over-represented, contributing roughly half the members, followed by Madras. Teacher's board: "Reasons for Failures = weakness Bengal, despite having its own active political organisation (the Indian Association, 1876), sent only about 5 members to the first INC session, and only after being informed at the last moment. Until 1905, most INC members were high-caste Hindus: about 40% Brahmins and the rest from other upper castes. Impact: the INC's claim to represent the whole nation was weak, and a weak claim of representativeness hurt the success of every INC programme. Weaknesses: Representation Bombay Presidency 38 Madras 21 Punjab and the "North-Western Provinces and Oudh" 10 (NWP 1836 and Oudh's administrations were placed under one head in 1877) Bengal-Bihar-Orissa-Assam (the extensive region) only 3 Total 72 Who is missing? On the heading he fans in the excluded: Low Muslim %, women (non-WEMC), peasants, workers and LC (lower castes). Beside the 1885 row: "all India not represented" (the last letters are cut off at the slide edge). Under "First two decades, elites" he writes 1885-1905. Why Bengal's turnout was low (slide). The 2nd Indian National Conference was held in Calcutta by the Indian Association (1876) just before the INC session, so leaders such as Surendranath Banerjea (SNB) found it difficult to attend. The handout's reason is that Bengal was informed at the last moment. Both can be true; learn both. Madras (slide): educationally advanced by 1885 but less politically organised than Bengal and Bombay, so it had less political influence. Handout versus slide on Bengal's numbers at the first session: the handout says Bengal sent "only about 5 members"; the slide's table counts the Bengal-Bihar-Orissa-Assam region as only 3 (the slide's region is wider than the handout's "Bengal"). The teacher did not mark either. Treat it as "very few (3 or about 5)" and do not give a single exact number in the exam unless the question quotes one. Bombay 38 + Madras 21 + 10 + 3 = 72 is the slide's own sum. The period of the composition figures differs. The handout says 1892-1905 (Hindus 90%, Muslims about 6.5%; 20% landlords, 40% lawyers, 15% traders) and "until 1905" for high-caste dominance. The slides print 1892-1909 for the same figures. The teacher's own ink for the elite row is 1885-1905. Quote the figures (90%, 6.5%, 40%, 20%, 15%) and write the period as "1892 to the early 1900s" if unsure. 3.2 Low Muslim participation Very few Muslims participated in the early INC. Badruddin Tyabji of Bombay became the first Muslim President of the INC at the Madras session of 1887: a notable exception. In the period 1892-1905,Hindus were 90% of members and Muslims only about 6.5%. Within the Hindu membership, Brahmins alone were roughly 40%. (The slide: the remainder were non-Brahmin Hindus, many upper caste, plus Muslims, Parsis and Christians.) Muslim participation dropped dramatically after the 1890s, and the INC made no concerted effort to reach out to the Muslim community. There was arrogance in this: a belief that the absence of a strong Muslim political party until 1906 meant no urgent effort was needed. When cow-killing riots broke out in 1893, the INC stayed silent and did not condemn the violence. Beside Tyabji's Madras session (1887) he underlines "Madras session." Beside the 1886 rule he writes "Calcutta session, President = Dadabhai Naoroji." On the right: census: Muslim population = 20%, against the INC's 6.5%. So Muslims were one-fifth of the people but about one-fifteenth of the INC. 3.3 The 1886 rule: avoiding social questions Because the INC wanted unity above all, it chose its fights carefully. Ask: why did it pick only Indian-versus-British issues, and what did that cost? To maintain unity, the INC took the pragmatic but damaging decision to avoid all social questions (caste, religion, social reform) until 1907. This was deliberate. Formal political resolutions (governance, civil services, economic demands) were the arena of the Congress. Communally sensitive social reform questions (caste, religion, personal law) were kept off the agenda because they risked splitting the fragile Hindu-Muslim-Parsi coalition before it had properly formed. The logic: national political unity had to be built first; raising caste or religious reform in the INC would invite the very divisions the British hoped to exploit. Teacher's board: Concept (1886 Social Qs) What counts as a "social issue"?H-M (Hindu-Muslim), UC-LC (upper caste versus lower caste), Women, and CLASS issues: working class versus capitalist class, and peasants versus the landed class.Why the 1886 rule? (1) to prevent the perception that the INC is pro-"xyz" group and not for all Indians; (2) to prevent disunity among Indians; (3) Decision: pick only issues where the opponent is a foreigner, so it is Indians versus Foreigner, which builds national unity; therefore won't pick social issues. He also sketches an empty triangle beside two stacks (UC, L, C and Landed/Capitalists, WEMC, Peasants, WC); the board gives no words, so read it as the class pyramid and check your notebook. PYQ Prelims 2000: Early Nationalist Movement (A-R) Prelims 2000, the slide has no tick on an option, but A = T (circled) and R = False can only mean (c). The bank key also says (c), and the next slide (Lecture 29, slide 17) prints the answer (c) A is true, but R is false. No conflict. On the PYQ the teacher underlines "weakness" and "narrow social base" and circles T for A. Over R's "narrow interests" he writes False. His reason, on the right: the INC did not take up inter-religious issues (it worked neither for Hindus nor for Muslims as such), and under the 1886 ruleIndian vs Indian issues were not picked up; Indian vs British issues were. So the movement had a narrow base of members, but it did not fight only for their narrow interests. 3.4 Commitment and social background Were the Moderates committed politicians? The commitment problem was real. Moderate leaders were mostly part-time politicians, with lucrative legal practices and other professional commitments. The INC was organisationally weak: it functioned more like an annual conference lasting three days than a genuine political party. (Handout analogy: the INC was the trade fair, not a company with a permanent office, year-round staff and a strategic plan.) Did their social background affect their politics? Yes. In 1892-1905 the INC membership was about 20% landlords, 40% lawyers and 15% traders, most from landed families. This shaped their positions: 1. No anti-Zamindar stand. They wanted PS 1793 extended outside Bengal, which was partly a fig leaf for protecting Zamindar interests: PS 1793 prevented the State from raising Land Revenue and so protected Zamindars from higher taxation. 2. They opposed the Punjab Land Alienation Bill of 1900, designed to stop indebted peasants from losing their land to moneylenders. It would have constrained land transfers, inconvenient for their class. 3. They did not champion working-class interests against Indian capitalists. Their stated position: only Indian Capitalism would remove poverty. They actively supported the workers of Assam Tea Gardens, but only because the plantation owners there were European. For labour reforms that would help Indian workers at the cost of Indian capitalists, they opposed them consistently. Weaknesses: Commitment and Social Background He underlines "3-day annual conference" (the board in Lecture 29, slide 6 calls it a "3 DAY annual DRAMA") and "but favoured Indian capitalists over the working class." The little sketch of circles on the right is an organisation tree (one head, a few leaders, a row below) with no words: check your notebook for what he said about a real party's structure. 3.5 The Lancashire Lobby and the Factory and Mines Acts Because leaders were landlords, lawyers and traders, their class interest met a British trade interest. Ask: was the opposition to the factory laws wrong, or only complex? The Lancashire Lobby argument. The British were not passing these labour laws out of sympathy for Indian workers.British textile manufacturers in Lancashire were heavily lobbying for factory regulations in India, because stricter rules would raise Indian production costs and reduce the competitiveness of Indian textiles against British goods in global markets. The Moderates understood this game. They argued that India's infant industries needed room to grow, and that heavy regulation imposed prematurely would crush indigenous industrialisation before it had begun, keeping India permanently a supplier of raw materials (and an export market for British manufactured goods) rather than a manufacturing economy. After "competitiveness of Indian textiles against British goods in global markets" he adds "as well as Indian market." So the Lancashire lobby hurt Indian textiles in the home market too, not only abroad. Teacher's board: a tariff example The tariff example.British manufactured goods entering India: British manufacturers lobbied for down or zero tariffs on them. Example: a British good of Rs 100 with a 50% import duty sells at Rs 150, against an Indian good at Rs 130, so the Indian good wins (the board marks this as "if India has been independent", that is, if India could set its own duty). On the right (Britain): an Indian good at 100 pounds with a 50% import duty becomes 150 pounds, against a British good at 130 pounds: the British good wins at home. So tariffs protect whoever sets them. Factories Act 1881 Ripon 80-84 Applied to factories with 100 or more workers.Banned employment of children under 7.Restricted working hours for children aged 7-12 to 9 hours per day.Mandated fencing of hazardous machinery "Famous, therefore imp" (underlined imp); he underlines "children under 7", "working hours" and "9 hours per day" and "fencing of hazardous machinery" and adds "+ 4 monthly holidays" Factories Act 1891 Lansdowne 88-94 Extended coverage to factories with 50 or more workers.Raised the minimum working age from 7 to 9, and the upper child-labour age (definition of child) from 12 to 14.Capped women's working hours at 11 hours per day with a 1.5-hour rest interval "not imp" Indian Mines Act 1901 Curzon 99-05 The first major regulation of mining conditions. Set a minimum age for child labour in mines and improved working conditions for women and children underground "not imp" The 1881 Act is the one to know (the teacher: famous, so important): 100 workers, under 7 banned, 7-12 limited to 9 hours, machinery fenced, plus 4 holidays a month (ink). The 1891 and 1901 Acts are marked not imp: know them only as the expansion (50 workers; ages 9 and 14; women 11 hours) and the first Mines Act. The handout's closing remark on these Acts (the slide prints it as a box): whether the Moderates were right or wrong to oppose them is a complex question. The Lancashire Lobby motive was real, the British were not philanthropists, but the consequence of Moderate opposition was that Indian workers, including children, continued to labour under harsh conditions for longer than necessary. 3.6 Why Moderate politics failed: the two structural problems The failure came from two structural problems that reinforced each other: 1. They did not represent the masses Roughly 90% Hindu, overwhelmingly drawn from the lawyer and landlord classes: not a cross-section of India, but a sliver 2. They distrusted the masses They refused to mobilise them, fearing that popular agitation would turn violent and become an uncontrolled mass movement Consequence A movement that neither represented the people nor threatened to unleash them carried no real pressure. The government could easily ignore petitions from a few hundred educated professionals with no mass base. Without the threat of popular disruption, the British could easily ignore the Moderates

Because the Moderates were gradual, the chapter closes on their goal, their methods and the verdict. Ask: why were they called mendicants, and what did Gokhale say in their defence? Goals. Their goal was limited: Self-Government within British rule. They wanted only the removal of the undesirable aspects of British rule, not British rule itself; as Surendranath Banerjea put it, to end "Un-British Rule." Their ultimate vision was Self-Government like Canada or Australia:dominion status, not independence. Teacher's board: GOAL OF INC The Indian National Movement was a movement of GRADUALISM, e.g. in its GOALS. The goal ladder: Limited Self-Government (1885-1906);Self-Government within the Empire (1906), which he lists as "SG / Home Rule / SG on lines of Australia and Canada / Swaraj";Dominion Status (1916), but the words "Dominion Status" were not used (the 1916 goal was "equal status with other self-governing dominions of the empire"); 1928: Dominion Status (named, underlined); Purna Swaraj (1929), circled. This chapter's Moderates belong to the first rung (1885-1906). Methods.Prayers and petitions to the government; resolutions at annual sessions; the press to express opinions; a rich culture of debates.No mass action. No agitation on the streets. Their approach was Gradualism. Teacher's board: ADOPTION How the Moderates came to their methods, in three stages (the board says "ADOPTION").Stage 1: the Brown Sahib (educated Indians who copied the British) faces discrimination (the board writes "You vs white, children Biological"; it reads as the picture of an adopted child set against the white family's biological children, which fits the title ADOPTION; check your notebook). Stage 2: petitions and requests.Stage 3: protesting letters (articles), like WhatsApp messages, and long debates. Stages 2 and 3 are "for legitimate demands." His memory image at the top right: "Think like a one-sided love story's lover": he keeps asking, writing and waiting for a reply that does not come. Goals and Methods: flow of five boxes Beside No mass action he writes [FIRM BELIEVERS of Ro Law]: they refused the street because they believed in the Rule of Law. Beside Gradualism he writes [LTD SG to SG on lines of Australia / Canada]: the gradual path runs from Limited Self-Government to self-government like Australia and Canada. 4.1 The label: "Strategy of Mendicancy" [the slide has no ink here] Their critics, and later the Extremists, called the Moderate methods the "Strategy of Mendicancy," that is, begging. The label captured the reality that their methods created little pressure on the British. 4.2 Defence of the Moderates (Gokhale, 1913) To be fair to them, Gokhale noted in 1913 that had the Moderates not followed these methods, the British would not have allowed the formation of the INC at all. And the culture of direct confrontation with the colonial government had not yet developed. A movement that begins with petition and prayer is not necessarily weak: it is building the institutions and culture of politics for a country that had never had a national political organisation.The INC of 1885 was the beginning of something, not the end.

the Moderates wanted it abolished 1860 Income Tax (teacher's board, with 1868: the Moderates wanted lower taxes) 1861 Indian Councils Act: ILC = Executive Council + 6 to 12 additional members, half non-officials (teacher's ink) 1868 Income Tax (teacher's board); Limit the State, by law. In the West the monarchy was limited step by step (Britain without a written Constitution, France with one). In India the opponent was a foreign power, so Step 1 for the Moderates was to limit the colonial State, with a good Constitution as the instrument. They drew on Utilitarianism (the greatest good of the greatest number, through laws) and Liberalism (rights, rule of law, a constitution). Only the State's own doors. Constitutionalism meant Responsible Government, protected rights and Rule of Law. Constitutional methods meant using only the channels the State provides: elections, the Legislature, the Judiciary, RTI, CPGRAMS, Citizen Charters and petitions (the teacher adds FIR, Court case and NOTA). Gandhi's Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience sit outside, as extra-constitutional mass struggle. Critics, not rebels. The Moderates knew British rule was exploitative, yet they believed in its Providence: if pressurised, the British could modernise India. Their goal was Limited Self-Government within British rule, because the masses were not yet ready; the long vision was Canada or Australia with British citizenship. Banerjea wanted an end to Un-British Rule, and Bonnerjee called the INC loyal to the British and their well-wishers. Eleven asks, no answers. Four were political: abolish the 15-member India Council, expand the ILC and PLCs with at least 50% indirectly elected members, give genuine powers, and Indianise the services (exam in India and Britain, age 23). Seven were economic: cut military spending (the Boxer Rebellion 1899-1901), a volunteer army, trial by jury, repeal of the Arms Act 1878, lower land revenue and no Salt Tax, PS 1793 extended, and an end to Assam tea indenture. None was met. Who was in the room. At the first session in 1885, 72 delegates came: Bombay 38, Madras 21, Punjab and NWP and Oudh 10, and only 3 from Bengal-Bihar-Orissa-Assam (the handout says Bengal about 5). They were upper-caste Western-educated professionals; Hindus were 90% and Muslims about 6.5% of the INC against 20% in the census. Tyabji, the first Muslim President (Madras 1887), was the exception. The 1886 rule. At the Calcutta session of 1886, under Dadabhai Naoroji, the INC decided to avoid social questions (Hindu-Muslim, upper-lower caste, women, class) until 1907, so that it would not look pro-one-group or split. It would pick only fights where the opponent was a foreigner. In 1893 it stayed silent over the cow-killing riots, and Muslim participation fell. Landlords' politics. In 1892-1905 about 20% of members were landlords, 40% lawyers and 15% traders, and the leaders were part-time politicians in a three-day annual conference. So there was no anti-Zamindar stand (they wanted PS 1793 extended), they opposed the Punjab Land Alienation Bill of 1900, and they backed Indian capital over labour (Assam tea only because the owners were European). The Lancashire game. British textile makers in Lancashire lobbied for Indian factory rules to raise Indian costs; the Moderates replied that infant industries needed room or India would stay a raw-material supplier. The Acts were the Factories Act 1881 (Ripon 80-84; imp), the Factories Act 1891 (Lansdowne 88-94) and the Indian Mines Act 1901 (Curzon 99-05). The verdict is complex: the lobby's motive was real, but Indian workers, children included, suffered longer. Prayer, petition, protest in print. They sent prayers and petitions, passed resolutions at annual sessions, used the press and debates, and avoided all mass action, as firm believers in the Rule of Law. The teacher's 3P is Prayer, Petitions, Protests in the press; critics, later the Extremists, called it the Strategy of Mendicancy. A sliver with no lever. Two problems reinforced each other: they did not represent the masses (about 90% Hindu, lawyers and landlords) and they distrusted the masses and would not mobilise them. A movement that neither represented the people nor threatened to unleash them could be ignored. The teacher's four power factors: claim, masses, demands, methods. A beginning, not the end. Gokhale said in 1913 that without these methods the British would not have allowed the INC to function, and that the culture of direct confrontation had not yet developed. The goal itself moved on: Limited Self-Government 1885-1906, Self-Government within the empire 1906, Dominion Status 1916 and 1928, Purna Swaraj 1929.
