Story so far: the chapter has two halves, the Moderates' positives and the Drain. Ask: which of the three positives on the board comes first? Teacher's board: the two questions of the chapter The chapter has two halves: (I) the Moderates and (II) the Drain.(I) Moderates.GOAL = LTD SG, not Purna Swaraj (his shorthand: limited self-government, and "x" over Purna Swaraj; SG he defines on slide 21 as the power to do L, E, J on our sovereign functions). Methods = Gradualism, "3Ps," Constitutional methods.(II) Drain. The drain is wealth moving from India to Britain ("Home"). The starred warning: "wealth is not always equal to rupees," which the next slide explains. Teacher's board: "(Q) +ves of moderates", branching to (1) "Non-Drain Theory" and (2) "Drain Theory" The answer frame for "positives of the Moderates":(1) Non-Drain Theory: the project of national building and the culture of parliamentary politics (the INC session functioned like a Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha session), which he links with a circled ICA 1892 (see Chapter 28; the board does not write the reason: check your notebook). (2) Drain Theory:the WEMC (Western Educated Middle Class) Moderates defeated the narrative of WMB (the White Man's Burden) through press, speeches and books. This is the structure of the rest of the chapter.

Because India had no single political community, unity came before rights. Ask: how did the 1886 rule, the 1888 veto and the 1889 clause each serve unity? What was the first goal the INC declared? At the very first INC session in 1885 in Bombay, the Congress declared its goal as "building national unity." This was not an accident. India in 1885 was a land of regions, languages, castes and religions, with no pre-existing sense of a single Indian political community. The Moderates understood that building such a community was the first task, even before demanding rights from the British. So they made a deliberate choice to focus only on issues common to all Indians. In 1886, Dadabhai Naoroji laid down an informal INC rule: the Congress would take up only political questions, not social or class questions, because social issues could divide Indians against each other. He underlined "building national unity" and "common to all Indians," and drew a slanted line from 1886 to it: Naoroji's rule is the method that delivers the goal. He underlined "only political questions, not social or class questions" and "Congress = a platform against colonial rule." The handout's bracket explains the rule: only issues where it was Indians against the British, and not Religion Hindu vs Muslim Caste Upper Caste vs Lower Caste Gender Men vs Women Class Working Class vs Capitalist Class Land Ryots vs Landlords The Congress was to be a platform against colonial rule, not a forum for internal Indian disputes. For Hindu-Muslim unity the INC took two concrete steps: 1888 INC decision (the communal veto):no resolution would be passed by the INC if the majority of Hindu or Muslim members disagreed with it. 1889 Minority Clause: the INC demanded that the British government reserve seats in the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) and the Provincial Legislative Councils (PLCs) for religious minorities, in proportion to their share of the population. Both show the Moderates tried to build a Congress that worked for all Indians. The 1889 clause is notable: it was the INC itself, not the Muslim League, that first formally demanded minority representation in legislative councils. He underlined "No INC resolution would pass" and added in the margin: "Br have ML1906 veto power on constitutional progress -> Partition of India = appeasement." [The board is partly cramped; read it as: the British gave the Muslim League (1906) a veto over constitutional progress, and that led to the Partition of India, which he calls appeasement. Check your notebook for his exact wording.] Teacher's board: "Communal VETO -> ML1906 -> Pakistan" (ML1906 and Pakistan underlined) A communal veto normally leads to trouble: "Communal VETO -> ML 1906 -> Pakistan."But here, the INC's veto was different:anyone who is a member of the INC has agreed to its ideology, which is Secularism and National Unity. So there was trust that the communal veto would not be misused for dividing India or for divisive politics. And a linked point: in the Constituent Assembly, reservation on the basis of religion was ruled out. Why? Answer: Pakistan. Rotating sessions, non-host President Each session was held in a different part of the country, and the President was specifically not from the host region. The logic: a Bengali leader presiding in Calcutta builds nothing new.A Marathi leader presiding in Calcutta, speaking to Bengali concerns, builds an all-India leadership and creates inter-regional bonds that would not exist otherwise. The handout's picture: a Bengali delegate or newspaper reader sees a Marathi president describe the problems of Bengal's peasants, and begins to see him as his national leader too; the Marathi leader, by visiting Bengal, becomes aware of Bengal's issues. This is nation building through simple structural design. Prelims 2013, the Naoroji trap. Statement 3 ("stressed the need for eradication of all social evils before anything else") is false: Naoroji's 1886 rule kept social questions out of the INC. Only statement 1 (exposed the economic exploitation of India) is right: answer (a). (The same PYQ is tagged again in section 3.2.)

items.t: 2 · Building a culture of parliamentary politics
items.x: Because unity needed a shared habit, INC sessions copied parliament. Ask: which parts of a Lok Sabha sitting did a session reproduce? How did INC sessions contribute beyond passing resolutions? The INC sessions were consciously modelled on parliamentary practice. A President functioned like a Speaker.Members spoke, debated and voted on resolutions.For India, this was new. Watch a Lok Sabha session today: the procedures, the order of speaking, the formal adoption of resolutions all have roots in the culture built by INC sessions from 1885 onwards. That is why it can be said that the modern political era in India, in a true sense, began with the INC. He underlined "In a true sense, India's modern political era began with the INC." On the board (slide 23) he writes the same idea as "INC session functioned like LS/RS session," linked to ICA 1892 (see Chapter 28).

items.t: 3.1 · The case for supporting Indian capitalists
items.x: Because the Moderates wanted a modern economy, they backed capitalists. Ask: why was this pro-industrialisation and not anti-poor? Why did the Moderates support Indian businessmen? The question causes confusion: supporting capitalists sounds against workers and the poor. But the Moderates' position was not anti-poor: it was pro-industrialisation. Industrialise like the West India needs to industrialise like the West. 19th-century industrialisation ran on capitalism.Every major industrialised country (Britain, the US, Germany, Japan) industrialised on the backs of its capitalist class No communist model yet Communist-led industrialisation (Soviet Russia) was born only in 1917 and showed results only after 1929. In the 1880s and 1890s that model did not exist. The Moderates worked with the tools available Indian capitalists were struggling They were not powerful monopolists. They were under severe competitive pressure from British imports flooding Indian markets and from British businesses operating inside India with the government's backing. An Indian capitalist in 1890 needed support, not criticism No class notes for this section: slide 28 carries the same text with no ink from the teacher. The slide's wording "not anti-poor, pro-industrialisation" is the handout's own.

Because the ICA 1892 disappointed them, the Moderates built their sharpest idea. Ask: why is wealth not always equal to rupees? What is the most important intellectual contribution of the Moderates? Without question it is the Drain Theory: the systematic, evidence-based argument that British rule was economically exploiting India, not developing it, and that the entire claim of the White Man's Burden (WMB) was false. The theory gained particular prominence after the bitter disappointment with the Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892), which failed to deliver any meaningful reform (see Chapter 28). Core idea: the British were using their political control over the Indian State to extract economic benefits for Britain. This was not charity or development: it was exploitation. The Moderates proved it with data and argument, building an economic critique of colonialism that was sharp, factual and difficult to counter. Ahead of its time:Lenin and Lala Lajpat Rai would later argue along similar lines, that colonialism is the product of British capitalism needing new markets and raw materials. The Moderates reached this conclusion through an economic lens well before it became a standard argument in global socialist circles. He underlined "evidence-based,""White Man's Burden was false,""disappointment with the ICA 1892" (circling the year 1892), "Britain used its political control over the Indian State to extract economic benefits for Britain," and "colonialism as the product of British capitalism." On the board (slide 23) the Drain Theory is "WEMC Moderates defeated the narrative of WMB" through press, speeches and books. The architects Romesh Chandra Dutt (R.C. Dutt) Former ICS officer turned economic historian. Wrote The Economic History of British India (Vol. I, 1902) and India in the Victorian Age (Vol. II, 1904). A data-driven account of how British land revenue policy, trade regulation and fiscal management impoverished India. Gave the theory its historical depth and empirical backbone Dadabhai Naoroji Poverty & Un-British Rule in India (1901): the most systematic presentation of the theory and a landmark text in the economic history of colonialism globally MG Ranade Often called the father of Indian economics He underlined the two Dutt titles with their years,the Naoroji title with 1901, and "father of Indian economics" (Ranade): these are the book-and-date matches. The handout figure adds facts that are not in the handout's running text (it is a flow chart on the page, placed by the handout near the Drain Theory material). It is the source for the Prelims 2015 match (Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer, R.C. Dutt are all economic critics) and for Prelims 1997 (Gokhale). The figure's flow order is a layout, not a sequence in time. This second handout figure is a summary of the Moderates' contribution: the Drain Theory is called the world's first economic critique of colonialism, "before Hobson, Lenin." (The handout's running text says Lenin and Lajpat Rai argued similarly later.) The "British Committee 1889" and "India journal" entries are not explained in this chapter. Prelims 1996 (answer d), Prelims 2008 and Prelims 2013:Sir Syed Ahmed Khan is the one who did not believe in Naoroji's Drain Theory (1996). 'Un-british' (as in Un-British Rule) is Dadabhai Naoroji (2008). The most effective contribution of Naoroji is exposing economic exploitation (2013: only statement 1). Prelims 2015:Naoroji, G. Subramaniam Iyer and R.C. Dutt were all economic critics: answer (d) 1, 2 and 3. Two concepts the teacher builds before the mechanisms Rupees are not wealth.One keyboard sells for Rs 100. If the RBI prints Rs 20 more, the same keyboard sells for Rs 120: that is inflation, but the value is the same (still one keyboard). So money (rupees) and value (wealth) are different things.If a country exports minerals, rupees and forex come in, but wealth goes out: his example is a poor African country selling minerals to the outside world.Think of the Middle East with crude oil and natural gas: to prevent the ill-effects of this drain, the Middle East is trying to use its forex for diversifying and developing its economy. This is why the first board (slide 19) warns "wealth is not always equal to rupees." [The slide's "Rs" is the rupee sign.] Teacher's board: "How Drain & Swaraj connected?" Answer: "Br misused its control over our Sovereignty / Sov Fns To ensure Drain of wealth from India" Teacher's board: "Concept: Rs vs value" How are Drain and Swaraj connected?Answer: Britain misused its control over our sovereignty (sovereign functions) to ensure the drain of wealth from India.Why was there a drain? Because we did not have SG (self-government), which is the power to do L, E, J (legislative, executive, judicial functions) on our own sovereign functions. This is the same L, E, J shorthand as in Chapter 8 and Chapter 10. Drain Theory in one line: "The misuse of political power over the State of the Colony for the economic benefit of the Colonial Power." (Handout and slide 36.) The handout's closing note: this made the economic critique inseparable from the political demand for Swaraj: without self-rule, the drain could never be stopped. Teacher's board: "IF Q on Drain of wealth" branching to "Pre (IR) in Br" [1757-1813; left: "1757-65 Plassey PLUNDER", "(LR) 1765+"] and "Post IR in Br (1813-1947)" The answer frame "If a question is on the Drain of wealth": split it into Pre-IR in Britain (1757-1813) and Post-IR in Britain (1813-1947).Pre-IR (1757-1813):the Plassey Plunder (1757-65) and Land Revenue (LR) from 1765 onwards.Post-IR (1813-1947): the later mechanisms. But "if the question is on the Drain THEORY given by the MODERATES, write the post-1813 drain" (he underlined Post 1813 Drain). Why: the Industrial Revolution in Britain ran 1750-1850; the EIC was a trader; in 1813 the EIC's monopoly on British business with India ended, and industrialised Britain got access to the Indian economy. Pre-1800s or pre-1813? The handout and slide 38 title the first period "Pre-19th Century (pre-1800s)" and the second "19th Century (1813 onwards)." The teacher's board (slide 22) draws the split at 1813 (pre-IR 1757-1813, post-IR 1813-1947). Use the teacher's 1757-1813 split; the "pre-1800s" label is the slide's shorthand.

items.t: 3.3 · Impact of British industrialisation on India
items.x: Because Britain industrialised, India was reshaped as raw-material source and market. Ask: where did the artisans go when no factory opened? What exactly did British industrialisation do to India? How British industrialisation changed India Before British IR: India = net exporter of finished goods (textiles, handicrafts) British industrial capitalism: India = (1) a raw-material source + (2) an export market for British factories Commercialisation of agriculture: cotton, indigo, jute (and opium) grown for British factories, not for food Handicrafts destroyed: artisans lose domestic and export markets; no Indian factories to absorb them Forced into agriculture:disguised unemployment; agriculture overburdened British industrial capitalism converted India into a source of raw materials and an export market for British factories. Before British industrial dominance, India was a net exporter of finished goods (textiles, handicrafts, processed goods). After, India became a net exporter of raw materials, while finished goods flooded back in as imports. This process is the commercialisation of agriculture: Indian agriculture was reoriented away from food crops and towards cash crops and raw materials for export to British factories. The peasants no longer grew what they ate; they grew what Britain's mills needed: cotton, indigo, jute, opium (Prelims 2018). The handout's analogy: an African country that exports crude oil and imports refined products and machinery: the raw material goes out cheap, the finished product comes back expensive. "Br sells FGs (finished goods) to India, therefore India = [an export market] for Britain." He underlined "(1) raw-material source,""(2) export market,""Britain commercialised Indian agriculture,""(cotton, indigo, jute)," "Opium," and "Handicrafts destroyed." Teacher's board: "CROPS" splitting into "Food" and "Cash crops" (boxed; Jute, Sugar, Tea etc, Cotton; "Input (Raw Material) for Industrial Sector") Crops split into Food crops and Cash crops.Cash crops (jute, sugar, tea, cotton, as on his board) are inputs (raw material) for the industrial sector.Commercialisation of agriculture (cash crops, his "B") pushed out food crops ("A"), leading to FOOD INSECURITY [FAMINES]. [The circled A and B float on the board; reading A = food and B = cash crops follows from the last line, "B = Commercialization of Agri >>> A -> Food Insecurity". Check your notebook.] Teacher's board: "Br MACHINE MADE GOODS" branching to "Cheaper" and "Better in Quality" Why machine-made British goods beat Indian handicrafts: they were cheaper and better in quality.Cheaper because of mass production:the factory setup is a one-time cost (his example: 100 crore); the first Bisleri bottle costs 100 crore, but rapid and mass production has a low additional cost, so the Nth bottle's average cost is Rs 1. And the contrast of people: an artisan uses skill, hands and tools to make crafts (goods); a worker works with physical labour on machines to produce manufactured goods. The Indian handicrafts sector was destroyed. Indian artisans lost both domestic and export markets. Since there was no industrialisation of India (no Indian factories came up to replace the handicrafts), the artisans had nowhere to go. They could not become factory workers and were forced back onto agriculture. The handout's contrast: an artisan uses skill and hands; a factory worker uses labour and machines. The two are decentralised and rural versus centralised and urban. When the artisan is pushed off his trade but no factory exists, he falls back on the land. The result is disguised unemployment in agriculture: too many people on too little land, each doing far less productive work than they could. This is why the agriculture sector became overburdened. The handout: in a modern economy the worker works in machine-based factories and agriculture employs a small fraction. Britain achieved this transition. India was denied it. Teacher's board: two circles Two circles:in GDP terms the economy can be mostly industrial (agriculture a small wedge), yet in employment terms agriculture can still be the big circle: "Even in an industrialised GDP, agriculture can be over-burdened." (This is the point behind disguised unemployment.) He adds a link to the "effect of AI" [written as "Link: effect of AI"; the board gives no more; check your notebook for what he said]. Prelims 1999, 2018 and 2020 land here.1999: no independent development of industries because of the absence of heavy industries (a) (not scarcity of capital or resources, not the rich preferring land). 2018: the economic result of British rule in the 19th century was commercialisation of agriculture (c) (not export of handicrafts, not growth of Indian factories, not urban growth). 2020: the first-half-of-19th-century impact of the Industrial Revolution was that Indian handicrafts were ruined (a) (no machines, no railways, no heavy duties on British imports). The transport revolution The transport revolution is part of the Industrial Revolution, and it contributed to the Drain.The steam engine (1769) later led to (1) machines, (2) ships and boats, (3) railways.The Suez Canal (1859-69) reduced the distance by 4,500 miles (his note: 9,000 km) (his sketch: the route from Britain round Africa against the shorter route through Suez). Impact on India: "LOOT escalated." And a verdict: "Awesome stuff for the colonisers = hell for the people of the colonies." Miles against kilometres. The handout and slide 36 say the Suez Canal cut the India-Britain sea distance by 4,500 miles. The teacher's board writes "4500 miles (9000 Km)" and says "to the Arabian Sea." One mile is about 1.6 km, so 4,500 miles is nearer 7,200 km; the board's 9,000 km does not match. Hold 4,500 miles (the figure in both handout and slide). The revolution in transport made the drain worse, not better.Steam-powered railways, steam-fitted ships, paved roads, modern ports and the Suez Canal (built 1859-1869) made it cheaper and faster to extract raw materials from India and ship finished goods back. "Paved roads" he glosses as "Pakka roads." And on the one-line Drain definition he defines "State": an organisation that rules (T) and (ppl): territory and people [the "T" is circled; read as territory]. So "State of the Colony" means the organisation that rules the colony's territory and people, which Britain controlled and misused for its own economic benefit. Teacher's board: "Transport Revolution = Part of (IR)" with yellow "contributed to Drain" Teacher's board: "Rail-ROAD-PORT infra" The board shows the rail-road-port system as a one-way pump.In India (circle 1): raw materials (1.1) travel by rail and road to the port (1.2); by sea they go to Britain (1.3), to the British port (1.4), and by rail to the factory (e.g. Lancashire) (1.5).Finished goods (1.6) leave the factory, cross the sea (1.7) and come back to the Indian port, then by rail and road to the urban areas, which are the market (1.8).Demand comes from the rich with buying power; Indian factories are at an infant stage (crossed out). And the legend: "Rail-Road infra in India [1850s] by Dalhousie 48-56 for faster movement of the army." [The code is smudged on the slide, read as "48-56"; it matches the handout's "Dalhousie 48-56".]

Because the drain had to run through some channel, the notes list the mechanisms before and after 1813. Ask: which mechanism needed no army, only a policy? How exactly did the money leave India? What were the specific mechanisms? The notes distinguish two periods. 3.4.1 · Pre-19th century (pre-1800s) Misuse of the Dastaks Duty-free trade passes originally granted only for the EIC's own goods, but misused by Company servants for private trade (the teacher: "Loss of TAX revenue for India") Plassey plunder + Land Revenue (LR) The Plassey plunder of 1757-65, plus LR extraction from British India beginning 1765. The LR of Bengal, Orissa and Bihar formally began with the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 (see [[10 Chapter 10]]) Result: the gold flow reversed Earlier, gold flowed into India as payment for Indian goods. After Plassey and the acquisition of LR rights, gold flowed out of India "PRELIMS" is written above the title and the period line is underlined. He underlined "misused by Company servants for private trade" and noted "Loss of TAX Revenue for India." (The Dastak and the Plassey Plunder are the subject of Chapter 10.) 3.4.2 · From the 19th century (1813 onwards) The modern colonial relationship developed: colony = source of raw materials and export market. The 19th-century mechanisms, as the teacher numbers them (1) The colony's new role: a source of raw materials plus an export market for British factories (2) Absence of protective tariffs: no import duty on British goods until World War I (1914-19) (3) Exchange rate manipulation: the rupee-to-pound rate managed to benefit British businesses (4) Council Bills (post-1833): tax-financed trade; India got no forex for its exports Components of the Drain: 19th Century (1813 onwards) Also: the EIC's own forex earnings (for example opium exported to China) taken to London "PRELIMS" is written above the title. He numbers the mechanisms (2) tariffs, (3) exchange rate, (4) Council Bills (CBs), with the colony's new role as the first (see section 3.3). He underlined "World War I (1914-19), when protective tariffs were applied for the first time." And a margin note: "(1858) Council = India Council; Bill = like (Cheque)" [the last word reads like "cheque" and is underlined; it is partly unclear: check your notebook]. (2) Absence of protective tariffs How a tariff protects: the numbers.A British finished good costs Rs 100; an Indian finished good costs Rs 110.(a) India is independent: it puts a 20% import duty at the economic frontier, so the British good costs Rs 120 against the Indian Rs 110: the Indian good wins.(b) India is a colony of Britain: 0% customs duty, so the British good costs Rs 100 against the Indian Rs 110: the British good wins.The "economic frontier" is guarded by the customs service (IRS Customs under the Ministry of Finance).Case (a) is post-1947 import substitution. The bottom sketch: goods go in and out of a country, and forex moves the other way. No import duty was imposed on British goods entering India to protect Indian manufacturers. This policy lasted until World War I (1914-19), when protective tariffs were applied for the first time. The result: British goods flooded Indian markets and Indian manufacturers could not compete. Teacher's board, circled (2): "Br (FG) Rs 100" enters across a vertical line, the "Economic Frontier" (starred: "IRS (Customs) under Mo Finance") (3) Exchange rate manipulation How a weak currency boosts exports:an Indian manufacturer exporter, X, sells a product at $1 in the international market.Case A: $1 = Rs 50, so X earns Rs 50.Case B: $1 = Rs 100 (a weaker rupee), so X earns Rs 100: Rs 50 extra.The extra rupees buy one more factory and more workers, so more goods are produced: GDP and exports rise."This was done by China 1978 onwards." And on the colonial side: "British kept the rupee STRONG, or the pound weaker than ideal" [my reading of why this matters: Indian exporters were denied this boost, and British exports stayed competitive in India; the board states only the two lines]. Exchange rate manipulation: the rupee-to-pound rate was managed in a way that benefitted British businesses (the slide: keeping British exports competitive in India). The handout's analogy: China has at times been accused of keeping its currency artificially undervalued to make Chinese exports cheaper;the British did something similar in reverse, managing the exchange rate to keep British exports competitive in India. Teacher's board: "E.g Teacher's board, circled (3): "How Weak Currency -> To Greater exports", example of an Indian manufacturer exporter, Mfr (X) An example of the interplay of monetary and fiscal policy:the exchange rate is a monetary policy tool; corporate taxes are a fiscal policy tool.Step 1: a weak rupee raises GDP and makes the industrialist richer. Step 2, after some years, taxes (corporate taxes) are raised: the stimulus given earlier is now taken back. [The slide is a side example on how the two policies work together; it is not about the British.] (4) Council Bills (post-1833): tax-financed trade This is the most complex mechanism; "CBs, next slides." (The board slides 43 and 44 build it.) Teacher's board: Council Bills mechanism The Council Bill mechanism, step by step.A British importer who wants Indian goods gives forex to the Secretary of State (SoS) for India in London, and gets a CB (Council Bill) in return.He comes to India with the CBs; the Government of India (GOI) takes the CBs and gives him rupees: "Indian taxpayer rupees."He buys Indian goods and leaves.Ideally, India would get (1) forex in and send (2) goods out. Here, India gets CBs in (not forex) and sends goods out. Council Bills: tax-financed trade (post-1833) A foreign importer wants Indian goods: instead of paying forex to India directly... He buys Council Bills in London: pays the India Council in forex, which STAYS in London He uses the Bills in India: presents the Council Bills to purchase Indian goods The GOI pays him in rupees: from Indian taxpayer money Net result: India got NO forex for its exports; the Indian taxpayer financed the trade The Secretary of State (SoS) for India held India's foreign exchange in London. When a foreign importer wanted Indian goods, instead of paying forex directly, he bought Council Bills (CBs),promissory notes issued by the India Council in London. He paid for them with his forex, which stayed in London. He then used the CBs in India to purchase Indian goods, and the GOI accepted the CBs and gave Indian rupees to the importer. The handout's picture: a foreign buyer gives dollars not to India but to a London office and gets a voucher; he uses the voucher in India to buy goods and gets rupees. India got rupees (its own currency) but never the forex for its exports. And the rupees to pay the importer came from Indian taxpayers. So India did not get forex for its exports; Indian taxpayer money financed this trade. The EIC's own forex earnings The EIC earned forex by exporting Indian goods, for example opium exported to China. This forex too was taken to London and did not return to India. 3.4.3 · Home Charges "imp for Prelims."The Drain splits into two heads: (1) Home Charges, and (2) things that are not Home Charges. The next board defines Home Charges. Teacher's board: "Home Charges = Britain" (Britain underlined) Teacher's board: "imp for Prelims" (underlined, top right) "Home" in Home Charges means Britain, not India.To understand it you must think like a British nationalist:you go to a cafe; the cafe provides you goods and services and charges you rupees; why did money move from your pocket to the cafe's pocket? Because the cafe provided goods and services to you and charged for it.The cafe is Britain, you are India: India pays forex to Britain and gets goods and services (G&S) back. So Home Charges are what India was made to pay Britain for goods and services Britain claimed to provide. [The circled word before "Charges for it" on the board is unclear, probably "so": check your notebook.] From here on, no class notes: the list below is from the handout only (the lecture reached this point on slide 46). The handout's definition."Home" here means Britain, not India. Home Charges were charges that India was made to pay for goods and services supposedly provided to India by Britain or the Secretary of State. Each item carries the British justification of the day. Salaries, pensions and training costs of British officials and soldiers They gave their careers to the service of India Dividends to EIC shareholders The EIC gave governance service to India by running the Company State Interest on loans taken by the EIC Loans taken to meet expenses of the GOI Interest on foreign debt Debt incurred for India's administration and development Expenses of the Secretary of State for India and the India Council in London (earlier the Board of Control) (no justification written) Purchase of stores and goods for India by the SoS (stationery, steel and other supplies) (no justification written) Payments to the British War Office for weapons purchased for India's defence, and for use of the Royal Military in crises such as 1857 (no justification written) Interest on FDI, paid to British businesses that invested in India To attract FDI for India's development The army abroad. The handout adds: the use of the British Indian Army abroad (campaigns in Afghanistan, Africa, China) was not technically a Home Charge, because India was not receiving a service: it was giving one to the Empire. Those war expenses were charged directly to the Indian budget as military expenditure, a separate and equally egregious drain that falls outside the category of Home Charges. Prelims 2011: the handout contradicts itself on statement 3. The PYQ's key is (d) 1, 2 and 3: statement 1 (support for the Indian office in London), statement 2 (salaries and pensions of British personnel engaged in India) and statement 3 (funds for waging wars outside India by the British). But the handout's note above says the army's use abroad is technically not a Home Charge.For the exam, answer (d), as the key and the handout's own alert say; keep the note as the conceptual distinction (payments for services Britain claimed to give India are Home Charges; imperial campaigns charged to the military budget are a separate drain). The Home Charges section has no class notes beyond the "Home = Britain" café board, so the teacher's view on statement 3 is. The net effect: double drain through asymmetric trade (no class notes) (i) Net exporter of raw materials. India shipped out more raw material (cotton, jute, indigo, tea, opium) than it imported, on paper a "positive" trade balance. But the forex India earned was also drained through Council Bills, Home Charges and guaranteed FDI interest. So India shipped out wealth (raw material) and its export earnings too: a double drain. (ii) Asymmetric trade. India did not receive an equivalent value of finished goods back: British finished goods (cotton textiles, machine-made products) flooded India tariff-favoured, but their total value was less than the raw material India shipped out. "Guaranteed FDI interest" is explained in section 3.5 under Railways (a guaranteed 5% a year in London). The handout does not give a separate number for the drain here.

items.t: 3.5 · Did British rule modernise India? The debate (no class notes)
items.x: Because the British claimed benefits, the Moderates answered each. Ask: what did each answer count that the British claim left out? Were there any genuine modernising benefits that justify the drain? This debate was structured by the Moderates themselves: the British made certain arguments in their favour, and the Moderates (and later historians) developed counter-arguments. A calibration before the debate. A 2022 estimate by Utsa Patnaik puts the total value of the drain at $45 trillion at 2022 prices. Whatever modernisation happened, it happened as an unintended by-product. No part of it was done for India. Whole section: no class notes yet. The lecture ended at slide 46 (the Home Charges definition), so the teacher's ink and reasoning for railways, canals and the "only 2%" rejoinder are not in the slides. Everything below is the handout. Railways Railways linked India internally and to the world economy through rail-to-port infrastructure Purpose:Dalhousie 48-56 introduced railways in 1853 primarily for faster movement of the British army:military control was the original purpose, not economic development  Direction: railways connected Indian markets and sources of raw materials to ports, and through ports to British manufacturers. They did not connect Indian markets to Indian manufacturers  Technology:very limited transfer, and only in low-technology areas like bridge-building and tunnelling  Real goal: to create investment opportunities for British railway companies  Guarantee: British capitalists got a guaranteed 5% annual interest on their invested capital, paid in pound sterling in London The 5% started the moment the FDI was made, so investors earned 5% even in the years the railway was under construction and earning nothing. Once the railway ran, if it failed to earn 5% in any year, the GOI made up the deficit. At any point, the investors had the right to sell the railway back to the GOI at a price equal to the exact total FDI. So if FDI was 100 pounds, they got at least 5 pounds a year from the day of investment, and if they wrapped up before 99 years, they also got 100 pounds back.FDI became an FD (fixed deposit with simple interest paid every year). That led to wasteful construction: profits were private, losses were public.The same money could have been invested in irrigation for India's food security. The by-product was real:by 1947 railways covered 78% of India.Feeder roads from Indian factory hubs to the railway lines let Indian businesses eventually use the network. Railways also increased people-to-people contact across regions, strengthening national unity and the inter-regional bonds the Indian National Movement would depend on. The railway date and the board. The handout says Dalhousie 48-56 introduced railways in 1853; the teacher's board (slide 37) says the rail-road infra came "in India 1850s by Dalhousie 48-56 for faster movement of the army." The two agree: 1853 falls in the 1850s, and the purpose is the army. (The Dalhousie chapter is Chapter 14.) Canals British-built canals became a role model for Asia and helped develop irrigation infrastructure and food security Quantity: by 1947 only 25% of cultivated area was under public irrigation  Geography: canals were built only in non-Permanent Settlement 1793 areas (Punjab, western UP, coastal Madras), where land revenue could still be increased. Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, locked under the Permanent Settlement of 1793, saw little canal investment  Access: canal water was not free; only rich farmers could afford it  Result:recurring famines in the 1860s and 1870s, and as late as the Bengal Famine of 1943, are proof there was no genuine food security The British response to famine was a series of Famine Commissions: the Strachey Commission (1880), the Lyall Commission (1897) and the MacDonnell Commission (1900),but their recommendations were rarely implemented with seriousness. The famines kept recurring because the structural problem was never addressed: extractive land revenue, export-oriented agriculture and inadequate irrigation. The British rejoinder: "the drain was only 2%" The drain was only 2% of India's export value in the early 1900s. This small amount paid for real development: it attracted FDI into railways, roadways and irrigation Quantity:GDP growth was not substantial  Quality: growth was regionally uneven, and investment in irrigation, health and education remained low  Neither the quantity nor the quality of development justified what India paid as the drain  Naoroji's argument: even if 2% sounds small, it was surplus capital. Invested in India instead of drained to Britain, it would have compounded over decades and generated significant GDP growth.It is not the absolute percentage that matters: it is what it could have become The handout's savings-account picture: 2% of your income seems small, but invested and compounded over 50 years, it becomes substantial wealth. The drain robbed India of that compounding effect, year after year. Drain Theory's central claim is structural: a colonial power using political control to redirect economic surplus. This made the economic critique inseparable from the political demand for Swaraj: without self-rule, the drain could never be stopped. The last PYQ alerts of the handout Prelims 1997 (answer b).M.C. The handout: the AINLF was founded in 1918, the Moderate splinter from the INC under leaders like Surendranath Banerjea and Tej Bahadur Sapru (the handout words this as "after the Surat Split aftermath when Moderates left INC"; hold the date 1918). Setalvad = eminent jurist, later the 1st Attorney General of India;B.N. Rau = Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly;Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer = member of the Constituent Assembly's Drafting Committee. The wrong options: Swaraj Party, Madras Labour Union, Servants of India Society. Handout figure: Gokhale 1866-1915, Gandhi's political master, Servants of India Society 1905 Poona. Prelims 2011 (answer d) is discussed under Home Charges in section 3.4. A land with no single people. In 1885 the first INC session at Bombay declared its goal as building national unity. India was a land of regions, languages, castes and religions with no pre-existing single political community, so the Moderates decided that building one came before demanding rights from the British. One versus only. In 1886 Naoroji laid down the informal rule that the INC takes only political questions, not social or class ones, so the fight is Indians against British and not Hindu against Muslim, upper against lower caste, men against women, worker against capitalist or ryot against landlord. In 1888 the INC added a veto (no resolution if the majority of Hindu or Muslim members disagree) and in 1889 the Minority Clause, the INC's own demand for reserved seats in the ILC and PLCs. The host never presides. Each session was held in a different part of the country and the President was never from the host region. A Marathi leader presiding in Calcutta and speaking to Bengali concerns builds an all-India leadership and inter-regional bonds, nation building by simple design. A parliament before a parliament. The President functioned like a Speaker and members spoke, debated and voted on resolutions, which was new for India. Today's Lok Sabha procedures have their roots in the culture of INC sessions, so the modern political era began with the INC. Why back the capitalists? The Moderates were not anti-poor, they were pro-industrialisation: every industrialised country had risen on its capitalist class, communist industrialisation was born only in 1917 and showed results after 1929, and Indian capitalists were struggling against British imports and British firms in India. The Drain Theory. After the disappointment with the Indian Councils Act of 1892 the Moderates built the Drain Theory: an evidence-based argument that Britain used its political control over the Indian State for its own economic benefit, so the White Man's Burden was false. Naoroji (Poverty & Un-British Rule in India, 1901), R.C. Dutt (1902 and 1904) and Ranade (father of Indian economics) made it, spread by press, speeches and books. How British factories rebuilt India. Before British industrialisation India was a net exporter of finished goods. Afterwards it was a raw-material source and an export market: farms grew cotton, indigo, jute and opium for British mills, handicrafts were destroyed, and artisans with no Indian factories to join were forced into an overburdened agriculture. Steam, rail and the Suez shortcut. The steam engine (1769) later brought machines, ships and railways, and the Suez Canal (1859-69) cut the sea distance by 4,500 miles. The teacher's board shows the rail-road-port loop carrying raw materials out and finished goods in, with railways built under Dalhousie 48-56 for the army, and he writes that the loot escalated. Plunder first, policy later. Before 1813 the drain was Dastak misuse, the Plassey plunder of 1757-65 and land revenue from 1765. After 1813 it was policy: no protective tariff until World War I, a managed exchange rate that favoured British business, and Council Bills in which the importer's forex stayed in London and the GOI paid rupees from taxpayers. The cafe bill and the double drain. Home Charges are what India paid Britain for goods and services Britain said it gave, Home meaning Britain. The eight heads include salaries and pensions, EIC dividends, loan and foreign-debt interest, India Office costs, stores, War Office payments and FDI interest, so India lost raw material and the forex it earned, a double drain. Railways, canals and only 2 per cent. The British pointed to railways (but with a guaranteed 5% in London, army purpose, 78% coverage by 1947), canals (but only 25% irrigated, outside Permanent Settlement areas, water not free) and said the drain was only 2%. Naoroji replied that 2% was surplus capital that would have compounded, and the chapter closes that the critique was inseparable from the demand for Swaraj.
